**ʿIbādah: The Verb That Contains a Whole Life**

"Worship" here is the Qur'an's comprehensive term, *ʿibādah* — the same word al-Fātiḥah put at the center of the prayer, *"You ˹alone˺ we worship"* (1:5). Its root covers servitude, obedience, and adoration at once, and its scope in Quranic usage is a life's entire orientation rather than a liturgical segment. The creation of the two orders is stated as its purpose elsewhere without ambiguity: *"I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me"* (51:56). Read with that verse, the command of 2:21 is not adding an activity to human life but naming the activity human life is for. The exegetes' standard gloss — worship as the utmost humility joined to the utmost love — keeps the term from collapsing into either fear alone or affection alone. And the command's justification is embedded in its own relative clause: *Who created you*. The Maker's claim on the made is the argument; nothing else is offered, because nothing else is needed. A thing that was made owes its making its orientation, and *ʿibādah* is that orientation with a name.

**“Your Lord”: The Title That Argues**

The command names its object *rabbakum* — your Lord — and the choice of title carries the verse's whole persuasion. *Rabb* is not primarily a word of power; it is the nurturer-owner, the one who raises what he has from stage to stage, the title al-Fātiḥah set over the worlds. To command worship in the name of the *rabb* is to ground obligation in received care: you are not addressed by a stranger with force but by the party who developed you from what you were. The prohibition that will close verse 22 — no equals — is already prepared here: a Lord who created your fathers cannot have partners invented by sons.

**Laʿalla: A “Perhaps” That Functions as a Promise**

The purpose clause — *laʿallakum tattaqūn*, so that you may become mindful — uses one of the Qur'an's characteristic particles, *laʿalla*, which classical grammarians gloss as expectation: perhaps, perchance, with the hope that. The particle raised a theological question the commentaries address directly: hope implies uncertainty, and uncertainty implies a heart in suspense — states unfitting to God. Two reconciliations dominate. One holds that God's "perhaps" is equivalent to a promise, since nothing can stand in its way; the expectation is certain from the divine side. The other attaches the hope to the subject of the sentence rather than to God: *you* are the ones for whom the outcome stands open, and the particle describes your position, not His. The second reading has the better grammar and the richer effect. The command genuinely hands the worshipper something to become: taqwā is offered as a real possibility that the act of worship genuinely produces, and the openness in the particle is the space where human freedom lives inside a divine sentence.
verses.22:
> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺

**The Evidence Is the Furniture of the World**

The verse answers the command of verse 21 not with syllogism but with surroundings. Its argument is a list — earth, sky, rain, fruit — and every item is something the addressee is already using. The rhetorical strategy is worth naming: revelation does not here prove God from abstractions but points at the furnished condition of the listener's life and asks him to read the furniture as evidence. Each piece carries a maker's mark. The earth is *firāsh*, a spread resting place; the sky a *bināʾ*, a built canopy; the rain a descent with a purpose; the fruit an output with a beneficiary — "for you," stated twice. The list moves from structure to supply: first the house, then its provisioning system. By the time the verse reaches its prohibition, the reader has walked through his own daily life as an exhibit, and the prohibition lands not as decree but as the only conclusion the exhibit supports. This is the Qur'an's most characteristic argument form — cosmology as testimony, geography as witness stand.

**A Bed and a Building: Domestic Words for Cosmic Things**

The two nouns chosen for earth and sky collapse the cosmic into the domestic. *Firāsh* is bedding, a place spread for rest — the earth described not as a planet but as a mattress laid out for the addressee, fitted to his body, neither too hard nor too hostile. *Bināʾ* is construction, an edifice — the sky as a raised roof, and the same root the Qur'an uses for buildings humans erect. The pairing produces a house: floor and ceiling, and the inhabitant between them. The register is deliberate and it does theological work. A house implies a householder; bedding implies someone who cared whether the sleeper was comfortable; a built roof implies a builder who calculated loads. The extended furnishing continues elsewhere in the Book — mountains set as stabilizers so the earth does not shake, and broad pathways for finding the way (21:31) — each feature an installed fixture. The verse's argument from design is therefore not Paley's watch found on a heath but something more intimate: you are not examining a mechanism, you are lying in a bed someone made.

**“Knowingly”: The Adverb That Turns Prohibition Into Indictment**

The final sentence is short and its last word is the blade: *fa-lā tajʿalū li-llāhi andādan wa-antum taʿlamūn* — do not set up equals to Allah *while you know*. After the list of verses 21–22, no one can plead ignorance of the Builder; the knowledge is built into the furniture, delivered with the fruit, recited in the very verses being read. The word *andād*, equals or rivals, names the specific idolatry of partnership: not denying Allah but assigning peers beside Him — intermediaries credited with independent power, causes treated as causes-in-themselves, favors thanked to the wrong hand.

**The Greatest Sin, in the Prophet's Own Ranking**

The prohibition's rank is fixed in a verified report. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd asked the Prophet ﷺ directly: what is the greatest sin in the sight of Allah? The answer: *"That you set up a rival unto Allah though He alone created you"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4477). The ḥadīth's logic is the verse's logic compressed — creation cited as the very ground that makes rivalry monstrous — and Bukhārī filed this report under a chapter headed by this verse of al-Baqarah, joining the two texts officially. The rest of the ranking sharpens the first place: asked what comes next, the Prophet ﷺ named killing one's child for fear of sharing food, then adultery with a neighbor's wife. The triad is coherent: a sin against the Creator, a sin against life, a sin against lineage — the three orders this verse's world rests on. That the greatest of the three is theological rather than bloody tells the reader how the Qur'an prices harm: the misdirection of worship outranks murder because it corrupts the source from which every other right flows.
verses.23:
> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true

**“Our Servant”: The Title That Carries the Claim**

The revelation is described as *mā nazzalnā ʿalā ʿabdinā* — what We have sent down upon Our servant — and the single word *ʿabd* carries the verse's whole biographical argument. The Qur'an does not name Muḥammad ﷺ here but titles him, and the title is the lowest and highest a person can hold: slave, servant, one who owns nothing and speaks for Another. The choice answers the objectors' actual case, which was never that the text lacked beauty but that its author was visible — a known man, in a known town, with a known history of neither scribal training nor poetic apprenticeship. The Qur'an supplies that biography as evidence rather than embarrassment: the *unlettered Prophet*, *"whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel"* (7:157), who could not read the scriptures he is said to have absorbed. A forgery requires sources; this author had none. The servant-title therefore does humility-work and argument-work in the same breath — the man is small enough that the book cannot be his.

**One Sūrah: The Deliberately Minimal Quantum**

The demand is graduated down to its floor: *bi-sūratin min mithlih* — one sūrah of its like. Not the whole Book, not ten chapters — a single unit, and the Qur'an elsewhere records the demand having been pitched higher before: bring ten sūrahs like it, forged if you must (11:13); bring a Book like it (28:49 — cited in the classical lists of the graduated challenge). The gradation is a documented feature of the challenge verses, which appear in Yūnus, Hūd, and al-Isrāʾ as well, and the Isrāʾ formulation removes the final limit of even collective effort: *"If ˹all˺ humans and jinn were to come together to produce the equivalent of this Quran, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other"* (17:88). One sūrah is thus the minimum testable unit of a claim whose maximum version spans two species. The commentators note this verse is Madinan while its parallels are Makkan — the challenge was not exhausted by its first audiences but re-issued to a new city with new doubters, and stands re-issued to every century since.

**“Call Your Helpers Other Than Allah”**

The second clause extends the challenge from the individual to his whole alliance: *wa-dʿū shuhadāʾakum min dūni Llāh* — summon your witnesses, your patrons, your gods-beside-Allah. The phrase *min dūni Llāh* is the same construction verse 22 used for the equals set up in worship, and the reuse is a hinge: the helpers invoked in the literary test are of the same order as the rivals forbidden in the creed. The verse quietly argues that every false god is now on trial as a co-author — if the idols are real powers, let them co-sign a sūrah. The objectors are invited to mobilize everything their worldview contains: poets, soothsayers, ancestral deities, jinn confederates of the kind the Qur'an names as whisperers of elegant deception (6:112). The demand is phrased as generosity — bring all the help you trust — and functions as exposure: the challenge will be refused by the same mouths that professed the helpers, and the refusal will itself testify which of the two claims the claimants actually believed.

**The Silence of Fourteen Centuries as Evidence**

The challenge's career is part of its argument, and the verse leaves that career open on purpose. The condition — *in kuntum ṣādiqīn*, if you are truthful — converts every subsequent century into testimony. Hostile regimes possessed the motive, the poets of two classical golden ages possessed the craft, and the Arabic grammatical tradition itself grew up around this text with every tool needed to imitate it; the record contains no surviving work accepted as meeting the demand, from enemies who would have gained everything by meeting it. The verse's final word to the doubter is therefore not *believe me* but *try* — and the next verse states what follows when the trying fails, as the verse already knows it will.
verses.24:
> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers

**The Conditional That Answers Itself**

The verse opens by completing the test of verse 23, and completes it before anyone has taken it: *fa-in lam tafʿalū* — but if you have not done it — *wa-lan tafʿalū* — and you will never do it. The second clause, set off in this translation by dashes, is an interruption of the conditional by certainty. The particle *lan* is Arabic's strongest future negation, and the commentators draw the grammatical-theological point precisely: a conditional from Allah is not an expression of uncertainty, just as the "perhaps" of verse 21 was not an expression of anxiety. Divine "ifs" state the logic of the situation from the human side while the divine side already holds the outcome. The effect on the reader is singular — the challenge is issued in full seriousness *and* its failure is announced in the same breath, so that the trial functions as revelation rather than information: the point was never to learn whether they could, but to let them discover, by trying or by flinching, what they are.

**An Aside Spoken Over Their Heads**

There is a shift of addressee inside the dash that deserves attention. "If you do not" addresses the doubters; "and you will never do it" is spoken about them — a confidence delivered past them, to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, in the middle of a sentence directed at the objectors. Rhetorically the aside is devastating: the doubters are being examined and, simultaneously, their exam results are being read aloud to the proctor. The device also protects the challenge's sincerity. Had the verse said simply *you will fail*, it would be a taunt with no test; had it said simply *if you fail*, the confidence would be absent. Holding both in one sentence, the Qur'an performs perfect knowledge and perfect fairness at once — the door genuinely open, the outcome genuinely known, and the known outcome stated publicly so that the failure, when it arrives, arrives without excuse. The hypocrites of this sūrah's opening lived by managing appearances; this aside announces a courtroom where appearances are read before they are worn.

**A Fire With Fuel Named**

The consequence clause introduces the Fire with an engineering detail: *allatī waqūduhā al-nās wa-l-ḥijārah* — its fuel is people and stones. The commentators identify the stones as sulfur, the burning mineral of the classical imagination, and as the idols themselves, the objects of the worship that led their votaries in — and the Qur'an elsewhere states the idol reading outright: *"Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell"* (21:98). The fuel list is thus a moral equation: the worshipper and the worshipped burn together, and the false god becomes, in the only transformation it ever manages, an aggravator of its devotee's fire. The same phrase is turned on the believers elsewhere as pastoral warning — *"Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones"* (66:6) — which confirms the description is meant to be taken concretely by every party. A hell of abstraction frightens no one; a hell with a fuel specification is designed for the imagination, and the imagination is where choices are actually made. The main verb of the verse is easy to skim past: *fa-ttaqū* — then guard yourselves, then fear — the imperative of the very root that named the sūrah's opening people, the *muttaqīn*. The structure is worth stating plainly: the threat is not the verse's point; the command is. "Fear the Fire" is taqwā given an object, and the whole verse exists to move taqwā from disposition to decision.
verses.25:
> Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever

**The Counter-Announcement, in the Same Breath**

One verse after the Fire is prepared, the imperative turns: *wa-bashshir* — and give good news. The command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and through him to everyone who will ever carry a message of joy, and its recipients are named in the Qur'an's standing formula: *alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — those who believe and do righteous deeds, faith joined to its works in the pairing this sūrah used at 2:3. The juxtaposition with verse 24 is not decoration but structure: the two announcements share one grammar of preparedness, one audience of the living, and one present moment in which the hearer must locate himself.

**“This Is What We Were Given Before”: Memory Inside Paradise**

The strangest and richest clause in the verse is the dwellers' own remark. Given fruit, they say: *this is what we were given before*. The majority reading takes "before" as the earthly life — the fruits of Paradise arriving in the forms of the fruits of this world, so that the first bite in eternity triggers recognition. The commentators then draw the theology out of the homesickness: the world's fruit was the sample, Paradise is the delivery; the familiar form is kept so that the reward is *recognizable as the fulfillment of a life actually lived* — this world is not forgotten there, only its bitterness removed, which is why the Qur'an's standing description of the dwellers is that no fear comes upon them and they do not grieve (2:62). A minority reading places "before" inside Paradise — each fruit resembling the one previously tasted there. Both readings serve one purpose: continuity of personal memory across the boundary of death. The reward is not absorption into novelty but the completion of a biography the dweller still owns and can quote.

**Mutashābih: Same Face, Different Taste**

The verse explains the recognition with one loaded word: they are given fruit *mutashābih* — resembling, similar, the translation glossing it *looks similar ˹but tastes different˺*. The exegetes read the resemblance three ways: identical appearance with transformed taste; or uniform excellence — no fruit of Paradise has an inferior grade, so every specimen resembles every other in perfection; or the remark as wonderment rather than comparison, since the dwellers are recognizing names and forms while the realities exceed both. The word choice carries a second cargo for the attentive reader: *mutashābih* is the same term Sūrah 3 will use for the Qur'an's elusive verses (3:7) and that Sūrah 39 uses for a Book whose parts resemble each other in harmony (39:23). A lexicon links Paradise's fruit to the Book's texture: familiarity on the surface, inexhaustible difference underneath, recognition that deepens instead of exhausting. The dwellers' conversation over fruit is, in miniature, the reader's conversation with revelation — every return to the familiar thing yields an unfamiliar taste.

**Khulūd: The Clause of Permanence**

The verse closes on the word that seals both houses: *hum fīhā khālidūn* — they will be there abiding, *khulūd* the Qur'an's standing refrain for the inhabitants of the Garden and the Fire alike. Lexically the root denotes staying, duration, a thing's persistence in its place; from the mouth of Allah the commentators read it as the promise that upgrades duration into eternity, since His word cannot expire. The Qur'an sometimes reinforces the clause — abiding *forever* — and sometimes qualifies it, *as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills* (11:108), which the exegetical tradition debates without dissolving, ending in a verse the same passage supplies: *a generous giving, without end*. This verse states the permanence flatly, and the flatness is part of the good news: a joy announced as temporary would not be news at all, since the heart's objection to every earthly good is exactly its expiry. The rivers flow, the fruit recurs, the spouses remain, and the clause of *khulūd* removes from all of them the one defect that made every provision of verse 22 bittersweet — the deadline.
verses.26:
> Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—

**A Parable Defended Before the Attack Lands**

The verse opens in the middle of an argument its hearers were having: *inna Allāha lā yastaḥyī an yaḍriba mathalan mā baʿūḍatan* — Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of a mosquito, or of anything above it, which the commentators read as anything beyond it in smallness. The occasions reported behind the verse name the objectors and their objection: the hypocrites, stung by the parables of verses 17–20; or Jews scoffing that God would deign to compare idols to a fly (22:73) or the protectors taken beside Him to a spider's house (29:41); or idolaters pressing the same complaint. In every version the charge is one of dignity — such images are beneath divine speech. The verse answers not by raising the images but by lowering the objection: *lā yastaḥyī*, He does not shy away, does not hold back out of propriety. The answer implies a principle of revelation that runs through the whole Book: truth selects its own images, and the selection is made by fitness to the point, not by the social rank of the objects. A God who furnished the world with gnats can speak with gnats.

**The Mosquito and the Scale of Signs**

The choice of *baʿūḍah* — mosquito, gnat — is exact for the argument being answered. The objectors measured divine speech by the grandeur of its contents; the verse answers by naming one of the smallest creatures that still exists, is formed, feeds, reproduces, and does work in the world no elephant can do. If the objection is that small things cannot carry meaning, the mosquito refutes it by existing at all: the creature that is beneath dignity in the objectors' scale is not beneath creation in the Maker's. The classical scholars drew the corollary into the doctrine of signs — every existent, at every scale, is an *āyah*, and the sign-value of a thing lies in its craftedness, not its size. The clause "or what is even smaller" then pushes past the limit of the visible: whatever lies below the mosquito's scale — what the ancients could only posit, and later ages would actually see — belongs to the same field of signs and the same freedom of divine speech. The verse is, incidentally, one of the Qur'an's standing answers to every aesthetics of the sublime that excludes the small.

**A Message That Actively Divides**

The verse then states its most difficult doctrine without softening: *yuḍillu bihi kathīran wa-yahdī bihi kathīran* — by it He leaves many astray and guides many. The "it" is the parable — the same small utterance functioning as guidance and as straying simultaneously, and the commentators press exactly this: the effect described is stronger than being ignored. Revelation denied is not neutralized in the denier; it works on him, moving him further from what it says. The verse echoes the sealing of 2:7 and the sickness-increased of 2:10 as one continuous mechanism: divine speech is active substance, and the moral condition of the receiver determines the direction of its action — medicine or irritant, light or dazzle, the same sky that waters the valley deafening the men of the storm. Many scholars read here the Qur'an's fullest statement that guidance and misguidance both pass *through* revelation rather than around it: no one is misled by the Book who was not already positioned to be. The doubles — many astray, many guided — refuse the comfort of rarity in both directions.

**Al-Fāsiqūn: Straying With a Qualification**

The final clause restricts the damage: *wa-mā yuḍillu bihi illa al-fāsiqīn* — He leaves none astray by it except the rebellious, the *fāsiq*. The word comes from a root meaning to exit, to break out — used of the date that bursts its skin, of the animal that leaves the herd — and in Quranic usage names the person who has stepped outside a binding order: the covenant-breaker, the one who transgresses while knowing the line. The *fāsiq* is misled *by* the parable because he was already out of position relative to truth; the parable reveals and completes the exit he began. The exegetes identify the *fāsiqūn* of this passage with the hypocrites just described — men whose rebellion was not ignorance but breach — and the verse by this hands its reader the test in advance: what this speech does to you will tell you where you are standing.
verses.27:
> those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers

**Which Covenant? Three Candidates and a Preference**

The exegetes identified the broken covenant variously, and the range is instructive. The widest reading takes it as the primordial covenant of human nature — the scene in al-Aʿrāf where Allah drew the descendants of Adam from his loins and asked *"Am I not your Lord?"* and they answered, *"Yes, You are! We testify"* (7:172) — a pact every person signs before birth and can breach after. A second reading, favored by al-Rāzī, takes it as the sworn expectation of the pre-Islamic Arabs: *"They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community"* (35:42) — an oath broken the moment the warner arrived. A third confines it to the specific covenants made with the People of the Book. Weighed together, the readings are not rivals but concentric rings of the same offense: every human being holds the first covenant, the Arabs of the revelation's audience added the second, and the scriptural communities the third. "After it has been affirmed" — *baʿda mīthāqih* — fits all three: in each case the bond was established, witnessed, and confirmed before the breaking. The verse prosecutes no one for ignorance; it prosecutes the confirmed and betrayed.

**Severing What Was Ordered Joined**

The second breach — *yaqtaʿūna mā amara Llāhu bihī an yūṣala* — severs what Allah commanded to be connected, and the commentators' first application is kinship: the ties of blood whose maintenance the Qur'an legislates from its opening pages — *"Be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties"* (4:1) — and whose severance it pairs, exactly as here, with corruption in the land: *"Now if you ˹hypocrites˺ turn away, perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ˹ties of˺ kinship!"* (47:22). The pairing in both sūrahs is not accidental but analytic: kinship is the first society, the training ground of every bond, and a person who can cut the ties he was born into has rehearsed the cutting of all the rest. Other exegetes widen the referent to everything Allah ordered joined — faith and practice, the prophets as one brotherhood, the community and its teachers, the People of the Book and the confirmation of their own scriptures in this Qur'an. One classical note adds a barb for Madina's Jews: the tie to this Prophet was itself kinship, Isaac and Ishmael being brothers. Every reading keeps the same structure: a commanded connection, deliberately cut.

**Corruption in the Land — the Passage's Third Return**

The third breach is *yufsidūna fī al-ard*, and the phrase is by now a signature of this sūrah's opening: the charge the hypocrites deflected while claiming to be peace-makers (2:11), the verdict that stripped the claim from them (2:12), and now the defining trait of the *fāsiq*. The recurrence completes an identification — the peace-making of verse 11 and the covenant-breaking of verse 27 are the same phenomenon at two depths, and the land's corruption is what both produce. Read with the two breaches before it, the corruption has a precise etiology: when the bond with Allah is cut and the bonds between people are cut, the ground itself inherits the severance, since the land in Quranic thought is not a neutral stage but a participant that registers the moral state of its inhabitants — corruption spreading on land and sea by what human hands have done (30:41). The three breaches form one ecosystem of damage: vertical, horizontal, environmental. A generation that keeps covenants and kinships farms a different earth than one that does not, and the verse states the farming as fact rather than metaphor. The verdict uses the market vocabulary the passage has been accumulating: *ulāʾika humu al-khāsirūn* — it is they who are the losers, *khāsir* being the merchant who returns from a venture with less than he carried out, bereft, or in the word's other shade, simply *lost* — having mislaid the road or the self. The restriction grammar — *ulāʾika hum* — repeats the sūrah's verdict formula, and the repetition lets the opening's ledgers be compared side by side: the God-conscious who are the successful (2:5), the traders who bought error with guidance and profited nothing (2:16), and now the covenant-breakers who are the losers.
verses.28:
> How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**A Question That Is an Argument**

The verse opens with an interrogative of impossibility: *kayfa takfurūna bi-llāh* — how can you disbelieve in Allah? Not "will you," not "do you dare," but *how* — the question that challenges the mechanics rather than the audacity of a position. The implication is that disbelief, examined against the believer's own biography, becomes incoherent: not wicked, which it also is, but unperformable with open eyes. And the argument the question unfolds is not cosmological or scriptural but autobiographical — it is built entirely from things that happened *to the addressee*. You were dead. You were given life. You will die. You will live again. You will be returned. Every clause is a stage of the reader's own record, known by direct experience or by the experience of every person he has ever lost. The verse by this relocates the debate about God from the sky to the self: the evidence is not out there at a distance to be assessed; the evidence is the assessor. The "how" now has its full force — with what instruments, drawn from whose life, is this denial being conducted?

**Four Stages and a Return**

The commentators count the verse's itinerary in stages: lifelessness before birth; life given for the world; death at the term; life restored at the resurrection — and then, governing all four, the return to Allah. The Qur'an states the same arithmetic from the other side, in the confession the dead will make: *"Our Lord! You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice. Now we confess our sins. So is there any way out?"* (40:11). Two deaths, two lives, one unanswered question. The symmetry is the verse's engine: resurrection is not a new kind of divine act requiring new evidence but the repetition of an act the addressee has already been the object of. Whoever finds the second giving of life incredible must first explain the first — and the first is not in dispute between the verse and its hearer, since the hearer exists. The argument's structure is thus *a fortiori* in the oldest sense: if the harder thing (life from no life at all) has been done to you, the easier thing (life again from a life already lived) cannot coherently be denied by you.

**What “Dead” Means Before the Beginning**

The first stage — *kuntum amwātan*, you were dead things — required the exegetes to define a pre-biographical death, and their readings converge on hiddenness. One strand takes it materially: the person's existence in the substance of the body — in the loins of the parents, in the dust of the earth, as raw material not yet a someone. Another takes it lexically: the Arabs called a thing "dead" when its traces were effaced and it was not mentioned or remembered — death as unremembrance — and the Qur'an supplies the gloss in its own idiom: *"Is there not a period of time when each human is nothing yet worth mentioning?"* (76:1). Ibn ʿArabī read the stage metaphysically: not sheer nothingness but non-manifestation — the person held, unexpressed, in divine knowledge, "dead" only to the world, fully real to the Knower. The readings agree on what matters for the argument: before the first life there was a true state of absence from the world, and the passage from that absence to a speaking, denying self was not performed by the self. Every person's first predicate, in the verse's grammar, is *was not* — and every subsequent claim to independence is made from borrowed existence.

**Life as a Loan From the Hand Being Denied**

The hinge of the verse is its second clause: *fa-aḥyākum* — then He gave you life. The verb is Allah's, the object is the reader, and the gift is the very capacity being used to refuse it. The Qur'an elsewhere generalizes the point into a doctrine of total dependence: provision, hearing, sight, and hearts are all loaned faculties whose loan can end (as in 67:23's inventory — He produced your hearing, your sight, your faculties, and little thanks you give). Verse 28 keeps the inventory to its two largest items — being and being-again — because two are enough: a creature who did not originate himself and does not terminate himself is bracketed at both ends by the Giver, and the middle he calls his own is a span between two donations.
verses.29:
> He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**Everything in the Earth — For You**

The verse's first clause is a deed of gift: *khalaqa lakum mā fī al-ard jamīʿan* — He created for you whatever is in the earth, *all of it*. The preposition *lakum*, "for you," is the operative word; the Qur'an repeats the gift-formula across sūrahs — cattle, crops, the sea's yield, the night and day — and states its general principle elsewhere: *"He ˹also˺ subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all by His grace"* (45:13). The comprehensive *jamīʿan* forecloses every carve-out: not some resources, not the useful ones, not the ones a particular civilization happens to exploit — everything in the earth, including what no generation has yet found a name for. The clause therefore reads forward as well as backward: ores no ancient market knew, forces no classical physics dreamed of, are inside the gift's scope. The verse is the Qur'an's ground-title for human use of the world, and its breadth is matched only by its condition — a gift *for you* is a gift with a purpose, and the purpose was stated ten verses earlier, in the command to worship the Giver.

**The Jurisprudence and the Limit of “For You”**

Islamic law built on this clause, and the building has two walls. The first is permission: what was created for human use is presumptively lawful — the default of things in the world is permissibility until a text restricts it, a principle the jurists derive from exactly this verse's generosity. The second wall is limit: "for you" states a beneficiary, not an owner absolute. The classical ethic of the gift follows: use without waste, extraction without corruption, possession held as trust — the same three bonds verse 27 listed, now seen from the property side. A covenant-breaker corrupts the land (2:27); the land corrupted is the gift misused; the misuse is not primarily economic but theological, a tenant redecorating the house as if he held the title.

**Istawā: Turning Toward the Heaven**

The second movement begins with a verb the Qur'an deploys in creation contexts with deliberate weight: *thumma istawā ilā al-samāʾ* — then He turned toward, or directed Himself to, or established Himself over the heaven; the translations vary because the verb's range is wide, and this very verse renders it "turned towards" while elsewhere — *the Most Compassionate, ˹Who is˺ established on the Throne* (20:5) — the same word pictures enthronement. The commentators' shared minimum is purposeful attention: *istawā* carries the sense of addressing a task completely, the way a builder turns from the foundation to the frame. The *thumma*, "then," marks an order of disclosure rather than divine delay — the Qur'an's creation sequences consistently narrate stages for a hearer who can only take them in sequence. The movement of the verse is architectural: the floor furnished first (the earth, for you), then the raising of the structure above it — canopy in verse 22, seven-fold edifice here. The reader is being walked through his house in the order a house is made: ground, then roof, then the inspection clause that closes the verse.

**Seven Heavens: The Numbered Sky**

The heaven's formation is given a number: *sabʿa samāwāt*, seven heavens — stated flatly, without explanation, and the Qur'an returns to the figure with structural detail: *"˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other. You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate"* (67:3), the layered construction also appearing in the six-days narrative of Fuṣṣilat (41:12) and in al-Ṭalāq's pairing of seven heavens with the like thereof in earths (65:12) — earths upon earths, as the early commentator Mujāhid read the cosmology: heavens above heavens, earths above earths. The classical exegetes ranged freely over the figure — atmospheric layers, celestial spheres, orders of being — and the Qur'an's own usage declines to legislate among them, fixing only three claims: the sky is plural in order, layered rather than a single dome; the layering is flawless, an engineered perfection the eye can test (67:3 challenges it directly); and the structure, however many of its floors lie beyond human sight, was built with the same "for you" orientation as the floor the reader stands on. Seven, in Semitic usage, is also the number of completeness — and the completeness claim is exactly the one the verse's closing clause will ratify.
verses.30:
> ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”

**Khalīfah: A Word That Named an Office and an Era**

The announcement's key term is *khalīfah*, and its semantic range shaped Islamic political vocabulary for a thousand years. The word comes from *khalafa*, to come after, to succeed, to replace — and it carries both directions of the relation at once: one who comes *after* another, and one who stands *in for* another, a deputy. The title *khalīfat rasūl Allāh*, successor of the Messenger of Allah, shortened to *khalīfah* and anglicized as caliph, is the historical deposit of this verse's word. But the Qur'an's own usage is wider than any throne. Here and in al-Anʿām the term spans the species: *"He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you"* (6:165) — succession as the human condition, coupled to testing. In Ṣād it narrows to an office with a job description: *"O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land, so judge between people with truth"* (38:26). Both layers are present in the announcement: humanity as such succeeds — on the earth, after its prior orders of life — and particular humans deputize, administering justice in the name of the One who placed them.

**The Angels' Question: Two Readings and a Weighing**

The reply is the scene's puzzle: *Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?* The question quotes two specific crimes, and the exegetes split on where such specifics came from. The first reading gives the angels experience: the earth had prior inhabitants — the jinn-tribes of the Ibn ʿAbbās narrative, who spread corruption and shed blood before being driven off — and the angels generalize from a known record. The second reading, al-Rāzī's preference, makes the question an expression of wonder rather than doubt or objection: the angels marvel at a wisdom that wills a blood-shedder for vicegerent, without impugning the wisdom. Weighing them, the question's precision favors the first — corruption and bloodshed are named, not guessed — while angelic impeccability favors the second, since wonder cannot sin. The tradition harmonizes: they knew the type because Allah had disclosed it to them, and they asked to understand, not to object. Notably, the two crimes they name are this sūrah's own charges — corruption in the land (2:11, 2:27) and the shedding of blood it will legislate against — as if the angels quoted the file on humanity that al-Baqarah is in the middle of documenting.

**The Iblīs Material and How the Tradition Grades It**

The commentaries attach a body of narrative to this verse — Ibn ʿAbbās's report of Iblīs as al-Ḥārith, an angel of the tribe called al-ḥinn, custodian of Paradise, sent against the earth's earlier corrupters, filled with pride at the victory, taunting Adam's lifeless clay body for forty years, flying in and out of it: *you are nothing*. The reports are vivid and they are graded by the tradition itself. Al-Rāzī and others note that the angelic-tribe specifics cannot be relied upon — they carry the fingerprints of popular narrative — because the Qur'an settles the question of Iblīs's kind in its own text: *"but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord"* (18:50). An authority like Ibn ʿAbbās would have known that verse. The method lesson is preserved inside the exegetical tradition rather than imported into it: lore is weighed against the Qur'an's explicit statements, and where they diverge, the lore is demoted. What survives the grading is the order-of-creation datum the Qur'an itself supplies — the jinn fashioned earlier, from scorching fire, while man was made of sounding clay (15:26–27) — enough to ground the prior-inhabitants reading without the mythology.

**“While We Glorify and Sanctify”: The Credential in the Question**

Embedded in the angels' question is their self-description: *wa-naḥnu nusabbihu bi-ḥamdika wa-nuqaddisu lak* — while we glorify Your praise and proclaim Your holiness. The two verbs name the angelic office: *tasbīḥ*, declaring Allah beyond every defect, and *taqdīs*, the related sanctification — some commentators read the pair as one act, we glorify You while praising You. The Qur'an's own cosmology deepens the puzzle: *"The seven heavens, the earth, and all those in them glorify Him. There is not a single thing that does not glorify His praises"* (17:44). The answer the scene will develop — taught names, a tested creature, worship chosen where it could be refused — supplies what universal glorification lacks: the *tasbīḥ* of a being that could have corrupted and shed blood, and did neither.
verses.31:
> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”

The reply to the angels' question — *I know what you do not know* — is now unpacked, and the unpacking is not an argument but a lesson plan: *wa-ʿallama Ādama al-asmāʾa kullahā*, He taught Adam the names, all of them. The demonstration to follow will show why the announcement of verse 30 was made in confidence: the being the angels questioned has just been equipped with something the questioners do not have, and the equipment is public, examinable, and about to be examined.

**Which Names? The Exegetical Range**

The commentators debated the inventory, and the debate maps the verse's reach. Ibn ʿAbbās read the names as the vocabulary of human discourse — man, sea, mountain, down to the kettle, the whole working lexicon by which people name and address their world. Mujāhid took the widest scope: the names of everything, a complete nomenclature of existence. Others proposed narrower lists — the names of the angels, or of Adam's descendants. Al-Ṭabarī preferred the last, partly on a grammatical ground worth recording: the pronoun used for the presented things is *hum*, the plural reserved for persons, where non-persons normally take the feminine singular — though the commentators concede the rule is not absolute, citing counter-instances like the beasts referred to by *hum* in 24:45. Al-Rāzī drew the linguistic corollary: Adam was taught all the languages of the earth, and his descendants specialized into particular tongues over time. Weighing the readings, the grammatical argument for persons is strong but defeasible, and the safest construal keeps both poles — the names of things and of people, objects and offspring, the lexicon and the genealogy. The verse is claiming, at minimum, that the first man was given the complete naming-capacity: everything in his world could be called, classified, and addressed.

**The Presentation and the Demand**

The scene's staging is precise: *thumma ʿaraḍahum ʿalā al-malāʾikah* — He presented them to the angels. What was presented, the commentators note, is either the named objects themselves or the names — the exhibit is deliberately not itemized, and the omission is the point of the following clause: *anbiʾūnī bi-asmāʾi hāʾulāʾ*, tell Me the names of *these*. The demonstrative "these" presumes a display the angels are looking at and the reader is not shown; the narrative withholds the inventory from everyone except the parties being tested. The demand's closing condition — *in kuntum ṣādiqīn*, if you are truthful — imports the sūrah's idiom of testing: the same conditional closed the literary challenge of 2:23, *if what you say is true*. Truth-claims in the Qur'an are consistently cashed out in performance — produce a sūrah, name the exhibits — and the condition here is not a doubt of angelic honesty but the standing rule of the scene: what you claim to know, demonstrate. The angels made a claim in verse 30 about their glorifying and sanctifying, and about the corruption of the announced heir; the demonstration will sort the claim.

**Naming as the Root of the Human Estate**

The verse's largest claim is anthropological. What distinguishes the human being in the Qur'an's founding story is neither sinlessness — the angels hold that — nor strength, nor age in creation, but taught, comprehensive, articulable naming. Every human science extends this endowment: taxonomy, grammar, law, medicine, astronomy are unfoldings of *al-asmāʾ*, the capacity to fix a name to a thing and by this to hold the thing in discourse, transmit it, deliberate about it. The Islamic tradition read the verse exactly so — the superiority of knowledge over worship-only, the scholar's rank above the merely devout — and the story's outcome institutionalized the lesson: the demonstration of naming settled the hierarchy of the scene without conflict, without a single act of power. Authority in this narrative is decided by curriculum. The vicegerency announced in verse 30 turns out to be an epistemic office — deputy of the One Who knows all things (2:29), equipped with the names, installed over the earth that was furnished for him — and the reader inherits the estate with the capacity that conveys it: whatever you can truly name, you can truly steward.
verses.32:
> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**The Answer Begins by Exonerating the Questioned**

The angels' reply opens before it confesses: *subḥānaka* — glory be to You, Allah be declared beyond every defect. Faced with a demand they cannot meet, the angels' first act is not self-defense and not despair but the vindication of the wisdom that framed the test — the same *tasbīḥ* they named as their office in verse 30, now performed at the exact moment it costs something. The exegetes note the pattern the Qur'an keeps: whenever divine action could be misread as defective — a decree, a judgment, an attribution of guidance and straying — *subḥānaka* or *subḥānahu* intervenes to sever the act from every imperfection.

**The Limitation the Verse Exists to Record**

The commentators draw the scene's formal conclusion from this reply: the verse records the limitation of angelic knowledge — not its weakness but its boundedness, specifically in universal comprehension. The angels know truly what they know; their knowledge simply does not extend to the whole, and verse 30's question was generated from inside that boundary. Read against the reply of verse 33 — *I know what you reveal and conceal* — and against the announcement of verse 29 — *He has knowledge of all things* — the scene arranges three epistemic ranks in one frame: the Knower of all things; the creature taught all the names; the creatures taught their functions. The ranking retroactively absolves the angels' question in verse 30 of every charge of insolence: it was the honest output of a bounded knower contemplating an unbounded decree. And it establishes the Qur'an's standing treatment of angelic error-adjacent speech — wonder, question, confession — as the behavior of knowers who are certain of their limit and therefore never pretend past it. The limitation is not their shame; it is their *tasbīḥ* in epistemic form.

**Two Names to Close: The Knower and the Wise**

The confession ends by naming the resolution the angels cannot articulate: *innaka anta al-ʿalīm al-ḥakīm* — You are truly the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The two names answer the two difficulties of the scene with surgical fit. *Al-ʿalīm* answers the knowledge gap — what we cannot name, You know; the exhibits are inside Your science even when they are outside ours. *Al-ḥakīm* answers the wisdom gap of verse 30 — the placement of a blood-shedding vicegerent, the withholding of comprehensive naming from sinless worshippers, the design of a test its first-takers will fail: every item has a purpose the Wise holds even where the knowing cannot trace it. The pairing is one of the Qur'an's most frequent closings, and its logic here is that knowledge and wisdom are the two attributes a bounded creature must posit whenever he meets a boundary: that the Knower has the fact I lack, and that the Wise has the reason I lack. The angels model the complete act of confession — limit admitted, both perfections affirmed — in a single sentence, and the sentence becomes the pattern.

**The Sentence the Tradition Learned By**

This reply entered Islamic practice as the learner's standing prayer. The classical etiquette of study opens sessions with *subḥānaka* and this confession, and the great Qur'anic supplication for increase — *My Lord, increase me in knowledge* (20:114) — is recited in the spirit of a verse that makes all knowledge a taught gift to be requested rather than a possession to be displayed. The liturgical reuse is not incidental; it reads the scene as normative. Every student occupies the angels' position at some hour: confronted with material he cannot name, tempted either to bluff or to despair, and this verse supplies the third option the scene enacted — glorify, confess the exact limit, name the Teacher's two perfections, and wait for the instruction. The prayer of al-Fātiḥah, *Guide us along the Straight Path* (1:6), is the same posture in petition form; the angels' confession is its declarative twin.
verses.33:
> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**The First Act of Office Is Instruction**

The demonstration proceeds by command: *yā Ādamu anbiʾhum bi-asmāʾihim* — O Adam, inform them of their names. The verb is *anbiʾ*, from the root of *nabaʾ*, news, and *nabī*, prophet — the announce-verb the Qur'an reserves for significant disclosure, here in its first human instance. The vicegerent's inaugural act is thus not governance, not judgment, not worship in the liturgical sense, but teaching: he addresses the angels, and what he gives them is information they lack. Read with verse 32's confession, the exchange is a liturgy of two offices: the functionaries confess their limit, the namer supplies it, and the gap between them is closed by knowledge moving in the direction the Teacher set.

**“Did I Not Tell You”: The Reserve Unsealed**

The divine speech returns to the angels with a self-quotation: *a-lam aqul lakum innī aʿlamu* — did I not say to you that I know? The reference is to verse 30's reserve, *I know what you do not know*, and the quotation marks the demonstration as the reserve's unpacking: what the angels did not know was the naming-capacity now exercised in front of them. The knowledge claimed is then given its full scope in two pairs — *ghayb al-samāwāt wa-l-arḍ*, the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and *mā tubdūna wa-mā kuntum taktumūn*, what you reveal and what you were concealing. The first pair is cosmological: nothing hidden in either order of creation — the seven heavens of verse 29 and the furnished earth — falls outside this knowledge; the Qur'an states the same scope as a standing attribute, *"˹He is the˺ Knower of the seen and the unseen—the All-Great, Most Exalted"* (13:9). The second pair is personal: the knowledge turns from the cosmos to the addressees' own interiors. The verse thus welds the two orders the reader is tempted to separate — the vast and the private — into one claim, held by one Knower, in one sentence.

**What Was Concealed: The Exegetical Candidates**

The final phrase — *what you used to conceal* — generated a literature, because the narrative does not name the concealed thing. One strand reads it as Iblīs's pride: if the tradition's placement of him among the prostrators is accepted, his interior refusal was present in the scene and known, the concealed item being the self-preference that his later open defiance will display. A second strand, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, reads it as a thought attributed to the angels themselves — that Allah never creates a thing nobler than them — with the counter-observation that on this reading what they "concealed" was a virtue, their settled knowledge of their own rank, and their acceptance of Adam's excellence in the scene was then without objection. Weighing the candidates, the text's refusal to specify is itself informative: the demonstration's force does not depend on which interior is meant, because the claim being proved is the *knowledge*, not the inventory. The Knower cites concealment generally, and every hearer supplies his own instance — which is how the verse achieves its pastoral aim: it is addressed to a reader who also has an unspoken item, and the reader knows which one it is without the text telling him.

**The Trial Closed, the Estate Confirmed**

Verses 30–33 form a complete movement, and its parts interlock: announcement (30), question (30), reserve (30), curriculum (31), test (31), confession (32), demonstration (33), ratification (33). The vicegerency stands at the end on three pillars the scene has exhibited — comprehensive taught knowledge, confessed limitation, and interiors transparent to the One who placed them. The angels' question is answered not with information about the future but with an installed fact: the blood-shedder exists now, and he can name everything in the room. The reserve of verse 30 — *I know what you do not know* — is discharged as far as discharge is possible for a bounded knower: the hidden good was shown in its first specimen, and the rest remains with the Knower, which is exactly where the angels' confession left it. For the reader at the end of the first juzʾ-section of al-Baqarah, the estate is now fully titled — earth furnished (29), heir announced (30), heir equipped (31–32), heir installed and the installation ratified by omniscience (33) — and the narrative is ready to record what the heir did with the estate, beginning with the command that comes next.
verses.34:
> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful

**One Exception, and the Qur'an Names Its Species**

*Illā Iblīs* — except Iblīs. The exception is grammatically tiny and cosmologically enormous, and the Qur'an elsewhere removes all ambiguity about its nature: *"but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord"* (18:50). He was no angel who fell; angels in the Qur'an's doctrine do not rebel — they do not have the equipment. He was a creature of the jinn, made of fire before man's clay (15:26–27), elevated by long worship into the company of angels, and addressed with them by the command. The distinction matters for everything that follows. A sin committed by an angel would impugn the order of heaven; a sin committed by a will-bearing creature among sinless company locates the fault exactly where the verse places it — in a freedom misused. The scene is thus staged with precision: the only being in the assembly capable of saying no is the one who says it.

**The First Sin Was a Comparison**

The Qur'an records Iblīs's reasoning wherever it retells this scene, and the reasoning is a syllogism: *"What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you? He replied: I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay"* (7:12). The sentence contains the whole pathology — a measurement of origins, a ranking of materials, and a verdict against the decree that outranks it. The exegetes' rebuttal is also embedded in the materials: clay receives, nurtures, and grows what is planted in it, while fire consumes what it touches; the comparison that flattered Iblīs was defective on its own terms. But the deeper indictment is structural. The first act of disbelief in the Qur'an's human-facing history is *qiyās* against a command — private judgment installed as a court of appeal over revelation. Every subsequent "I know better than the text" descends, in the Qur'an's genealogy of error, from this one sentence spoken standing while everyone else was prostrate.

**A Scene the Book Retells Five Times**

No narrative moment in the Qur'an is repeated more insistently: the command, the prostration, and the refusal appear in al-Aʿrāf (7:11–25), al-Ḥijr (15:28–44), al-Isrāʾ (17:61–65), al-Kahf (18:50), and Ṣād (38:71–78), each retelling adding a facet — the respite granted, the oath of ambush, the strategy against the straight path. Al-Baqarah's version is the most compressed of the five: the sin named, the ranking stated, the scene closed. The compression itself is a choice — this sūrah needs only the fact of the refusal, because its subject is the community that will face the refuser's war. The repetitions across the Book function as emphasis by distribution: the fall of humanity begins not at the tree but at the prostration, and every generation that reads any of the five accounts is told where its oldest enemy enlisted. Ṣād preserves his answer in the same six words (38:76) — the syllogism is stable across every retelling, which is how fixed ideas appear in transcripts.

**The Enemy Was Hired Before the Fall**

Structurally, the verse plants the Adamic drama's antagonist inside the vicegerency narrative. The angels feared corruption and blood from the new appointment (2:30); the first corruption in the story is committed by neither man nor angel but by the third party who has now declared war from inside the assembly. Humanity's temptation is thus older than humanity's sin: the whisperer was positioned before the fall, and his motive — the refused prostration — is recorded before the tree appears. The verse also carries a standing warning to its readers about the company sin keeps. Iblīs was no stranger to worship; the tradition describes aeons of devotion before this moment.
verses.35:
> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**“Do Not Approach”: A Boundary With a Margin**

The prohibition's verb is *lā taqrabā* — do not *approach* — and the choice of verb over "do not eat" builds a safety margin into the command. The forbidden act lies at the end of a path; the prohibition begins at the path's entrance. Islamic ethics drew the principle directly from this grammar: guard the haram by guarding its approaches — the glance before the look, the meeting before the act, the conversation before the commitment. The margin also sharpens the coming failure. When the tree is eaten, the couple did not merely cross a line but traversed a whole protected distance to reach it, which is why the temptation narrative in Ṭā Hā dwells on the approach — the whisper that walked them toward the tree step by step. A command framed as *do not approach* makes every deliberate nearness a partial transgression, and it teaches the reader of the verse that moral boundaries in this Book are defended in depth, not painted at the edge of the cliff.

**Which Tree? A Name the Qur'an Withholds**

The exegetical literature is full of candidates — wheat, the grapevine, the fig — and the Qur'an itself never names the tree, using only *shajarah*, a word broad enough for any tree, shrub, or woody growth. The commentators are candid about where the candidates come from: Jewish and Christian oral traditions, and perhaps Arabian lore, filtered into the tafsīr collections, much of it weakly attested in ḥadīth and some of it, as al-Ṭabarī's own material shows, no better than folklore. The withholding is a lesson in exegetical method that al-Rāzī states as a rule for the whole story: certain details are neither knowable from the text nor needed by it — *one should cease and refrain from being categorical, and God knows best*.

**Which Garden? The Dispute and Its Weighing**

A larger question divides the commentators: is this the Garden of Reward promised to believers, or a garden of trial prepared elsewhere? The consensus holds the first — it is *al-Jannah*, the definite, well-known Paradise — and answers the objections: Iblīs may have whispered from outside its bounds, and the promise that its dwellers are never expelled (15:48 — *"nor will they ever be asked to leave"* (15:48)) applies to those admitted as reward after the earthly test. The minority position, al-Rāzī reports and presses, notes real difficulties: Satan's lie inside a garden where *"never to hear any idle talk or lying therein"* is promised (78:35); the tempter's offer of a *"Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away"* (20:120), which would tempt no one already immortal; and the descent-verb *ihbiṭ*, used in this sūrah for ordinary travel (2:61) without implying vertical fall. Al-Rāzī's verdict is his method again: the proofs on both sides are weak and contradictory, so certainty is withheld — and the story's meaning survives either answer intact.

**The Wife Addressed Inside the Command**

The Qur'an does not name her in this verse or any other; she is *your wife*, and the traditions supply the name Ḥawwāʾ and the details of her creation. What the verse's grammar does supply is joint address: the command is spoken over both of them, the permission belongs to both, and the prohibition binds both. This is a structural departure from the Genesis account's sequencing, and its consequences run through the Quranic story. The temptation in Ṭā Hā is directed at Adam by name (20:120); the eating is joint; the confession is joint and in the dual and plural — *"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers"* (7:23). No woman is singled out as the entry-point of sin, no man as its victim; the responsibility is shared in the same sentence that shares the pardon. The unnamed wife of this verse is, in the Qur'an's moral universe, a co-addressed moral agent — present in the command, present in the slip, present in the received words of verse 37.
verses.36:
> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**How the Deception Worked: Selling Certainty**

The mechanics of the slip are supplied by the parallel accounts, and they show an attack on the one vulnerability the charter of verse 35 had left open. The Garden offered everything except guaranteed continuation — and Satan sold exactly that: *"O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?"* (20:120). The offer targeted not appetite but fear of loss, and al-Rāzī's observation sharpens it: a promise of eternal life is tempting only to someone whose eternity feels contingent — which is also one of his arguments that the garden of trial was not yet the Garden of Reward, where permanence is the floor and no such bait could work. Ṭā Hā adds the second instrument: he swore to them that he was their sincere adviser (20:119 — the oath recorded in al-Aʿrāf and Ṭā Hā). The deception thus ran on two rails — a guarantee against the terror of ending, and a sworn claim of goodwill — and both rails are still in service in every temptation since.

**“Descend, All of You”: The Plural and the Enmity**

The command *ihbiṭū* is plural, and the exegetes read the addressees as Adam, his wife, and their progeny — sometimes with Iblīs and his progeny included — the couple standing as representatives of the whole company. Ṭā Hā carries the same formula: *"Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other"* (20:123). Readers of the verse are by this told something about their own residence: the war declared in verse 34 did not end at the expulsion; it was given a new theater with a permanent garrison. To live on earth is to live inside a declared enmity, and the guidance promised in verse 38 is the supply line for the side that keeps the covenant.

**A Residence and Provision — With a Clock**

The earth's description is two nouns and a deadline: *mustaqarr* — a dwelling place, a settled station — and *matāʿ* — provision, enjoyment, furnished means; both *ilā ḥīn*, until a time. The commentators range over the dwelling: the earth as abode, in the sense of 40:64 — *"It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy"* (40:64) — or the graves as the true *mustaqarr* of the body. The readings can stand together, since every dwelling before the grave is provisional and the grave itself is a station on the way. The deadline is read as death, or the Resurrection, or an appointed term known only to Allah. The effect of the clause on the whole story is to make the earth a furnished leasehold: comfort is real — provision is promised in the same breath as the enmity — and comfort is terminal. The verse that expelled humanity from a garden also outfitted the exile: residence, rations, a clock, and an enemy. Three of the four are mercies; the fourth is the test.

**An Expulsion That Was Also an Installation**

Read back through verse 30, the descent changes character. The original announcement was never "I am placing a vicegerent in the Garden" but *"I am placing a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth"* — the earth named as the office's seat before the man existed. The garden residence and the slip and the descent were all, on this reading, stages in a single appointment: the vicegerent was educated, tested, forgiven, and then installed at his post, with his adversary also on site and his guidance also en route (2:38). The angels' question of verse 30 receives its fullest answer here — the corruption and blood they feared are real possibilities of the office, but the office was never designed for the innocent; it was designed for the repentant, for creatures who slip and receive words. The verse is thus an expulsion only in its grammar. In its function inside the sūrah it is an induction: humanity enters the earth not as a convict but as a posted deputy, briefed on the enemy, provisioned for the term, and expected at every fall to do what Adam is about to be shown doing — take the words and turn.
verses.37:
> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**Words Received, Not Composed**

The verse's pivot is a single verb: *fa-talaqqā Ādamu min rabbihi kalimāt* — Adam *received* words from his Lord. The reception is from a direction the reader must not miss: the words of repentance were authored on the divine side first and handed down, so that the sinner's first true act of return was itself a gift. A person cannot repent with his own resources, the verse teaches, because the fall has damaged precisely the resources repentance needs; so Allah supplies the sentence. The commentators identify the words variously, and the identifications form a small library of the tradition. The dominant reading takes them as the confession preserved in al-Aʿrāf: *"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers"* (7:23). Others report Adam's plea in three questions — Did You not make me a vicegerent? Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit? Does Your compassion not outstrip Your wrath? — with the divine "yes" to each as the received words. Others again say the words were the rites of the pilgrimage taught to him, or a formula of tawḥīd and self-accusation recorded by al-Rāzī: *There is no god but You; glory be to You and praise; I have wronged myself, so forgive me*. The plurality is itself informative: the tradition agrees on the mechanism — repentance is taught before it is offered — while leaving the syllables open.

**The Acceptance Runs Ahead of the Return**

Sequence the clause carefully: Adam received the words, *then* He turned to him. The acceptance is attached to the receiving, not to a completed program of amendment — no penance is interposed, no waiting period, no expiation enumerated. The verse's two closing names ratify the speed: *al-Tawwāb*, the Accepter of Repentance in the intensive form — the repeatedly-turning, the One whose nature is to accept — and *al-Raḥīm*, the Most Merciful, the particular mercy of al-Fātiḥah's third verse now at work at the lowest point of human history. The verse is, in practice, the charter of verse 36's leasehold — the earth is survivable because the Accepter of Repentance is in office.

**Adam Confuted Mūsā: The Verified Reading of the Fall**

The ḥadīth corpus supplies the scene's most famous epilogue, verified in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: Adam and Mūsā argued before their Lord. Mūsā opened the case — *O Adam, you are our father; you disappointed us and turned us out of Paradise.* Adam answered with a question about Mūsā's own honors: Allah favored you with His direct speech and wrote the Torah for you with His own hand — *do you blame me for a matter Allah had decreed for me forty years before He created me?* And the Prophet ﷺ concluded, three times over: *so Adam confuted Mūsā* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6614). The tradition's logic requires care, because it is often misused. Adam's appeal to decree is not a sinner's excuse offered before repentance — that appeal the Qur'an forbids — but a forgiven man's statement about a closed case: the matter had passed through words, through acceptance, through the turning of verse 37, and after pardon the only true description left is the decree. The ḥadīth thus reads verse 37 forward: once repentance is accepted, the fall belongs to Allah's prior knowledge and to mercy's record, and blame is no longer the correct grammar.

**The Door the Sūrah Will Keep Reopening**

*Al-Tawwāb* makes its first appearance here, and it does not make its last: the name returns in this sūrah at the legislation of the calf's aftermath (2:54), in Abraham's prayer for the city (2:128), over the pardon of the three who stayed behind in a later campaign (9:118 in the wider Book), and wherever a breach is followed by a way back. Its placement at the head of human history is architectural — repentance is installed as constitutional before a single law is given, so that the law will arrive to creatures already provisioned with its remedy. The verse also answers, retroactively, the angels' fear of verse 30. The creature who sheds blood and corrupts is real; but so is the creature who receives words and turns, and the second description is the one Allah chose to seal with two of His names. The fall narrative closes here — forgiven, installed, briefed — and the next verse re-reads the descent-decree to the whole species as a covenant with terms.
verses.38:
> We said, “Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**The Second Descent Widens the Address**

The command to descend was given in verse 36; here it is repeated — *ihbiṭū min-hā jamīʿan*, descend from it, all of you — and the repetition marks a shift of register from event to constitution. The first descent expelled a family and an enemy from a garden; the second installs a species on an earth under stated terms. The plural *all of you* carries the widening: the exegetes read the address as reaching beyond Adam and his wife to their progeny — every child of the couple is a party to the descent — and in some readings Iblīs and his progeny are inside the same plural, the two camps dispatched together to one theater. The effect on the reader is immediate and personal. This is not a story being watched but a decree being served: the "you" of the descent includes whoever recites the verse, already resident on the earth, already inside the enmity, and now handed — in the same breath as the exile — the terms of residence.

**Idhā: When, Not If**

The guidance clause is built on a particle that does quiet theological work. *Fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum minnī hudan* — then *when* guidance comes to you from Me — the construction combines the conditional *in* with the emphatic *mā* and the heavy *nūn*, and the commentators read the combination as certainty wearing the grammar of contingency: guidance's arrival is not in question; its timing is left open. The preposition *minnī* — from Me — fixes the source, foreclosing every candidate substitute: no guidance arrives from the earth you descend to, from the enemy stationed there, or from the self that slipped once already. The parallel in Ṭā Hā states the outcome's symmetry: *"Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺"* (20:123). Guidance, in the charter of the descent, is a delivery service with a named sender and guaranteed dispatch — the earth is never left without it, and every generation lives inside some radius of a prophet, a book, or a remainder of either.

**Two Guarantees: No Fear, No Grief**

The promise attached to following is the Qur'an's standing formula of security: *fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* — no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve. The commentators' analysis of the pair gives it its full psychology: *khawf* concerns what has not happened — the future and its threats; *ḥuzn* concerns what has — the past and its losses. The two affections between them occupy the whole of mortal time, and the formula's double negation empties both. The guided soul is described as inhabiting an unafraid present: not protected from events, but released from the two taxes the mind levies on events — dread in advance and sorrow behind. The same formula recurs as the description of the Garden's people throughout the Book — *"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (2:62) — which means the promise of this verse is not postponed to Paradise: the state it names begins in the following, here, and completes there. The descent took humanity out of a garden of provision; the charter offers a garden of the heart, portable across the enmity, to whoever follows the delivery.

**Four Acts Containing All Things**

The tradition preserves an expansion of this charter reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: when Adam descended, Allah revealed to him that four acts contain all things, for him and his children. One is for Me — worship Me and associate nothing with Me. One is for you — the reward of what you do. One is between you and Me — you supplicate, and I respond. One is between you and your fellow humans — treat them as you love to be treated. The fourfold scheme is a complete constitution of the descent, and its correspondence to the verse is exact: worship answers the guidance's first demand; personal reward answers the following's guarantee; supplication-and-response names the living link between the descended and the Sender; and the golden rule legislates the social floor of a theater occupied by enemies.
verses.39:
> But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**The Other Clause of the Charter**

Verse 38 wrote the descent's guarantee for the followers of guidance; this verse writes its complement, and the two form a single legal instrument. *Wa-lladhīna kafarū wa-kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — and those who disbelieve *and* deny Our signs. The doubling of verbs is not rhetorical padding; it distinguishes two acts that often travel together but are separable in principle. *Kufr* is the settled state — unbelief as a condition of the person, the covering-over of what the heart has been shown. *Takdhīb* is the punctual act — calling a specific sign a lie, rejecting this proof, that messenger, these words. A person can drift into kufr without ever confronting a sign; the combination named here is the aggravated case — the state confirmed *and* the evidence refused, refusal layered on disposition until the two interlock. The charter of the descent is by this complete before the descent is lived: two roads out of the same garden, both announced to the same plural "all of you," neither hidden.

**Aṣḥāb al-Nār: A Citizenship, Not a Visit**

The verdict names the deniers *aṣḥāb al-nār* — companions, people, inhabitants of the Fire. The word *ṣāḥib* denotes one who keeps company with a thing, whose relation to it is settled and customary: the companions of the cave, the people of the right hand, the traveler's companion on a road. Applied to the Fire it says more than destination — it says belonging. The Fire is not a place these souls pass through but a polity they inhabit, and the idiom pairs exactly with the Garden's own people in verse 25's *hum fīhā khālidūn* and its surroundings. The Qur'an sorts humanity, at the end of its first charter, into two citizenships, and the citizenship language does deliberate work against a common evasion: the hope of a temporary sentence, a purgatorial interval, a fire that exhausts itself.

**Khālidūn: The Permanence Clause, Second Filing**

The final sentence — *hum fīhā khālidūn*, they will be there forever, abiding — repeats the permanence clause that closed the Garden's description, and the repetition is symmetrical by design. The same word, the same grammar, the same flatness, filed for both houses. Whatever is promised there is promised here: no expiry, no parole by lapse of time, no erosion of the sentence by its own duration. The exegetical discussions that surround *khulūd* — the exception clause *except what your Lord wills* (11:108), the intensifier *forever* appended elsewhere — apply to both filings and are handled by the tradition in both directions, with the overwhelming reading holding eternity for the settled inhabitants of each house. The clause's function in the charter is argumentative as much as descriptive: it is permanence that makes the earthly choice weighty.
