For the recital's addressees the demonstration has an edge — a community that demanded to *see* Allah received instead the one sight that proves the unseen's power over their own bodies: death reversed on themselves. The demand of verse 55 failed; the evidence that actually arrived was stronger than what was demanded, because it was lived rather than viewed.

**Gratitude as the Purpose of Return**

The purpose clause — *so that perhaps you would be grateful* — is the recital's second filing of the same formula: verse 52's pardon ended with *so perhaps you would be grateful*, and verse 53's gift of the Scripture will end with its own *laʿalla*, that perhaps you would be guided. The particle states the divine intent behind the act without guaranteeing its landing: the raising makes gratitude possible, not automatic. The clause also identifies what resurrection is *for* in this recital. The raised are not raised as trophies of power — the verse does not end with "so that you would know that I am able," though the knowledge is implied — but as debtors restored to the capacity of thanks. A dead man cannot be grateful; a forgiven calf-taker cannot serve; a struck-down community cannot keep a covenant. Every reversal in the recital reopens the same closed circuit between gift and acknowledgment, and gratitude is the circuit's name. The verse by this binds the resurrection to the sūrah's economy of verse 47: favors are remembered or lost, and the greatest favor — life returned from death — is filed here with its purpose attached, so that no later reader can receive the story as spectacle without receiving its claim.

**Reversal Is Allah's Standing Method**

Verse 56 does not stand alone in the Qur'an, and its companions fix its genre. Later in this same sūrah, a man passing a ruined city asks how Allah could bring it back to life, and is answered by being killed for a century and raised — *"So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life"* (2:259) — with his food unfresh and his donkey's bones reclothed in flesh as the evidence laid out around him. Abraham asks to be shown how the dead are given life, and is walked through four birds scattered on hilltops and called back in haste (2:260). ʿĪsā is given the raising of the dead as a sign of his mission, *by Allah's Will* (3:49). The pattern across the filings is constant: reversal is demonstrated to a questioner, a passerby, a prophet, a community — always to witnesses, always with the same verb-family, always as proof of the general rule rather than as exception to it. Verse 56 is the filing addressed to a whole people at once. Its placement here — before the manna, before the city, before the rock — makes reversal the foundation of the wilderness narrative: everything the recital gives this community afterward is given to people who have already been dead and returned, which is the sūrah's way of saying that every favor in the file arrives on top of the first one.
verses.57:
> And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves

**Provision That Nobody Produced**

The verse files the wilderness economy in its purest form: shade from above, food from above, and between them a people that farms nothing. No sowing precedes the manna, no herding precedes the quails, no labor stands anywhere in the sentence — the verbs are all divine (*We shaded, We sent down*), and the only human verb is the one commanded: *eat*. The desert is the setting the Qur'an chooses deliberately, because it is the one habitat where provision cannot be mistaken for production: no rain-cycles, no soil, no stored harvest to credit. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same provision with the same grammar — *"We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, 'Eat from the good things We have provided for you'"* (7:160) — and both filings attach the same concluding principle. The structure makes this the recital's clearest case of unconditioned niʿma: the people had just died and been raised (verse 56), had not yet been asked for anything, and the provision arrived before any demand. The verse's placement in the sequence — after resurrection, before the city's test — puts pure gift at the center of the wilderness years, so that every failure around it is measured against a baseline that cost the recipients nothing.

**Ghamām: The Cloud That Shelters and Splits**

The shade is *ghamām* — a word the Qur'an reserves for clouds with theological careers. This is the cloud-cover under which Allah will appear at the end of the age: the sūrah itself asks whether the deniers are waiting for Allah to come *in the shade of clouds, along with the angels*, at which point the matter is settled (2:210). It is the cloud into which the sky splits on the Day the angels descend (25:25). The same noun shading a camp in the desert and framing the final theophany is not accidental vocabulary: *ghamām* is Allah's chosen medium of presence-with-veil — near enough to shelter, opaque enough to protect. For a people who had demanded to see Allah plainly and been struck for it (verse 55), the arrival of the shading cloud is a second answer to the same demand: you asked for unveiled sight and received stroke; here is the unveiled impossible thing given in its bearable form — His provision covering you as a roof, His presence near you as shade. The wilderness tradition of a cloud leading and covering the camp thus enters the Qur'an as doctrine rather than logistics: the ghamām is the mercy-version of the manifestation the demanders asked for.

**Eat: The Command Against Prohibition**

The speech inside the verse is an imperative with a strange object: *eat from the good things We have provided for you*. Strange because eating requires no command — hunger commands it — and because the Qur'an elsewhere has to argue against the opposite impulse: *Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?* (7:32). The command to eat the ṭayyibāt is a standing ruling against religious self-starvation, and the sūrah's addressees knew both failure modes the ruling targets: communities that forbid their own lawful foods in the name of piety (4:160 will file the prohibition as punishment-shaped-law), and communities that receive provision without receiving it as provision. The word *ṭayyibāt* carries the whole ethic: the good, the wholesome, the clean, the lawful — one Arabic term doing the work of four English ones, naming food that is simultaneously sound in substance and sound in permission. To be commanded to eat the ṭayyibāt is to be told that the good thing given is to be enjoyed, not merely consumed, and not ascetically refused. The verse's manna is therefore doctrine as much as diet: grace arrives as good things, and the correct response to good things is to eat them gratefully, which is the only command the speech contains.

**The Wrong That Lands on the Wrongdoer**

The verse closes with the principle the whole recital runs on: *the evildoers did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves*. The sentence is the mirror of verse 54's diagnosis — you wronged yourselves by taking the calf — and of the wider Qur'anic rule that Allah is beyond the reach of harm, so every sin's damage settles in the sinner's own account. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's parallel filing ends identically (7:160), which marks the principle as the fixed frame of the wilderness narrative rather than a comment on one lapse. The clause also answers the question verse 55's stroke raised about divine severity: the stroke, like the sin it answered, harmed its recipients and not its Sender — severity and provision run through the same arithmetic, in which Allah's acts are pure giving or pure ordering, and the entire variable of harm sits on the human side of the ledger.
verses.58:
> And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**A Second Entry Into a Given Land**

The verse's command has the shape of a gift with a liturgy. A people fed for a generation in the open desert is told to enter a city and eat freely, wherever they please, from what it holds — and the entry is fenced with two small requirements: a posture and a word. The first half of the command is deliberately unrestrictive — *eat freely from wherever you please* places no boundary on the table — and the restrictions attach not to the eating but to the entering. The structure replays, with a difference, the first entry-command of the sūrah: Adam was placed in the garden with the same open table, *eat as freely as you please* (2:35), and one restriction — the tree. Here the restriction is inverted into a positive rite: instead of one thing withheld, one thing asked — humility at the gate, absolution on the lips.

**Which City the Command Named**

The city is unnamed in this verse, and the exegetes' candidates follow the geography of the conquest: Jerusalem, Jericho, other cities of Syria or Jordan, and — al-Rāzī's minority reading — Egypt itself. The identifications turn on a historical problem the verse leaves open: Moses never entered the Holy Land, so a command spoken under his leadership would either predate the conquest or belong to Joshua's campaign at Jericho. Al-Rāzī's Egypt reading dissolves the problem by relocating the scene: the punishment of the following verse, he reasons, fits the period before any entry into the Holy Land, and Egypt — the land of their torment — would then be re-entered as a land of provision, the reversal complete. The stronger evidence runs the other way. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same command with the city named: *"Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please"* (7:161), and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ joins the gate-entry to the covenant's catalogue: *"We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, 'Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility'"* (4:154). The identification with Jerusalem — or with a city of the Holy Land entered at the conquest — carries the Qur'an's own explicit glosses, while the Egypt reading rests on inference. The unnamed city of this verse is named twice elsewhere in the Book, and the naming settles it.

**Ḥiṭṭa: One Word for the Whole Liturgy**

The spoken requirement is a single word: *ḥiṭṭah* — rendered here *Absolve us*, literally an unburdening. The grammarians' reading of its force is exact: al-Zamakhsharī takes it as a cognate-accusative invocation, "unburden us an unburdening" — the way Arabic compresses a whole petition into its verbal noun, so that the word is not a description but a request in its shortest legal form. The word's content completes the posture's work. A bowing body could still carry a boasting heart; the prescribed speech forecloses it, because *ḥiṭṭah* names the speaker's condition — burdened, in need of removal — and names nothing about the speaker's merit. There is no room in the word for *because we fought*, *because we kept the law*, *because our fathers were righteous*; the entire entry-theology of the covenant is compressed into a noun meaning take this load off. The verse by this makes the liturgy a doctrinal instrument: what a people says at its threshold of blessing discloses what it believes about the blessing. Islamic practice keeps the pattern in its own entry-formulas — the duʿāʾ of the mosque's door, the greeting of peace at every threshold — and the ancestor of the whole genre stands here: one word, spoken entering, that assigns the gift to the Giver and the burden to the only Remover.

**Forgiveness and Increase at the Threshold**

The promise answering the word is double: *We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers*. The first half meets the petition — *ḥiṭṭah* asks for removal, and removal is pledged, maghfira for their line of sins: the calf, the demand, the wilderness record. The second half exceeds it, and the exceeding is attached to a named group: the *muḥsinūn*, the good-doers, the people whose worship carries excellence. The promise's structure is thus the sūrah's whole economy of grace in two clauses — the floor is forgiveness for the asking, and the ceiling is multiplication for the excellent — with both opened by a bowed entry and a four-letter word. The multiplication clause also does specific work in this context. The city's table was *eat freely from wherever you please*; the promised increase says that the material gift is the lesser half of what the threshold offers. A community entering in humility receives not only the city but a rising curve inside the covenant — reward that compounds for those who do the asking well. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's filing carries the same double promise (7:161), which marks it as the standing terms of entry rather than a one-time offer: wherever the gate of a divine gift is opened, forgiveness and increase are posted on it together.
verses.59:
> But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness

**The Changed Word**

The verse's first clause reports one of the smallest sins in the Qur'an and one of the most heavily answered. The command had been a posture and a word (verse 58); the response was a substitution — *the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say*. The verb *baddala* is the Qur'an's technical term for replacement: not mispronouncing, not forgetting, but swapping the commanded thing for another thing in its place. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same clause with the same verb and adds the qualifier that sharpens it: *"But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say"* (7:162) — *among them*. The substitution was not the whole camp's act but a faction's, and the naming matters: the recital indicts precisely and does not smear. What the qualifier also exposes is the social anatomy of the sin — a liturgy commanded to everyone, corrupted by some, and not corrected by the rest, since the punishment that follows lands on the community's file as a whole. The changed word is the smallest possible act of covenant-breaking, and that is why the verse treats it as the largest kind of sign: what a people does with one commanded syllable discloses what it will do with a scripture.

**What They Said Instead**

The reports supply the substituted words, and they supply two versions. The famous reading has them replacing *ḥiṭṭah* — absolve us — with *ḥinṭah*, wheat: the petition for forgiveness turned into a request for grain, the liturgy of the gate converted into shopping. Al-Zamakhsharī pressed the obvious objection: these people did not speak Arabic, so a wordplay between two Arabic nouns cannot be what happened, and the report's wit does not survive translation into the scene. The objection is sound as far as it goes, and the hadith literature preserves the Prophet's ﷺ own version of the substitution, which is different in wording and identical in kind. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records it: the Children of Israel were told to enter the gate in prostration and say *ḥiṭṭah*, *"but they changed (Allah's Order) and entered, dragging themselves on their buttocks and said, 'Habatun (a grain) in a Sha'ratin (hair)'"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4641). The substitution in the ḥadīth is still a food-word — a grain, in a hair — but the mechanism the Prophet ﷺ emphasizes is the change itself, whatever the syllables: the commanded petition was replaced by a trivial phrase, and the commanded posture by its inverse. The stronger reading holds both reports together at the level they agree on: the word was changed because the word was the test, and a people unwilling to ask for absolution will always find a smaller sentence to say in its place.

**A Punishment From the Heavens**

The response arrives as *rijz min al-samāʾ* — punishment from the heavens. *Rijz* is the Qur'an's word for penal affliction: the same noun names the plagues sent upon Pharaoh's people when they broke each promise (7:134), the affliction sent on the people of Lūṭ's cities (29:34), and — in its other register — the whispering pollution of Satan (8:11). The commentators read the heaven-sent rijz here as a plague, the identification supported by the word's use for the Egyptian plagues and by al-Rāzī's related reasoning that this punishment belongs to the period before any entry into the Holy Land. The clause's direction — *from the heavens* — answers the scene's geography: the sky had been this community's benefactor for a generation, dropping shade (verse 57) and dropping food; the same sky now drops the penalty, and the verse states the symmetry without comment because the symmetry is the comment. Nothing on earth mediated the punishment; no army, no famine-cycle, no natural cause is named. A liturgy mocked at a gate is answered by a dispatch from the direction the gift came, and the answer's precision — *upon them for their rebelliousness*, the cause stated in the sentence — keeps the punishment inside the covenant's own logic: not rage but consequence, filed against a named act.

**Why a Word Carries This Weight**

The disproportion between the sin's size and the punishment's weight is the verse's deliberate lesson, and the sūrah explains it by pairing this scene with a later charge against the same community's scholars: *"a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it"* (2:75). Words are the covenant's medium: promises are words, liturgy is words, scripture is words, and the demand to *say* ḥiṭṭah was a demand to let the mouth ratify what the heart knew — that the city was gift, the table was provision, and the guests were burdened sinners at a merciful Lord's door. Verse 42 had already legislated the principle for the scholars — do not mix truth with falsehood, do not conceal it knowingly — and verse 59 shows the principle's wilderness origin: the first corruption of a divine word on this community's record was committed with the mouth, at a gate, in a single substituted sentence.
verses.60:
> And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**A Prophet's Prayer for Water**

The verse opens with need rather than command: Moses sought water for his people — *istisqā*, the seeking of drink, a prophet reduced to the desert's one question. The Qur'an states the prayer and moves immediately to the answer, and Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same sequence with the same economy: *"We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, 'Strike the rock with your staff.'"* (7:160). The form of the scene became Islamic practice: the prayer for rain, ṣalāt al-istisqāʾ, established in the Prophet's ﷺ sunnah and performed to this day when the rains fail — a community asking its Lord for water through its imam, in the grammar this verse first wrote down. The detail worth holding is the direction of the asking. The people's thirst is real; the prophet does not lecture them about it but carries it upward. The recital elsewhere shows this community's needs expressed as complaint (the food fatigue that follows in the file); here need is expressed as intercession, and the answer comes through the intercessor's channel. The verse thus distinguishes, without naming the distinction, two ways of being needy before Allah — the way that asks Him through His appointed, and the way that demands of Him as a customer — and grants the first without a word of rebuke.

**The Staff Again**

The answer is an instruction addressed to a tool: strike the rock with your staff. The staff is by now the recital's standing instrument. At the sea the same command produced the same grammar — *"Strike the sea with your staff," and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain* (26:63) — and the two filings together establish the pattern of prophetic miracle in the Qur'an: the extraordinary act is routed through an ordinary object wielded by an obedient hand. Nothing in the staff parts seas or opens stone; the verse's theology is that divine power does not bypass means but honors them, so that the means stay visible and the power stays unmistakable. The staff's own history deepens the choice: it was Moses's shepherd's stick — the one he leaned on and beat down leaves with for his flock, as he told the One who spoke to him at Ṭuwā (20:18) — and it became the sign-object of his mission. A herdsman's tool, retained through prophethood, is now the instrument of a nation's water. The Qur'an keeps selecting for its signs the objects people already carry, which is its standing answer to demands for spectacle: the miracle is not the absence of ordinary things but what obedience does with them.

**Twelve Springs for Twelve Tribes**

The struck rock yields structure, not just water: twelve springs gush out, and each tribe knows its drinking place. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf supplies the correspondence explicitly — *"We divided them into twelve tribes— each as a community"* (7:160) — so the water-system mirrors the camp-system, spring for tribe, and the miracle includes its own administration. The commentators elaborate with reports of a portable stone — carried through the wilderness, struck on each of four faces, three streams from each face, twelve in total — and with the reading that each tribe's spring was assigned by lot or by marking; the reports are tradition's furniture rather than the verse's content, and the verse's own point stands without them: grace arrived organized. A camp of twelve tribes at one water source is a riot; a camp of twelve tribes with twelve springs is a settlement.

**The Rock and the Heart**

The verse carries a second reading the sūrah itself authorizes. Fourteen verses later the same sūrah compares this community's hearts to stone — and to stone that waters: *"Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah"* (2:74). The comparison presumes exactly what verse 60 staged: rock is not barrenness in the Qur'an's mineralogy but potential — the hard thing that, struck in obedience, pours. The Sufi commentators drew the inference explicitly: Ibn ʿAjībah reads the stone as the heart, the staff as spiritual resolve (*himmah*), and the striking as the discipline that breaks the ego's hardness so wisdom and unveiling flow — twelve streams for the twelve faculties of a restored soul. The esoteric reading is legitimate precisely because verse 74 installs the rock-heart equation in the text; the historical event remains the verse's primary sense, and the symbolic reading rides on it rather than replacing it. Both registers converge on one claim: the water came from the hardest thing present, at a stroke performed in obedience, through a stick that was only a stick. The camp drank from a rock that day, and the recital keeps the scene on file for every later reader whose own hardness is waiting for the same command — strike, and what was stone will water twelve directions.
verses.61:
> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺. So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.” They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations

**The Complaint Against Heaven's Table**

The verse opens with the longest direct speech any wilderness generation addresses to its prophet in this recital, and the speech is a complaint about the menu. *We cannot endure the same meal* — the manna and quails, provision that fell from the sky without sowing, has become unbearable through repetition. Nothing in the speech accuses the food of being bad: the manna was ṭayyib, sent with a command to eat (verse 57). What the speakers cannot bear is *uniformity* — one food, day after day, with no market, no variety, no Egypt. The biblical record preserves the same complaint in the same wilderness: the people weeping for the fish and cucumbers and melons and leeks and onions and garlic of Egypt, and the quails granted in answer turning into judgment on the cravers (Numbers 11).

**Moses's Rebuke: The Direction of the Exchange**

The answer comes as a question that contains the whole verdict: *Do you exchange what is better for what is worse?* The verb is *istibdāl* — substitution, the same family the recital used for the changed word at the gate (verse 59) — and the question's force is in its direction-words. Better and worse here are not flavors but stations: the heavenly provision is the better, the earth's commons the worse, and the exchange is therefore a descent dressed as a purchase. The second half of the rebuke drives it home: *go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for*. The verb is *habaṭa*, to go down — the sūrah's word for Adam's exit from the garden (*descend from the heavens*, 2:36) and for every fall from a given station to an earned one. The crops are available; they have always been available; they grow wherever people farm, and the camp can have them the moment it accepts descent into the ordinary economy. The word *miṣr* in the command — rendered *any village* — carries the pun the exegetes debate: as a common noun it is a town, any town; as the proper name it is Egypt, and al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse's orthography requires the indefinite reading (*miṣran*, not *Miṣra*), so the command is go down to a town, not return to Egypt — though early readers heard the second meaning humming under the first. Both readings converge: what the demanders want is available anywhere below heaven, and getting it means leaving the table where heaven serves.

**Stricken With Disgrace and Misery**

The verdict arrives in two coverings and a burden. *They were stricken with disgrace and misery* — *ḍuribat ʿalayhim al-dhillah wa-l-maskanah*: abjection and destitution struck over them as a tent is struck over a camper, or a tax is struck on an account. The imagery of the verb is enclosure: the two conditions wrap the community, and the recital is not describing one bad season but a standing condition — the same sentence will be refiled in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān with the addition that the covering holds wherever they are found, except under a covenant with Allah and a covenant with people (3:112). The third element is active rather than passive: *they invited the displeasure of Allah* — *bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin min Allāh*, and the verb *bāʾū* is commercial in its root sense: they returned home carrying it, the way a trader returns carrying his goods. Wrath is filed as acquired property, earned and borne back, which is the sūrah's market idiom applied to the worst possible cargo. The two coverings and the burden together answer the complaint's logic exactly: the people who could not endure heaven's monotony receive earth's monotony as a permanent estate — disgrace that does not rotate, misery that does not vary — and the displeasure they carry is the receipt.

**Rejecting Signs, Killing Prophets**

The verdict names its grounds, and the grounds exceed the meal: *for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets*. A complaint about onions is being answered with a charge sheet of murder, and the connection is the recital's method rather than disproportion. The verse addresses the community across its whole history in the second person — the same inheritance logic that made descendants parties to the sea and the calf — and files the two capital crimes of that history: the signs rejected (the demand for sight, the changed word, the calf taken after the sea) and the prophets killed without right, a charge the Qur'an repeats across sūrahs (2:87, 2:91, 3:21, 3:112, 3:181, 4:155, 5:70) with the same *unjustly* — since no prophet's killing could ever be just, the adverb marks the killings as done against known truth. The sūrah will turn the charge into an argument at verse 91: a community that says *we believe in what was sent down to us* is asked why it killed Allah's prophets before, if belief is the claim (2:91). The meal-complaint sits inside that larger indictment because it shares its root: the rejecting of what Allah sends, in the form He sends it. The manna rejected was a sign handled exactly as the prophets were handled — received, resented, replaced.
verses.62:
> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**Four Names on One Promise**

The verse lists four communities and hangs one promise on all four: the believers — the Muslim confessors — the Jews, the Christians, and the Ṣābiʾūn. The third name is the verse's historical puzzle, and the exegetes' candidates map the puzzle's shape. *Ṣābiʾ* derives from a root meaning to leave one religion for another — or, in a second etymology, to rise, as stars rise — and pagan Arabs used it as a slur for the Prophet ﷺ himself, who had left the religion of his forefathers. The commentators propose identifications across a spectrum: monotheists with no book, rites, or prophet, saying only *there is no god but God*; angel-venerating worshippers who faced a qiblah and recited the Psalms; defectors from the People of the Book; followers of the religion of Noah; or star-influenced monotheists whom some classify as unbelievers.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The promise is stated in the Qur'an's fixed eschatological idiom: *their reward is with their Lord*, and *no fear upon them, no grief*. The two halves are the charter formula of this sūrah — the same pair that closed the descent's guarantee to Adam's children: whoever follows the guidance, *"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (2:38). The reuse is the verse's strongest structural signal: the people of verse 62 are being admitted to the charter's own promise, in the charter's own words, which places the verse inside the sūrah's first architecture rather than beside it as an exception. The formula's two negatives are precise about what salvation removes — fear of what is coming, grief over what was left — covering the future and the past in one stroke, the exact double anxiety the Last Day generates. And the reward's location — *with their Lord*, stored in His custody rather than distributed by any community's gatekeepers — removes the promise from every institutional claim: no priesthood, no lineage, no confession holds the keys to this verse's treasury. The reward is with the Lord of the four named groups, which is the verse's quiet way of saying He is one and His custody is single.

**The Parallel Filing in al-Māʾidah**

The Qur'an states this ruling twice, and the second filing confirms the first's permanence: *"Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (5:69). The parallel is near-verbatim, with one variation — the Ṣābiʾūn move ahead of the Christians in the order — and variation of order without variation of content is the Qur'an's way of filing a principle rather than an occasion. A concession to a moment is stated once; a standing rule is restated in a later sūrah, in a different context, with the same clause carrying the same weight. Al-Māʾidah's filing sits among verses on communal difference and judgment — God will decide between the communities on the Day of Judgment — which frames the rule there as eschatological business belonging to Allah alone. The double filing also answers the historicist reduction from within the text: whatever historical group the Ṣābiʾūn were, the ruling's grammar — whoever believes and does good — is built to outlive every candidate identification, and the second sūrah's repetition publishes that intent.

**Before Islam or After? The Abrogation Debate and Its Better Answer**

The exegetes ask whether the verse's promise runs past the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and three answers have their grounds. The first limits it: the verse concerns Jews, Christians, and Ṣābiʾūn who kept their original faith before Islam and, when the Prophet ﷺ came, acknowledged him — people like Salmān al-Fārsī, Abū Dharr, and the monks Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Baḥīra; on this reading the labels name communities, and the condition names their faithful members' completion in Islam. The second claims abrogation: a view cited from Ibn ʿAbbās holds that 3:85 — whoever seeks a religion other than submission, it will not be accepted — cancels this verse. The counter-principle defeats it on the tradition's own terms: abrogation applies to legal rulings and commands, not to descriptive statements, and least of all to statements about persons' standing with Allah in the hereafter; verse 62 is description, not legislation, and survives. The third, al-Zamakhsharī's, reads *those who believe* ironically as the hypocrites — outward confessors lumped with the named groups, against whom the verse's second half then defines true believers. The reading collapses without it: nowhere else in the Qur'an does *those who believe* mean hypocrites, and a Jew who followed Muhammad's law would simply no longer be called a Jew. The stronger construction keeps the plain sense and reads the condition as the verse does — creed, eschatology, and good works as the substance the labels stand for, with the commentators' common gloss that true belief after the mission's publication includes acceptance of the Messenger, since rejecting a prophet one has truly known is not belief in Allah but belief on one's own terms.
verses.63:
> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**Raised Over You: The Exegetes' Two Readings**

How the mountain stood over the camp divides the commentators, and both sides have grounds. The majority reading is literal and total: the mountain — Sinai itself, or a mass torn from Palestine — was uprooted, made to move, and held suspended above the Israelites like a canopy, the fear of its fall the sanction behind the pledge. The alternative reads the phrase as idiomatic: the mountain loomed above them, the way English says a danger *hung over* a people, and the looming was the theophany's terror — the thick cloud, the smoke like a kiln's, the violently shaking mountain of the Exodus account, with its standing order that whoever touches the mountain dies. The Qur'an's own elaboration settles the question toward the literal. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf describes the scene with two details no idiom needs: *"We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them"* (7:171). A mountain *like a cloud* — spread above them as shade is spread — and a community that *thought it would fall*: both details belong to a suspended mass, not to a looming landscape, and the second detail records the camp's own perception, which is exactly what the literal reading claims. The looming-idiom reading remains possible as language but must explain away 7:171's specific imagery; the stronger reading keeps both verses at face value. The mountain was held over them, and they looked up.

**Hold Firmly, With Strength**

The speech under the mountain is the covenant's clause: *hold firmly to that which We have given you, and observe what is in it*. The first verb — *khudhū*, take, seize — is governed by *bi-quwwah*, with strength, which the exegetes read as earnestness, seriousness, and settled resolve: take the Scripture the way a drowning man takes a rope, with the whole body's commitment. The strength is not intellectual assent but grip. The second command — *remember what is in it* in one reading, *observe its teachings* in this translation's rendering of *udh-kurū mā fīh* — makes memory a term of the covenant: the contents are to be held in recall, recited, kept present, because a book unremembered is a book not held. The same command is filed at verse 93 with the mountain scene repeated and the covenant's object named as obedience, and again in al-Aʿrāf with the identical words and identical purpose clause (7:171) — three filings of one signing. The object held is *what We have given you*: the Torah, as the commentators state plainly, the book given at the forty nights' end (verse 53). The verse by this connects the recital's two mountain scenes — the gift received by Moses above and the covenant gripped by the people below — into one transaction: the Book descended, and the descent's condition was strength of hold and permanence of memory.

**So Perhaps You Will Become Mindful**

The clause of purpose is the covenant's stated end: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — so that you may become god-fearing. The recital's purpose clauses have been accumulating — pardon for gratitude (52), the Book for guidance (53) — and this one names the deepest target, the virtue the sūrah opened with: guidance is for the mindful (2:2), and the Scripture's holding is for mindfulness. The taqwā named here is also the covenant's only adequate sanction, which reorders the mountain scene: the mountain hanging overhead produces fear of falling, but the verse wants fear *of Allah* — and the difference between the two fears is the distance the Scripture must carry the community. Verse 63 is thus the sūrah's statement of how a people under terror becomes a people under conscience: the terror is the door, the grip is the road, and mindfulness is the arrival.

**The Sūrah's Covenant Register**

Verse 63 is the third filing of the covenant in this sūrah's first hundred verses, and the register is cumulative by design. Verse 40 states the covenant bilaterally — fulfil yours and I will fulfil Mine. Verse 53 files its instrument — the Scripture and Criterion given. Verse 63 stages its signing — the pledge taken under the canopy, with the terms spoken: hold, remember, become mindful. Verse 93 will refile the same scene with the community's answer recorded, and al-Nisāʾ gathers the whole package — the Mount raised for the covenant, the gate entered with humility, the Sabbath kept, the firm pledge taken (4:154) — into a single indictment list. The repetition is the covenant's own method: a bond of this weight is not signed once but re-read at every station, and the Qur'an's habit of refiling Sinai across sūrahs treats the covenant as a living instrument each generation re-enters. That is why the address is second-person — *We took a covenant from you* — spoken to Madinans about a mountain they never stood under: the pledge runs with the Scripture, and every community that receives the Book receives the scene. The verse's last word is its first demand: mindfulness. Everything else — the fright, the grip, the memory — is scaffolding around a single objective, and the scaffolding comes down, in the sūrah's own telling, the moment the community lets go.
verses.64:
> Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers

**Turning Away After Everything**

Three words carry the verse's indictment: *turned away, afterwards*. The verb *tawallā* is not the glancing-off of inattention but the deliberate turn of the back — the same verb the Qur'an uses for the one who hears the call and walks the other way. Its object here is everything verse 63 assembled: the covenant taken, the mountain raised, the command to hold with strength. And the temporal marker *baʿda dhālik* — after that — is the aggravator. This was not a people who turned away in ignorance, before the demonstration; they turned away after the canopy, after the sea, after the resurrection of verse 56, after the pardon of verse 52. Every defense a reader might reach for (we did not know, we were not shown, we were never asked) has been pre-filed in the preceding twenty verses, and *afterwards* closes the file.

**Faḍl and Raḥma: The Two Names That Intercepted**

The interception runs through a pair: *faḍl* and *raḥma* — grace and mercy. The two nouns are not synonyms stacked for emphasis; they name distinct operations, and the pair's division of labor is exact. *Faḍl* is surplus: giving beyond what is owed, beyond what is earned, beyond the measure of the deed — the word the Qur'an uses for provision granted without accounting, for reward multiplied past the act's worth. *Raḥma* is tenderness toward the miserable: care that reaches a recipient in a condition it cannot remedy itself — the womb-root's mercy, moving toward need rather than toward merit. The turning-away community stood in need of both operations at once: it had earned less than it had (so surplus was required — faḍl), and it was in a condition it could not exit unaided (so descending care was required — raḥma). The pair appears across the Qur'an as the standing formula of rescue — the believers hold their direction of prayer through Allah's faḍl and raḥma, the sūrah's own verse on the qibla test closes on Allah as Raʾūf and Raḥīm toward humanity (2:143) — and its filing here, immediately after the turning-away, makes the theological point the recital keeps proving: the covenant survives its breaches because its divine side runs on grace-and-mercy rather than on match-and-mirror. The human side turns; the divine side's response is governed by names that do not.

**What the Mountain Could Not Do**

Verse 63's canopy produced a pledge; verse 64 records that the pledge did not hold. The pair of verses states, in the Qur'an's own sequence, a limit on terror: fear compels the tongue but does not convert the heart, and a covenant signed under a hovering mountain requires a different power to keep. The sūrah had already legislated the alternative — verse 45's method clause: seek help through patience and prayer, the disciplines that hold a person on the line after the line's terror has faded. Verse 63's own purpose clause said the same thing from the other end: hold firmly, remember, *so perhaps you will become mindful* — taqwā formed by grip and memory, not by fright. Verse 64 is the demonstration of why the purpose clause was needed. The raised mountain is thus given its exact weight in the recital's theology: enough to arrest a refusal, not enough to found a fidelity. What fidelity requires is the pair of this verse — grace that gives the turning-away community a second standing, mercy that keeps working on hearts the mountain could only shake. The sequence fright → pledge → turn → grace is the sūrah's whole account of how law alone fares with human beings, and it is why the recital never relies on severity twice: every terror in the file is followed by provision, every collapse by an intercepted verdict.

**Of the Losers**

The verdict intercepted is named in the sūrah's market idiom: *you would have been of the losers* — *la-kuntum min al-khāsirīn*. Loss, in this sūrah, is never vague misfortune but failed exchange: its opening portraits buy misguidance at the price of guidance and complete the purchase without profit (2:16); its hypocrites deal in deception that returns on the dealers; its deniers trade the eternal for the fleeting. To be *of the losers* is membership in that company — the people whose ledger shows capital spent on nothing. The commercial frame sharpens the counterfactual's arithmetic. The turning-away was itself a transaction: the covenant's obligations set down, the covenant's benefits retained as far as possible, the direction of trade reversed. What grace intercepts is not a mood but a deal — the completed sale of a delivered people's standing for the price of an unkept pledge. And the *min* of membership does its habitual work: the losers are a class, and the intercepted community was one clause away from enrollment. The sūrah's readers stand inside the same grammar. Every turning-away is a small purchase in the same market, and the verse states what keeps any buyer out of the losers' roll: not the buyer's discipline, but the two names that move before the transaction settles — grace upon you, mercy upon you.
verses.65:
> You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**The Test Engineered at the Seaside**

Sūrah al-Aʿrāf preserves the scene in full, and its details explain why the Qur'an calls the event a test: *"Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath. During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen. In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness"* (7:163). The arrangement is deliberate provocation by arrangement: a fishing town whose fish appeared, visibly, in abundance, only on the one day work was forbidden — appetite maximized exactly where law interdicted. The exegetes read the visible abundance as the test's precision instrument: the fish were not merely present but *shurraʿan*, surfacing in plain sight, engineered temptation in the town's own harbor. The Sabbath itself carried the covenant's weight — al-Nisāʾ lists its keeping among the terms of the firm pledge taken under the mountain (4:154) — so the weekly surfacing was a weekly audit of the pledge. The verse in al-Baqarah assumes the whole apparatus and states only the breach and the sentence, because for its first audience the apparatus was known: the town by the sea was a case recited in their own houses, and the Qur'an's reminder needed only the case number.

**The Town's Three Companies**

Al-Aʿrāf's filing adds the social anatomy of the breach, and it belongs to any honest reading of the sentence. The town held three groups: the transgressors, who fished; a company that warned and forbade; and a company that questioned the warners — *"Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?"* — answered by the warners with the sūrah's whole doctrine of public admonition: *"Just to be free from your Lord's blame, and so perhaps they may abstain"* (7:164). The answer defines the warner's two reasons: discharge — the obligation of forbidding evil falls on the one who knows, whatever the target's response — and hope — *perhaps* they will abstain, the same particle that governs the recital's purpose clauses. Verse 65's audience in Madina had just been addressed about this exact obligation: the scholars who preach righteousness and exempt themselves (2:44). The town scene is that verse's case law. When the warning was ignored, the outcome sorted the companies: *"We rescued those who used to warn against evil and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment"* (7:165). The rescued are named by their warning — not by their fishing-abstinence alone but by their standing in the breach and speaking. The third company's fate the exegetes debate; the text's emphasis falls where the warners' answer put it: the blame discharged is the blamer's own salvation.

**“Be Disgraced Apes”**

The sentence is four words: *kunū qiradatan khāsiʾīn* — be apes, disgraced. The imperative of being — *kun* — is the Qur'an's creative command, the word that makes rather than requests; the transformation is filed as divine speech act, instantaneous and total. *Khāsiʾūn* adds the condition attached to the new form: driven away, disgraced, banished — the word used elsewhere of a dog slinking off and of the punished cast out from favor. Al-Aʿrāf files the same sentence with its precondition: *"But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, 'Be disgraced apes!'"* (7:166) — persistence first, transformation second; the sentence lands after the warning was refused and the violation hardened into custom. The exegetical debate over the transformation's mode is old: the majority reads it bodily and literal — the Qur'an's plain statement, confirmed by al-Māʾidah's mention of people Allah reduced to apes and pigs (5:60); Mujāhid read it as hearts transformed while bodies remained, comparing the metaphor of 62:5 — *"The example of those who were entrusted with ˹observing˺ the Torah but failed to do so, is that of a donkey carrying books"* — where the animal is admittedly likeness. The bodily reading is stronger: the Qur'an distinguishes clearly between its *mathal*-parables, which announce themselves as likenesses, and its *masakh*-transformations, which are stated as events; 5:60's phrasing — reduced to apes and pigs — describes a fate, not a figure. The metaphorical reading keeps the moral truth the literal one contains: the form followed the nature. A people whose humanity had become purely appetitive — surfacing fish as the only object of thought — received the body of the appetite they lived by.

**No Progeny: The Line That Ends**

The sentence raises the question every generation asks of it, and the Prophet ﷺ answered the question directly. When the metamorphosed peoples were mentioned before him — the monkeys, and as one narrator recalls, the pigs — he said: *"Verily, Allah did not cause the race of those which suffered metamorphosis to grow or they were not survived by young ones. Monkeys and swine had been in existence even before"* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2663b). The ruling has two clauses, and each does theological work. The metamorphosed left no offspring: the transformation was terminal for the transformed, a dead end rather than a new species — which answers the naturalist objection that today's apes would then be human descendants, and preserves the punishment's character as extinction-of-a-people rather than origin-of-a-kind. The ḥadīth by this fixes the punishment's semantics: *masakh* is not evolution but verdict — a soul's removal from the human register, complete with the loss of what makes human life continue, posterity. The transformed did not become ancestors; they became a case, which is exactly how verse 65's continuation files them.
verses.66:
> So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing

**“To What Is Before It and Behind It”**

The nakāl's range is stated in a spatial-temporal formula the exegetes read three ways: *li-mā bayna yadayhā wa-mā khalfahā* — for what is between its hands and what is behind it. The dominant reading is temporal: for the generations present at the event and the generations after — the punishment's deterrence running forward through time, every later community a beneficiary of the town's sentence. The second reading keeps the idiom spatial — *between the hands* meaning ahead, in front: for the surrounding settlements of that region and those behind them, the deterrent working geographically across the neighborhood that watched the fish-traps fill. The temporal reading carries the verse's main weight, because verse 66 exists to explain why the story is being recited in Madina centuries later: the audience of the recital *is* the *mā khalfahā*, the behind-it, receiving the sentence as it was designed to be received — at a distance, through speech, as restraint.

**Mawʿiẓah: The Admonition and Its Addressees**

The second filing of the punishment is *mawʿiẓah* — admonition, exhortation, lesson — and its addressees are named: *li-l-muttaqīn*, for the God-fearing. The word carries both registers the classical lexicons record: counsel that draws the hearer toward good, and reprimand that pushes from evil — the single term covering the lesson's two faces, because a warning is simultaneously an invitation. The addressee-naming is the verse's most deliberate stroke. A punishment made nakāl addresses everyone through fear; the same punishment made mawʿiẓah addresses the muttaqīn through recognition. The distinction is the sūrah's own opening distinction — the Book as guidance *for the God-conscious* (2:2), a benefit that lands only where the landing-conditions exist. A lesson requires a faculty to receive it, and taqwā is that faculty: the settled carefulness about Allah's bounds that lets a person hear an old sentence as addressed to himself. Without it the same story is anecdote — entertainment at the ancestors' expense, or tribal polemic, or nothing. The verse thus splits its own audience: the nakāl restrains the outward person in whoever hears it, and the mawʿiẓah reforms the inward person in whoever fears. Both are mercy; the second requires cooperation, which is why it is restricted by name rather than by exclusion — the God-fearing are not a tribe but a condition, and the condition is open to every hearer the recital reaches.

**How a Punishment Becomes a Lesson**

The mechanism by which an event centuries dead performs this double work is the recital itself, and the verse is the recital's statement of purpose. The town's transformation is inaccessible to the senses now — no ruins of apes, no surviving witnesses — yet the nakāl operates because the event was preserved in revelation and is being read aloud in Madina. The Qur'an's own narration is the delivery system of the lesson: the same speech that files the punishment enacts its forward reach, carrying it across the generations the formula names. This is why the Qur'an insists on its stories as *aḥsan al-qaṣaṣ*, the best of narrations (12:3), and files its penalties with narrative care — the punishment of Pharaoh's body preserved explicitly so that it may become a sign for those who come after (10:92), the Sabbath-town narrated across three sūrahs. Every major penalty in the Book carries its transmission clause, and verse 66 is the clause in its purest form: the event's afterlife as lesson is part of the sentence. The reader's position in the mechanism deserves exact statement, because it defines what reading this verse is doing: to receive the mawʿiẓah is to be the *mā khalfahā* functioning as designed — the punishment completing its second purpose in the heart of someone the town never met. A lesson unlearned is a nakāl half-executed; the verse files the audience as the sentence's remaining half.

**The Saved Companies and the Lesson's Full Text**

The mawʿiẓah's content is larger than the transformation, and the fuller filing in al-Aʿrāf shows why. That sūrah's account preserves the town's three companies — the breakers, the warners, and the questioners of the warning — and preserves the outcome's sorting: the warners rescued, named by their warning (7:165). Read as one lesson, the case teaches more than *do not break the bound*. It teaches the structure of a community under test: that transgression in a town is never only the transgressors' affair, that standing in the breach with a spoken warning is itself a form of keeping the Sabbath, and that the rescue is attached by name to the warning rather than to private abstention. The questioners of al-Aʿrāf's account — why bother warning the doomed? — voice the fatigue the lesson exists to answer, and the warners' reply (discharge before Allah, hope for the target) is the lesson's positive text. Verse 66's two nouns thus divide the case's teaching cleanly: the nakāl is the negative half, the fate of the breakers restraining every hearer from the engineered breach; the mawʿiẓah is the positive half, the fate of the warners instructing every God-fearing hearer what to do in a town where the fish surface on the forbidden day. A lesson with only its first half produces fear without direction; the Qur'an files both.
verses.67:
> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”

**The Sūrah Named for a Cow**

The longest sūrah of the Qur'an takes its title from this episode: al-Baqarah, the Cow. The naming is itself an exegetical act — of the sūrah's hundreds of rulings, narratives, and arguments, the tradition's chosen identifier is a story about a commanded sacrifice and the reception it met. The episode is also, as the commentators note, unusually detailed by Qur'anic standards: where the Book typically compresses a narrative to its moral geometry, this one runs across several verses of dialogue, question and answer, specification and response. The detail is the reason for the naming. The sūrah's central subject is how a covenant community handles what it is given — scripture, provision, commands — and no scene in the recital displays the handling's failure mode as precisely as a command received with a sarcasm-question. The cow-episode is al-Baqarah in miniature: a divine order, minimal in its terms; a human reception that converts the order into an occasion; and a negotiation that costs the receivers everything the order was going to give them cheaply. A sūrah that legislates prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, debt, and war names itself after this exchange because the exchange determines whether any legislation will be carried at all.

**A Command With No Specifications**

The order arrives in six words: *Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow*. Its remarkable feature is what it lacks. No age, no color, no lineage, no number — an indefinite noun, *baqarah*, any cow. In a law-code whose later sūrahs will specify sacrificial animals down to their condition and season, this command is maximally general, and the generality is the test's design. A specific command tests obedience's precision; a general command tests obedience's willingness. Any cow would have discharged the order, which means the entire difficulty of the episode was manufactured by the receivers: the command's ease was total, and everything hard about it entered through the response. The order said *a cow*; the dialogue will end with a cow so specified that only one in the region answers the description — and the distance between those two points is the verse's moral geography.

**The Prophet's Refuge**

Moses's answer is not anger, correction, or argument — it is *istiʿādha*: *I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant*. The prophet treats the mockery-accusation as a contagion to be fled rather than a charge to be answered, and the refuge-formula reveals his diagnosis: to trade jest for jest, to meet derision with heat, is to join the *jāhilūn* — and the word in Qur'anic usage names far more than missing information. *Jahl* in this Book is a disposition: the settled preference for one's own way over known truth, the active state the prophets are warned against joining — *do not be one of those ignorant* is the address to a prophet grieving others' denial (6:35); Noah is warned not to ask *about what you have no knowledge of*, lest he fall into ignorance (11:46); Joseph prays to be kept from yielding *and falling into ignorance* (12:33). In all three the ignorance is moral motion, not cognitive lack — and the same word, in its social form *jāhiliyyah*, will name the entire pre-Islamic order of tribal insolence. Moses's refuge therefore answers the mockery-question at its root: you ask whether I jest; I seek Allah's protection from the condition that would make me jest with a command of Allah, or answer your jest in kind. The prophet models the only safe handling of derision aimed at revelation — neither absorbing its frame nor returning its tone — and the model became Islamic etiquette: the answer to *are you joking?* is not a joke but a refuge.

**Excessive Questioning Destroys**

The scene the verse opens is the Qur'an's case law for a principle the Prophet ﷺ stated as legislation. Asked, when Hajj was made obligatory, whether it applied every year, he declined the question three times and then said: *"Leave me with what I have left to you, for those who were before you were destroyed because of excessive questioning, and their opposition to their apostles. So when I command you to do anything, do it as much as it lies in your power and when I forbid you to do anything, then abandon it"* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337). The ḥadīth names the cow's questioners explicitly as the destroyed-people archetype — *those who were before you* — and states the mechanism: questioning multiplies obligation, and multiplied obligation breaks compliance. The man who asked *every year?* risked making Hajj annual by asking; the people who asked *what cow?* made their one-cow order into a unique-cow hunt. The ḥadīth's second clause gives the standing rule of Islamic legislation in its place: commands are to be fulfilled to capacity, prohibitions abandoned outright — the whole duty stated without interrogation, because interrogation is how duties grow teeth. The verse and the ḥadīth together fix the cow-episode's function in the sūrah: not an anecdote about one reluctant sacrifice but the founding precedent for how a community should receive its law — act on the general, ask only what action requires, and treat the itch to specify as the itch the destroyed peoples died of.
verses.68:
> They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”

**“Your Lord”: The Pronoun of Distance**

The question that opens the negotiation carries its diagnosis inside its grammar: *call upon your Lord* — *rabbika*, your Lord, not our Lord. The pronoun will stand unchanged through the whole exchange — *your Lord* in every question, three times running — and its consistency rules out accident. A community inside its covenant says *our Lord*; a community conducting business with its prophet about a command it has not accepted says *your Lord*, locating the obligation on the messenger's side of a line it has not yet crossed. The Qur'an's dialogue preserves distances exactly this way, and the exegetes hear the distance here: the questioners stand at arm's length from the command even while asking about it, treating the order as Moses's property to explain rather than Allah's claim on themselves. *Are you joking?* became unsayable once Moses took refuge; the same refusal now wears the vocabulary of inquiry — *call upon your Lord, ask Him for us, let Him clarify* — deference in form, deferral in function.

**Neither Old Nor Young: The Specification of the Middle**

The answer arrives with the divine formula attached — *Allah says* — and specifies age: *neither ˹too˺ old nor ˹too˺ young, but in between*. The two excluded terms are *fāriḍ* — the over-aged animal, past work and past milk, tough and spent — and *bikr* — the uncalved heifer, too young for the service. The commanded animal is *ʿawānun bayna dhālik*, a mature one between the two: in its full strength, neither declining nor unformed. The specification of the middle is the Qur'an's recurring signature of excellence, and the sūrah itself supplies the doctrinal parallel: the community of this revelation is made *an upright community* — *ummatan wasaṭan*, a middle nation — set between extremes to stand as witnesses over humanity (2:143). The Arabic *wasaṭ* carries both meanings at once: the midmost position and the excellent one, since the middle of a thing is its balance-point and its strength. Applied to the cow, the rule produces the best available animal — full of life, fit for sacrifice, neither a worn-out beast offered cheaply nor a calf offered prematurely. Applied to the soul, which the esoteric commentators do immediately, it produces the law of spiritual timing: Ibn ʿAjībah reads the specified age as the season of self-correction — the soul neither too old, its habits set and change grown costly, nor too young, feeling itself immortal and seeing no need. The command's first specification is thus also its most transferable: whatever is offered to Allah is offered in its middle strength, and the middle strength of a life is now.

**“So Do As You Are Commanded”**

The answer closes with a clause that is not specification but rebuke: *fa-fʿalū mā tuʾmarūn* — so do what you are commanded. Its placement is the verse's sharpest stroke. Allah has answered the question fully, and in the same breath redirects the questioners from asking to doing — the answer given, and the command to act on it restated, so that the clarification cannot become the ground of a further clarification. The clause is the divine version of the prophetic rule the ḥadīth legislated: leave me as I have left you; when I command, do as you are able (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337). And the sūrah's wider legislation names the danger the clause fences: believers are warned not to ask about matters which, once made clear, may distress them — questions whose answers convert latitude into obligation (5:101). The cow's questioners are living inside exactly that mechanism in reverse: they ask, and each answer obligates. The rebuke-clause is mercy offered at the first round — the door back to the cheap obedience still open, the original command still standing in full force under the new specification. That the questioners will pass through it and ask again is what turns the episode from instruction into case law: the verse records the last moment when *do as you are commanded* was the whole remaining task.

**The Soul in Its Middle Season**

The esoteric reading the verse invites is not decoration but application, and its structure follows the specification exactly. The cow to be sacrificed is the egotistical soul, and the age-rule is the rule of the work's timing. Too old: the soul whose habits have calcified, whose appetites have become character, for whom the knife of discipline arrives after the flesh has set — the change possible still, but at the cost the over-aged animal names. Too young: the soul that has not yet tasted consequence, that feels its days inexhaustible and its reform always postponable — the calf of a life not yet formed enough to have anything to give up. Between them stands the *ʿawān*: the soul in its working strength, old enough to know what it carries and young enough to set it down — and the sūrah's own middle-nation verse (2:143) confirms that the between-position is where Allah stations the communities He intends to keep. The reading also preserves the historical event's primacy, which is the rule of every sound esoteric reading of this recital: the cow was a cow, slaughtered in a wilderness camp, at the end of a negotiation that cost its conductors dearly — and the soul-rule rides on that event because the event is true. What the verse commands its first hearers to slaughter, it commands every later reader to identify: the animal in between, the season that is now, the obedience that grows expensive by the hour. *So do as you are commanded* — the clause spoken over a cow, standing over every middle season since.
verses.69:
> They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”

**The Beautiful Sacrifice Across the Scriptures**

The colour specification places this scene inside a wider scriptural pattern. The Torah's own cow-ordinance — the red heifer of Numbers 19 — specifies an animal by hue: red, without blemish, on which no yoke has come, sacrificed outside the camp and burned with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet, its ashes kept for the purification of those who have touched the dead. The two ordinances share their decisive marks: a cow defined by a specified colour, unblemished, unworked — and both connect the animal to death's pollution, the biblical rite by statute and the Qur'anic narrative by event, since this cow's slaughter will be joined to a murder case in the recital's close. The differences are equally instructive: Numbers files a permanent ritual law; al-Baqarah files a single commanded act embedded in a story about how commands are received. Neither text quotes the other, and the parallel's value is not source-criticism but theology: both testaments agree that the sacrifice offered for the gravest matters is a *specified* one — marked out, unmistakable, costly in its very definition. Islamic practice keeps the same principle in its own sacrificial law: the animal for the ʿīd is to be sound, unblemished, and the best within the offerer's means — beauty and soundness as the standing marks of what is fit to be given to Allah.

**The Definition of What You Love**

Read at its longest range, the verse states a rule about divine definitions. The questioners asked Allah to specify the object of their sacrifice, and the specification that arrived describes beauty — an animal intense in colour, pleasing to the eye, singular among its kind. The Qur'an elsewhere ties righteousness to exactly this structure: giving of what one cherishes, the love of the object being the measure of the gift (3:92). A sacrifice costs what its object is loved for, and the colour clause is quietly assembling a sacrifice of maximum cost — not because Allah requires expense but because the questioners required definition, and the defined is always dearer than the generic. The verse's pastoral transfer is direct. Every reader carries commands stated in indefinite nouns — give, forgive, speak, stop — and every reader knows the first question of the negotiation: specify for me exactly what, exactly which, exactly how much. The cow's answer stands over all of it: the more precisely you ask Allah to define the sacrifice, the more precisely the definition will find what you love. The bright yellow cow, pleasing to see, is not the Qur'an's description of a difficulty but of a gift — the kind of object worth giving — and the tragedy of the negotiation is only that its conductors reached that description by the expensive road.
verses.70:
> Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”

**The Third Question, and the Confusion That Grows**

The exchange's final question returns to its first's exact wording — *make clear to us which cow* — as if the two intermediate answers had never been given. Age specified, colour specified, the description now carrying marks no ordinary animal matches; and the questioners report the opposite of what specification should produce: *all cows look the same to us*. The verb is *tashābaha* — the things have become mutually similar, indistinguishable, confusable — and the report is the verse's central datum: information has accumulated and clarity has decreased. Confusion arrived as the fruit of their method: three rounds of interrogation conducted at a distance (*your Lord*, still, in this third question) have produced the epistemic state interrogation always produces when it replaces action — paralysis wearing the vocabulary of care.

**In Shāʾ Allāh Arrives at the Third Round**

The question ends with the narrative's first conditional formula: *then, Allah willing, we will be guided to the right one*. The phrase is the correct one — the Qur'an legislates it explicitly for every future-tense intention: *"And never say of anything, 'I will definitely do this tomorrow,' without adding, 'if Allah so wills!'"* (18:23–24) — and its arrival here, in the third round, carries the weight of its lateness. The exegetical tradition draws the inference directly: had the people coupled their first response to the command with *in shāʾ Allāh* — had they received the order with surrender instead of interrogation — any cow would have answered, and the negotiation would never have begun. The formula that makes asking lawful is the formula that makes acting possible, and the questioners discover it only after two rounds of its absence have cost them. The verse leaves the sincerity of the discovery open, and the openness is precise: *in shāʾ Allāh* can be the speech of submission or the idiom of a culture, and only the slaughter will show which it was. The narration's closing verdict on the whole exchange — that they slaughtered, but almost did not — suggests the formula arrived on the tongue before it arrived in the will. The conditional, spoken at the right moment, hands the outcome to Allah; spoken at the third round, it documents how long the questioners kept the outcome in their own hands.

**“We Will Be Guided” — to Which Guidance?**

The question's stated purpose is guidance: *then we will be guided to the right one*. The word is the Qur'an's greatest term — *hidāyah*, the guidance the sūrah opened by naming as its own content, the Book as guidance for the mindful (2:2) — and its appearance here, attached to cow-identification, is the verse's sharpest irony. The questioners use the vocabulary of salvation for the project of specification: guidance, in their sentence, means being shown which animal to buy. The narrowing is diagnostic. Guidance in the Qur'an's primary sense is directional — the whole of a life oriented toward Allah — and the command standing before these speakers was already guidance in that sense, complete and sufficient: *Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow*. To obey it was to be guided; the guidance was in the command, not in the cow's description. What the questioners seek is guidance's opposite in function — information without obligation, clarity purchased at the price of delay. The verse does not mock the word's use; it shows the word's demotion. When a divine command is received as a problem to be solved rather than a direction to be walked, the highest vocabulary the receivers have gets conscripted into the solving — *we will be guided* — and the guidance shrinks to fit the task. The sūrah's readers are left holding the distinction the questioners lost: guided to the right cow, or guided, in the sense the Book was sent for.

**The Adab of Asking**

The three rounds together compose the Qur'an's instruction on the etiquette of inquiry, and its positive model stands elsewhere in the same revelation. The disciples of ʿĪsā ask for a table spread from heaven — a request granted, but granted with the sternest conditional warning attached anywhere in the Qur'an: belief required, disbelief after the sign answered by a punishment unlike any other (5:112–115). The pattern across both scenes is constant: asking Allah's prophets to produce specifications and signs is possible, is sometimes answered, and always costs. The alternative the recital keeps filing is the believers' standing formula — *we hear and obey* (2:285) — the two verbs in their proper order, hearing completed by doing, with inquiry occupying the space action leaves rather than the space action needs. The distinction the verse installs is not between asking and never asking; Islamic law is built on questions put to the Prophet ﷺ and answered. It is between the question that serves performance — *how shall I do this?* asked by one already moving — and the question that replaces it, asked at a distance, in the conditional mood, while the command waits. The cow's questioners are the second kind's founding case, and their *in shāʾ Allāh* at the third round is the verse's mercy: the correct formula, arriving late, still carried them to the slaughter. The etiquette is learnable from their invoice: ask what obedience requires, couple every intention to the divine will from the first word, and remember that the field looks most uniform from the farthest distance.
verses.71:
> He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly

**The Nearest Cow Would Have Sufficed**

The tradition's summary of the whole exchange is a single prophetic sentence: it is preserved in the exegetical record that the Prophet ﷺ said, had they taken the nearest cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them. The sufficiency statement is legislation in miniature, and it generalizes into the rule the ḥadīth corpus states in full: *"Leave me with what I have left to you, for those who were before you were destroyed because of excessive questioning"* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337). The cow's negotiation is the destroyed-peoples archetype the ḥadīth names — the case study behind the rule. Its mechanism is now fully visible in the completed episode: a command received with general terms is cheap and sufficient; the same command interrogated acquires specifications, and each specification transfers cost from the law to the law's addressees, until sufficiency has to be purchased back at the market's ceiling. Islamic jurisprudence built its interpretive ethics on the counterfactual. The schools' standing maxim — do not ask into what your obligations could become — descends from this verse's invoice; the jurists' preference for leaving general texts general, and for acting on commands at their plain face, is the nearest-cow principle made method. The verse thus legislates twice: once in its narrative, showing the cost of interrogation, and once in its silence — the sufficiency that stood at the first word, unclaimed, while three questions assembled its replacement.

**The Unspent Offering and the Cherished Gift**

The completed portrait — unyoked, sound, unblemished, saturated in colour, pleasing to the eye — describes the most valuable animal the definition could construct, and its value is the verse's quiet claim about sacrifice. The Qur'an's rule of giving runs in the same direction: *You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish* (3:92) — the measure of the gift being the love of the object given. The cow's specification assembles exactly such an object: not the old beast past work, whose slaughter is disposal, but the sound one in its full strength, beautiful to look at, expensive to buy. Islamic sacrificial practice keeps the principle in its own rulings — the ʿīd animal to be sound, mature, unblemished, the best within the offerer's means — and the cow-episode is the principle's narrative filing: what is offered to Allah is offered from the unspent and the cherished, not from the remainder. The questioners assembled this offering without intending it. They sought specifications to postpone a sacrifice and received the description of the finest sacrifice their region contained; the stall produced the standard. The verse leaves the irony standing and draws its lesson: the object of obedience, fully defined, always turns out to be costly — which is not the definition's defect but its purpose, since the cost is where the offering becomes an offering.

**The Soul That Never Bore the Yoke**

The esoteric reading the recital invites completes here its most exact application.
