Ibn ʿAjībah's commentary takes the cow as the egotistical soul and reads each specification as the soul's required condition at the sacrifice: in its middle age, neither calcified nor unformed (verse 68); beautiful through goodness, the colour of a soul pleasing to its Lord (verse 69); and here — *not employed to till the soil or water the fields* — a soul never broken to the world's plowing, whose strength was not spent cultivating appetites and irrigating desires. *Wholesome*: free of the defects that bind — the crack of greed, the limp of attachment. *Without blemish*: no streak of another colour in its yellow, no divided allegiance in its surrender. The reading keeps the history primary — the cow was slaughtered in a wilderness camp by a reluctant people — and rides on the text's own choice of marks: the unyoked animal is an image the narrative supplies, not one the commentator imports. The soul's sacrifice, fully specified, is always *almost not* performed: the knife is easy and the readiness is the expensive item, which is why the verse ends where it ends — not on the portrait but on the flinch.
verses.72:
> ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed

**“Allah Revealed What You Concealed”**

The verse's closing clause is its theology in six words: *and Allah is the one who brings out what you were hiding*. The concealment is double — the killer hiding his act, the community hiding its knowledge, its suspicions, its complicities of silence — and the clause names Allah as the discloser of both. Nothing in the verse suggests the disclosure was invited: the camp disputed; it did not pray for resolution. The disclosure is divine initiative against a stalled human case, and the initiative states the principle the whole recital runs on: concealment is not a stable state before Allah. The sūrah has been filing the principle since its head — the One who knows what the breasts conceal, before whom the hidden and the manifest stand equal — and verse 72 is the principle enacted as narrative: a case with no witnesses, no confession, and no human route to truth receives truth from the only party who has it. The clause's tense is also precise: *mā kuntum taktumūn* — what you *were* hiding, the imperfect of a settled practice. The concealment had become the community's operating condition; the disclosure breaks a habit, not a moment. And the verse announces the disclosure while withholding its manner — the how of the case's resolution belongs to the recital's next movement, and the withholding keeps this verse's weight where it belongs: on the fact that Allah discloses, which is the fact every concealer in every generation is being told.

**Why the Murder Comes After the Cow**

The chronological order of events and the narrative order of verses diverge here, and the divergence is the Qur'an's pedagogy. In time, the murder preceded the command: the killing happened, the dispute arose, and the sacrifice was ordered as the instrument of resolution. In narration, the command comes first (verse 67), the negotiation fills four verses (68–71), and the case is disclosed last (72). The effect on the reader is exact: for four verses the reader occupies the questioners' position — holding a command whose rationale is undisclosed, watching a sacrifice specified without apparent purpose, sharing the camp's ignorance of why a cow. The disclosure at verse 72 then arrives for the reader as it arrived for the community: after the obedience, as its vindication. The narrative order by this argues against the order modern readers instinctively impose on commands — rationale first, then compliance — and files the divine order: compliance first, rationale after, sometimes long after, sometimes only at the end. The questioners' sin, read inside this structure, sharpens: they interrogated a command whose wisdom was not merely present but concrete, pending, and about to save their community from a feud. The verse's placement teaches every holder of an unexplained command where the explanation is: on the far side of the performance, in Allah's keeping, arriving when its arrival does the most good.
verses.73:
> So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand

**The Brief Return**

The reports converge on what the blow accomplished: the slain man, struck with the piece of the sacrificed cow, returned — briefly, bodily, lucidly — and named his killer, after which the body went back to its death. The tradition preserves the details with variations (the length of the return, the exact question put to the revived man, the identification's aftermath among the accusers), and the Qur'an's own text states none of them: the narration compresses the entire event into its principle, leaving the incident to the reports. The compression is deliberate and theologically exact. What the verse needs from the miracle is not its plot but its demonstration — that Allah gives life to the dead — and the plot's omission keeps the reader on the demonstration. The return's temporariness, which the reports agree on, matters for the demonstration's logic: this is not a resurrection unto life, like the raising of verse 56 that returned a community to its years. It is a resurrection unto testimony — the dead man restored for exactly as long as the truth needs a mouth, then released. The miracle's economy is perfect: the minimum animation that discharges the disclosure, no more. A God who needed to impress would have kept the man alive; the verse's God raises the dead the way the case requires and files the event as a sign rather than a spectacle.

**“Thus Allah Gives Life to the Dead”**

The verse's central clause generalizes the event into doctrine: *kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā* — thus, in exactly this manner, Allah gives life to the dead. The demonstrative *thus* does the argumentative work: what you have just been told is not one story but one sample, and the sample certifies the rule. The recital had already filed the rule's first instance on this community's own bodies — raised after death at verse 56 — and the Qur'an's wider catalogue stands behind both: the man of the ruined city, killed for a hundred years and brought back with his food unfresh and his donkey's bones reclothed in flesh (2:259); Abraham, shown the mechanism at his own request — *"Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste"* (2:260) — life reassembled from scattered parts at a call; ʿĪsā's commissioned sign, *I will heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead to life— by Allah's Will* (3:49); even the calf's animation, a handful of dust from the messenger-angel's hoof-prints cast on moulded clay (20:96). Across every filing the grammar holds: life is Allah's to give, to withdraw, and to give again, and the giving-again is no more difficult than the giving. The cow's fragment is the catalogue's smallest entry and its most forensic: resurrection demonstrated not on a prophet's question or a passerby's wonder but on a murder case, in public, with a legal consequence — the dead made to testify, the living made to understand.

**So That You May Understand**

The purpose clause names the sign's target faculty: *li-ʿallakum taʿqilūn* — so that you may reason, understand, use your ʿaql. The recital's purpose clauses have been graded: gratitude after pardon (52), guidance after the Book (53), mindfulness after the covenant (63) — and understanding after the resurrection-sign. The choice of ʿaql is exact, because the sign is an argument. A miracle aimed at awe would overwhelm; a miracle aimed at understanding reasons — it places a demonstrated case (this dead man lived again, visibly, last week) beside an undemonstrated universal (the dead will live again, finally) and lets the mind close the distance. The sūrah has been conducting this pedagogy since its opening charge that the Book's audience must use its reason, and verse 73 is the recital's clearest instance of a sign functioning as evidence rather than as power-display. The clause also rebukes, silently, the negotiation that preceded it. The questioners wanted certainty by specification — truth defined until it could be held without risk. The disclosure gives certainty by demonstration — truth enacted before witnesses, requiring no specification at all. Understanding, in the verse's usage, is what happens when a person lets a shown thing teach him; the whole cow-episode is what happens when a person tries to make a commanded thing safe before doing it. The sign closes the case and the case closes the argument: Allah shows, the shown is understood, and the understanding is the sign's stated purpose.

**The Valley That Greened**

The tradition preserves the Prophet's ﷺ own answer to the question this verse exists to preempt — *how* does Allah revive the dead? — and the answer keeps the demonstration's register. Asked the question directly, the exegetical record relates, he answered with a scene rather than a metaphysics: have you passed through a barren valley, and passed it again, and found it green? *Even so is the resurrection.* The analogy is the Qur'an's own standing one — the dead land revived by sent-down water, filed dozens of times across the Book as the visible proof of the invisible promise — and its power is that it asks nothing of the hearer but eyes already used. The verse's *thus* gathers both: the forensic raising in the wilderness camp is the demonstration, the greening earth is its repetition in every reader's reach, and the understanding the purpose clause asks for is the act of seeing the second in the first.
verses.74:
> Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**The Mountain That Would Have Crumbled**

The Qur'an presses the comparison to its limit elsewhere, and the limit convicts the heart outright: *"Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have certainly seen it humbled and torn apart in awe of Allah"* (59:21). A mountain — the largest, hardest, most immovable thing in the visible world — is posited as the recipient of this revelation, and the predicted result is humility and rupture. The hearts addressed in verse 74 received the same class of signs and remained intact. The premise of both verses is that creation is not insensate: the mountain at the theophany crumbled to dust while Moses watched (7:143), and the Qur'an states the general rule without exception — *"There is not a single thing that does not glorify His praises—but you ˹simply˺ cannot comprehend their glorification"* (17:44). Stones crashing down in awe are therefore not a poetic fiction but a disclosure: the mineral world lives inside a worship the human ear cannot parse. Against that background the hardened heart is not only unresponsive but counter-natural — the one creature in the verse's universe failing to do what rocks do, surrounded by a creation that fears, gives, and opens, holding the single exception.

**The Trunk That Wept for the Remembrance**

The tradition preserves the comparison enacted in the Prophet's ﷺ own mosque, and the enactment is the verse's standing proof. When the pulpit was built and the Prophet ﷺ left the palm-trunk he had been leaning on during the sermon, the trunk cried out — the ḥadīth of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī says it cried like a child — and he descended, embraced it, and quieted it, then explained: *"It was crying for (missing) what it used to hear of religious knowledge given near to it"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3584). Dry wood, in the presence's absence, grieving the cessation of remembrance — while hearts of flesh, addressed by the recitation directly, stay dry. The scene is verse 74 in reverse: the third rock's crumbling awe witnessed in a mosque post. It also answers the verse's unspoken objection — that stones cannot really fear, that the language is figurative. The Prophet ﷺ treated the trunk's grief as real enough to embrace, and the Qur'an's creation-theology says the same of every thing: nothing is outside the glorification of 17:44. The hardened heart of verse 74 is thus surrounded on every side by witnesses more responsive than itself — rivers from stone, fissures pouring, mountains humbled in hypothetical, a trunk weeping in fact — and the final clause closes the courtroom: *Allah is never unaware of what you do* (2:74), the audit running whether or not the heart feels it.

**Hardening Is a History, Not a Nature**

The verse's *even then* has a parallel filing that supplies the mechanism. Sūrah al-Māʾidah states the sequence flatly: *"But for breaking their covenant, We condemned them and hardened their hearts. They distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold"* (5:13). The order is causal and it begins with the human side: covenant broken first, hardening after. The divine hardening the verse names is not an arbitrary infliction but a settled consequence — the heart that repeatedly refuses becomes progressively unable, the way a joint repeatedly dislocated goes slack. Verse 74's placement confirms the reading: the hardening follows the cow's miracle, which follows the resurrection of verse 56, which follows the sea — a generation hardened *after* evidence, which is the only hardening the Qur'an ever indicts. Every sign received without response deposits a layer; the recital is filed in second person — *your hearts* — so that no reader watches the process as a spectator.

**Water and the Heart the Revelation Softens**

Against the hardness, the Qur'an keeps filing the counter-case, and its imagery is exactly this verse's: water and stone. The same sūrah struck the rock and brought twelve springs (2:60); the revelation's effect on receptive creatures is stated in Sūrah al-Zumar — the best message, a Book of consistent repeated lessons, *"which causes the skin ˹and hearts˺ of those who fear their Lord to tremble, then their skin and hearts soften at the mention of ˹the mercy of˺ Allah"* (39:23). Trembling then softening: the sequence of the third rock, run in a human body, produced by recitation. The comparison is total — what Allah's speech does to the God-fearing skin and heart is what the strike did to the wilderness rock, and what the mountain's hypothetical humbling (59:21) says speech would do to stone itself. The hardened heart of verse 74 is therefore defined precisely: it is the organ that received the same water and did not split. The verse's commentators connect the symbolism deliberately — water as the standing figure of life, from the sky (22:63), from under the earth (39:21), in human creation itself (21:30) — and set against it the lifeless heart. The closing clause then leaves the diagnosis in Allah's knowledge: He is not unaware of what hearts do with the water they are given, and the file remains open — the recital continues past this verdict, which is itself the mercy the verse's last word withholds from saying.
verses.75:
> Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it

**Taḥrīf: The Word for Corruption**

The charge names its crime with a technical term: the verse's *knowingly corrupt it* renders *yuḥarrifūnah* — they distort — from a root meaning to slant, to twist, to make oblique. *Taḥrīf* is the Qur'an's standing word for the mishandling of revelation by its custodians, and it runs as a thread through the Book: the changed word at the gate (2:59), the distortion with tongues that makes listeners think the twisting is from the Book (3:78), words taken out of context with *we listen and we disobey* substituted for *we hear and obey* (4:46), hearts hardened and words distorted as one paired consequence (5:13). The verse's specification is the aggravator within the family: the distortion happens *after understanding* and *knowingly* — this is not drift, mistranslation, or the entropy of copies, but informed misdirection by people who comprehended exactly what they were changing. The lexical root reinforces the picture: a slant is not a break. Taḥrīf keeps the text's body and moves its direction — the words survive, the meaning is rotated — which is why the crime is invisible to outsiders and requires the diagnosis only revelation can supply. The verse indicts a specific professional failure: custodians converting custody into manipulation, and it does so to an audience that includes every later custodian of any text.

**“After They Understood”: Knowledge as the Aggravator**

The circumstantial clause — *knowingly*, after they had understood — is the verse's legal center, and it repeats the sūrah's standing aggravation. Verse 42 forbade mixing truth with falsehood *while you know*; verse 44 charged the preacher who exempts himself *although you read the Scripture*; verse 59 filed the changed word at the gate. The consistent principle: the weight of a distortion is proportional to the understanding of the distorter. An ignorant error is corrigible by teaching; an informed corruption is a decision, and decisions are what the audit judges. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the full form of the crime: *"They say, 'It is from Allah'—but it is not from Allah. And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly"* (3:78) — the distortion completed by its attribution, the twisted meaning sold with the divine warranty attached. Verse 75's clause by this excludes every softening reading. This is not a text that grew obscure over centuries, not a tradition that drifted in transmission, not scholars honestly divided — it is comprehension followed by contradiction of the comprehended, which the Qur'an treats as the specific sin of custodians, and which is why the believers' expectation is being corrected: a party that corrupted the word knowingly will not be moved by hearing it again correctly. The argument they lost was never informational.

**Text or Meaning: The Tradition's Own Debate**

Islamic scholarship debated for centuries what taḥrīf historically was — alteration of the transmitted text or corruption of its interpretation — and the debate belongs to any honest reading of this verse. The maximalist position, epitomized by Ibn Ḥazm in the fifth Islamic century, held that the Jews and Christians actually changed the text of their scriptures, excising and inserting. The earlier commentators were notably less eager to claim this, and al-Rāzī's reasoning is the tradition at its sharpest: the prophecies of the coming Prophet could not have been physically removed from a text as widely distributed as the Torah, since excision at that scale would require a collusion of copyists across communities too large to conceal — so what shifted, he argues, was interpretation: texts requiring careful thought acquired, over time, a normative reading drifted from their intent. Al-Rāzī himself concedes the asymmetry — a less widely distributed text could be altered without detection. The verse's own wording inclines the balance toward his reading: distortion *after understanding* describes minds working on a comprehended text, and the companion verses specify tongues and context-shifting (3:78, 4:46) rather than erasure. What both sides agree on is the operative fact for the verse's purpose: by the Prophet's ﷺ time the received interpretation stood against the received text, and the custodians knew it.

**Do Not Grieve Yourself to Death**

The question the verse puts to the believers — do you still expect? — is one the Qur'an puts to its Prophet ﷺ in the same terms, and the parallels mark this verse as pastoral instruction before it is polemical record. To a messenger whose hope for his people was consuming him, the Book says that Allah leaves astray and guides whom He wills, *so do not grieve yourself to death over them* (35:8); and again: *perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message* (18:6). The grief named in those verses is the same appetite verse 75 questions — the sincere person's investment in an outcome that is not his to produce. Against naiveté: the case file exists so that each refusal is met with recognition rather than shock — the distorters of verse 75 have heirs in every negotiation, and the believer who knows the type is neither surprised nor broken by it.
verses.76:
> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”

**Two Rooms, Two Scripts**

The verse stages a scene in two rooms. In the first, the meeting: faces turned to the believers, the confession ready — *we believe*. In the second, the private circle: the same faces turned to each other, the counsel running the other way — *will you disclose to them what Allah has opened to you?* The architecture is hypocrisy in its literal sense, the double script of a community maintaining two truths and managing the traffic between them. The sūrah filed the identical pattern at its head, in its portrait of Madina's hypocrites: *"When they meet the believers they say, 'We believe.' But when alone with their evil associates they say, 'We are definitely with you; we were only mocking'"* (2:14). The echo is nearly verbatim, and its function is taxonomic: the verse is telling the believers that the double-speech they are encountering from some scholars of the Scripture is not a new species but the sūrah's third type wearing different clothes. The two rooms are also the verse's evidence-theory: a confession contradicted in private is not a confession at all but a move in a negotiation, and the Qur'an records both moves in one sentence so that the first can never again be taken at face value.

**“Do You Not Understand?” — Reason Conscripted by Concealment**

The counsel ends with the sūrah's refrain turned inward: *do you not reason?* — *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn*, the same rebuke Allah aimed at the scholars who preached righteousness and exempted themselves (2:44), quoted now by corrupters to each other. The quotation is the verse's irony at full voltage. The ʿaql-audit that runs through the recital — reason demanded at every station, its absence diagnosed as the root failure — appears here in the mouths of the audited, deployed not to find truth but to enforce silence about it. *Do you not understand* means, in the private room: do you not see the tactical cost of honesty? The word keeps its shape and inverts its function, which is exactly what taḥrīf does to texts (2:75): the body preserved, the direction rotated. The verse by this completes a pairing with its predecessor: 75 charged the distortion of Allah's word after understanding; 76 shows the understanding in active service of the distortion — reason running the concealment campaign, foresight budgeting disclosure. The sūrah's theology of intellect receives its negative case law here: ʿaql is a faculty with no moral guarantee, and its employment by a frightened conscience produces the most efficient hypocrisy — one that can argue for its own silence.

**What Allah Had Opened to Them**

The object of the feared disclosure is *mā fataḥa Allāhu ʿalaykum* — what Allah has opened to you — and the openings the exegetes enumerate define what the private room was guarding. The phrase covers the knowledge Allah gave them and made easy to them: the Torah's rulings; the descriptions of the coming Prophet lodged in their own text, whose disclosure would hand the Muslims their argument complete; the punishments their history had earned, whose recounting would let the believers say — as some traditions report the Muslims did say — that Israel's nobility before Allah was spent. Each candidate reading converges on one fact: the dangerous material was *their own*, revelation in their custody, and the believers' growing mastery of it was the crisis the private room convened to manage. This is the verse's connection to the sūrah's earlier charges — the signs sold for a paltry price (2:41), the truth concealed knowingly (2:42) — now shown in deliberation: concealment is not passive withholding but a governed policy, with councils, arguments, and peer pressure against the leakers.

**The Recitation of the Closed Door**

The verse's deepest work is done by its existence. A recitation revealed in the open, recited in the mosque, memorized in the market, quotes at length what was said behind closed doors — the counsel, its reasoning, its closing rebuke — and the first people to recognize the quotation's accuracy were the people quoted. For the believers of Madina the scene was evidence of a specific kind: the Prophet ﷺ had not attended those councils, and no informant could have carried their content in this compression; the recital's reach into the private room was itself the argument that its source stood outside every room. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān files the same exposure with the same anatomy — *"When they meet you they say, 'We believe.' But when alone, they bite their fingertips in rage"* — and draws the verse's general law: *Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart* (3:119). The two rooms are, before Allah, one room; the partition the conspirators built runs between themselves and each other, never between the scene and its Recorder. That is the verse's permanent edge for every reader: the counsel of closed doors is already transcribed, the disclosure they feared has occurred in the only forum that decides — and the believers' advantage in that forum was never information but the fact that they said the same thing in both rooms.
verses.77:
> Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal

**A Theme With No Exception in the Book**

The knowledge of hidden and manifest is the Qur'an's most ubiquitous divine attribute after mercy, and its ubiquity is the verse's warrant. Sūrah al-Naml states it in the same pairing: *"And surely your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal"* (27:74) — hearts specified, the seat of the private room named as transparent. The same declaration recurs across the revelation — Allah knows what is in the souls, knows the secret and the more secret, knows what the breasts conceal — in verse after verse the recital could cite (21:110, 24:29, 28:69, 33:54, 36:76). The divine names gather it: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted — the pairing that closes the sūrah's own verse of the Throne (2:255). The cumulative effect is a cosmology without interior walls: there is no category of the concealed that functions as concealment before Allah, and every human institution built on that category — secrets, cabals, double scripts, the managed disclosure of verse 76 — is built on a local fiction. The verse's question form (*do they not know?*) presumes the answer is available knowledge: this is not esoteric doctrine but published revelation, stated so often that ignorance of it is itself a choice. The conspirators of the previous verse knew it as text and forgot it as fact — which is the precise failure the question exposes.

**The Practical Atheism of the Private Room**

The question's target is not unbelief but inoperative belief. The men of verse 76 affirmed the Lord, the revelation, and the Day — their counsel quoted all three. What their conduct denied was the bearing of those affirmations on the room they were sitting in: a plan built to keep knowledge from Allah's witnesses, as if the witnesses were the whole jury. Islamic moral theology has a name for the structure — living as though the unseen were absent, the practical atheism of hearts whose creed is sound and whose calculations exclude it. The sūrah's opening had diagnosed the same condition from the other side: the disbelievers warned that a seal has been set (2:7), the organ of reckoning closed; verse 77 describes its softer variant, where the reckoning is acknowledged verbally and omitted operationally. The distinction the verse installs is between knowledge-that and knowledge-in-force: they know *that* Allah knows, and the question asks whether they know it in the way that reorganizes behavior. The answer their counsel gave is on record — a disclosure policy with no line-item for divine awareness — and the policy is the verse's indictment. This is why the question is addressed to *them* in the third person rather than as a rebuke spoken to their faces: it is diagnostic speech, filed for the believers' education, describing a condition the recital's audience is being inoculated against.

**One Attribute, Two Readings of the Same News**

The knowledge verse 77 announces is the recital's most double-edged fact, and its two edges are filed in the sūrah itself. Against the concealer it is threat without remainder: no strategy survives contact with an omniscient opponent, and the litigation posture of verse 76 — managing evidence before the Lord — is revealed as the one unwinnable case. Toward the sincere it turns as comfort with the same remainder: the nearness the sūrah will state in its own terms — *I am truly near. I respond to one's prayer when they call upon Me* (2:186) — is the identical attribute experienced from the other side. The heart's concealed prayer, the unspoken grief, the goodness nobody witnessed: all of it is known, which means none of it is lost. The two readings are not different doctrines but one fact meeting two postures — the hidden contents of a soul that fears exposure, and the hidden contents of a soul that trusts. The verse's placement between the exposure of hypocrisy and the recital's continuing audit fixes its function as the passage's ground rule: everything filed after it — the ransom, the distortions, the claims about the Fire, the covenant breaches to come — is evidence in a court whose judge reads the sealed file as easily as the open one. *Do they not know?* The question is the recital's standing invitation to move from the first room to the second, and to discover that there was only ever one.
verses.78:
> And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate

**Ummī: What the Word Carries**

The term — *ummiyyūn* — is doing careful work. In the usage the exegetes settle on, an *ummī* is one who cannot write, or cannot write well: the condition of the majority in a world where literacy was a trade. The commentators note the qualification honestly: literacy in Arabia, Jewish and Arab alike, was partial — some read and wrote fluently, some managed a rudimentary script, and the fully literate were a small fraction of the whole. A minority opinion attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word differently — a people acknowledging no prophet and no revealed book, called *ummiyyūn* precisely for that opposition to the Books of Allah — but the tradition itself marks this reading as unconvincing against the ordinary sense of the word. The term carries a second life in the Qur'an that makes its appearance here resonate: the coming Prophet is announced as *the unlettered Prophet* whom they find written in their own Torah and Gospel (7:157), and Sūrah al-Jumuʿah describes a Messenger raised *from among the unlettered* (62:2). Illiteracy in the recital's vocabulary is neither insult nor virtue but a condition — and the verse's illiterate are defined by it tragically: cut off from the Book by the very lack that, in another people, would make the Book's arrival among them the miracle it became.

**Amānī: The Lies and the Stories One Wants**

What the illiterate have instead of the Scripture is named in the Arabic *amānī* — rendered here *lies* — a word the tradition reads from two sides, and both sides belong to the verse. On one reading it means the reports they are told: their knowledge of Scripture is exactly what their scholars choose to say it is, religion received secondhand from the same class the previous verses convicted. The double sense is the verse's diagnosis in a single term: without access to the Book, the laity cannot distinguish what was transmitted from what was consoling, and the class above them, as verses 75–76 established, has both the means and the motive to blur the line. *Amānī* is scripture-by-rumor plus scripture-by-wish, and the illiterate hold it with full confidence and zero ground.

**The Corruption Chain, Top to Bottom**

Read in sequence, verses 75 through 78 describe a system, and the system is the verse's real subject. At the top: scholars who heard Allah's word, understood it, and distorted it knowingly. Around them: a private council governing what may be admitted in public, afraid of their own scripture's contents reaching rival hands. Beneath them: the illiterate majority whose entire religion is what the council permits to circulate — hearsay shaped above, conjecture held below. The flow runs one way: the literate manufacture the distortion and the unlettered consume it, and the consumer's inability to check is what makes the manufacturer's crime profitable. Accountability in the recital attaches at both ends of the chain — the verse files the illiterate's condition as culpable ignorance, the ignorance of those who took a religion on terms that made verification impossible by construction. For the young Muslim community hearing this recitation, the anatomy was immediate equipment: they were being told why the scholars of Madina would not simply hand their congregations the truth if it were shown them — the congregations had no independent access to the truth to begin with, and the custodians' position depended on keeping it that way.

**The Unlettered Nation and the Book It Cannot Alter**

The verse's irony completes itself in the community addressed. The Prophet ﷺ described his own people in the same term: *"We are an illiterate nation; we neither write, nor know accounts"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1913) — the ḥadīth's context is the lunar calendar, a ruling that fasting follows the seen crescent rather than calculation, and its self-description is exact: an *ummī* ummah. Yet the Qur'an's preservation runs through precisely this condition as its instrument. The revelation given to the unlettered Prophet was lodged not in manuscripts held by a class but in mass-recited memory — thousands of chests carrying the same text, generation upon generation, a transmission model in which the hearsay chain of verse 78 is structurally impossible: where every layperson carries the Book itself, no council can manage what the laity know. The contrast is the recital's quiet argument for its own audience. Israel's Scripture became, in the verse's description, a text the many could not check and the few could slant; the Qur'an answers by making its whole community the manuscript. The illiterate of verse 78 are pitiable and culpable at once — and the ummah hearing the verse is being shown, in the same breath, what its own unletteredness was arranged to prevent.
verses.79:
> So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned

**With Their Own Hands**

The phrase the verse builds on is physical: the Scripture distorted *with their own hands* — and the Arabic beneath the translation is more literal still, naming those who write the book with their hands. The emphasis is deliberate and it narrows the indictment to an act of production. Verse 75 charged distortion of a word heard; this verse charges authorship — hands putting ink where Allah put nothing. The phrase *with their own hands* strips the crime of every mediating excuse: not inherited error, not drift in transmission, not the entropy of copying, but original composition by identifiable people at identifiable desks. The exegetes preserve the historical forms the charge took: accounts of writings composed and pawned off on the unlettered for small profit, and the graver account — the alteration of the prophecies describing the coming Prophet, the very portraits lodged in the Torah (7:157) reshaped so that the descriptions would fit something else. The mechanism is the fullest form of the slant the sūrah has been tracking: first the meaning is rotated inside the text, then, when rotation is not enough, the hand writes a new page and the new page enters circulation wearing the old warranty. The verse's specificity is its universality: it is addressed to every age's forgers, and every age has produced candidates, inside every tradition that keeps its faith in books.

**“Then They Say: This Is from Allah”**

The writing alone is not the crime's summit; the attribution is. *Then they say, "This is from Allah"* — the manufactured page is issued with the divine warrant attached, and the lie acquires its full structure: not merely falsehood but falsehood sold as revelation. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the same act in the same terms and adds the aggravation: *"They say, 'It is from Allah'—but it is not from Allah. And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly"* (3:78). The theological gravity is in the direction of the lie. To deceive a person is to wrong a person; to speak in Allah's name without Allah is to enlist the divine authority itself as the instrument of the wrong, making God — in the eyes of the deceived — the sponsor of the fabrication. The buyer of the forged page does not merely hold an error; he holds an error he believes Allah guaranteed, which immunizes it against every future correction: to question the text becomes, for him, to question God. This is why the recital ranks the crime above the distortions before it. Distortion slants a truth still present; authored attribution replaces the truth with a counterfeit wearing omnipotence as its seal — and the counterfeit's victims defend it with the sincerity real faith deserves.

**The Fleeting Gain**

The clause of commerce supplies the motive and completes the indictment: the distortion is done *seeking a fleeting gain*. The forgery is an industry — composition, warranty, sale — and the Qur'an files it under the sūrah's running economics of the sacred, which began at verse 41 with signs exchanged for a cheap price and will recur wherever the recital weighs spiritual capital against worldly cash. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān joins the two crimes in one sentence: *"Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain"* (3:187) — the same custodians, the same covenant to disclose, the same small money on the other side of the scale. The phrase *fleeting gain* is the verse's own commentary on the transaction's arithmetic: an infinite authority, borrowed without right, liquidated for cash that will not outlive the seller. The tradition's historical gloss — writings sold to the unlettered of Arabia at small profit, the altered prophecies preserving a position and its revenues — keeps the motive concrete: this is not error seeking truth but truth's costume seeking income. And the price being paltry does not soften the verdict; it sharpens it. The recital's repeated astonishment is that the sacred is sold cheap — that hands which have touched the warranty of heaven settle for so little.

**The Standing Indictment**

The verse was revealed about forgers in Madina's Scripture-market and has never since lacked addressees. Every tradition that keeps its faith in texts breeds the verse's crime: fabricated reports composed for patrons, rulings purchased, histories written to order and warranted with the sacred name — and the Islamic tradition's own response to verse 79 is its proudest institutional achievement. The sciences built to police attribution — the criticism of transmission chains, the grading of narrators, the discipline that made a report's warrant a researchable object rather than an asserted one — exist because this verse exists: a revealed immune system against the forgery of the sacred, developed by a community that took the woe personally and spent centuries engineering the checks the illiterate of verse 78 never had. The verse by this reads in three registers at once: a historical indictment of specific hands, a permanent law of religious economics in which the counterfeit's price is always paltry and its woe never partial, and a standing instruction to every generation to keep the question verse 76's conspirators feared alive in their own houses — what Allah has actually revealed, distinguished by evidence from what hands have written and tongues have warranted.
verses.80:
> ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”

**The Parallel File in Āl ʿImrān**

The same claim is quoted again in the Qur'an, and the second filing supplies the diagnosis the first leaves for the rebuttal to deliver: *"This is because they say, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a few days.' They have been deceived in their faith by their wishful lying"* (3:24). Two additions carry weight. The deception is located *in their faith* — not beside it, not in politics or profit, but inside the piety itself, which is where a false assurance does its damage: the doctrine of numbered days did not merely misdescribe the hereafter, it reorganized a community's relationship to its own sins, making repentance optional and reform affordable. And the origin is named: *their wishful lying* — fabrication with a history, a doctrine built rather than received, which connects this claim directly to the economy of verses 78–79: the illiterate holding hearsay as certainty, the hands writing what tongues warrant as divine. The numbered days are the output of that machine — an *amānī*-doctrine in the full sense of verse 78, both a story told and a story wanted, the wish for a cheap exit from the Fire wearing the dress of a revealed schedule.

**The Two-Pronged Rebuttal**

The answer comes as a command — *Say* — and it is a disjunction that leaves the claim nowhere to stand. First prong: have they *taken a pledge from Allah* (2:80)? If the numbered days are a divine promise, produce the covenant — the document, the warrant, the moment Allah committed Himself to the term. And the prong carries its own trap: *Allah never breaks His word* — if such a pledge existed, it would indeed be honored; the rebuttal does not question Allah's fidelity but the pledge's existence. No scripture given to this community contains the term, and the community whose file the sūrah has been building holds a documented history of covenant-breaking from its own side (2:40 and 2:63 among them) — a party in default invoking a contract it never signed. Second prong: or are they *just saying about Allah what you do not know* (2:80)? If there is no pledge, then the claim is not a disputed interpretation but speech about God without knowledge — the epistemological crime the recital has been charging since verse 75, where distortion followed understanding, and verse 78, where conjecture replaced the Book. The disjunction is exhaustive and both exits are convictions: either you hold a covenant you cannot produce, or you are authoring eschatology without a source. The claim's advocates have no third option, and the verse's brevity is the confidence of an argument that knows its ground. The verse must be read with a precision the Islamic tradition itself drew, because mainstream Islamic theology does hold that some who enter the Fire eventually leave it. Third — the distinction on which everything turns — there is a difference between saying *Allah will not remove a believer from the Fire* and saying *Allah never promised to remove him*: Allah may act beyond His promises, and the absence of a pledge does not bind His mercy. The sin verse 80 indicts is therefore not the hope of release but the claim of a contract: the numbered-days doctrine is a self-issued covenant, and the rebuttal's first prong — a *pledge from Allah*? — is the permanent test of every cheap assurance in every age: release belongs to Allah's mercy, which He may extend; it cannot belong to a schedule, which no one can sign for Him.

**Saying about Allah What You Do Not Know**

The second prong outlives its occasion and becomes the verse's general law. *Saying about Allah what you do not know* (2:80) is the recital's formal charge against ungrounded theology — speech about God without warrant, the sin that sits beneath the forgery of verse 79 and above the conjecture of verse 78, naming in one clause the whole corruption chain's common root. The verse installs a rule of procedure for religious claims: assertions about Allah's dealings — His promises, His punishments, His terms — require a source from Allah, and where the source is absent, the assertion is not opinion but attributed lie. The pastoral transfer to the recital's audience is immediate and uncomfortable. Every religious community generates its numbered days: assurances of national exemption, calculations that cap the consequences of collective behavior, doctrines that let a people sin on schedule. The forms change — the structure of verse 80's claim is the structure of every "God would not punish us, His people, beyond this" ever preached. The rebuttal does not change either. If yes, produce it. If no, then know that the mercy you are counting on is real — 39:53 forbids despairing of it — but it is Allah's to give on His terms, not yours to schedule on your own, and the difference between hoping in an unbound mercy and claiming a bound one is the difference the verse's two prongs were revealed to draw.
verses.81:
> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**Residents, Forever**

The verdict itself uses the sūrah's standing eschatological formula: evildoers become *the residents of the Fire*, and they are *there forever*. The same sentence closed the recital's opening portrait of denial — those who disbelieve and reject the signs are the Fire's residents, there forever (2:39) — and its reappearance here ties the numbered-days claim to the denial it sprang from: the doctrine of a bounded Fire was a privilege claimed by people whose position the sūrah has already ruled on. *Residents* — *aṣḥāb*, companions, the people of a place, belonging to it as it belongs to them — is the verse's psychology in one word: this is not visitation but citizenship, and citizenship in the Fire is the fixed form of the character the two conditions described. *Forever* — *khālidūn… abadan* — doubles the permanence, and the doubling answers the claim's arithmetic exactly: against days numbered, duration without number. The justice of the formula reads through the encompassment: what the person built around himself in a finite life is made the shape of his infinite one, the enclosure he earned becoming the residence he keeps. The Qur'an's eschatology does not present the Fire as a caprice imposed on strangers to it but as the consummation of an encompassed self — which is also why the door the verse leaves open, in the word *encompassed*, has been the hope of every sinner who has not yet been closed over.

**The Verse in the Theological Wars**

Few Qur'anic sentences were argued over as fiercely in Islam's formative centuries, and the argument defines the verse's reception. Read maximally — *evil* meaning any grave sin — the verse became the Khārijī and Muʿtazilī proof-text: the unrepentant major sinner, they held, is the Fire's resident forever, the Muʿtazilah assigning him an intermediate station in this world and perdition in the next. The mainstream position read the two conditions together and refused the maximization: the evil that encompasses is disbelief and association, not the failures of a believer struggling inside his faith, and the Qur'an's own texts bound the reading. *"Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills"* (4:48) — the unforgivable named, everything below it placed inside the divine will. And the recital's own open door: *"O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins"* (39:53) — a verse addressed to the exceeded-limit people precisely so that no encompassment short of final rejection would be read as sealed. The mainstream synthesis keeps both edges: the believer's grave sin does not make him the Fire's resident forever, and no sinner may presume the mercy while continuing the earning — because the verse's terror is real, its conditions are exact, and the space between a lapse and an encompassment is the space repentance exists to keep open.

**The Anatomy of Encompassment**

The image at the verse's center — sin closing over its owner — describes a process the sūrah has already documented from the adjacent side. The hardened hearts of verse 74 were hardened *after* the signs, layer upon layer, each unresponded evidence depositing stone; the encompassment of verse 81 is the same accumulation seen from inside the water. A first sin is a wound; repeated, unrepented, defended, it becomes a habit; the habit becomes a character; the character becomes an enclosure — the point at which the person no longer has his sins but is had by them, and the verse's second condition is met. The tradition's moral psychology takes the image literally as diagnostic: a ḥadīth of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim pictures trials presented to hearts as a reed mat is woven stick by stick — every heart impregnated by them takes a black mark, every heart that rejects them a white one — until hearts sort into two kinds, and the engrossed state is reached not by a single enormity but by the refusal of many small breaches (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 144a). *Balā* overturns the numbered days, and the overturned claim's lesson survives in inverted form: there are no cheap schedules, and the only number that matters is how long the encompassment is allowed to continue before it is no longer possible to leave.

**The Audit of Earning**

The verse closes the numbered-days episode by installing its permanent law: the Fire is not a tariff but a wage, and wages follow work. The *kasaba* that opens the formula is the recital's whole economics of the self in one verb — every person earning, daily, the residence he will occupy, the sūrah having just indicted a community for earning its religion as revenue (79) and its eschatology as comfort (80). The encompassed sinners of verse 81 are the final case of the same principle stripped of its excuses: no forged warranty, no national exemption, no schedule — only the closed account of a self that earned enclosure and receives it. The verdict's symmetry with the promise the recital keeps beside it is the verse's balance for its audience: the same formula, the same forever, stands ready on the other side of the ledger for belief and righteous work, and the sūrah will file it immediately. For the reader under audit — and the recital addresses every reader as audited — the verse's function is to destroy the two false comforts it was revealed against. Against presumption: identity purchases no term, and no people has a pledge it cannot produce. Against despair: the encompassment is not the state of the struggling, and 39:53 remains open until the water actually closes. Between the two, the verse leaves the only ground the recital ever offers — the earning, today, in whichever direction the hands are moving.
verses.82:
> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

**Two Conditions: Belief and Work**

The formula's subjects are defined, like the verdict's, by a double condition: belief joined to good works. The pairing is the sūrah's standing definition of the saved — it opened the Book's own portrait of the God-wary, who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and give from their provision (2:3–4), and it carries the sūrah's first promise of the Garden: *"Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow"* (2:25). The two terms are joined in every instance because neither completes the formula alone: belief without righteous work is a claim the recital has just spent verses auditing — the confession of verse 76's meeting-room, true-sounding and empty in practice; work without belief is the charity of a heart encompassed by something other than Allah. *Āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — believed and did the ṣāliḥāt, the things that set right, the acts that repair — is Islam's shortest complete description of a human being in proper order: the heart anchored in the unseen, the limbs discharging what the heart holds. The verse's conditions are by this the mirror of verse 81's: against earning that encompasses, belief that grounds and work that rectifies; against a character closed over itself, a character open upward and outward, and the two characters receive their two eternities.

**Residents of the Garden**

The verdict's wording is reused and its change of object changes everything: *they will be the residents of Paradise* — *aṣḥāb al-jannah*, the companions of the Garden, the same word of belonging that verse 81 gave to the Fire. Belonging is the verse's psychology as it was the verdict's: the Garden's people are not visitors admitted on sufferance but inhabitants whose nature has been fitted to the place, as the Fire's residents were fitted to theirs. The sūrah has already furnished the residence — rivers flowing beneath the Gardens, fruit provisioned, purified spouses, and the standing clause of permanence (2:25) — and verse 82 files the title deed: this furnishing is not metaphor offered to console but estate conveyed to owners. The term *aṣḥāb* also carries the company its root implies: the residents of the Garden are each other's, a companionship the recital will elsewhere describe in mutual facing and conversation, the society of the saved as part of the salvation. Against the private room of verse 76 — conspirators managing knowledge among themselves in fear — the Garden's company is the same human need for one another, transposed into a house where nothing needs managing: what the two-faced community sought in concealment, the residents of the Garden have in open belonging.

**Forever, on Both Sides of the Line**

The closing clause is identical to the verdict's: *they will be there forever*. The shared eternity is the verse's answer to the numbered days, and it answers from the side of promise rather than threat. The claim of verse 80 capped the Fire at a countable term on the strength of an identity; the recital's actual doctrine removes the cap from both houses — the Fire's forever and the Garden's forever stand on the same grammar of permanence — and the effect on the reader is a single reorientation: nothing in the hereafter is temporary, so everything rides on which forever a life has earned. The permanence is also the verse's comfort in its deepest form, because the human grief the Garden answers is the grief of ending: every good the world gives is leased, and the lease's shortness poisons the holding. A Garden held forever removes the poison at its root — the sūrah's phrase *there forever* appears in its earliest promise (2:25) and returns here as the settled law, and the tradition reads the sequence as deliberate: the believer's smallest act inside the double condition is being stored against an unending balance, which is why the recital can ask a whole community to spend its wealth, its safety, its very selves (as verse 84 will demand of a covenant-people) without the arithmetic of loss ever closing. Forever on both sides of the line is the recital's way of making this life's every choice infinite-stakes and its every sacrifice infinite-return.
verses.83:
> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent

**The Charter of the Covenant**

With the eschatological interlude closed — the numbered-days claim rebutted, the two eternities filed — the recital returns to its central exhibit and quotes the covenant itself. *And remember when We took a covenant from the children of Israel*: the verse sets down the terms in the order a complete life requires them. First the vertical bond — *worship none but Allah*. Then the circle of obligation widening outward: *parents*, then *relatives*, then *orphans and the needy* — the claims of blood, of kinship, of helplessness. Then the whole of society in a single clause — *speak kindly to people*. And finally the two standing rites, *prayer* and *alms-tax*, the daily and the material disciplines that keep the charter in force. The exegetes recognize the list's genre immediately: it belongs with the Qur'an's great universal commandment-passages, the decalogue of Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:151–153) and the long ethical charge of Sūrah al-Isrāʾ (17:23–39), which the tradition counts among the *muḥkam* — the clear, foundational verses on which the rest of revelation stands. What is being quoted here is therefore not a tribal contract but the moral constitution of revealed religion itself, the same charter in every prophet's hand — which is precisely why its violation, filed in the verse's closing clause, indicts something deeper than one community's history.

**Allah's Right, the Servant's Right**

The charter's first term is its foundation, and the Prophet ﷺ once stated it as a paired doctrine of rights. Riding behind him on a donkey, Muʿādh was told: *"Allah's right on His slaves is that they should worship Him (Alone) and should not worship any besides Him. And slave's right on Allah is that He should not punish him who worships none besides Him"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2856). The covenant of verse 83 opens with exactly this right — worship none but Allah — and the ḥadīth supplies the reciprocal: the servant who keeps the first term holds a promise against punishment, the divine counterpart to the human obligation. The pairing explains why the charter begins where it does. Every other term — kindness, speech, prayer, alms — is a branch of the first; a kindness performed for social credit, a prayer offered to be seen, an alms given to purchase standing all fail at the root the root-term plants: that the act belongs to Allah alone. The sūrah's own theology of forgiveness draws the same line from the other side: association with Allah is the sin whose forgiveness He has not placed in the ordinary economy (4:48). The covenant is thus offered on a single non-negotiable condition, and its fivefold social and ritual elaboration is what that condition looks like when it is lived — a structure the recital now holds up against the record of the people who received it first.

**The Four Claims of Kindness**

The social terms of the charter are ordered by nearness, and the ordering is instruction. Parents first: the Qur'an honors them with a standing emphasis — the command runs through the Book in passage after passage (17:23, 29:8, 31:14, 46:15) — and the exegetes note that the duty binds whether the parent believes or not, pointing to Abraham's restraint with his unbelieving father (19:42–48) as its outer limit case; the prophetic tradition crowns the mother specifically, in the saying that Paradise lies at the mothers' feet. Then *relatives* — in the Arabic *dhū al-qurbā*, the possessors of nearness — the ring of blood whose claims the Qur'an files again and again beside the poor (2:177, 4:36, 17:26). Then *orphans* — the *yatīm*, classically the child whose father has died, the minor stripped of its provider and protector, whose case the Book legislates at length (4:3–10, 6:152, 107:2). Then *the needy* — the claim of want itself, owing nothing to kinship, resting entirely on the covenant. The sequence walks outward from the household to the stranger, and its moral logic is deliberate: kindness is trained on the near and tested on the far. A community that keeps the inner rings while neglecting the outer has not kept the charter, and a community that performs for strangers while devouring its own orphans has performed, not obeyed. The four claims together define the covenant's horizontal face — and the recital's audience is being shown what Allah considers the minimum furniture of a just community, in terms no one hearing it could call particular to any tribe.

**Prayer and Alms-Tax: The Ritual Seal**

The charter closes as the sūrah's own address to the believers closed at its start — with prayer and zakāh, the pair the recital has joined since verse 43, where the community hearing this history was told: *establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down* (2:43). The pairing is the covenant's machinery: prayer keeps the first term alive in the body's daily rhythm, alms-tax keeps the kindness-terms alive in the property's annual circulation — the vertical bond rehearsed five times a day, the horizontal claims discharged as an obligation rather than a mood. Whether read as command or as covenant-statement, the terms are identical, and their identity with the Muslim community's own obligations is the verse's silent transfer: the charter taken from the children of Israel is the charter taken from every people given a revelation, the same five terms in the same order — God, kin, the helpless, the tongue, the rites.
verses.84:
> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness

**A Covenant of Blood and Homes**

The recital moves from the universal charter to a specific bond, and the specificity sharpens the charge. After the five terms of verse 83 — worship, kindness, speech, prayer, alms — this verse quotes a covenant in two prohibitions: *that you would neither shed each other's blood nor expel each other from their homes*. The two protected goods are the most elementary a community has: life and dwelling, the person and the place the person belongs to. And the covenant's grammar makes both goods reflexive — *each other's* blood, *each other's* homes — so that the crimes it forbids are not crimes against strangers but against the self extended: the brother's blood is your blood, the neighbor's house is continuous with your own. The exegetes read the verse as continuing the account of the earlier Israelites, the covenant of the community's founding laid beside the charter of the previous verse — and the pairing is deliberate in its architecture. Verse 83 bound the community upward and outward, to Allah and to people; verse 84 binds it inward, to its own members, in the two things no member may take from another. A people whose charter is perfect but whose internal bond is broken has religion without community, and the recital is about to document exactly that condition — which is why this verse first fixes the bond's terms and, in its second half, its ratification.

**You Gave Your Pledge and Bore Witness**

The verse ends where a contract ends: *you gave your pledge and bore witness*. The double formula is legal language, and its doubling is the point — the covenant was not merely received but confirmed, and confirmed twice over. The pledge is the community's own act of binding itself; the bearing of witness, in al-Rāzī's and al-Ṭabarī's readings, is either direct attestation — we heard, we accept, we testify to this bond — or presence itself, the standing of the whole group at the event as its witnesses. Either way the effect is evidentiary: a covenant witnessed cannot later be disowned, because the disowning party is on the witness list. The recital's method of address presses the point home. *Your* covenant — the second person runs through the sentence, so that the pledge belongs to the community as a present fact rather than an ancestral event, and every generation that says *we are the people of that covenant* re-signs the witness roll in the act of saying it. This is the verse's quiet machinery for everything that follows: the coming indictment will not be arguing that the bond was unclear or unwitnessed. The terms were elementary — do not kill each other, do not expel each other — the pledge was given, the witnesses were the pledgers. What remains to be examined is conduct, and conduct against a witnessed covenant admits no defense of ignorance.

**The Group and the Individual: Two Ways to Inherit a Crime**

The verse's communal address raises the question the tradition faced directly: how can a later generation be bound, or indicted, by a covenant its ancestors ratified? The exegetical discussion distinguishes two inheritances. The first is passive implication — the way children suffer from parents' crimes, the way a household pays for its head's debts: a burden carried without choice. The second is active participation — and here the principle turns moral: where individuals glory in a group identity, holding its honors as extensions of the self, they expose themselves to the crimes attached to that identity as well. The boast and the burden are one package; a people that says *we are the chosen* has claimed the choosing and the chosen's conduct together. This is the mechanism by which the "sins of the fathers" pass justly to later generations — not by blood but by identification: the descendant who accepts the ancestral glory without repudiating the ancestral crime ratifies the crime, and his ratification is real because his acceptance of the glory was real. The verse's second-person grammar operates inside this logic. *We took your covenant* — the address treats the community across its generations as a single moral person, and the treatment is fair on the community's own premises: a people that remembers its covenant as *ours* has already merged its account with the covenant's.
verses.85:
> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do

**The Ransom Paradox**

The indictment's turn is its strangest feature: *and when those expelled come to you as captives, you still ransom them*. The same community that drove out its own now pays to free them — expel with one hand, ransom with the other, the crime and its expiation performed by the same people in the same war. The exegetes locate the verse's central question in precisely this contradiction: believing part of the Book and disbelieving part refers, on al-Ṭabarī's reading, to the clash between the expulsion — which violates the Book — and the ransom — which accords with it. The paradox is not hypocrisy of the simple kind but of an intricate kind, and its intricacy is what makes the verse's question so cutting. The ransom is genuine virtue: freeing captives stands in the Qur'an's own ethic among the highest acts — Sūrah Muḥammad legislates the treatment of war captives as release *by grace or by ransom* (47:4) — and the Prophet ﷺ made it a standing command of the community's duty: *"Give food to the hungry, pay a visit to the sick and release (set free) the one in captivity (by paying his ransom)"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5373). The verse does not fault the ransom. It faults the selectivity — a community that keeps the commandment which costs money and breaks the commandment which costs power, that honors the Book in the captive-market and tramples it on the battlefield, in the same week, with the same hands.

**Some of the Scripture, the Rest Rejected**

The verse's central question generalizes the case into a permanent category: *do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?* The wider sense of *kufr* the exegetes mark here is rejection and denial of specific truths rather than atheism of God — the expulsion and the alliances are hypocrisy and immorality enacted, and in the Qur'an's moral arithmetic such acts are inseparable from a measure of unbelief, because a truth one systematically disobeys is a truth one has functionally denied. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ will legislate the category in full: those who believe *in some and disbelieve in others* — the selective believers — are made disbelievers in truth by their selection (4:150–151). The mechanism the verse exposes is the treatment of revelation as a menu: the comfortable terms taken, the costly terms left, the selection itself performed by appetite rather than by the Book. And the selection is never random — it runs, in every age, along the line between commandments that cost money and commandments that cost power. The ransom costs money and was kept; the prohibition on expulsion cost tribal position and was broken. The verse's question is addressed to every community that keeps a Scripture, because every community that keeps one keeps it partly, and the partial pattern is legible the moment one asks which terms are honored and what each honored term costs.

**Disgrace Here, the Harshest Punishment There**

The sentence is doubled across the two worlds: *disgrace in this worldly life* and *the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment*. The worldly half is exposure — *khizy*, the shame of a community whose contradiction becomes public, its covenant-breaking visible to the very neighbors it made its allies; the recital itself is part of that disgrace, quoting the private arithmetic of expulsion and ransom in the open mosque for the city to hear. History ran the sentence to its letter in Madina's following decade, as tribe after tribe of the three lost its place in the city — the expulsion its own hands had normalized returning as its own fate. The otherworldly half carries the verse's distinctive superlative: not punishment simply but *the harshest* — a degree reserved here for the selective believers, and its logic reads back through the passage: one who never received the Book sins in ignorance; one who received it, ratified its covenant, witnessed it, and then rationed it has sinned against light, and the light aggravates the sentence. The closing clause returns the whole scene to the standing audit — *Allah is never unaware of what you do* (2:85) — the same sentence that closed the hardening of hearts at verse 74, framing this entire stretch of the recital: nothing in the two rooms, the battlefield, or the captive-market escapes the file, and the double punishment is filed against a crime the Judge watched completely.

**The Whole Book, or the Menu**

The verse leaves its audience with the choice its question implies, and the choice is the recital's demand on every Scripture-keeping community. Belief in the Book is not subscription to selected clauses; it is standing under all of them, including the ones that cost what the honored ones never touch. The Muslim community hearing the recitation was being vaccinated in real time: its own charter — the covenant of verse 83, the bond of verse 84 — contained the same costly terms, and the same wars, alliances, and exiles would come for it in its own generations, wearing the same justifications the verse strips bare. The ransom paradox is the verse's permanent diagnostic, and it works in both directions. Keeping the cheap commandments while breaking the expensive ones is selective belief condemned here by name; and performing the expensive ones as a cover for the cheap ones' violation — ransoming the captive the same hands expelled — is the aggravated form, because it dresses the rationing as piety.
verses.86:
> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped

**The Name of the Transaction**

Two sentences close the case the previous verse opened, and the first is a diagnosis: *these are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world*. The recital has reached the underlying form of every crime it has filed in this passage. The distortion after understanding, the two rooms' two scripts, the expulsion and the ransom, the covenant rationed — each is now named as one act wearing different clothes: a purchase. The verb is the market's own — buying and selling — and the sūrah has been building this economics of the sacred since its early verses: the signs exchanged for a cheap price (2:41), the souls sold for a price the sūrah elsewhere calls miserable indeed (2:102), the book written by hands and sold for a fleeting gain (2:79). Verse 86 states the general law behind the ledger: every sin against known revelation is a trade in which the Hereafter is the currency and the world's life the merchandise. The trade's structure explains the selectivity the previous verse indicted — the cheap commandments kept, the costly ones broken — because a trader selects by price: what the world pays for is bought, what it does not pay for is left on the shelf, and the shelf's contents are the covenant's expensive terms. The verse's demonstrative — *these are the ones* — points at a defined class rather than a moment of weakness: the people whose governing orientation has become the transaction itself.

**“Will Not Be Reduced”**

The sentence's first clause answers the passage's earliest false comfort with total precision: *their punishment will not be reduced*. The numbered-days claim of verse 80 had promised a schedule — the Fire's touch capped at a count; this clause removes not only the schedule but every mitigation below it: no reduction, no lightening, no gradation of the sentence once it begins. The two negations of the verse work as a pair against the two resources a condemned party reaches for — the sentence's intensity and the sentence's isolation — and the first negation binds the intensity. The exegetical discussion of verse 80 had carefully preserved Islam's actual doctrine: release from the Fire is possible for whom Allah wills, and intercession is real (11:107); al-Rāzī's distinction stood between a promise of release, which no one holds, and a possibility of release, which Allah has not closed. Verse 86 addresses the traders specifically, and for them the text is flat: no تخفيف — no lightening. The precision matters for the verse's justice. This is not the general metaphysics of Hell but the sentence of a defined class — those whose orientation became the trade of eternity for the world — and the unmitigated wording marks the class's defining feature: they already had the covenant, the witness, the charter, and the visible costs of every term. A reduction is a mercy applied to weakness; the trade of the Hereafter is not weakness but settled policy, and the sentence matches the policy's permanence with its own.

**The Trade Is Still Open — Until It Isn't**

The verse names a class and sentences it, and its pastoral edge is that the class has open enrollment in every generation, with the enrollment form the reader recognizes: the small preference of the immediate over the eternal, repeated until it becomes orientation. Every deferred prayer for a meeting, every dishonest word for a contract, every alliance kept against a commandment broken, every expulsion performed and ransom paid — the trade rarely announces itself as a sale of the Hereafter; it presents as management of this week. The recital's remedy for the trader is the recital itself: verse 86 exists to be heard mid-transaction, to name the purchase while the buyer still holds the goods and can put them down. The door the sūrah keeps open stands open here — *do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins* (39:53) — and its width is exactly the width of the trade's reversibility: what was sold can be renounced, the covenant re-signed, the orientation turned, and the class-exit is repentance, the one transaction the recital never caps. But the verse's two negations mark where reversibility ends: at the sentence. *Not reduced, nor helped* is spoken from the far side of the last opportunity, and its finality is the verse's mercy to the living — the trader who hears it while hearing still works is being told, in the plainest terms the Book has, that the counter closes, that the merchandise was never worth the price, and that the audit clause beneath every verse of this passage is running while there is still something the audit can receive.
verses.87:
> Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others

**Clear Proofs and the Holy Spirit**

The chain's final named link receives the verse's fullest description: *We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit*. The clear proofs — *bayyināt*, the things that make plain, that demonstrate — are read by the exegetes as the Gospel itself (al-Ṭabarī), or the miracles: healing the sick, raising the dead, quickening the shape of a bird (3:49), the announcements from the unseen — or both together (al-Rāzī). The holy spirit's identification runs in three streams: usually the Archangel Gabriel (Ibn Kathīr); or the name by which Jesus quickened the dead; or the Gospel — a reading al-Rāzī notes sits awkwardly with Sūrah al-Māʾidah's juxtaposition of Gospel and spirit as distinct gifts (5:110), where Allah recounts strengthening Jesus *with the holy spirit* alongside the Book and the signs. What the readings share, al-Rāzī observes, is the sense of life-giving: bodily quickening or the nourishment of heart and intelligence — the spirit as the divine instrument by which dead things live. The term's reach runs back to the first creation: the spirit breathed into Adam when Allah proportioned him (15:29), the same gift the sūrah's own verse of the Throne will name among what Allah keeps as His own (2:255's *the spirit, of His command*). Jesus, in this verse, is thus documented with the maximum equipment a messenger carries — Book, proofs, spirit-support — and the documentation is deliberate: the coming question will ask what a community did with a prophet furnished like this, and the furnishing removes every plea of ambiguity.

**Arrogance, Rejection, Killing**

The escalation is three steps and the verse compresses them into one clause: *you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others*.
