Second, the demanders never proposed their lists as satisfiable: the Quraysh's final clause — *even then we will not believe* — confesses the list's function, and the verse classifies the confession before it is made. *The same was said by those who came before* is therefore not merely a historical observation but a predictive law: the wording will recur, because the heart recurs; and the heart's recurrence means every generation's demanders are the archive's demanders, speaking its sentences, awaiting its answers.
verses.119:
> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**Sent With the Truth**

The verse answers the demanders of verse 118 not with more signs but with the mission's definition, and the definition opens with its warrant: *We have surely sent you with the truth*. The preposition carries both senses the tradition holds together — sent *in* truth, the mission's substance true, and sent *with* truth, the messenger furnished with it — and either sense answers the demand at its root. The demanders asked for direct speech and spectacular signs as conditions of belief; the verse declares that the condition has been met in a form they did not specify: a Messenger carrying truth. The emphasis particle — *innā*, We have surely — puts the sending beyond question: not a claimant's self-presentation but a divine act stated by its actor. The truth he is sent with is the recital's whole content — the signs made clear, the Book confirming what preceded, the guidance the demanders' hearts lack the certainty to receive — and the verse's placement makes the point structural: between the demand (118) and the disposition of the opponents (120, whose content the recital will file in its own place), the mission stands defined, complete, and independent of its reception. The truth's arrival does not await the audience's terms; the audience's judgment awaits the truth's arrival, and it has arrived.

**The Two Titles**

The mission's function is named in the paired titles the Qur'an gives its messengers: *a deliverer of good news and a warner* — bashīr and nadhīr, the two active participles that run as a fixed pair through the Book (6:48, 17:105, 34:28, and the prophetic catalogs beyond). The pairing is the revelation's two-handed delivery: one hand carries the promise — the gardens, the rivers, the no-fear-no-grief formula this sūrah has been filing — and the other carries the threat, the Fire and its residents and the sentences pronounced on the traders and the distorters. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ states the pairing's purpose in its completion-clause: messengers came *delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after the coming of the messengers* (4:165) — the excuse-removal that makes the mission's delivery total. Neither title alone accomplishes it: good news without warning invites presumption, the numbered-days comfort of verse 80; warning without good news invites despair, which the sūrah elsewhere forbids in the widest terms. Together they leave the hearer without shelter in either direction — the promise real, the threat real, the choice genuinely open, the excuse genuinely gone. The pair also defines the messenger's office against the demanders' expectations: they wanted a spectacle-performer and a voice from the cloud; the mission is a herald's office, and a herald's authority is his message, not his fireworks. The recital has watched both hands at work across a hundred verses, and the verse names the worker.

**Not Accountable for the Residents**

The verse's second sentence draws the mission's boundary, and the boundary is its mercy to the messenger: *you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire*. The exegetes note the clause's grammatical readings — you will not be questioned about them; you are not answerable for them; and, less preferred, an imperative do not ask about them — and the preferred readings converge on one ruling: the messenger's account covers delivery, not outcome. The absolution belongs to a family the Qur'an repeats at every station where the Prophet's ﷺ grief at refusal surfaces: *you are not responsible for people's guidance — it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills* (2:272); the consolation of Sūrah Fāṭir — do not grieve yourself to death over them (35:8); Sūrah al-Ghāshiyah's closing definition of the office — *you are not there to compel them* (88:22). The family's consistency marks a doctrine: guidance is divine property, refusal is human property, and the messenger stands between them as carrier — honored with the trust, exempt from its verdicts. The clause's wording deserves attention: the Fire's people are named *residents* — aṣḥāb, the belonging-term verse 81 fixed — so the absolution concerns people whose verdict is already characterized, and the messenger is released from accountability for a sentence he did not author and cannot repeal. The recital had prepared the same lesson for its wider audience at verse 75, correcting the believers' expectations of their interlocutors; here the correction is addressed to the correction's own first holder — the one whose sincerity made every refusal cost him most.
verses.120:
> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**A Satisfaction With One Condition**

The verse states a categorical impossibility in the grammar of never: *never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith*. The particle combination — *lan* with the *until*-clause — produces the verse's precise claim: the displeasure is permanent, and its terminus is a single condition, the Messenger's adoption of the objectors' religion. The exegetes confirm that the verse ratifies the reading of the passage before it: the demands of verse 118 were taunt rather than inquiry (al-Qushayrī's note), because a demand whose satisfaction is defined as the demanders' conversion of the answerer was never a demand for evidence. Al-Thaʿlabī supplies the historical texture — the qibla's turn from Jerusalem to the Kaʿbah had generated resentment among both communities, and truce-proposals functioned as delaying tactics aimed at turning the Prophet ﷺ from his course — which shows the condition operating in live negotiation: concessions offered, alliances dangled, satisfaction promised, all indexed to one non-negotiable surrender. The verse's insight into negotiation deserves its full statement. Ordinary disputes have settlement points — interests traded, positions adjusted, partial satisfactions built. The dispute this verse describes has no settlement point short of total conversion, because the displeasure is not about terms but about the Messenger's existence as Messenger: a truth received from Allah is precisely what the condition demands he cease to hold. Against such a condition, every concession is waste and every partial agreement is purchase of time for the other side — which is why the verse's answer is not a counter-proposal but a definition.

**Millah: The Word for a Community's Way**

The condition's object — *their faith* — translates *millah*, and the word's range shapes the verse's claim. Millah is not bare belief but the religious law, the way that defines a community: the term the Qur'an uses across a dozen stations for the total pattern of a tradition — the millah of Abraham, upright and unaffiliated with the later communities (2:135's context, 3:95, 4:125, 16:123, and the prophetic confessions from Noah's ship to Joseph's prison, 7:88, 12:37, 14:13, 18:20, 22:78, 38:7). To follow a millah is to enter a community's whole order — its law, its direction of prayer, its definition of the righteous past. The verse's condition is therefore maximal in its wording: not adjustment of some rulings, not adoption of some practices, but entry into the way as way. The maximality exposes the condition's function. A demand that could be met partially would be a negotiating position; a demand that can only be met totally is a statement that no negotiation is intended. And the two named communities' mills, in the recital's account, share the feature that makes the condition impossible for a Messenger: each is defined in part by the rejection of what comes after its own scripture — the exclusivism the recital quoted at verse 111, the *none will enter except us* that verse 121's following-logic dismantles from within. The Messenger asked to follow either millah is asked to follow a way whose own logic denies his standing — the condition contains its own refusal, which is the verse's first proof that the plea for satisfaction was never sincere.

**The Impossible Conditional**

The verse's third sentence takes the form of a hypothetical addressed to the one person for whom it is impossible: *if you were to follow their desires after all the knowledge that has come to you*. The conditional's addressee is the Messenger ﷺ, whose following of desire after knowledge is excluded by the office the recital has defined — and the impossibility is the sentence's method. The Qur'an's rhetoric repeatedly legislates to the community through address to its head: the case stated at its maximum clarity, in the person least able to fulfill it, so that the law's severity lands undiminished on everyone for whom fulfillment is possible. The clause's terms carry the sūrah's standing aggravation. *Their desires* — ahwāʾ, the whims and appetites, the same word-family the recital contrasted with knowledge since verse 75: following desire after understanding is the named structure of informed corruption. *After the knowledge that has come to you* — the aggravator in its exact form: not ignorance but post-knowledge reversal, the sin the whole passage has been prosecuting. And the consequence clause states the reversal's total cost: *there would be none to protect or help you against Allah* — the walī and naṣīr vocabulary of verse 107, the patronage-monopoly declared there, now applied as the defector's sentence. Sūrah al-Māʾidah legislates the same prohibition to the office in the same terms: judge by what Allah has revealed, *and do not follow their desires over the truth that has come to you* (5:48). The two verses together make the conditional a law rather than a warning: for every holder of knowledge, the following of another's desire over received truth forfeits the divine protection that knowledge was held under — and the forfeiture is total, because the protection had no second source.
verses.121:
> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**Following as the True Recitation**

The verse defines the Book's real readers, and the definition turns on a verb with a double root-sense that the exegetes exploit deliberately. *Yatlūnahu* — they recite it — comes from *talā*, which carries both recitation and following: to recite the Book and to follow it are, in the word's own structure, one act seen from two sides. Many of the commentators prefer the following-sense as the verse's operative meaning — those who follow the Book *as it should be followed* — and the preference is doctrinal rather than merely lexical. Recitation without following is the performance the passage behind this verse has been prosecuting: the hearers-and-disobeyers of verse 93, the reciters whose Scripture testified against their conduct. Following gives the verse's standard its content: to follow the Torah properly, al-Ṭabarī specifies, is to abstain from what it forbids and partake of what it allows — the Book's permissions and prohibitions taken as operative law rather than inherited text. Al-Rāzī adds the interior condition: proper recitation is done with humility, the reader's posture matching the text's claim. The verse by this installs a three-layer standard — read, obey, revere — and makes belief in the Book a function of all three: *it is they who truly believe in it*. Belief is not assent beside the Book but the Book's own operation in a life, and the verse's first sentence is the recital's answer, in positive form, to everything the hundred verses before it filed in negative: the distortion, the rationing, the casting behind backs all failed the same standard this verse states.

**Who Holds the Book Here**

The subject's identification runs in two directions in the exegetical tradition, and both belong to the verse's design. Al-Ṭabarī records the reading that takes *those We have given the Book* as the Muslim believers — the community holding the Qur'an, reciting-and-following it as it should be — and the reading that takes them as the learned among the Jews who follow the Torah faithfully, the remnant the recital keeps sighting at every station. The double reference is not confusion but the verse's method: the standard it states is Book-generic, and every community of a Book is measured by it, so the subject-phrase denotes whoever actually meets the standard — the Muslim follower of the Qur'an and the Jewish follower of the Torah alike, and only them. Sūrah al-Māʾidah supplies the same division inside one community: *had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provision from above and below — some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil* (5:66). The uprightness-and-evil split is the verse's two classes restated: the following few and the rejecting many, divided not by affiliation but by conduct toward the held text. The reading's consequence for the Madinan moment is precise: the verse is not a blanket transfer of election from one people to another but the installation of a criterion that cuts through every people — and the community hearing it inherits the criterion along with the promise, since *those We have given the Book* includes them from the moment the Book was given.

**The Torah That Leads Onward**

The tradition draws the standard's sharpest consequence for the verse's historical subjects, and the consequence runs through the Torah's own content. To follow the Torah as it should be followed is, on al-Ṭabarī's reading, ultimately to follow the Prophet ﷺ — because the Torah demands it: the unlettered Messenger whose description its holders *find written in their Torah and the Gospel*, whom they are commanded to honor, support, and follow (7:157). The logic is the confirmation-argument the recital has been running since verse 89: a Book truly followed leads its follower to whatever the Book itself testifies to, and a testimony refused is proof that the Book is not being followed but used. The converse completes the circle — to reject the confirmed Messenger is to reject the confirming Torah, since the rejection contradicts the text the rejecter claims to hold. Sūrah al-Māʾidah states the obligation from the Gospel's side in the same grammar: *let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it — and those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are truly the rebellious* (5:47). The verse's two classes thus sort themselves by a single test available to both communities: does your following of your Book carry you to the truth your Book announces? The followers whom verse 121 pronounces believers are, on this reading, the scholars of Israel who followed their Torah into the mosque of Madina — and the recital's audience knew such people by name, the converts whose faith the verse vindicates against both their former community's taunts and any believer's suspicion.
verses.122:
> O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others

**The Refrain Returns**

The verse is a return, and the return is its meaning. Seventy-five verses earlier, the sūrah opened its address to this community with nearly the same sentence: *O Children of Israel! Remember all the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others* (2:47). The two verses are twins in wording and function, and their placement marks the architecture of the recital's longest movement: the address to Israel begins at verse 40 with the covenant-call, states the twin commands of remembrance and preference at verse 47, files a hundred verses of record — the charter, the witnessed bond, the contradiction in Madina's wars, the trade, the covered hearts, the rejected Messenger, the demands, the never-pleased condition — and closes at verse 122 with the twin commands repeated word for word. The structure is an inclusio, the rhetorical frame that seals a section by restating its opening, and the sealing is deliberate: the movement that began with *remember* ends with *remember*, so that everything filed between the two stands enclosed inside the command. The repetition also does the work only repetition can do. The first hearing came before the record; the second comes after. The community addressed at verse 47 had been asked to remember before the recital enumerated what was to be remembered; the community addressed at verse 122 hears the same command with the enumeration complete — every favor re-filed, every breach documented, every excuse answered. The refrain's return is therefore not redundancy but summation: the same two clauses, now carrying a hundred verses of evidence inside them.

**Honoured Above the Others**

The second clause restates the preference whose meaning the movement has spent a hundred verses correcting: *how I honoured you above the others*. The honoring — *tafḍīl*, the preferment — is stated at verse 47 and repeated here without qualification, because the qualification is the record between the two statements. The preferment was real: messengers from within the community, Scripture in its custody, favors no contemporary people received in such number. And the preferment's meaning was operational, not ontological — election to a covenant whose terms the recital quoted in full (83), a bond witnessed (84), and a practice that violated both. The misuse the movement documented ran in three directions, and the refrain's return closes all three: the preferment read as exemption — the numbered days of the Fire (80), the death-wish challenge's exclusive paradise (94); read as monopoly — the *none will enter except us* of verse 111, classified there as desires; and read as identity-sufficiency — *we believe only in what was sent down to us* (91), answered by the killing of their own prophets. The honoring was a trust with tasks: worship none but Allah, kindness to the four rings, the goodly word, the prayer and alms — and the second hearing of the clause, after the tasks' documented refusal, carries the correction inside the repetition. The verse does not withdraw the honor; the recital nowhere says the favors were taken back. It re-files the honor at the close of the evidence, which leaves it standing in its only sustainable sense: a historical preferment for a covenant's service, held by a people the service defined, and lost wherever the service was refused — the remnant excepted, as always, the few whose honoring and whose honoring-keeping were one fact.
verses.123:
> And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given

**The Twin Verse and the Frame's Second Edge**

This verse is the recital's second filing of the same eschatology, and the twin's existence is the frame's construction. Verse 48 stated it at the movement's opening: *guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another — no intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given*. Verse 123 states it at the movement's close with the same four negations and one variation of order: ransom now precedes intercession, where the opening verse placed intercession first. The variation is small and its effect is real. At the section's opening, the sequence moved from mediation to price; at its close, the price leads — and the closing position lands after a hundred verses in which ransom figured as a live communal practice: the tribes ransoming the captives their own hands had expelled (85), the ransom-paradox indicted as selective belief, the market of souls sold and bought running through the movement's whole economics. The Day on which *no ransom will be taken* is thus filed, at the frame's second edge, against the community that treated ransom as its characteristic virtue and its characteristic evasion at once. The inclusio the twin verses build encloses the Israel-movement inside one eschatological fact: whatever the record contains — favors, breaches, trades, ransoms, excuses — the section begins and ends at a Day where none of the record's social instruments function. The frame is the movement's interpretive key, and the key says: everything filed between these two verses was filed under a jurisdiction whose courtroom admits no representative.

**Intercession and Its Permission**

The verse's unconditional negation of intercession must be read against the Qur'an's full doctrine, and the full doctrine is its qualification rather than its contradiction. Intercession exists in the recital's eschatology — but as permission, never as right: the sūrah's own verse of the Throne will state the condition in its question-form, asking who can intercede with Him *except by His permission*, and the qualification runs through the Book wherever intercession appears. The verse here negates the intercession the claimants assumed: the automatic mediation of ancestors, the patron-saints' standing credit, the community's collective merit cashed for its members — intercession as a social route operating on the Day the way patronage operated in the world. That route is closed absolutely, and its closing is the verse's target: the same assumption the numbered-days doctrine made (80), the same reliance on ancestral standing the preferment-claim carried (111, 122). Where Allah grants intercession by permission — as the tradition's intercession-reports describe for the Fire's believing inhabitants — the grant is divine mercy exercised, not a debtor's right collected, and the distinction is the verse's whole point. The Day takes no ransom and accepts no intercession *from the case's own resources*; what arrives by the Judge's permission is not the case's resource but the Judge's gift. The verse therefore does not legislate despair — the recital keeps 39:53's open door standing — but it destroys the two false comforts the movement's defendants actually held: the tariff purchased by lineage, and the advocate retained by affiliation.

**The Individualism of the Day**

Beneath the four negations runs the verse's positive doctrine, and the doctrine is the individual soul's arrival alone. *No soul will be of any help to another* — the nafs, the self, is the Day's only unit of account, and the verse's grammar enforces the singularity: soul to soul, each carrying what each sent. The doctrine answers, in one clause, the movement's central error: every form of collective assurance the recital prosecuted — the national Fire-tariff, the ethnic paradise-monopoly, the *what was sent down to us* loyalty, the preferment read as property — assumed that group membership transmits standing across persons. The Day is defined as the jurisdiction where transmission fails: no soul's righteousness flows to another's account, no soul's ancestry modifies another's sentence, no group's file is opened for its members. The recital has been building this individualism from its own earlier stations: the engrossed sinner of verse 81 earning his residence personally, the formula of verse 82 keyed to whoever believes and does good, the sending-economy of verse 110 filing every good under its sender's own name. Verse 123 states the individualism as eschatological law, and the law's edge runs against every reader's default: the human instinct to arrive represented — by family, by community, by saint, by the merits of the dead — is the instinct the four negations dismantle, clause by clause. What survives the dismantling is the verse's actual demand: a soul that has made its own provision, because on the Day named, provision made by anyone else is not transferable, and provision made by transfer was never provision at all.
verses.124:
> ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”

**The Patriarch Begins With a Test**

The recital turns from the Children of Israel to their covenant's root, and the first fact it files about the patriarch is not his lineage, his calling, or his vision but his examination: *when Abraham was tested by his Lord with commandments, which he fulfilled*. The verb — *ibtalā* — is the trial-verb, the testing of a person against a demand whose weight is real; the object — *kalimāt*, words — the exegetes read as the commands themselves, the divine words that arrived as tasks. The text specifies none of them, and the silence is the verse's first teaching: the itemization matters less than the fulfillment, and the recital records the patriarch's standing not by cataloguing his trials but by certifying their completion. The test-first structure also answers, in advance, the theology the previous section closed against. The honor the Children of Israel claimed as possession (122) is shown here in its actual form: precedence earned through examination, the favored man favored *after* the commands were fulfilled. Sūrah al-Najm states the certification in its own compact line — *and Abraham, who perfectly fulfilled his covenant* (53:37) — and the two verses together give the patriarch's file its header: tested, fulfilled, certified. The office that follows in the verse is granted onto that record, not before it.

**What the Words Were**

The commentators differ widely over the commandments' content, and the spread of their readings maps the patriarch's whole received legacy. One stream takes the words as commands instituting bodily purity — the grooming, cleansing, and ritual disciplines the tradition traces to Abraham, including the practices of natural fitness the Sunnah preserves. A second stream reads them as the rites of the pilgrimage: the circumambulation of the House, the running between Ṣafā and Marwah, the stoning of the pillar — the ḥajj in its full apparatus, which Muslims consider Abrahamic in origin, instituted at this station. A third takes the words as trials of suffering rather than statutes: the circumcision undertaken in old age, the sacrifice of the son (37:102's scene), and the fire his people built for him — the fire answered by the command the sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ preserves: *O fire! Be cool and safe for Abraham!* (21:69). The three streams are not rivals so much as strata: purity-commands, pilgrimage-rites, and survival-trials together compose the patriarch's received biography, and each stream's evidence is textual within the larger Qur'an. The weighing the verse itself supplies is structural — it reports the testing and the fulfillment without adjudicating the list, which tells the reader where the emphasis belongs: whatever the words were, they were completed, and the completion is what the office is built on.

**The Tested Pattern as Inheritance**

The verse's transfer is in the office's nature. An imām is followed, and what Abraham's imāmah makes followable is the tested pattern: commands received, commands fulfilled, appointment granted, concern for the line answered with a moral condition. Sūrah al-Furqān preserves the pattern as every believer's prayer — *our Lord, grant us pious spouses and offspring, and make us models for the righteous* (25:74) — the imāmah-words turned into supplication, the office opened to whoever prays for it on its terms. The recital's audience — a community two generations old, already generating its own claims of precedence — received in this verse the constitution of religious authority as Islam holds it: leadership earned under examination, conferred by Allah, inherited only by the righteous, and measured at every generation against the man who fulfilled. The children of the covenant, hearing their own file closed at verse 123, now hear its root opened at verse 124 — and the opening sentence tells them, and every later claimant, that the covenant's first holder got it by passing a test, and keeps it by the answer given to his question about his children.

At the third, it is simply information: not all of Abraham's descendants will be virtuous — a fact Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt states outright: *We blessed him and Isaac as well. Some of their descendants did good, while others clearly wronged themselves* (37:113).
verses.125:
> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

**The Standing-Place of Abraham**

Between the two institutions stands a specific commandment: *take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer*. The maqām — the standing-place — is identified in the tradition first as the physical station: the stone near the Kaʿbah said to bear Abraham's footprint, held in its enclosure beside the House to this day. The exegetes record wider readings — the maqām as the ḥajj-rites in their entirety, or as the pilgrimage's other stations, ʿArafāt, Minā, Muzdalifah — and the readings share a claim: whatever Abraham stood on or stood for in the House's service is consecrated as prayer-ground. The tradition preserves the commandment's occasion in two accounts. In one, the Prophet ﷺ took ʿUmar by the hand at the stone and said, *this is the standing-place of Abraham*; ʿUmar asked, *shall we take it as a place of prayer?*; the Prophet ﷺ answered that he had not been commanded to — and before the day's sunset the verse descended with the command. In the account ʿUmar himself narrated, preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, he wished aloud to the Prophet ﷺ, *I wish we took the station of Abraham as our praying place* — and the revelation came: *and take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 402), one of the three matters in which ʿUmar reported his Lord agreed with him. The two accounts differ in who spoke first, and the difference is immaterial to the verse's fact: the prayer-site at the patriarch's stone is legislated here, in a form — *you may take* — that some exegetes read as imperative and others as declarative, the community's practice settling the reading. The stone's function completes the verse's Abrahamic architecture: the imām of verse 124 leaves a footprint, and the footprint's place becomes the community's prayer-ground — leadership followed literally, at the point of standing.

**“Purify My House”**

The verse's second half records the charge laid on the builders: *We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House*. The covenant-verb — *ʿahidnā* — makes the purification a commissioned trust, and al-Ṭabarī specifies the content: cleansing the House from idolatry and from doubt. The two objects of purification define the masjid's negative and positive conditions — no false object of worship inside it, no false posture of heart toward it — and the charge's tense carries its history: for Abraham, purification meant maintaining the House in the state it was instituted in, a standing custodianship; the tradition then records the custody's long erosion, the idols' arrival, and the restoration — the Prophet ﷺ returning the House to its Abrahamic condition at the conquest, the charge fulfilled a second time by the descendant of its first trustees. The purification-clause also binds this verse to verse 114 with a knot the recital ties deliberately: the House's existence is for the circlers, the meditators, the bowing and prostrating — and whoever fills it with anything else, or bars anyone from these, is charged with the ruin the earlier verse sentenced. *My House* — the possessive is the clause's warrant: the purification standard is not the trustees' preference but the Owner's purpose, and the purpose is named in the three classes the charge serves.

**Father and Son, Jointly Entrusted**

The charge names two trustees, and the second name is the verse's argument to its audience: *Abraham and Ishmael*. The patriarch of verse 124 and the son whose line the Arabian hearers claimed are joined in one custodianship — the House built and purified by both, its covenant held by both, its prayer-ground marked by one and legislated for all. The joint trusteeship does precise polemical work in the recital's Madinan moment. The Israelite claim ran through Isaac's line exclusively; the Arabian claim ran through Ishmael's; the verse files the House as the two brothers' common work, under their common Father's God, which makes the House older than the division and superior to both claims. The purification-charge addressed to both also states the recital's covenant-law from verse 124 in operative form: the office descends through righteousness held jointly, not through lineage held exclusively — and the wrongdoer's exclusion the patriarch heard applies to every trustee of every generation, of either line. For the Muslims hearing the sūrah — a community praying toward this House within months of the verse's revelation, their qibla legislation about to arrive — the verse installed their direction's full pedigree: the House they faced was not a Makkah landmark but a divine institution, made center and sanctuary, charged to two prophets, purified for three classes of worshipper, its patriarch's footprint legislated as their prayer-site. The community's newest practice was given the oldest title-deed in the recital's possession.
verses.126:
> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**The Patriarch's Civic Prayer**

The verse records the second of Abraham's two prayers for the House's setting, and this one is urban: *my Lord, make this city secure and provide fruits to its people*. The petition's two terms are the two goods a settlement lives by — safety and supply — and their order is doctrinal: security first, because provision cannot be enjoyed where fear governs, and worship cannot be gathered where the roads are unsafe. The city is Makkah, the barren valley the patriarch had settled his household in with the prayer Sūrah Ibrāhīm preserves: *our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House, so that they may establish prayer — so make the hearts of people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, so perhaps they will be thankful* (14:37). The two prayers are one petition across decades: the valley without cultivation asked for fruit, the city asked for security, and both asked on the House's account — the settlement's goods requested for the sake of the worship it hosts. The same sūrah preserves the prayer's third term, the patriarch's fear for its interior: *make this city secure, and keep me and my children away from the worship of idols* (14:35) — security and provision bracketing the one danger that would void both, the idol inside the safe, fruit-bearing town. The verse's prayer is therefore a complete civic theology in one sentence: safety for the body, fruit for the body's life, and — in the clause that follows — the qualification that reveals what the body's goods are for.

**The Sanctuary Declared**

The prayer's first term — *secure* — received its historical ratification in the tradition's most documented declaration. On the day Makkah was taken, the Prophet ﷺ stood in the city and stated its status: *"Allah has made Mecca a sanctuary, so it was a sanctuary before me and will continue to be a sanctuary after me. It was made legal for me — that is, I was allowed to fight in it — for a few hours of a day. It is not allowed to uproot its shrubs or to cut its trees, or to chase or disturb its game, or to pick up its lost things except by a person who would announce that publicly"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1833) — with the tradition's single recorded exception, when al-ʿAbbās asked for the idhkhir-grass used by the goldsmiths and for graves, and the Prophet ﷺ granted it. In another formulation of the same announcement, the tradition dates the sanctity to the day the heavens and the earth were created and extends it to the Day of Resurrection, with the killing inside it permitted to no one before or after. The declaration's content is Abraham's petition made law: the city *secure* — not merely peaceful by circumstance but inviolable by statute, its safety a ruling rather than a condition. The statute's granularity in the ḥadīth — the shrub, the tree, the game, the lost article — extends the sanctuary past human blood to the city's whole living furniture, and the few-hours exception of the conquest confirms the rule by marking its only breach as unique, dated, and closed. The verse's prayer is thus answerable in the historical record: asked at the House's founding, legislated at the city's return, and the *āmin*-root binding it to verse 125's *amn* ties the city's security to the House's sanctuary as one institution.

**Fruits in the Barren Valley**

The petition's second term carries the geography's standing miracle. Makkah sits in a valley the patriarch's own prayer described as without cultivation (14:37) — no orchards, no fields, no water-command of its own — and the fruit asked for it is not agricultural produce but commercial and pilgrim provision: the goods carried in because the House draws the carriers. The prayer's mechanism is stated in 14:37 itself — *make the hearts of people incline toward them* — the fruit routed through inclination, the supply created by love of the destination, and the history the verse's audience knew ran exactly on that mechanism: the caravans of winter and summer, the market fairs of the pilgrimage season, the barren town fed by its own drawing-power. The recital's audience was also hearing the petition's purpose-clause, which 14:37 states and verse 126 assumes: *so that they may establish prayer*, *so perhaps they will be thankful*. The fruits are instrumental — provision for a worshipping settlement, supply ordered to gratitude — and the instrumental ordering is what the answer's second half enforces from the other side: the provision arrives for all, but it is received rightly only where the gratitude runs, and where it does not, the enjoyment is booked as respite and the destination as evil. The verse leaves the two receptions standing side by side in one city: the believer fed and thankful, the disbeliever fed and respite-held, the same fruit, the same security, two destinations — and the difference between them located, as the recital always locates it, in what the fed heart does with the feeding.
verses.127:
> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**The First House**

The Qur'an states the House's rank in its own terms, and the statement is the verse's doctrinal anchor: *surely the first House of worship established for humanity is the one at Bakkah — blessed, and a guidance for all people* (3:96). The name *Bakkah* is the verse's own antiquarian evidence — an alternate form of Makkah that the tradition connects to the biblical Valley of Baca in the Psalms (84:6), a link the commentators note across the two scriptural archives. The firstness claimed is of establishment *for humanity* — the earliest house set up for human worship, which is compatible with the Adam-lore and independent of it: whatever the foundations' age, the House's standing as humanity's first appointed sanctuary is the Qur'an's own assertion. Sūrah al-Ḥajj supplies the building's commission from its other end: *when We assigned to Abraham the site of the House* (22:26) — the location designated, the builder placed at the designated point, with the charge that follows in that verse running exactly parallel to verse 125's purification-command. The two verses together fix the building's theology: the site is assigned, not chosen; the House is established, not invented; and the raisers' work, however monumental in its labor, is execution of a divine plan whose firstness, blessedness, and guidance-function belong to the plan rather than to the masons. The verse's audience — a community praying toward this House, months from legislating the direction permanently — received in these clauses their qibla's full credentials: first, blessed, guidance, assigned, raised by the two names their own genealogies traced to.

**“Accept From Us”**

The builders pray while they build, and the prayer's single petition is the verse's spiritual center: *our Lord, accept from us*. The request names the work's actual risk. Construction can fail structurally — but the patriarchs, raising a house whose site was assigned by Allah, do not pray about walls; they pray about standing. The deed's acceptance is not guaranteed by the deed's correctness: an act can be complete in its performance and unaccepted in its account, and the prayer confesses the gap — acceptance belongs to the Receiver, not to the act's arithmetic. The tradition's grammar of acceptance runs through the recital: the fast accepted, the charity received, the pilgrimage *mabrūr* — each pairing a completed human act with a requested divine response, and each keeping the response on mercy's side of the ledger. The prayer's timing is its instruction: it is spoken *during* the raising, not after it — the builders' hands moving while their tongues ask, the acceptance sought for work in progress, which makes the prayer a continuous liturgy of labor rather than a closing ceremony. The two Names that seal the petition state the acceptance's mechanism: *You are indeed the All-Hearing* — the prayer reaches its addressee, the asking is not spoken into vacancy; *the All-Knowing* — the work and the intention behind it are both held in knowledge, the seen stones and the unseen sincerity registered together. The hearing answers the prayer's utterance and the knowing answers the prayer's unspoken content, and the pair is the builders' complete warrant: nothing in the raising — not the effort, not the fear of inadequacy, not the intention no colleague can verify — falls outside the two attributes the petition names.

**The Two Builders**

The verse joins the two names in one sentence of joint labor, and the joining is the recital's genealogical politics at its most concrete. Abraham, the imām tested and appointed at verse 124; Ishmael, the son of the Arabian line, named here not as attendant but as co-raiser — the foundations lifted by both, the prayer said by both (the verse's grammar puts the petition in their shared mouth), the acceptance sought for both. The tradition's accounts of the building divide the labor between them — one laying stones, one handing them, in the reports the exegetes preserve — and whatever the division's details, the verse's headline is partnership: the House's construction belongs to the two lines' common ancestor-pair, and the prayer over it is a single prayer in a dual voice. For the recital's Madinan audience the fact carried its full charge. The Israelite claim ran through Isaac; the Ishmaelite line ran to the Arabs; the House now being raised in the narrative stood as the work of both brothers under their father, its purification-charge (125) laid on both, its acceptance-prayer uttered by both — an institution older than the division of the lines and jointly owned across it. The verse by this performs, in narrative form, the covenant-law verse 124 stated in doctrine: the office and the trust descend through fulfillment and righteousness, held here by father and son together, with the wrongdoer — of either line, of any generation — excluded by the answer Abraham received. The two builders pray as one party, and the House they raise is, in the recital's design, the standing rebuke to every later monopoly of the patriarchs.
verses.128:
> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**A Nation That Submits**

The prayer's second petition extends the first across generations: *and from our descendants, a nation that will submit to You*. The word *umma* names not a family but a community — a people gathered by a shared orientation, the term the Qur'an uses for the constituted bodies of religious history. The petition is the patriarch's answer to his own question at verse 124: asked whether the covenant would run through his offspring and told it does not extend to wrongdoers, Abraham now prays the only prayer that question permits — not that his descendants hold the office by blood, but that a nation of them be *made submitting*, the covenant's condition fulfilled in them by the same grace requested for himself. The exegetes ground the petition's scope in a general principle: kin hold the first claim on a person's care and concern — al-Rāzī's note, anchored in the Qur'an's own command to the believers: *protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones* (66:6). The patriarch's prayer models the principle at its prophetic height: the imām's first congregation is his line, and the line's good is not its precedence but its submission. The petition's wording also carries the recital's covenant-law forward: a nation *that will submit* — the qualifying participle attached to the community as its defining mark, so that the nation asked for is constituted by the posture rather than the genealogy, and every later member qualifies by the same clause. The prayer thus builds, inside the House-raising scene, the community that will inherit the House — an umma defined at its founding petition as submitters-made, descendants in form, muslims in content.

**“Show Us Our Rituals”**

The third petition asks for the liturgy itself: *show us our rituals* — *manāsik*, the word whose range the tradition sets out as the pilgrimage-rites, the sacrificial practice, and worship's forms in general. The verb — *show us* — is the petition's doctrine: the rites are seen before they are performed, given before they are invented. No prophet in the recital designs his community's worship; the forms descend, are assigned, are shown — as the House's site was assigned (22:26) and the standing-place legislated (125). Sūrah al-Ḥajj states the principle across the communities: *for every community We appointed a rite of sacrifice, so that they may pronounce Allah's Name over the livestock He has provided* (22:34) — appointment and provision from one side, pronouncement from the other, the liturgy's two-party structure fixed. The petition's humility is its instruction for the recital's audience: the patriarchs, custodians of the first House, ask to be shown how to worship in it — the builders requesting the liturgy of their own building. The question embedded in *our rites* is equally instructive: which forms belong to this House, this community, this covenant? The prayer leaves the answer entirely with Allah, and the answer arrived in the tradition's record as the complete ḥajj — the circling, the running, the standing, the sacrifice — held in Islam as Abrahamic institution, its forms received, its showing granted. Between the submission asked in the first petition and the rites asked in the third stands the prayer's complete order: orientation first, form second — the submitting heart before the shown ritual, because the rite without the orientation is the empty house of verse 114's indictment, maintained in stone and abandoned in function.

**“Turn to Us”**

The fourth petition is the prayer's most tender clause: *and turn to us in grace* — *tub ʿalaynā*, the tawba-verb in its divine direction. The tradition's grammar of tawba is reciprocal, and the reciprocity is the clause's whole content: the human being turns toward Allah in repentance, and Allah turns toward the human in acceptance — one word, two motions, the meeting named from each side. The sūrah filed the mechanism at its origin-station: Adam received words from his Lord and the turning was accepted (2:37) — the first repentance, its vocabulary given, its reception guaranteed. The patriarchs' use of the verb carries no claim of known sin; it is the servant-posture in its pure form — the creature asking the Lord to keep the relation turned, the face-to-face of grace maintained, whatever in the servants' state requires the turning. The two Names sealing the petition are chosen from the prayer's own request: *the Accepter of Repentance* — *tawwāb*, the intensive form, the One whose turning is abundant, repeated, ready; *Most Merciful* — *raḥīm*, the mercy that meets the turning where it lands. The pairing is the verse's theology of return in two words: the request to be turned to is addressed to the One whose Names already answer it, which is the recital's standing structure of duʿāʾ — the petition built on the attribute that grants it, the asking shaped by the Giver's self-description. For the community hearing the prayer, the clause legislates the liturgy's interior: rites shown, submission made, and over both the continuous turning — the worship that keeps asking to be received, at the House whose builders never stopped asking.
verses.129:
> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**A Messenger From Among Them**

The builders' prayer reaches its final petition, and the petition names the community's future guide: *our Lord, raise from among them a messenger*. The preposition carries the prayer's whole ecclesiology — *from among them*, minhum: the messenger requested is not sent at the nation from outside but raised up from within it, of its substance, speaking its tongue, sharing its valley and its House. The request completes the sequence begun two verses back: a submitting nation asked for (128), and now, from that nation's own body, the guide whose office will keep it submitting. The verb — *raise* — is the Qur'an's standing word for prophetic commissioning, and its vertical sense belongs to the petition: the messenger is raised the way the foundations were raised at verse 127, a lifting from within the material, the community's own stock elevated to its guidance-office. The recital's audience heard the petition with its answer in their ears: Sūrah al-Jumuʿah states the fulfillment in near-identical terms — *He is the One Who raised for the illiterate people a messenger from among themselves* (62:2) — the ummī community of the sūrah's own portrait (2:78's illiterate, the nation that neither writes nor calculates, in the Prophet's ﷺ description) receiving the raised messenger the patriarchs asked for. The petition is the recital's bridge across the centuries: the House's builders praying for the House's future congregation's guide, and the guide arriving from among the congregation, in the lineage the prayer named — the answer carried by the son whose co-labor verse 127 had just honored.

**The Book and the Wisdom**

The second office's two objects carry a pairing the Qur'an deploys as a fixed formula, and the formula's breadth is the tradition's evidence for its meaning. The Book — *al-kitāb* — is read most often as the Qur'an, the delivered text in its written-recited form. The wisdom — *al-ḥikma* — is understood in the exegetical tradition as the Sunnah: the Prophet's ﷺ exemplary sayings and doings, the Book's embodied commentary — or, more broadly, the knowledge and understanding of the religion the Book's delivery produces (al-Ṭabarī's range). The pairing's recurrence across the Qur'an settles its import: the Book and wisdom are named together as what Jesus received (3:48, 5:110), as what the Children of Israel were given (45:16), as what the House of Abraham received (4:54) — a formula, in the tradition's reading, for revelation's two modes wherever it descends: the text delivered and the understanding given, the word and its realization, the recitation and its application. The pairing also answers, in its structure, the communities the recital has just documented failing: a Book held without wisdom is the Torah rationed and cast behind backs (85, 101) — text preserved, understanding refused; and wisdom claimed without the Book is the desires called guidance (120). The petition asks for both offices in one messenger because the community's health requires both hold — and the answer's history is the tradition's demonstration: the Book memorized in ten thousand chests, the wisdom recorded in the Sunnah's corpus, the pairing maintained as the two hands of one inheritance.

**The Purification**

The third office is the petition's goal-term, and its placement last marks it as the work's completion: *and purify them*. Tazkiya — the verb of purification and growth at once — names the soul-craft the messenger performs: cleansing from the coverings the recital has catalogued (the sheathed hearts, the drunk-in calf-love, the black-marked mat-weaving), and growing the soul toward the states the recital promises (the white hearts the trials cannot harm, the no-fear-no-grief formula's holders). The purification-office is what separates the messenger from the librarian: a deliverer of texts transmits; a purifier transforms, and the petition asks for both because a community holding the Book unchanged is the recital's documented tragedy — the Torah in custody, the hearts hardened, the covenant cast at every station. The office's mechanism is the recital's own: the revelations recited do the purifying as they are received — the message that softens skins and hearts at Allah's mention (39:23's operation), the signs clear for people of sure faith (118) — and the messenger administers the reception, pacing the delivery to the community's capacity, as the Prophet ﷺ did with the companions whose formation the tradition records year by year. The petition's three verbs now show their architecture: recitation supplies the purifying agent, teaching supplies its application, purification is the effected state — and the community that receives all three is the umma the patriarchs asked to be made submitting (128), submitting not in name but in cleansed hearts.

Sūrah al-Jumuʿah extends the answer past the first congregation — the messenger sent to them *and to others of them who have not yet joined them* (62:3), the prayer's reach covering every generation the recitation now includes.
verses.130:
> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

**Millah: The Faith Named**

The object of the possible rejection — *the faith of Abraham* — translates *millah*, the term the recital defined at verse 120 as a community's whole way: not a creed held but a pattern lived, the total order of belief, practice, and direction. Abraham's millah is therefore everything the file just documented: the submission asked as gift, the commands fulfilled under test, the House and its rites, the prayers for nation and messenger, the covenant held on righteousness rather than blood. The Qur'an's contest over this millah is its historical occasion: the communities of Madina each claimed the patriarch — the Jews through the Israelite line, the Christians through their scripture's genealogy, the Arabs through Ishmael and the House — and each claim implied that Abraham's faith was that community's property. The verse answers every claim at once by naming the millah independently of all of them, and Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the independence as doctrine: *Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness, and was not a polytheist* (3:67). The patriarch's faith precedes the denominations that claim it — the uprightness, the ḥanīf-posture, the submission — and the verse's question by this acquires its full edge: the communities rejecting the Messenger who carries Abraham's millah forward are rejecting, by the recital's account, the faith of their own claimed ancestor, and the rejection is filed not as theological difference but as the fool's lightness.

**Chosen in Both Worlds**

The verse's second sentence states the patriarch's standing in the two worlds, and the double statement is the rejection-question's warrant. *We certainly chose him in this life* — the iṣṭifāʾ, the selection the Qur'an records for a short list of its figures: Mary chosen above the women of the worlds (3:42), Moses chosen for the message (7:144), Adam (20:122), the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the sūrah of the Angels (35:32), the prophets collectively (6:87) — and Abraham, chosen with the emphatic *certainly*, his selection spanning the worldly life in office, honor, and function: imām, builder, answered supplicant, the direction of a community's prayer. *And in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous* — the second-world term of the selection: not merely saved but enrolled, placed among the ṣāliḥūn, the company the patriarch's own prayer-work kept naming. The two clauses together answer the millah-contest from the standing side: the faith whose rejection is foolishness is held by a man doubly certified — chosen here, righteous there — and the certification is divine speech, not communal claim. The verse also quietly settles the lineage-question of verse 124 from the patriarch's own side: the covenant did not extend to the wrongdoers among his offspring, and the patriarch himself stands at both worlds' head — the office's first holder, whose holding is the pattern every claimant of his name is measured against. Chosen, fulfilled, enrolled: the three verbs of the patriarch's file leave the rejection-question with no respectable answer, which is exactly what the question asserts.

**The Continuity of the Two Laws**

The exegetes read the verse as the recital's statement of continuity between the patriarch's law and the Messenger's, and the reading is the verse's structural function in the sūrah. Al-Qushayrī's note states the principle: the Law of Muhammad ﷺ retains the Law of Abraham except where it abrogates it — the continuity qualified by the naskh-doctrine the sūrah legislated at verse 106, so that the two mills stand in the relation the recital's own jurisprudence defines: one religion across its dispensations, its forms adjusted by the Owner of the kingdom (107), its substance unchanged. The concrete evidence runs through the passage just filed: the ḥajj-rites held in Islam as Abrahamic institution — the circling, the standing-place, the showing requested at verse 128 — and the tradition's tracing of the bodily purities, the grooming and cleanliness disciplines, back to the patriarch's fulfilled commands (124's first exegetical stream). The continuity-reading gives the verse's question its second edge. The millah is not a museum-piece the communities honor while practicing otherwise; it is a living law, carried forward in the rites the Muslims of Madina were performing and the Messenger they were following — so rejecting the Messenger is not preserving Abraham's faith but abandoning its transmission, the chain the verse's own six-station file documented link by link. The fools the question names are, in the recital's Madinan moment, precisely the claimants who honored the patriarch's name while rejecting his millah's arrival — and the verse files the contradiction as the definition of safah: lightness toward the heavy thing one claims to hold.
verses.131:
> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**The One-Word Command**

The verse files the patriarch's defining moment in its smallest possible form: a command of one word. *When his Lord said to him: Submit* — *aslim*, the imperative of the same root whose participle the builders' prayer requested at verse 128 (*make us submitters*). The command's singularity is its content: not a list, not a ritual, not a doctrine — the whole religion in one verb, the orientation before the specification. The root-command also explains the prayer of verse 128 in retrospect: the patriarchs asked to be *made* muslim because the making had been *commanded* — the imperative arrives first, and the submission that answers it remains, at every station of its holder's life, a thing asked for. The commands fulfilled at verse 124 — the purities, the rites, the trials — are this command's specification; the fire and the knife were its tests; and the one word remained the sum, which is why the verse can state the patriarch's entire standing in one sentence of dialogue.

**“I Have Submitted”: The Answer in the Perfect Tense**

The response is as short as the command and carries one grammatical feature the exegetes mark: *aslamtu* — I have submitted — the perfect tense, the completed act. The answer does not say *I will submit* and does not negotiate terms, delay, or conditions; it reports the submission as already accomplished at the moment of speaking, the response and the command meeting without interval. The recital's audience knew the contrast-answer: the community of verse 93, commanded under the raised mountain to hold firmly and obey, replied *we hear and disobey* — the same command-structure, the split response. Between the two answers the recital's whole moral geography lies: the perfect-tense *I have submitted* and the inverted *we hear and disobey*, the patriarch's file and Israel's file, the millah and its rejection. The answer's object completes its scope: *to the Lord of all worlds* — the submission directed not to the command's occasion but to the Commander's universal lordship. The phrase — *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — is the recitation's own opening address, the Fātiḥa's second line (*all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds*), and its appearance in the patriarch's mouth ties the Muslim's daily prayer to the patriarch's defining answer: every reciter of the Fātiḥa speaks the object of Abraham's submission in every prayer of his life. The worlds named are the plural of every realm — human, jinn, angelic, seen, unseen — and the submission is to the Rabb of the whole plurality, which is the verse's quiet completion of the millah-contest: a faith whose object is the Lord of all worlds cannot be any single community's property, because its object owns the claimants.

**Islām Before Islam**

The verse's verb is the recital's evidence for a claim the whole Qur'an makes: the submission named here is older than the name the Muslim community carries. The tradition states the principle plainly — *islām*, while the proper name of the religion brought by Muhammad ﷺ, is generalized in the Qur'an to mean the primordial religion, the true religion as such, the fundamental orientation of the soul toward God that is universal and stands among the bequests the prophets leave their children. The verse is the principle's founding exhibit: Abraham, centuries before the Mosaic law and centuries more before the Qur'an, receives the command *aslim* and answers *aslamtu* — and the exchange is the same religion the recital's own community bears by name. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān legislates the identity's exclusivity from the other side: whoever seeks a way other than islām, it will not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he is among the losers (3:85) — the submission-pose named as the only accepted orientation across every dispensation. The verse by this performs the recital's genealogical politics in one dialogue: the patriarch is not a proto-Jew, not a proto-Christian, not an Arab ancestral cult-figure — he is a muslim in the Qur'an's precise sense, the first word of whose religion is the word commanded to him, and every community that claims him claims a submitter, which is a description of posture rather than of party. The command's universality is its inheritance-law: the millah passes to whoever answers it, and the answer has never been restricted to a lineage — the same lesson verse 124's covenant-condition stated in legal form, here stated in dialogue.
verses.132:
> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**“Allah Has Chosen This Faith for You”**

The counsel's first clause states the children's position, and the statement is grace before demand: *indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith*. The verb is the iṣṭifāʾ of verse 124 and verse 130 — the divine selection, the same word used of the patriarch's own choosing — now applied to the religion itself as the children's portion. The clause's theology is precise in its prepositions: the faith is chosen *for you*, *by Allah* — the religion arrives as gift before it stands as task, the selection divine before the holding is human. The verse by this installs the correct order of the religious life: the children are not told *choose this faith* but *this faith has been chosen for you* — their freedom operates inside a prior grace, the way the patriarch's own submission was commanded before it was answered (131). The named object — *this faith*, the millah in its submission-form — is the religion verse 131 defined: islām as the primordial orientation, the universal pose, what the prophets bequeath. And the choosing's agent answers the millah-contest one final time from inside the family scene: the faith the patriarchs transmit is not a tribal inheritance but a divine selection — held by the children not because their fathers held it but because Allah chose it for them, a ground that stands for every generation the choice reaches and falls away for every claim that cites the fathers alone. The counsel's first clause is thus the recital's whole doctrine of election in one sentence: chosen by Allah, chosen for the children, chosen as this — the submission the dialogue of verse 131 enacted.

**“Do Not Die Except in Submission”**

The counsel's second clause is its famous imperative, and its form is the verse's most striking feature: *so do not die except in a state of full submission*. Death is not chosen — no one commands the hour of his dying — and the command therefore addresses what the hour arrives to find: the state, not the event. The imperative is a command about living whose term is set at dying: arrange the whole of life so that death, whenever it comes, comes upon a submitter. The tradition named the doctrine this verse legislates — the good ending, ḥusn al-khātima — and its logic is the recital's own anthropology: the state at death is the sum of the life's direction, the heart's last posture continuous with its practiced posture, and the one who lives submitting dies submitting by the same necessity that verse 93 filed in the other direction: the heart made to drink its loves carries them past the boundary. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān legislates the identical clause to the Muslim community directly: be mindful of Allah as He deserves, *and do not die except in submission* (3:102) — the patriarchs' deathbed counsel converted into the ummah's standing law, which is the verse's proof that the waṣiyya was never addressed to one family. The command's severity is also its mercy: it makes every moment continuous with the last one, so that the deathbed requires no emergency conversion — the submitter arrives at death already in the state death is commanded to find. Between the two clauses the counsel's whole architecture stands: the faith given by selection, the life ordered toward the exit — gift and task, grace and vigilance, in the two sentences a dying father spent his last words on.

**The Counsel to Every Child**

The verse's transfer is in its address: every reader is somebody's child, and the waṣiyya reaches whoever inherits a faith. The counsel's two clauses are the inheritance's two questions. Has the faith come to you as chosen — received as selection before it is held as identity, the gift-order of verse 128's petition intact? And is your life arranged toward the commanded exit — the daily posture continuous with the deathbed posture, the submission practiced at the scale of hours so that it stands at the scale of the end? The recital's audience heard both questions with their own bequest in hand: the Qur'an itself is a waṣiyya to its hearers, this sūrah's hundred-verses-plus of covenant, audit, and patriarch-file the counsel's elaboration, and the Messenger ﷺ raised from the prayed-for nation (129) its living transmitter. The verse installs the community's self-understanding as children of a bequest — not owners of a property but heirs of a charge, with the charge's terms stated: the faith is chosen for you, so do not die except in submission. Between the two patriarchs' deathbeds and the recital's Madinan moment, the counsel travels unchanged, which is the verse's final proof of the millah's identity: what Abraham said to his children and Jacob said to his, the sūrah says to its — one sentence, three generations of speakers, one posture required of every hearer, and the exit-command running until the Day verse 123 described, where the states the deaths found are filed, and no soul arrives except as it lived.
verses.133:
> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**The Sons' Answer**

The reply is the verse's creed, and its structure moves in three steps. *We will worship your God* — the personal term first: the sons receive the faith as their father's God, the deity of a lived relationship they were raised inside, the continuity of the household's worship. *And the God of your forefathers — Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac* — the historical term second: the fathers named, the lineage's three patriarchs listed in an order the verse makes remarkable. Ishmael stands between Abraham and Isaac — the Arabian uncle named among the fathers, in a list the Israel-line's descendants speak, and the inclusion is the recital's genealogical reconciliation in the sons' own mouth: the House's two builders (125, 127) are both ancestral to the worship confessed here, the family's two lines joined in one God-list. The exegetes note the verse's noun-choice with matching care: *your God* translates *ilāh*, the common noun for deity, not the proper Name — the sons confess the object's oneness before they speak its name, and the confession's third step states the oneness: *the One God* — *ilāhun wāḥid*, the singularity that makes the three fathers' God one God rather than three household deities. The answer closes where the whole section has been heading: *and to Him we submit* — the islām-clause, the patriarchs' counsel (132) answered in the patriarch's own house, the submission-pose of verse 131 spoken by the twelve. Sūrah Yūsuf preserves the same confession from one son's mouth a lifetime later: Joseph in the Egyptian prison following *the faith of my fathers — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob* (12:38), the list recurring, the submission restated — the deathbed creed become the tribes' standing formula in its best son.

**The Patriarchs Cannot Be Owned**

The verse is the recital's argument, in narrative form, against every exclusive claim on the patriarchs, and the argument's force is that the scene is the claimants' own. The Qur'an's general case runs through this section: Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian (3:67); his millah is submission, held by whoever answers its command (130–131); the covenant excludes the wrongdoer of any line (124). Verse 133 supplies the case's decisive exhibit — the deathbed itself, with the Israel-line's own father asking the worship-question and his own sons answering in the terms the recital legislates: one God, the fathers' God including Ishmael, and submission to Him. The answer the tribes' founder received is the answer the Qur'an preaches, which makes the Madinan claimants' rejection of the Messenger a rejection filed against their own founding scene: the patriarchs, in the tradition's reading, were followers of the pure religion of Abraham — primordial monotheism, which is to say islām in the verse's own closing word — and the communities that claim them while rejecting the submission-formula contradict, the recital asserts, the only witnessed testimony about what the patriarchs actually transmitted. The verse's witness-question thus inverts at its close: the claimants were not present at Jacob's deathbed, but the recital was — and what it reports is a creed with no exclusivity clause in it, no lineage-reservation, no millah-property: the God of all the fathers, one, submitted to. The patriarchs belong to whoever holds their sons' answer, and the answer's text is quoted here in full, so that the belonging is adjudicated by the scene rather than the claim.

**The Scene as the Section's Seal**

Verse 133 closes the recital's Abraham-cycle, and the closing scene gathers the cycle's whole argument into a room. The test and its fulfillment (124) end in the question every fulfillment faces: will it survive into the children? The imāmah conditioned on righteousness (124) stands confirmed: the office passed through the answer, not the blood. The House built and purified (125), the city prayed for (126), the building's acceptance requested (127), the submitting nation and its messenger asked (128–129) — every petition lands in this scene's confession: the nation submitting, in its patriarchal nucleus, answering at the deathbed of Israel's father. The millah beyond denomination (130), the one-word command answered in the perfect tense (131), the bequest commanding the submitted exit (132) — all three verified in the sons' closing clause: *to Him we submit*. The recital seals the section with the formula its next movement will legislate for the Muslim community in the same terms, and the seal's message to every claimant of every patriarch is the verse's standing challenge: the witness-question runs against all of them — you were not present, the testimony is recited, and the testimony contains the creed. Whoever holds the creed holds the fathers; whoever rejects it is rejected by the scene, whatever his lineage. The deathbed of Jacob remains the recital's examination-room for every child of the patriarchs, and the twelve sons' answer remains on the record — your God, the God of Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac, one God, submitted to — waiting at every generation's exit for the voice that will speak it as its own.
verses.134:
> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

The long appeal to Abraham that began with his covenant and his imamate has just ended with his deathbed, and this verse draws the line under the whole account. "That was a community that had already gone before" — *qad khalat*, they passed, they are gone, their case is finished. The generation of the patriarchs lived, chose, believed, struggled, and died, and what they accumulated went with them into their own reckoning.

**Kasab: Deeds as Property**

The verb the verse uses for what the dead and the living alike hold is *kasaba*, to earn — and the same root, depending on context, carries the sense of committing or perpetrating. The double edge is deliberate. A deed in the Qur'an's moral economy is not an event that evaporates; it is an acquisition that attaches to its doer the way a purchase attaches to a buyer. What a person "earns" becomes his property in the only ledger that survives death, and the property can be a burden as easily as a treasure. The vocabulary of earning also explains why the verse phrases both halves identically — *for them* what they earned, *for you* what you earned. There is no qualitative difference between the ancestors' account and the descendants': the same verb governs both, the same ownership rules apply to both, and the same audit awaits both. Death closes the earning, not the ownership; what was acquired remains acquired, held by the dead in a custody no living relative can reach into. That is why the verse can say so flatly that "for them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned": the sentence structure of ownership. Their earnings are in their hands; yours are in yours. No transfer mechanism exists between the two accounts, in either direction.

**No Soul Carries Another's Load**

The principle stated here in the language of earnings is stated elsewhere in the language of burdens. The sūrah of the Star records, as if reciting a creed already known, *"˹They state˺ that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another, and that each person will only have what they endeavoured towards"* (53:38–39). Two claims in two clauses: liability is non-transferable, and reward is proportional to effort. Together they seal the verse's argument. A sinner cannot offload onto his ancestor, and an heir cannot withdraw from his ancestor's balance. The Qur'an presses this point precisely because ancestral credit was a live currency in its first audience — lineage was identity, protection, and prestige, and the claim to have righteous forefathers functioned as a kind of moral insurance. The verse cancels the policy.

**A Community, Not a Clan**

The word for what has passed is *ummah* — a community defined by what it held together, its faith and its way, rather than by blood alone. That choice of word quietly redefines what the heirs inherit. From an *ummah* that has gone before, the living receive a direction: the creed it lived by, the pattern of its submission, the guidance it carried. What they do not receive is its credit. The distinction matters because the same sūrah has already fixed the rule at the top of Abraham's story: when God made him a leader for humanity, the imamate was explicitly withheld from wrongdoers among his own line — *"˹He said,˺ 'And ˹so will˺ some of your descendants ˹also˺.' ˹Allah˺ said, 'My covenant does not ˹extend to˺ the wrongdoers'"* (2:124). Rank in God's economy runs through conduct, not chromosomes. A clan boasts of its dead; a community continues their work.
verses.135:
> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**The Millah of Abraham**
