The command to eat the provided good things has a precedent in this same sūrah's history of the Israelites: the clouds shaded them, manna and quails were sent down, *"Eat from the good things We have provided for you"* (2:57) — the identical formula, spoken over the wilderness table. And the verse records what followed: *the evildoers did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves* — the same provision, received by one generation with transgression and rebellion. The two tables stand beside each other in the sūrah deliberately: provision plus gratitude is this verse's covenant; provision plus self-wronging was that generation's failure. The difference is not in the food — both tables were furnished by the same Provider with the same class of good things — but in the second course, which is thanks. This is why the verse makes gratitude conditional on worship rather than optional for it: the manna generation had the permission and lost the benefit, and the believers are handed both in one sentence so that the history is not repeated at their own tables. Every meal offers the choice the wilderness offered: eat and remember the Provider, or eat and wrong the self.
verses.173:
> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Word "Only" and the Short List**

The verse opens with a restriction on restriction: *He has only forbidden you* — four items, and the four exhaust the divine prohibition of food. The "only" is the verse's argument in one word. Against the tribes that forbade whole classes of their cattle to themselves, against the ancestral customs that bound what God had loosed, against the footsteps that walk the pious toward invented prohibitions, the revealed law presents a list so short it can be memorized in a breath: carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in another's name. Everything else on the earth's table stands under the permission of the previous verse.

**The Name Over the Throat**

The fourth item establishes the positive ritual the community performs at every slaughter: the pronouncing of God's Name. The sūrah of the Pilgrimage legislates the same act over the sacrificial camels — *"pronounce the Name of Allah over them when they are lined up ˹for sacrifice˺"* (22:36) — and Islamic practice fixed the formula as the *basmalah* spoken at the cut. The theology is precise and answers the meal's deepest question: who made this death lawful for my life? The animal dies because a human needs it; the Name declares that the taking happens under God's permission and in His direction, converting a killing into a receipt. Meat from which the Name is absent is not by this carrion in the physical sense; it is meat whose killing belongs to no one's stated accountability — or worse, to a named rival. This is why the verse's list ends with the dedication-prohibition rather than beginning with it: the first three items protect the body and the decree; the fourth protects the meaning of the act, and meaning is the verse's real subject. The table of the believers is a table at which every death has been declared to its Owner, and the declaration is what separates eating from mere consumption.

**A Ruling the Qur'an States Three Times**

This verse is one of the Qur'an's most exactly repeated laws, and the repetitions mark its constitutional status. The sūrah of the Bee states it in near-identical words: *"He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (16:115). The sūrah of the Cattle states the principle without the list: *"Why should you not eat of what is slaughtered in Allah's Name when He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you—except when compelled by necessity?"* (6:119). And the sūrah of the Table, in the Medinan period's final legislation, expands the list to its full detail — carrion, blood, swine, the dedicated-to-others, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, the partly eaten by predators, the altar-sacrificed, the divining arrows — with the same necessity exemption standing (5:3). The expansion confirms rather than revises: the later verse elaborates the carrion category into its modes of death and keeps the fourfold core intact. A law repeated verbatim across Meccan and Medinan revelation, then detailed without disturbance, is the tradition's picture of a ruling beyond abrogation — the food law's permanent floor.

**Forgiving and Merciful as the Law's Frame**

The verse closes with the two names — All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — and their placement is the final lesson. They follow the necessity clause rather than the prohibitions, covering the eater who crossed the line under compulsion, the one who erred in measuring his necessity, the one whose past meals were eaten before the law arrived. A food legislation could have closed with vigilance: Allah watches what enters your mouths. This one closes with absolution, and the absolution is attached precisely where human beings will fail — at the boundary cases, the famines, the mistakes, the years of ignorance before the permission and prohibition were revealed. The whole passage from the address to humanity to this verse is by this framed by mercy at both ends: the enemy declared (2:168), his methods exposed (2:169), the ancestral refusal refuted (2:170), the uncomprehending flock parabled (2:171), the believers' grateful table set (2:172), and the four doors closed with the key of necessity in the lock and forgiveness on the frame. The community that receives this law is told, in the act of receiving it, that its Lawgiver expects to be thanked at the table and expects to forgive at its edges — and both expectations are mercy.
verses.174:
> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment

**The Concealment Gets Its Price Tag**

The curse-verses on concealment (2:159–162) return here with a new element: the motive. The concealers are not only hiding; they are hiding *for a price* — trading the Book for a fleeting gain, the same traffic the sūrah condemned in its portrait of the editors of Scripture: woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say "this is from Allah," to sell it for a little price (2:79). The verse renders the transaction with a physical image of unusual violence: what they swallow is not the gain but fire — they *consume nothing but fire into their bellies*. The parallel in the sūrah of the Women fixes the same image to a neighboring crime: those who devour the property of orphans are, in truth, eating fire into their bellies (4:10). Both verses run the same accounting: the wealth sought by corrupting religion is not lost, not confiscated, not merely forbidden — it is *converted*. The price of the hidden truth arrives in the belly as the Fire that truth would have saved them from, and the conversion happens now, invisibly, at the moment of the profitable sin.

**God Will Not Speak to Them**

The second penalty is the withholding of speech: Allah will neither speak to them on the Day nor purify them. Āl ʿImrān states the identical sentence over those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain: *"Allah will neither speak to them, nor look at them, nor purify them on the Day of Judgment"* (3:77) — the same crime drawing the same threefold withdrawal, with the look added there. But the Qur'an also describes God speaking on the Day — questioning all of them about what they used to do (15:92–93), questioning those to whom the messengers were sent and the messengers themselves (7:6), and telling the damned *"Be despised in there! Do not ˹ever˺ plead with Me ˹again˺!"* (23:108). Al-Rāzī harmonized the texts with precision: the plain sense of this verse and 3:77 is total silence, but in light of the questioning-verses it must describe a punishment within speech — God will not speak to them words of peace and welcome. He compared it to the intimacy of a king, whose displeasure is shown by exile and the cutting off of contact, and suggested the angels will be the ones who speak to people that Day. Al-Ṭabarī read it as God not saying things agreeable to them; al-Qurṭubī added the linguistic observation that Arabs say "he did not speak to him" of a man who is angry. The speech withheld is not communication but favor — and for souls arranged entirely toward God, the withdrawal of His address is itself the fire.

**The Anatomy of the Fleeting Gain**

The phrase *fleeting gain* deserves the weight the verse places on it. The gain is characterized not by its size but by its duration — little and passing, a price that cannot be spent twice, in a market that closes at death. Against it the verse sets what was sold: revelations, clear proofs, guidance — goods whose value the sellers themselves acknowledged, since concealing something proves you know it is worth hiding. This is the same accounting the sūrah applied to the traders of the Hereafter for this world (2:86) and the covenant-sellers of Āl ʿImrān, who will have *no share in the Hereafter* (3:77) — a phrase that reads as the balance sheet: their share was taken early, in cash, and the account is closed.

**Placed Between Patience and the Law**

The verse's location in the sūrah is part of its argument. It arrives after the patience-triad with its formula of return and its blessings (2:154–157) and before the great definition of righteousness (2:177) and the legislation of retaliation, bequest, and fasting that follows. Between the patient poor who say *to Allah we belong* and the community about to receive its civil law stands the figure of the religious profiteer — the scholar-class sinner whose crime is the precondition of every other corruption, since a community can only be misled where guidance was withheld. The sūrah has now named this figure from every side: the truth hidden knowingly (2:42), the testimony concealed (2:140), the recognition like a father's knowledge of his child (2:146), the curse and its exception (2:159–160), and here the price, the fire, and the silence. The legislation that follows — blood-money, bequests, the fast — is addressed to a community whose knowledge is assumed intact, and this verse is the guarantee that its keepers were warned: the words you carry are not inventory. They are the speech of the One who can withhold His own.
verses.175:
> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire

**The Verb of Purchase**

The Qur'an's word for this transaction — *ishtaraw*, they purchased — belongs to a family the Book uses with bitter consistency for bad spiritual trades. The same verb described those who sold God's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain (3:77), those who trade the Hereafter for this life (2:86), and elsewhere those who purchase diversionary talk to mislead from God's way. The choice of commercial language is not decorative; it imports the whole apparatus of the market into the moral life — price, preference, exchange, profit — and then audits it. A market transaction is rational when the buyer values what he receives more than what he pays; the verse's claim is that these traders paid guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment, meaning they paid more than they received by an infinite margin, and did it knowingly, since the concealment of 2:174 presupposed knowledge of exactly what was being sold. The image convicts not only the sin but its stupidity: the Qur'an's profiteers are never shrewd operators but men who cannot do arithmetic, and the market metaphor exists to show every reader the ledger they are keeping with their own choices.

**"How Persistent They Are in Pursuit of the Fire"**

The verse's exclamation has taxed the commentators precisely because its surface is strange: what is praised — or mocked — is the traders' *patience*, their steadfastness, in relation to the Fire. The readings recorded by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī converge on a rhetorical question: what drove them to the deeds that brought them near the Fire? — or, what gives them such patience toward the Fire that they abandon truth for falsehood? The common sense, in al-Rāzī's summary, is simply: what made them do this? The irony is the engine of the sentence. Patience — *ṣabr* — is the sūrah's supreme virtue: the instrument the believers were commanded to take up (2:153), the quality whose bearers receive blessings and mercy (2:157), the grace promised good news (2:155). Here the same constancy appears in inverted form: a steadfastness in ruin, an endurance that spends itself hastening toward punishment. The traders have the virtue's structure — persistence through difficulty toward a goal — and the vice's direction. The exclamation thus does double duty: wonder at the magnitude of their self-destruction, and a warning that constancy itself is morally neutral until its object is named.

**Forgiveness Sold Back**

The second pair of the trade deserves its own attention, because forgiveness is the sūrah's standing offer. The passage immediately before ended with the Accepter of Repentance speaking in the first person (2:160), and the whole legislative arc about to begin — retaliation with its pardon, bequests with their equity, the fast with its ease — is forgiveness made institutional. The concealers are described as having held forgiveness and exchanged it: the revelation they hid was the vehicle of pardon for their communities, and by selling it they sold their own access to what it carried. The exegetical point is structural: guidance and forgiveness are the two goods revelation brings — knowledge of the way and absolution on the way — and the trade named here surrendered both at once, which is why the penalty of 2:174 fell on both faculties: the fire answers the belly's gain, the withheld speech answers the guidance, and the withheld purification answers the forgiveness. Each element of the sentence corresponds to an element of the sale. The verse is not adding imagery to the previous one; it is displaying its itemization.

**The Question Left With the Reader**

The closing exclamation is addressed, grammatically, to no one — it is wonder spoken aloud, the way a bystander says *how could he?* over a ruin. That unaddressed quality is its pedagogy. The verse does not answer its own question; no reason is given for the trade, because none exists that survives statement — that is the point of calling it a purchase of error at guidance's price. The sūrah will keep posing the same audit in different currencies — wealth traded for the Hereafter, oaths traded for gain, the self traded for appetite — and every instance inherits this verse's arithmetic. The traders of 2:174 thought they were selling religion for money; the verse corrects the invoice — they were buying the Fire, and paid for it with everything that could have saved them, and kept paying, patiently, to the end.
verses.176:
> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition

**Which Book?**

The exegetes asked whose Book the verse means, and the answers widen its reach. It could be the Qur'an — the Book the concealers around the Prophet were trading against. It could be the Torah and the Gospel, which on the Islamic account attest to the Prophet's truth, so that "differing about it" covers the questions of interpretation and distortion the sūrah has been prosecuting since its early verses (2:75). Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī both allowed the most comprehensive reading: the Book as God's Book collectively — Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an together — one revelation in successive installments, so that differing about it is differing about the whole enterprise of heaven's speech. The comprehensive reading is the strongest, because the passage's subjects have been plural throughout: the People of the Book who hide the testimony (2:140), the group that recognizes and conceals (2:146), the concealers cursed by all who curse (2:159). A single Book in three descents is exactly the object such parties can all be said to differ about, and it makes the verse the summary judgment on the whole sectarian argument the sūrah opened — the claim and counter-claim of Jew and Christian (2:135) resolved by the identity of what they were all given.

**Shiqāq: The Opposition Engrossed**

The verse's second clause names the condition of those who differ: they are in *shiqāq baʿīd* — far schism, deep opposition, the fracture-word the sūrah used of those who turn from the community's creed (2:137). The word's career in the Qur'an is consistent: the wrongdoers *totally engrossed in opposition* (22:53), the disbelievers *entrenched in arrogance and opposition* (38:2), the denier who has *gone too far in opposition* (41:52). Each instance pairs schism with a qualifier of depth or distance, and the image is spatial: opposition as a position taken far from something — not disagreement at close quarters, where correction is possible, but rupture with distance built in. The addition here, *regarding the Book*, identifies the axis of the rupture: the difference is not about weather or wages but about the one object whose whole function is to end differences. A book revealed in truth exists to be the common reference; differing *regarding it* is therefore not using a shared standard differently but destroying the standard — which is why the verse assigns no ordinary disagreement but far schism. The parties who quarrel over the Book have quarreled their way out of the only court that could have settled them.

**Differing About It, Not Differing With It**

The preposition carries a distinction the classical readers marked. To differ *with* someone about a text can be honest exegesis — the sūrah itself has modeled disagreement handled with grounds, reporting the exegetes' divisions and weighing them. What the verse condemns is differing that has the Book as its object in the sense of its casualty: readings that distort (2:75 — a group hears the word of God and then knowingly corrupts it after understanding it), concealments that subtract (2:174), trades that price it (2:175). The far schism is thus not pluralism but sabotage — difference manufactured from a text whose truth is known to the manufacturer. This is why the verse lands where it lands in the sequence: the traders' sentence (2:174–175), the reason (176), and then immediately the sūrah's positive counterpart — the definition of righteousness (2:177) that begins by believing in the Book and the prophets without distinction. The two verses are a diptych: far schism about the Book on one panel, and on the other the creed that holds every book together, makes no distinction between the messengers, and turns belief into the worked righteousness of orphans, travelers, captives, and pledges kept.

**The Distance Called Far**

The final word of the clause — *far* — deserves its own weight, because distance in the Qur'an's moral geography is measured from God. The wrongdoer is elsewhere described as having gone astray *far* (4:116's phrasing of distant error), and the Fire's own name for its inmates' condition is remoteness — the curse the previous passage defined as being distanced from mercy (2:159, 2:161). Schism about the Book is far, then, in the same sense: every act of distortion, concealment, and sale moves its author a measurable distance from the truth he still holds the text of, and the distance compounds, because each generation of readers inherits the corrupted copy rather than the clear original. The Book remains true where it is; the schismatics are simply far from it, and the far is where the punishment of 2:174–175 was already located.
verses.177:
> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**The Five Articles Before the Deeds**

The definition begins in belief, and the list it gives became canonical: belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets. These five are the principal articles on which the Islamic creedal statements are built, and they reappear as a unit in the sūrah of the Women's command to believe in Allah, His Messenger, the Book revealed to him, and the Scriptures revealed before (4:136). Their fullest canonical exposition is the famous ḥadīth of Gabriel, preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: the archangel, appearing as a traveling man, asks the Prophet to define *īmān*, and the answer enumerates belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree in its good and its evil — the same list, with the decree added. The ordering in this verse is instructive: God first, then the Day that gives moral life its horizon, then the unseen agents, then the books, then the messengers — creed before conduct, because the conduct that follows is unintelligible without it. The righteous are not defined as those who *do* the listed deeds but as those who *believe* the listed truths and do the deeds out of them.

**Wealth Given While It Is Still Loved**

The first deed named is charity, and its qualifier is the verse's psychological core: giving wealth *despite loving it* — or, on the reading that takes the pronoun as God's, *because of love for Him*. Al-Ṭabarī's explanation covers the first sense: parting with property even when one fears poverty or yearns for what wealth provides. The phrase has a twin in the sūrah of Man, where the righteous feed the poor, the orphan, and the captive — *and give food despite their desire for it* (76:8). The gift counted here is the one that costs, made while the hand still prefers to keep. The recipients are then listed in the order of social nearness and need: kinsfolk first — charity begins where obligation bleeds into love; orphans, whose guardianship the sūrah has legislated repeatedly; the indigent; the wayfarer stranded among strangers; the beggars; and the freeing of captives — wealth spent not on a person but against an institution, buying human beings out of bondage. Many jurists noted that this giving must be *beyond* the zakāh, since the alms-tax is listed separately later in the same verse: first the costly charity of love, then the fixed levy of law. The recipient list recurs at 2:215 and 4:36 and across the Qur'an's legislation of war-booty — one standing roster of the people a righteous economy is measured by.

**Patience in the Three Extremes**

The final deed is the sūrah's standing virtue, now specified by its three testing grounds: patience in misfortune (*baʾsāʾ*), in hardship (*ḍarrāʾ*), and in moments of peril. Al-Ṭabarī's glosses separate them: misfortune as challenges like poverty — the loss of means; hardship as matters like sickness — the loss of health; and the moments of peril as battle, the meeting of the enemy, the hour when the body's fear argues against the will's resolve. The three grounds cover the full geography of affliction — the purse, the body, the battlefield — and together they recall the test announced at 2:155 with its fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. The verse thus closes its definition where the passage began: the righteous are the patient of 2:155–157, described now in full dress. And the peril-clause points forward with deliberate timing: the sūrah is about to legislate retaliation (2:178), then war itself (2:190 onward), and the community about to receive those laws is first told that the law's operators must be defined by patience — in the feud's heat, in the wound's pain, in the battle's first hour.

**The True and the Mindful**

The verdict that closes the verse is double: *it is they who are true, and it is they who are mindful of Allah*. The first word — *ṣadaqū*, they were truthful, they proved sincere — answers a question the verse's own opening raised: who is telling the truth about righteousness? Not the one who points at his direction of prayer but the one whose creed, charity, worship, pledges, and patience are on record. The second — the reverent, the *muttaqūn* — names the quality the whole sūrah has been circling since its second verse, the Book given as guidance to the mindful. The restrictive construction of both clauses ("it is *they*") excludes the counterfeits the passage has just catalogued: the concealers who traded the Book (2:174–176), the far-schismatics, the direction-merchants of righteousness.

The Qur'an's insistence on this virtue runs through its portraits of the prophets — Ismāʿīl, who kept his word to his people — and its laws require the same fidelity of ordinary believers in 5:1 and throughout.
verses.178:
> O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment

**The Three Options of the Heir**

The verse's legal machinery places the homicide's outcome in the hands of the victim's next of kin, with the state holding the sword. Islamic law's developed doctrine gives the heirs three courses: demand retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*), carried out only by the authorities — the verse is understood to exclude vigilantism entirely; accept the blood-money (*diyah*), a monetary composition; or forgive outright. The options are mutually exclusive in practice: once one is executed, the other two are cancelled — an heir who has taken the diyah cannot afterward demand the life, and the reverse holds. Some jurists declined to treat retaliation and blood-money as equal alternatives in cases of clear, intentional homicide, holding that capital punishment must then follow; most left the choice with the heirs. A minority position recorded by Ibn Kathīr allowed the killer himself to refuse the composition and submit to the punishment against the heirs' will. The detailed literature that grew from this verse — direct versus indirect causation, standards of evidence, the manner of execution, the amount and payment schedule of the diyah, the state's role — is the measure of how much jurisprudence one sentence of revelation generated: the schools differ on the branches while the trunk, equivalence with the heir's option of mercy, is common to all.

**The Pardon and the Courteous Payment**

The second sentence legislates the mercy-case in two directions. *If the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian* — the wording is notable: the pardoner is called the offender's *brother*, a term of kinship the law keeps alive at the moment of maximum enmity — then let the pardon be followed honorably and the payment rendered with goodness. The exegetes read the double adverb as binding both parties: the heir who pardoned for money must not harass or inflate, and the offender's side must not delay or diminish; the settlement is to be performed with the courtesy that makes it a reconciliation rather than a truce. And the verse names this arrangement itself a gift: *that is an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy*. The alleviation, as the commentators specify, is the very existence of the blood-money option — that homicide, the gravest of crimes, admits of composition at all. The comparison with the Torah's own retaliation law was drawn by the exegetes: Deuteronomy instructs the eye-for-eye court to show no pity (Deuteronomy 19:21), while the Qur'an's parallel in the sūrah of the Table pairs the same lex talionis — a life for a life, an eye for an eye — with the sentence that whoever waives it charitably finds it an expiation for him (5:45). Rabbinic tradition too incorporated composition into its practice; the Qur'an's contribution is to make the merciful exit explicit, named, and rewarded.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Moral Sequence**

The placement of this legislation is argument. The verse before defined righteousness as creed, costly charity, established prayer, kept pledges, and patience in misfortune, hardship, and battle (2:177); the verse after will give the retaliation's rationale — life in the qiṣāṣ (2:179). Between the definition and the rationale, the sūrah installs the law that most needs both: the killing-law, given to a community of ex-feuders whose patience is about to be legislated for the battlefield. The sequence teaches that the retaliation is not an isolated penalty but a chapter of birr — the kept pledge includes the settlement signed over a grave, and the patience in moments of peril begins with the heir who could take blood and takes money, or who could take money and forgives. The Qur'an's criminal law here is continuous with its ethics: the same heart that gives wealth despite loving it is being asked to give vengeance despite loving that too, and the verse that demands the exchange supplies, in its own title for the arrangement, the reason it can be endured — an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy.
verses.179:
> There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺

The classical commentators measured this verse against the Arabs' own wisest saying on the subject, a proverbial line roughly rendered "killing is what wards off killing" — the ancestral formula the pre-Islamic Arabs considered the summit of legal wisdom.

**People of the Kernels**

The address that follows — *O people of reason*, ūlū al-albāb — is one of the Qur'an's honorifics, and its literal sense is an image: possessors of the *lubb*, the kernel inside the shell. The nut symbolism carries the epistemology: wisdom lies deeper than the surface, and the one who would be nourished by a thing must crack through to its inner truth. The title recurs wherever the Qur'an wants its hardest thinking done — in the pilgrimage's provisions (2:197), in wisdom's gift (2:269), over the verses precise and elusive (3:7), before the signs of the heavens and the earth (3:190), in the stories of the prophets (12:111), and a dozen places more. Its use here is pointed: the law of retaliation is exactly the kind of ruling whose surface — a killing commanded — repels the shell-level gaze, and whose kernel — life multiplied by deterrence, valuation, and limitation — is available only to the reader who cracks it. The verse does not address everyone; it summons the readers capable of holding a paradox, and it makes the holding itself an act of the intellect it honors.

**So That You May Be Mindful**

The verse ends by assigning the law a purpose beyond safety: *so that you may become mindful of Allah* — taqwā, the same end the fast will be given (2:183) and the same quality the bequest-legislation will call an obligation upon the reverent (2:180). The claim is strong: penal law is moral education. A retaliation system run by the state, bounded by equivalence, opened to pardon, and priced at life-for-life trains its community in precisely the dispositions taqwā names — restraint at the moment of rage, deference to a standard above the self, the habit of seeing every act answered. The feud trained the opposite virtues: initiative in vengeance, loyalty to the clan over the truth, escalation as honor. The law replaces the curriculum, and the verse states the pedagogy's goal: not merely a safer Arabia but a God-fearing one. This is also the verse's quiet answer to the objection that severity is unspiritual — the qiṣāṣ is not the enemy of mercy but its infrastructure, since the pardon-option of 2:178 is only meaningful where the right to punish is real; mercy without a sword behind it is not forgiveness but weakness, and the taqwā the verse aims at is built from both instruments, the fixed retaliation and the open pardon, working on the same heart.

**The Whole Arithmetic in One Line**

Read with its predecessor, the verse completes the sūrah's first legislation of blood. 2:178 built the machinery — equivalence against the feud, the heir's three options, the courteous settlement, the punishment of post-settlement transgression — and 2:179 supplies the machinery's reason for existing, so that the law is received not as a code of vengeance sanctioned but as an instrument of life deployed against vengeance. The Torah's own arithmetic is enlisted in the same direction elsewhere in the Qur'an: the ordinance given to the Children of Israel that whoever takes a life unjustly is as if he killed all humanity, and whoever saves a life is as if he saved all humanity (5:32) — the same valuation logic, the same weighting of each life with all lives. The Qur'an's shorter sentence does the same work inside penal law: one life taken is a wound to the whole body, and the measured answer to it is what keeps the whole body alive. The people of the kernels are asked to see it — the killing in the law and the life in the killing — and the seeing is itself the first exercise of the mindfulness the law exists to produce.
verses.180:
> It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**The Deathbed Gets a Law**

The verse uses the sūrah's legislative verb — it is *prescribed*, the same word that set the retaliation (2:178) and will set the fast (2:183) — and applies it to the hour of dying. When death approaches and the dying person leaves *khayr*, something of value, a bequest is to be made for parents and near kin in fairness. The word *khayr* — good — standing alone for property is established Quranic usage: whatever good you spend is for your own sake (2:272); the sūrah of the Chargers describes the human being as fierce in his love of good things, meaning wealth (100:8). The law's trigger is thus twofold: the approach of death and the existence of something to leave. The exegetes read the second condition as limiting the first — the bequest-legislation addresses those who die holding property, and it does not disturb the prior claims on that property, since debts and financial obligations must be discharged from the estate even after death. The verse installs the will as the dying person's last lawful act: a final disposition, bounded by fairness, supervised by the community, and owed to the people closest in blood.

**Parents and Kin, in Fairness**

The beneficiaries are named in an order that carries moral weight: parents first, then the near relatives. The fairness qualifier — *bi-l-maʿrūf*, in what is honorable and fitting — governs both the amounts and the manner, and the early commentators pressed its social edge: bequests are to be made first to relatives and only secondarily to others, and those who left relatives in need while bequeathing property to strangers were severely condemned. The ruling answers a standing temptation of the deathbed — the wish to make a grand gesture to a friend, a teacher, an institution, while the family that will survive the testator inherits poverty. The Qur'an's economy of charity consistently orders the claimants by nearness: the same roster of kinsfolk, orphans, and the poor structures the giving of 2:177 and 2:215 and the kindness-command of 4:36. Fairness here is therefore not equality but proportion to claim — the parent's claim, the child's, the dependent relative's — assessed by the honorableness the word *maʿrūf* denotes: what the community's best judgment recognizes as right, without the need for a schedule.

**The Two Limits the Law Grew**

From this verse the jurists developed the bequest's two famous restrictions, and both have textual anchors. The first: a bequest may not exceed one-third of the estate. The proof-text is the report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (1295): Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, gravely ill in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage and wealthy with only a daughter to inherit, asked the visiting Prophet whether he might give two-thirds of his property in charity — no; half — no; and the Prophet set the ceiling: a third, and even a third is much. Then the reason: it is better to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them poor, begging from people. The second restriction: no bequest may be made in favor of a person who already inherits by the Quranic shares — the widely transmitted prophetic saying "there is no bequest for an heir." Together the two rules protect the fixed inheritance system from the deathbed's affections and grudges: the shares of 4:11–12 stand untouched by wills, and the will's own space — the third, the non-heir — is preserved for exactly the cases the shares cannot reach.

**Before the Shares: The Arabian Background**

The verse also marks a transition in property history. Before the Quranic legislation, Arabian inheritance was agnatic — the male line took the estate, with custom excluding women and minors from succession entirely. The Quranic shares reorganized the field around fixed quotas for named relatives, including the women the custom had passed over: the male's share twice the female's, the daughter's half or two-thirds, the parents' sixths, the spouses' quarters and eighths (4:11–12) — all disbursed, as those verses repeatedly insist, *after the fulfilment of bequests and debts*, which is this verse's institution embedded in the arithmetic. Within that architecture the bequest of 2:180 holds its office: the testator's personal word, operating in the third, reaching the people and purposes the fixed shares do not name — the law's provision for the dying heart, fenced so it cannot trample the heirs.
verses.181:
> But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**The Sin Transferred**

The verse legislates for the moment after the deathbed: the will has been made, heard, and recorded, and the testator is gone. If anyone now alters it, the sin of the alteration falls *only* on those who altered — the wording is exclusive and deliberate. The transfer answers a question the situation itself raises: when a bequest is changed, whose account carries the wrong? Not the dead man's — his act was completed in fairness or in its absence, and the verse of exception that follows (2:182) shows the law's concern for his possible fault separately. Not the heirs who suffer from the change — they are its objects, not its agents. The sin attaches to the changer and stays there, undistributed: the executors who adjusted a figure, the witnesses who "remembered" different terms, the relatives who intercepted a bequest before it could operate. Al-Qurṭubī's reading of the verse establishes the rule's shape: a bequest validly made cannot be altered — the dead man's word acquires, at his death, a legal inviolability, and the living hands that touch it take on the whole of the touching's guilt.

**Hearing as the Trigger of Responsibility**

The condition in the verse — *after hearing it* — is not incidental but constitutive. The alteration condemned is the knowing one: the changer heard the will, from the testator's mouth or the witnesses' attestation, and then changed what he had heard. Hearing creates custody; custody creates the duty of fidelity; the change breaches both. The same structure governs the bequest's attestation in the sūrah of the Table, where two just men are to be called as witnesses when death approaches (5:106) — the institution exists precisely so that the hearing is official, the will is not a private whisper, and any later alteration is provably against a heard text. The verse by this protects the dying in the only way law can protect the dead: by deputizing the living. The witnesses, the executors, everyone within earshot of the bequest become its custodians, and the sin-clause tells them that custody is not honorary. What was heard must be delivered; the delivery is now their act, and its corruption is their sin alone.

**What the Verse Does Not Forbid**

The prohibition has a boundary the jurists drew carefully, and the boundary completes the law rather than weakening it. Al-Qurṭubī distinguished altering a valid bequest from correcting an invalid one: a bequest is not protected by this verse when it was itself unlawful, and such a bequest can be cancelled or modified without incurring the sin. The two examples he gives define the category — a bequest exceeding the third is reduced to the third; a bequest directing something forbidden, such as the gifting of wine, is nullified. The principle underneath is that the verse guards the testator's *lawful* word, not his wordlessness before the law: a will is inviolable inside the boundaries the previous verse set (the third, the non-heir, the fairness), and outside them it carries no protection, because the dead have no right to command sin. This reading is what connects 2:181 to its successor: the changer condemned here alters a bequest against the heirs' rights for his own ends, while the intervener excused there alters a bequest that was itself engineered against those rights. Same physical act — changing the will — opposite moral valence, distinguished entirely by which direction justice runs.

**All-Hearing of the Quiet Crime**

The verse closes with the two names, and their fit to the case is exact. The bequest is among the quietest of legal events: spoken on a deathbed, heard by two or three, committed to memory or a private page, and then tested at a moment when its author cannot testify. The alteration is quieter still — a number adjusted, a name omitted, a document lost, a witness persuaded — performed precisely where human oversight is thinnest, since the one person who could say *that is not what I said* is beyond saying anything. The names do the evidentiary work the case cannot otherwise have: the crime of altering a bequest is almost perfectly concealable from people and perfectly unconcealable from God, so the verse's deterrence is the same one the concealment-passages used (2:174) — the surveillance that survives every witness's death.
verses.182:
> Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Exception That Guards the Exception**

The previous verse made the will inviolable and charged every alteration to the alterer; this verse opens the one door through which alteration may lawfully pass. Whoever *fears* — suspects, apprehends, has ground to worry — an error or an injustice *from the testator himself*, and then sets matters right between the parties, carries no sin. The structure is deliberate and rare: a prohibition (2:181) immediately qualified by its necessary exception (2:182), so that the law's severity against changers cannot become a shield for a corrupt will. The sin the previous verse assigned to the changer is here lifted from the corrector, and the distinction between the two actors is the verse's entire content. Both change the document; one changes it against justice for gain and bears the sin alone; the other changes it toward justice against a wrongful instrument and bears none. The verse thus completes the bequest-legislation by installing a remedy inside the rule — the dead man's word is protected, but only insofar as his word was just.

**The Duty of the Living**

The correction the verse authorizes is not optional housekeeping but a communal obligation. Al-Qurṭubī states it as a communal charge: where a will's evident purpose is to sidestep the Quran's fixed shares of inheritance, the community must revise or void it. The actors are named with legal precision: *between them* refers to the heirs; *him* — the one who fears and sets right — is the trustee administering the will, its attesting witnesses (5:106), or whoever holds the charge, though some readings place the initiative with the heirs themselves. The no-sin clause then explains itself against the general rule: altering a will would ordinarily incur the sin of 2:181, but here equity outranks the dead man's directive — the correction is not alteration in the forbidden sense because it does not defeat the dead man's lawful word; it defeats his unlawful one, on behalf of the very system his word attempted to outmaneuver. Al-Rāzī's formulation gives the principle its edge: the corrector acts *for* the testator's real interest and *for* the heirs' right simultaneously, and a change that serves both against a documented injustice is the law repairing itself, not a person overriding the law.

**The Names That Close the Triad**

The bequest-legislation ends where it began, with mercy named: Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The two names do specific work here. Forgiveness covers the testator — the man whose will erred or inclined, who perhaps repented too late or never knew his bequest was janaf; the verse corrects his instrument without adding his sin to the changers' accounts, and the forgiveness named leaves his case with God rather than with the estate. And forgiveness covers the corrector — the executor who must judge a dead man's intentions, who may fear wrongly, who may adjust a will that was innocent after all; the no-sin clause is generous precisely because the judgment is hard, and the merciful names assure the hesitant intervener that an honest correction made in fear of injustice stands under pardon even where his fear proved mistaken. The triad of verses thus closes as a complete legal-moral unit: the command to bequeath in fairness (2:180), the protection of the bequest against the greedy living (2:181), and the correction of the bequest against the unjust dead (2:182) — each guarded from the abuse its own emphasis invites, and all three framed by the same names.
verses.183:
> O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺

**The Third Kutiba**

The verse begins with the sūrah's legislative formula — *kutiba ʿalaykum*, it is written upon you, it is prescribed — the same verb that established the retaliation in cases of murder (2:178), and the formula carries the same weight here: fasting is not recommended, not ancestral custom, not a spiritual option; it is written. The obligation it creates became, in its final form, the fast of Ramadan, counted by all the schools of law among the five pillars of Islam: complete abstinence from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn until sunset, across every day of the lunar month. The verse that prescribes it is addressed to the believers specifically — O you who believe — where the food permission had gone out to all humanity (2:168); the fast belongs to the covenant community, and its prescription dates, the exegetical sources record, to shortly before the Battle of Badr, in the second year of the Hijrah — the same season of legislation that gave the community its qiblah. A people turned toward the Kaʿbah, given its murder-law and its wills-law, now receives the law of its months: the body itself enters the legislation.

**So That You May Become Mindful**

The purpose clause names the fast's product: taqwā — mindfulness, reverence, the guarded consciousness of God that the sūrah has made the end of every law it legislates. The retaliation was given so that the community might become mindful (2:179); the bequest is an obligation on the mindful (2:180); and the fast is prescribed so that perhaps the fasting will produce the same quality. The fit between the discipline and the goal is exact, and it is why the verse needs no elaboration. Taqwā is the state of a person whose actions are governed by an unseen standard — who abstains from what he could take because a Presence he cannot see forbids it. Fasting is that state rendered physical and continuous: for the whole bright day, with food in reach and appetite intact, the fasting person abstains from what is otherwise lawful to him, and no observer can tell whether he is fasting — the discipline's compliance is invisible, its inspection internal.

**The Hunger That Teaches**

The pedagogy of the fast runs through the body, and the verse's prescription takes the whole body as its classroom. Hunger and thirst are the two appetites no human can argue with; for one lunar month the believer argues with them anyway, daily, and wins by abstention rather than satisfaction. The training generalizes immediately: the appetite that is refused at noon is the same faculty that must refuse the forbidden morsel of 2:168, the bribed judge of 2:188, the illicit gain of 2:174 — the fast is a rehearsal of every refusal the law will later demand, performed in the easiest case, where the refused thing is lawful and only the hour forbids it. The tradition drew the same conclusion from the fast's effects on speech and temper, requiring the fasting person to abstain from false and idle talk as well as food, so that the discipline covers the tongue and the appetite together. This is taqwā being manufactured: not the abstract reverence of doctrine but the drilled reflex of a body that has learned, thirty times running, that a command can stand between it and its desire — and a body that has learned this in the small case is being prepared for the large ones the sūrah is about to legislate, on the battlefield where appetite's cousin, fear, will make the same demands in the opposite direction.

**A Community Between Two Laws**

The verse's placement completes a legislative triptych that defines the new community from three sides. Blood was regulated — the feud replaced by equivalence, pardon, and mercy (2:178–179). Property was regulated — the deathbed governed by fairness, custody, and correction (2:180–182). Now the body is regulated — appetite governed by the month, the day, and the unseen standard of taqwā. The three laws answer the three domains in which human societies destroy themselves: violence, wealth, and desire; and the same purpose-clause runs through all three, so that you may be mindful. The fast is the triptych's central panel in a further sense — it is the one discipline every believer performs personally and daily, the retaliation being the rare case and the bequest the final one, and it therefore carries the community's moral formation through the ordinary month rather than the exceptional event. Between the sūrah's food permissions and its coming war-legislation, this verse installs the training ground: a people learning, one hunger at a time, that what God has written upon them is written for what it makes of them — and what it is making here, the verse says in its last word, is the reverent.
verses.184:
> ˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew

**The Days, Numbered**

The verse opens by describing the fast as *numbered days* — ayyām maʿdūdāt — and the commentators divided over what those days first named. One reading, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, identifies them with the days of Ramadan itself, the verse being a compact statement of the month-fast with its exemptions. The other reading identifies an earlier, shorter obligation: before Ramadan was legislated, the community is reported to have kept three days of fasting each month along with the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ, the tenth of Muḥarram — and this verse, on that account, prescribed those numbered days, with the Ramadan-verses that follow superseding them. The ʿĀshūrāʾ practice is well attested: the reports describe the Muslims fasting the tenth of Muḥarram, with some connecting it to the Jews' fast on that day, others to the day Noah's ark came to rest on the mountain. Al-Bukhārī preserves the decisive exchange (2004): the Prophet came to Medina and found the Jews fasting ʿĀshūrāʾ because it was the day God saved the Children of Israel from Pharaoh, for which Moses fasted in gratitude — and he answered, *we have more right to Moses than you*, fasting the day himself and commanding the fast (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2004). The numbering matters for another reason: a fast of counted days is a fast with an end, and the Qur'an's first word about the discipline is that its duration is finite, bounded, and known in advance — the ease-theme of the whole legislation stated in its opening noun.

**Those Who Can Bear It Only With Difficulty**

The third clause — *and upon those who can bear it only with difficulty is a redemption: the feeding of a poor person* — was read in two directions, and both readings are classical. The first, reported from the early community and recorded by al-Qurṭubī, treats the clause as an original option: in the fast's earliest legislation, whoever wished could feed a poor person for each day and not fast at all — a concession later withdrawn by the Ramadan-command that whoever is present in the month should fast it (2:185), which abrogated the choice and left the feeding only for those incapable. The second reading, which al-Qurṭubī preferred on the grammar, finds no abrogation: the root ṭ-w-q here denotes the ones who bear the fast with hardship rather than the ones who merely could but need not — the chronically ill whose condition will not lift, the elderly whose strength is spent — and for them the feeding of a poor person per day is not a purchased exemption but the substitute duty their incapacity creates. On this reading the makeup-days clause covers the temporarily unable, and this clause covers the permanently unable, and the two together leave no body without a law. The grammar that supports it is the reading's own evidence: the difficult-bearing are those for whom the fast remains possible but punishing, and the verse prices that punishment at a meal.

**Whoever Volunteers More**

The clause that follows — whoever volunteers good, it is better for him — was explained by al-Qurṭubī in two concrete directions. The volunteer may feed more than the minimum: a poor person for each day becomes two, and the extra is his own merit. Or he may keep feeding beyond the redemption, giving the poor even when the law's requirement is already discharged. The voluntariness is the verse's hinge between duty and virtue: the feeding is fixed at one poor person per day, but the good above the fixed amount is welcomed without limit, and the verdict on it is unambiguous — it is better. The same verse by this answers a question the exemption system always raises: whether concessions cheapen devotion. They do not; they relocate it. The one who cannot fast feeds; the one who feeds beyond the requirement has taken the fast's inner logic — hunger transferred into generosity — further than the fasting itself would have. The law's floor is exact, and above the floor the verse opens the voluntary ascent that the whole sūrah's charity-legislation has been describing since the spending-verses of its opening.
verses.185:
> Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful

**The Month Defined by Its Book**

The verse names the month and defines it — not by its fast but by its revelation. Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, as guidance for humanity, with the clear signs and the criterion. The priority of this definition is the verse's first lesson: the month is sacred because of what entered the world through it, and the fast is the human response to that entry, not its cause. The exegetes described the descent in two stages, following the Qur'an's own accounts elsewhere: the Book was sent down in its entirety to the guarded tablet in heaven — the preserved original of 85:22 — and thence to the lowest heaven of this world, from which the angel Gabriel brought it to the Prophet passage by passage, occasion by occasion, across twenty-three years. The month's connection to that descent is fixed by the Night of Power within it — the night better than a thousand months, on which the sending down occurred (97:1–2) — so that every Ramadan reenacts, in its fast and its recitation, the month the Book arrived. The believers do not merely fast in Ramadan; they fast in the anniversary of revelation, and the traditional month-long recitation of the whole Qur'an in the night prayers keeps the definition audible.

**Guidance, Clear Signs, Criterion**

The three descriptors the verse gives the Book map the ways a revelation guides. *Hudan* — guidance — is direction itself, the road named. *Bayyināt* — the clear signs, the manifest proofs — are the evidence along the road, the verses and demonstrations that make the direction recognizable as true rather than merely asserted. *Furqān* — the criterion, the separator — is the instrument of judgment, the standard by which right is distinguished from wrong, case by case. The same triad describes revelation's function throughout the Qur'an, and its presence here explains why the month of the Book is kept by the body: a criterion is not only read but practiced, and the fast is the practice in which the separation between the lawful and the forbidden is felt hourly — the morsel permitted at sunset and forbidden at noon is furqān made edible. The verse thus ties the month's two contents together: the Book that separates truth from falsehood, and the fast that trains the will in every smaller separation, so that the community holding both learns the criterion with its mind in the recitation and with its hunger in the day.

**Ease Intended, Not Hardship**

The reason clause is among the most-quoted sentences in Islamic legal literature: *God desires ease for you, and does not desire hardship for you*. The clause is not decoration; it is a hermeneutic key the jurists applied across the law. The exemptions of illness and journey are instances of the desired ease — the same Lawgiver who commanded the fast removed it from the bodies it would harm, and the removal is as much His will as the command. The principle generalizes: no hardship is laid upon you in the religion (22:78), and the Prophet's standing instruction to his envoys was to make things easy and not difficult, to give glad tidings and not drive people away. The verse by this installs mercy inside the legislation's logic — the fast is severe and the severity is bounded by the same hand, so the believer receives both the discipline and its limits as one gift. This is why the exemptions are not experienced as loopholes in the tradition but as evidence: the concession proves the Legislator's intent, and the intent explains why the obligated fast is undertaken joyfully rather than resentfully. A law whose author has declared that He desires ease is a law whose every harshness carries its own measured scope.
verses.186:
> When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺

**The Answer Without "Say"**

The verse carries a structural distinction visible on the page of the Qur'an itself. The sūrah is full of questions routed through the Prophet — they ask you about the new moons, *say*… (2:189); they ask you what they should spend, *say*… (2:215); they ask you about fighting in the sacred month, *say*… (2:217); they ask you about wine, about orphans, about the Hour — each time the answer is handed to the Prophet to deliver, the command *qul* interposed between question and reply. Here alone in the sequence, when the servants ask about God Himself, the *say* is absent: the verse moves directly from the question to *I am near* — God answering in His own person, without the prophetic relay. The commentators marked the difference and read it as intimacy legislated into the syntax: on every other subject the revelation speaks about God; on this one God speaks. The servant who asks where his Lord is receives not information transmitted but presence declared, and the first-person voice — *innī*, I, am — is itself the answer's content. The nearness is not a fact about God reported by a prophet; it is God's own word in the moment of asking.

**I Answer the Call of the Caller**

The declaration expands into a promise with the structure of reciprocity: when My servants call, I answer — *I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me*. The same promise grounds the Qur'an's great invitation elsewhere: call upon Me, I will respond to you (40:60); and its most urgent case is named in the sūrah of the Ants — who answers the distressed when he calls upon Him (27:62). The answering here is unconditional in form: the caller calls, and the response is given; no merit-clause qualifies it, no worthiness-test precedes it. The tradition supplied the mechanics of what answering means — the request granted, or averted evil substituted for it, or reward stored against the Day — but the verse's own claim is the bare reciprocity: the call does not fall into silence. The servants who asked *where* are told *how*: not at a place, but in the responding.

**Be Kind to Yourselves: The Voice and the Shout**

The nearness-verse generated one of the tradition's most practical corrections. Al-Bukhārī preserves the scene (6384): on a journey, the people raised their voices in proclamation and supplication until the Prophet called out — *O people, be kind to yourselves; you are not calling one who is deaf or absent — you are calling the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, and He is nearer to you than the neck of your riding animal*. The report applies this verse to volume: the shout assumes a distance the verse denies. If God is near, hearing, and seeing, then the raised voice does not improve delivery — it only exhausts the caller, and the exhaustion is the unkindness to the self the Prophet named. The correction reeducates the worshiper's imagination: prayer is not transmission across a gap but address to a Presence, and the Presence requires neither amplification nor repetition to hear. This is why the Qur'an's own instruction on the manner of calling pairs humility with secrecy — call upon your Lord humbly and in secret (7:55) — and why the tradition prized the silent dhikr and the night's whispered prayer: not because God hears them better, but because they confess what the loud prayer forgets — that the One called upon is already near, already hearing, already answering.

**Nearer Than the Vein**

The nearness declared here has a whole geography elsewhere in the Qur'an, and the verse is its legal center. God is closer to the human being than his jugular vein (50:16) — nearer than the body's own instrument of life; closer than the people between whom and their hearts He intervenes (8:24); and at the hour of death closer still — when the soul reaches the throat, We are nearer to him than you, though you do not see (56:85). The nearness has its eschatological form too: David's repentance was sealed with nearness and a beautiful return (38:25), and the Garden's own inhabitants are addressed by the name that repeats it — peace be upon you for your patience, the near ones. And the name itself, *al-Qarīb*, the Ever Near, stands among the divine names, paired with the All-Hearing in the very verses of this sūrah's Abraham-passages (34:50). Set against this constellation, the servants' question about location reads as the perennial human mistake — imagining transcendence as absence — and the verse's answer as its permanent correction: the God above the throne is the God nearer than the vein, and the fasting servant's whispered call travels a distance of zero.
verses.187:
> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**The Rule and Its Early Hardship**

The verse legislates by easing, and the reports behind it describe what was eased. In the fast's first years the night was not free: food and marital relations were permitted only until the night prayer, after which the fast effectively began — one school of reports even describing abstinence through the entire month's nights, with the concession coming only in response to the community's failure to keep it. The case the tradition names most often is ʿUmar's: he confessed to the Prophet that he had approached his wife after the night prayer, and the answer came that he had not been firm in holding to the original restriction — a rebuke accompanied by relief, since the verse that followed made the whole night lawful.

**Seek What God Has Ordained**

The permission is then enlarged: be with them now, and seek what God has ordained for you. The exegetes read the seeking in two directions, both rooted in the word's usage. It is the seeking of children — the marital night open to the generation the fast's daytime rule suspends, the ordinance of progeny continuing its course through the holy month. And it is the seeking of the Night of Power within those same nights — the night better than a thousand months, on which the Qur'an was sent down (97:1), sought by the worshiper in the month's latter part even as the marriage keeps its rights in the month's every night. The double reading composes the verse's vision of Ramadan's darkness: it is not a void between fasted days but a field of ordained goods — the children conceived, the night-prayer kept, the decree-night watched for — and the concession that freed the night for the marriage freed it for all of these at once. The wording *what God has ordained for you* keeps the emphasis where the easing placed it: the night's goods are not tolerations of the flesh but ordinances of the Lawgiver, licensed from the same hand that licensed the day's abstinence, so that the believer moves between the two without contradiction — the fast's discipline by daylight, the ordainment's warmth by dark, both commanded, both worship.

**The White Thread and the Black Thread**

The verse's most famous detail fixes the fast's beginning: eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct from the black thread of night. The idiom — the two threads as the first light against the last dark — was initially taken literally by some Companions, and al-Bukhārī preserves the case of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim (1917): he placed a black cord and a white cord under his pillow and watched them through the night, unable to tell one from the other, until the Prophet explained that the verse means the darkness of night and the whiteness of dawn. The report does double duty. It documents the community's scrupulosity — a man watching cords rather than guess at his fast's boundary — and it models the Qur'an's idiom being read as idiom: the threads are the horizon's two colors, not two objects, and the distinction is the true dawn's lateral spreading light against the night. The other reports of the verse's descent add the phenomenon's detail: the light of dawn appearing in the sky, the tops of mountains and houses catching illumination, the white thread emerging from the black. The resulting law is the fast's daily architecture — from true dawn to sunset, the boundary marked by light itself, so that every fasting community reads its obligation off its own sky, and ʿAdī's cords remain the tradition's emblem of literalism corrected by the Prophet's own exegesis.
verses.188:
> Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin

**Wealth Gets Its Food-Law**

The verse arrives between the fast-legislation and the war-legislation, and its position is its argument: after the month that trains the body to refuse lawful food at forbidden hours, the sūrah legislates the permanent refusal — wealth that may never be consumed at any hour, by anyone, however lawfully it is served. The mutuality matters: *between you* makes the property of every member of the community sacred to every other, and the verse by this completes the food-legislation it follows — 2:168–169 commanded eating of the lawful and the good and forbade the steps of Satan; this verse extends the same lawfulness from the plate to the purse.

**The Ruling That Cannot Make Lawful**

From that gloss grows the verse's central legal-moral doctrine: the separation of legal title from moral right. A court decides on evidence and procedure; it can be deceived, out-lawyered, or bought; and when it is, its judgment transfers possession but not entitlement. The tradition's proof-text is the report al-Bukhārī preserves from Umm Salamah (2680): the Prophet said — *I am only a human being, and people bring their disputes to me; some of you may be more eloquent in argument than others, so I may judge in favor of the one whose eloquence prevails. If I give someone what is in truth another's right, I am only giving him a piece of the Fire — let him not take it.* The hadith universalizes the verse's case: the judge is human, the eloquent litigant may win unjustly, and the prophetic verdict converts the ill-gotten award into its substance — fire, the same conversion 2:174 applied to the concealers' gain and 4:10 to the devourers of orphans' property. The briber of 2:188 has purchased exactly this: a favorable ruling that is, before God, a coal. The verse and the report together establish that the law's outer verdict and the soul's inner standing run on separate tracks, and the bribe is the attempt — always futile on the second track — to make the first serve the second's crimes.

**The Corruption of the Instrument**

The clause indicts more than the briber, and the tradition read it that way. A judicial system that can be proffered wealth is a system whose officers are for sale, and the Qur'an's legislation against bribery has its counterpart in its legislation of judges — the sūrah of the Table's command to judge by what God has sent down and its portrait of those who judge by other than it (5:44–45), the sūrah's own instruction that disputes be brought to God and the Messenger rather than managed privately. The bribe's social damage exceeds its private crime: each purchased verdict teaches the community that verdicts are purchasable, and the teaching destroys the instrument that 2:178–179 had just made the alternative to the feud. The retaliation-law replaced blood-vendetta with courts; the courts exist only while their judgments are trusted to track justice rather than money. The briber therefore commits a double betrayal — of the neighbor whose portion he covets and of the system whose integrity his neighbors' lives depend on — and the verse's placement immediately after the qiṣāṣ and bequest legislation is exact: blood regulated, wills regulated, and now the regulator itself, the court, fenced against the wealth that would capture it.

**Knowing as the Aggravator**

The last words of the verse deserve final weight, because they mark its difference from the errors of property the law also governs. Islamic jurisprudence legislates extensively for honest dispute — contested inheritances, unclear contract terms, mistaken boundaries — and provides courts precisely for cases where knowledge is genuinely divided. This verse is not addressed to those cases. Its target is the taker who *knows*: the claimant aware that the portion is another's, the briber certain his eloquence is purchasing what he has no right to. The knowledge clause strips the crime's usual camouflage — the self-narratives of entitlement, the *it's complicated*, the *technically I'm owed* — and leaves the act naked: a knowing hand, reaching past a known line, using the law's own instruments to do it. The same clause explains the verse's severity of framing: sins of ignorance are the ones repentance most readily reaches, and the sūrah has legislated repentance generously (2:160, 2:182); the knowing consumption of another's wealth is the sin committed with the conscience fully briefed, and its only remedy is the piece of Fire's return — restoring the portion before the verdict of the higher court, where no eloquence prevails and every ruling tracks the truth.
verses.189:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful

**The Question and the Redirect**

The verse follows the sūrah's familiar question-form — they ask you — and its answer performs a characteristic move: it declines the question as posed and answers the need behind it. The reports about what was actually being asked vary — some describe curiosity about the moon's waxing and waning, its physical mechanics; others describe a practical inquiry about the new moons' function — but the answer is the same in every case: *they are means of timing for people, and for the pilgrimage*. The redirect is the verse's method. Speculation about the celestial mechanism is not forbidden, but it is not what the community needs legislated; what it needs is to know what the moons are *for*, and the verse supplies the for: the religious calendar. The same pattern governs the sūrah's other question-verses — the inquiry about spending answered with the list of recipients (2:215), the inquiry about the sacred month answered with the hierarchy of sins (2:217) — revelation answering in the register of practice rather than theory, turning every question toward the life it must govern. The moon asked about as an object is answered as an instrument, and the instrument's user is the worshiper.

**Timing and Pilgrimage: The Calendar Built**

The two functions the verse names — timing for people, and the pilgrimage — cover the religious year's architecture. The lunar months order everything the community must date: Ramadan's fast begins with a crescent and ends with a crescent (2:185's completing of the number); the hajj belongs to months appointed (2:197), whose first is another sighting; the ʿīds, the zakāh-year, the ʿiddah of widows and divorced women (2:234), the months of the truce and the sacred months — all run on the hilāl's arithmetic. The pilgrimage is named separately because it is the calendar's summit: the one act of worship whose timing is collective and continental, drawing every community's sighting into a single convergence at a single place in a single month. By making the moons the means of both daily timing and the great gathering, the verse installs the sky itself as the community's clock and its compass-measure of seasons — a calendar not legislated by priests nor adjusted by rulers but posted monthly on the western horizon, where the herdsman reads it as reliably as the astronomer. The answer to the questioners is thus larger than the question: the moon they wondered at is the instrument by which the entire worship-life of the ummah keeps its appointments with God.

**The Spiritual Reading: Houses and Their Doors**

The Sufi exegetes, with Ibn ʿAjība at their head here, read the clause as the allegory its concreteness invites: everything in the religious life is a house with an appointed door, and the house is not entered by its back. Ibn ʿAjība's schema names the three houses and their nine doors — the house of the sharīʿah, entered by repentance, obedience, and reverence; the house of the ṭarīqah, by sincerity, purification, and virtuous character; the house of the ḥaqīqah, by concentration, contemplation, and gnosis. The principle generalizes beyond the schema: the knowledge that comes without its discipline of study, the spiritual station sought without its obedience, the intimacy with God attempted without the prayer He appointed — each is the back wall, and each fails for the same reason the Yathrib climber's scruple failed: it approaches a true destination by an unappointed route, mistaking the difficulty of the approach for its legitimacy.

**Enter by the Doors, and Be Mindful**

The closing commands gather both halves of the verse into one ethic. *Enter the houses by their doors* is the general principle extracted from the specific practice — appointed means for appointed ends, the lawful route however plain against the dramatic shortcut. *And be mindful of God, that you may prosper* attaches the principle to the sūrah's governing virtue and its governing promise: taqwā as the way, success — falāḥ — as the end, the same pairing the sūrah's opening gave its very first description of the guided (2:5). The two halves of the verse now read as one lesson in two registers. The moon: a wonder asked about as spectacle, answered as instrument — the celestial body's meaning is its function in the worshiper's calendar. The door: a scruple performed as extra-devotion, answered as error — the threshold's meaning is its appointment by the Lawgiver. In both cases the verse disciplines religious imagination toward obedience: not what seems marvelous (the moon's phases, the wall's ascent) but what has been made a means (the timing, the door). The questioners who came asking about the sky are sent home with a calendar and a doorway, and the verse's last word promises that the homecoming — through the door, by the months, in mindfulness — is where the prospering lives.
verses.190:
> Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors

**The First Permission, and the Dispute About It**

This verse opens the sūrah's legislation of war, and the tradition debated whether it opens the Qur'an's.
