The exegetes record the question directly: is this the first verse revealed permitting the Muslims to fight, or does that priority belong to the sūrah of the Pilgrimage's permission — granted to those being fought, for they have been wronged (22:39)? The reports supporting each are given, and al-Ṭabarī declines to decide, finding the narrations insufficiently conclusive — a characteristic exercise of his evidentiary discipline. What the verse's own context supplies is the setting: the reports of occasion place it in the period of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when the Prophet and his Companions set out for the ʿumrah unarmed and were turned back, and the settlement's terms left the community's relationship to Meccan violence unresolved. The legislation that follows addresses a people who have been persecuted, expelled, and fought for thirteen years, who have just been barred from their own sanctuary by treaty rather than battle — and the first word of the war-law to such a people is a limitation, not a license: fight *those who fight you*.

**In the Cause of God**

The command's first phrase sets the war's final cause: fight *in the path of God*. The formula excludes every other motive the Arabian battlefield offered — tribal honor, booty as end, vengeance as appetite, prestige as currency — and names the one legitimate aim: the cause that is God's, which the surrounding verses will define as the ending of persecution and the securing of worship (2:193). The cause-clause is thus the verse's first limit and its most comprehensive: a war fought in God's path is answerable to God's stated ends, and any operation serving another end has left the permission even if it keeps the vocabulary.

**Do Not Exceed the Limits**

The second command is the verse's famous prohibition: *do not transgress* — the iʿtidāʾ whose forms the tradition enumerated. The exegetes read the non-transgression as governing every excess the reciprocity could invite: killing beyond the combatants, retaliation beyond the injury, pursuit beyond the need — and the Qur'an's own parallel legislation of retaliation states the standard it applies here: if you retaliate, retaliate with the like of what was done to you (16:126); the recompense of evil is evil like it (42:40). The verse's closing names the divine disposition toward the excess: God does not love the transgressors — the same formula the food-legislation used of the wasters (2:168) and the sūrah will use again, marking transgression not merely as forbidden but as forfeiting love. The prohibition's placement is the verse's structural point: the permission to fight and the ban on exceeding it arrive in one breath, so the community never holds the license without holding its limit. Every war-law that follows — the Sacred Mosque's clause, the persecution's ranking, the cease-fire's acceptance — is the working-out of these two clauses together: fight the fighters, and fight them within bounds.

**The Verse Beside Its Neighbors**

Read against the Qur'an's wider peace-legislation, the verse's limits show their framework. The sūrah of the Examined Woman distinguishes the two populations precisely along this verse's line: God does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who did not fight you over religion nor expel you from your homes — God loves the just (60:8); what is forbidden is alliance only with those who fought and expelled and abetted (60:9). The peace-orientation is legislated independently: if they incline to peace, incline to it (8:61); the good-and-evil asymmetry of the sūrah of Explained in Detail commands repelling evil with what is better, until the enemy becomes as an intimate friend (41:34); and the patience-counsel to the Prophet himself is to bear what they say and depart from them courteously (73:10), with the reminder that he is not there to compel anyone (88:22). Against this background 2:190 is not an isolated permission but a bounded exception inside a scripture whose default is patience, kindness to the non-fighting, and peace when peace is offered — the exception's boundaries drawn by reciprocity and non-transgression, and its exercise governed by the cause that alone makes it God's.
verses.191:
> Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers

**Fitnah Is Greater Than Killing**

The verse's central declaration — *fitnah is greater than killing* — supplies the war's moral calculus, and the word's meaning here is fixed by the context and the exegetes together: fitnah as persecution, as the trial inflicted on believers to make them abandon their religion — torture, expulsion, the pressure that produced the martyrs of Mecca and the Hijrah itself. Some commentators read the word here in its sharpest sense as persecution culminating in shirk — the forcing of idolatry, the greater killing, which is the killing of the soul's allegiance. The declaration's logic is comparative and consequentialist in the precise sense: killing is terrible, and the verse does not soften it; but the campaign to destroy faith itself — the fitnah the Quraysh had conducted for thirteen years — is worse than the killing that resistance to it entails. The sūrah restates the same ranking in its sacred-month legislation: fighting in the sacred month is great, but barring people from God's path, disbelieving in Him, and expelling the Mosque's people is greater with God, and fitnah is greater than killing (2:217). The two statements together form the war-law's foundational weighing: the injury that justifies war is not death inflicted but faith attacked — and the permission to kill exists to end the greater killing.

**The Sacred Mosque's Regime**

The second half of the verse legislates the sanctuary: do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they fight you there; if they fight you there, fight them. The clause is the war-law's sharpest particular limitation, and its background is the sūrah's own: the Mosque's inviolability had been established in the Abraham-legislation (2:125–126), its security made a divine endowment, and the Hudaybiyyah context of these verses meant the community was currently barred from it by treaty — a people with every grievance and a standing permission to fight, legislated now to keep their swords sheathed at the very site of their exclusion. The regime the clause builds is conditional to the point of passivity: at the Sacred Mosque the believers may not start combat at all; the permission activates only inside an attack already begun there.

**Where the Permission Stops**

The verse's limits become fully visible against the Qur'an's asylum legislation. The sūrah of Repentance, dealing with the same post-war population, commands: if anyone of the idolaters seeks your protection, protect him until he hears the word of God, then deliver him to his place of safety (9:6) — the enemy not merely spared but escorted, given the hearing he fought against, and returned safe to his home. The same population the battlefield verse addresses is thus covered, outside battle, by a law of refuge; and the reports' prohibitions on killing non-combatants fence the battlefield itself. Read as one system, the permission of these verses reaches only the fighting enemy, in the fighting, without transgression (2:190), with the sanctuary held out of the war unless the war enters it, and with asylum, safety, and peace legislated at every margin — the moment the enemy inclines to peace, the whole apparatus stands down (8:61). The verse that sounds, in isolation, like the war-law's hardest sentence is in fact its tightest channel: killing permitted where persecution made killing the lesser evil, expulsion permitted where expulsion was the injury answered, the Mosque protected even against the justified army, and every exit from the fighting left open and commanded.

**The Recompense Named**

The verse's last phrase — such is the recompense of the disbelievers — attaches the counter-fighting at the sanctuary to a category the sūrah has used consistently: the punishment that is the crime's own shape returned. The disbelievers who made the Sacred Mosque an instrument of persecution — barring its worshippers from it (2:217), using its sanctity to shield their aggression — receive, when they fight there, the fighting they chose: the protection they violated withdrawn, the retaliation they invited arriving at the exact site and in the exact form of their violation. The phrase is judicial rather than vengeful: the recompense is described as theirs by right of their own act, the same structure the retaliation-law gave the murderer (a life for the life taken) and the transgressor after settlement (2:178). And it is bounded by that structure — the recompense of the fighters at the Mosque is the fighting at the Mosque, and no further: not their families, not the sanctuary's desecration, not the excess the previous verse named unloved by God. The verse ends, as it began, inside its limits: the permission specific, the sanctuary honored even in its violation, the fitnah named as the evil that outranks killing, and the recompense measured to the crime — the whole passage a war-law written, line by line, against the war it legislates for.
verses.192:
> But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Forgiveness Offered to the Persecutors**

The names at the verse's end do specific work against the specific enemy addressed. These were not neutral belligerents: they had tortured the early believers, boycotted their clan, driven them from their homes, killed some and apostatized others, barred them from the Sacred Mosque, and fought them at it. The verse that offers them God's forgiveness when they cease is offering, in practice, the pardon of everything the war-legislation just described — and it is the same forgiveness the sūrah extended to the concealers who repent (2:160), to the eaters of usury who desist (2:275, in the legislation ahead), to the wrongdoers who return. The Qur'an's economy of pardon is uniform: the sin is named at its full weight, and the door is left open at its full width, and the two statements never cancel each other. The fighters of 2:190–191 are addressed at full weight — the killing permitted against them, the expulsion answered, the fitnah ranked above murder — and the door is then opened by two divine names, so that the passage's last word about the enemy, before the war's object is stated, is not the sword but the mercy. A war-law that ends its permission in forgiveness is legislating the war as a means whose end is peace with the enemy himself, not merely peace from him.

**The Mercy That Precedes the Battle**

The verse also retroactively conditions the two before it. If the cessation is met with Forgiving and Merciful, then the fighting permitted before the cessation was never directed at the enemy's destruction as such — it was directed at the fitnah, and the enemy's person was always, in principle, a candidate for pardon. The mercy is not the war's aftermath but its premise: the permission to fight exists inside a scripture that has already decided, in its names for God, how it wants the fighting to end. This is why the tradition could legislate from these verses the whole conduct-code of restraint — the non-combatants spared, the sanctuary held, the excess forbidden (2:190), the asylum granted and escorted (9:6) — each rule an application of the same premise: the enemy is fought while he fights and received when he stops, and the receiving is divine before it is communal. The verse's placement between the hardest permission (kill them wherever you find them) and the war's final object (fight until there is no fitnah) is thus architectural: the mercy-clause stands at the hinge, so that the reader carries the forgiveness into the object-statement and the object-statement back into the permission — the war is fought to end persecution, and it ends, for the persecutor who ceases, in the names of pardon.

**The Community's Imitation of the Names**

The verse addresses God's disposition, but its legislation binds the community in the same direction. The next verse will make the binding explicit — if they cease, then no enmity except against the wrongdoers — and the whole treaty-context of the passage's descent, at Hudaybiyyah, is a lived instance: a community that had been barred from its sanctuary settled for a truce whose terms looked, to some of the Companions, like humiliation, and accepted them as the Prophet accepted them. The names at this verse's end supply the ethic behind that acceptance: a community whose Lord meets the ceasing enemy with forgiveness and mercy is a community forbidden from meeting him with remembered injury. The sūrah will legislate the same imitation elsewhere — forgive and overlook, until God brings His command (2:109); pardon the People of the Scripture's provocations and bear with them (5:13); repel evil with what is better (41:34) — and the war-passages are the hardest case the imitation is asked to carry. The verse therefore does double duty: it states the divine response to cessation, and it trains the believers' response to be its image — the enmity ending exactly where the aggression ends, the pardon offered because the Pardoner has already offered His, and the two names standing over the battlefield as the war's real conclusion.
verses.193:
> Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors

**Religion for God Alone**

The positive object — religion is for God — carries the legislation's theological core. The phrase excludes every rival sovereignty over conscience: the idols enforced by Quraysh's politics, the rulers whose state-religion the persecution served, the tribal order in which a man's worship followed his clan's feuds. Where religion is for God, allegiance is rendered to God and the political power withdraws from the soul — which is why the persecution's end and the phrase's fulfillment are one condition viewed twice. The verse's object is not the establishment of belief by force; belief compelled is not belief, and the Qur'an's own declaration that there is no compulsion in religion (2:256, in the legislation ahead) belongs to the same system: the war removes the compulsion that runs against God, and what remains is the field in which religion is rendered freely to its only proper Object. The tradition read the two verses together accordingly: the fighting until no fitnah is the removal of coercive idolatry's power, and the religion-for-God that follows is the free worship that power's removal makes possible — the sanctuary reopened, the pilgrim unbarred, the believer untortured, and every soul left, at last, alone with its allegiance.

**If They Cease, No Aggression**

The verse's second half is its brake, and the brake is absolute: if they cease, then no aggression — no iʿtidāʾ, no hostility — except against the wrongdoers. The cessation that ended God's enmity in the previous verse (the Forgiving, the Merciful) ends the community's here: the fighting stops at the persecution's stop, and continuing after the stop is itself the transgression the war-law opened by forbidding. The exception clause — except against the wrongdoers — was read by the exegetes in complementary ways: the aggression that remains lawful is against those who continue to wrong, so that the ceasing enemy is fully covered by the prohibition while the persisting wrongdoer remains within the permission; and some read the excepted wrongdoers as the persisting persecutors specifically, the fitnah's operators, against whom the enmity endures exactly as long as their wrong. Either reading yields the same law: the enmity is not against a people but against a wrong, and it survives neither the wrong's end nor its abandoner. The verse by this closes the circle the passage opened — fight those who fight you (2:190), kill them where you find them within the limits (2:191), forgive when they cease (2:192), and stop when the persecution stops (2:193) — each command bounded by the next, the whole legislation a corridor with walls on both sides: the wall against passivity in the face of fitnah, and the wall against war beyond fitnah's end.

**The Oppressors and the Enmity's True Object**

The final phrase redefines the enemy one last time: the enmity is against the oppressors — the ẓālimūn, the wrongdoers, the ones who commit the ẓulm that fitnah is. The naming is deliberate and de-tribalizes the war completely. The enemy of these verses is never the Quraysh as a people, never the Arabs of Mecca as a population, never an ethnicity or a lineage; it is the oppressor as a moral category — whoever operates the persecution, and only while he operates it. This is the verse's contribution to the whole passage's architecture: the war-law of 2:190–193 is indexed, start to finish, not to identity but to act — fight those who fight you, expel those who expelled you, fight fitnah until fitnah ends, and hold enmity only against the ones still wronging.

**The Passage as One Law**

Read as a unit, the four verses form the Qur'an's first complete war-code, and its shape is worth stating whole. The permission: fight in God's cause those who fight you, without transgression (2:190). The field-rules: the fighters wherever found, the expulsion bounded by the expulsion suffered, the fitnah named as the evil outranking killing, the Sacred Mosque held out of the war unless war enters it (2:191). The exit: the ceasing enemy met by God's forgiveness and mercy (2:192). The object and the brake: fight until persecution ends and religion is God's; if they cease, no aggression except against the persisting wrongdoers (2:193). Every clause is a limit on the clause before it — the permission limited by reciprocity, the field-rules limited by the sanctuary and the non-combatants the tradition drew from them, the object limited by the cessation, the cessation guaranteed by the divine names. A people thirteen years persecuted, freshly barred from their own sanctuary by treaty, are given this code — and its hardest sentence is the ranking of persecution above killing, while its last word about the enemy is pardon. The war these verses legislate is a surgeon's war: the fitnah cut out, the healthy tissue — the ceasing, the non-fighting, the asylum-seeking, the sanctuary — legislated inviolable, and the operation over the moment the disease is.
verses.194:
> ˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺

**The Sacred Things Named**

The plural — the sacred things, or inviolable things — was enumerated by the exegetes: the sacred month, the sacred land of Mecca, and the iḥrām, the ritual state of the pilgrim. Al-Rāzī records the sharper occasion behind the ruling: when the Meccans learned that the Muslims were forbidden to fight during the sacred months, they calculated that this restraint could be exploited — that Muslim quiescence in the holy time was a vulnerability to be attacked. The verse answers the calculation directly: if blood is shed against a Muslim in the sacred month, the shedder's own blood becomes liable in the sacred month; the inviolability of forbidden things is to be observed, but not to the point of self-destruction.

**Transgression as Measured Response**

The verse's middle clause commands retaliation in the same manner as the attack, and its wording is the exegetes' careful study: the verb used is the same root as transgression — *iʿtadā* — yet the response it commands is not seen as illegitimate, as the verb ordinarily implies. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the "transgression" ordered here is a legitimate answer to aggression, and could rightly be rendered "attack him in the like manner that he attacked you." The likeness is the law: the response is measured against the injury, equal in kind and degree, never exceeding it. The Qur'an states the same standard twice more — if you retaliate, retaliate with the like of what was done to you, though patience is better (16:126); the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent, while pardon and reconciliation carry their reward with God (42:40). Read with those texts, this clause is the war-law's proportionality rule in its plainest form: the believer may answer blow for blow, expulsion for expulsion, month for month — and the answer's legitimacy lives entirely in its likeness. Excess converts the responder into the transgressor the previous verse named unloved by God.

**The Fence Around the Fence**

Structurally, the verse fences the fence the war-code opened. 2:190 permitted fighting against the fighters and forbade exceeding; 2:191 extended the permission to the field and withdrew it at the sanctuary unless the sanctuary was attacked; 2:192–193 ended the enmity at the cessation and named persecution as the only object. This verse handles the case those rules leave hardest: the enemy who attacks inside the protected times and places themselves — the month, the precinct, the pilgrim-state — where the believer's own scruple might paralyze him. The answer keeps both truths intact: the protections stand (retaliation happens *in* a sacred month only *for* an offense in a sacred month — the sanctity is the occasion, never the casualty), and the believer is not left defenseless (all violations carry retaliation; the attacked may answer in kind). The verse by this completes a code in which nothing is unprotected and nothing is unprotected-able: sanctity without defense becomes bait, and defense without sanctity becomes the transgression the code forbids. Between the two, the measured retaliation in the sacred month is the narrow path the legislation walks.

**The Sacred Things in the Community's Memory**

The verse's ruling outlived its occasion and became the community's standing grammar of holy time. The four sacred months — Dhū'l-Qaʿdah, Dhū'l-Ḥijjah, Muḥarram, and Rajab — kept their inviolability in Islamic law, and the sūrah itself legislates the gravity of fighting within them: fighting in the sacred month is great, though barring people from God's path and expelling the Mosque's people is greater (2:217). The pilgrimage-legislation that follows immediately (2:196–203) then fills those same months with their positive content: the ʿumrah performed in Dhū'l-Qaʿdah that the verse's ledger commemorated became the pattern of the Prophet's own pilgrimages, all performed in the sacred time. Read forward, the verse is the hinge between the war-code and the hajj-code: the months in which blood may not be shed are the months in which the rites are kept, and the retaliation-for-violations clause exists precisely so that the rites' keepers are not prey. The sacred month for the sacred month is, in the end, the community's calendar defended — its holy time made inviolable not by the enemy's goodwill but by a law that answers every violation in kind, under the eyes of the God who is with the mindful.
verses.195:
> Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers

**The Command to Spend**

The verse sits between the war-legislation and the pilgrimage-legislation, and its first command supplies both with their economics: spend in the path of God. The war just legislated cannot be fought without expenditure — mounts, arms, provision for the fighters, support for their families — and the pilgrimage about to be legislated is itself a journey of means, incumbent only on those who can afford the way. The spending commanded is the wide infāq the sūrah has been legislating since its opening pages: charity in its every form, given where God's cause requires it, with the cause named first so that the spending's direction is fixed before its amount. The sūrah of the Hypocrites states the urgency of the same command from the other side: donate from what God has provided before death comes and the soul begs for a short reprieve to give (63:10).

**Destruction at One's Own Hands**

The second clause is the verse's famous prohibition: do not cast yourselves into destruction with your own hands. The idiom is emphatic about agency — the hands are named — and the exegetes divided over the ruin intended. The readings recorded by Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī converge on stinginess as the primary sense: one throws oneself into ruin by holding back from charity and from spending in God's way, or, in a related reading, by settling down with family and wealth and abandoning the struggle in God's path. The withholding is the self-destruction: the wealth kept does not save the keeper but ruins him, since the cause that goes unfunded is the cause that fails, and its failure returns on the community that could have carried it. A broader reading takes the clause at its plain sense — avoid everything that leads to self-destruction, including courting divine punishment by doing what God has forbidden — so that the prohibition covers both the miser's slow ruin and the reckless man's fast one. The hands named are the same hands the sūrah described eating fire (2:174) and devouring orphans' wealth (2:188's neighborhood): the instrument of taking, here commanded to let go.

**Abū Ayyūb's Correction at the Walls of Constantinople**

The verse's most famous application is a correction delivered on a battlefield decades after the revelation. The reports — preserved in the Sunan collections and quoted by the exegetes — describe a Muslim army before Constantinople, in which Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, the Prophet's own host in Medina, was serving as an old man. A fighter charged the Byzantine lines alone and was killed, and some of the soldiers said: he has thrown himself into destruction, quoting this verse against him. Abū Ayyūb corrected them: we know this verse better than you — it was revealed about us, the Anṣār. When God gave victory to His religion and its followers multiplied, we said to one another: it is time to go back to our estates and restore what we neglected of them; and the verse came down forbidding exactly that — the retreat into property and comfort after the cause had need of men. On Abū Ayyūb's authoritative reading, then, the destruction is not the soldier's bold charge but the community's quiet withdrawal into its wealth; the verse prohibits not courage misapplied but comfort preferred to duty. The report is the tradition's own guard against reading the clause as a counsel of mere caution.

**The Ruin of Despair**

A third reading recorded by Ibn Kathīr turns the clause inward, toward the sinner's own counsel of doom: some take the verse as addressed to people who, having committed a sin they believe unforgivable, go on sinning because they feel condemned in any case — and al-Ṭabarī describes the same movement as surrender to moral despair instead of turning in repentance. On this reading the self-destruction is the despair itself: the sinner who decides his case is closed has thrown himself into ruin with his own hands more surely than any sin could, because the open sin leaves repentance standing while despair cancels it. The reading fits the verse's context in the sūrah's economy of pardon — repentance legislated for the concealer (2:160), for the usurer who desists, for the whole community at every turn — and it balances Abū Ayyūb's correction from the opposite flank: the verse forbids both the recklessness that presumes on safety and the despair that presumes on ruin. Between the two presumptions stands the spender — the one whose hands are busy with God's cause rather than with his own destruction in either direction.
verses.196:
> Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment

**Complete Them, for God**

The verse opens the sūrah's hajj-legislation with the command to complete the ḥajj and the ʿumrah *for God*. The first word raised a legal question the exegetes pursued at length: is the ʿumrah obligatory like the ḥajj? The pilgrimage proper is one of the five pillars, universally held binding on every able Muslim who can afford the way — an obligation established by other texts, above all the verse in Āl ʿImrān making pilgrimage to the House a duty upon people for whoever can find a way thereto (3:97). The ʿumrah, the lesser visit, is generally counted voluntary in Islamic law, though some scholars require it as the ḥajj is required. Al-Ṭabarī records a reading of *complete* that harmonizes the positions: the command may mean that once a person enters either rite, he must finish it without interruption — parallel to the supererogatory fast, which becomes obligatory to complete once begun — so the ʿumrah can be commanded to be completed without being obligatory to start. Others take *complete* as "perform them according to their rules." What all readings share is the phrase *for God*: the rites are to be done for worship alone, not for trade, not for meeting people, not for display — an intention concretely embodied the moment the pilgrim enters iḥrām, the ritual state in which many ordinarily permitted things become forbidden.

**If You Are Hindered**

The second clause legislates the blocked pilgrim: if you are prevented from proceeding, send whatever offering is within reach. The hindrance covers anything that stops a pilgrim already committed — illness or injury on the road, a hostile party barring the way — and since the sick are exempt from setting out at all, al-Ṭabarī reasons the clause addresses obstacles arising *after* entry into iḥrām. The offering is specified almost unanimously as a sacrifice, a sheep at the minimum, with cattle and camels also named. The clause's historical ground is Ḥudaybiyyah itself: when the Prophet and his Companions were barred from the ʿumrah in the sixth year, they shaved their heads and slaughtered their animals right there on the road, not in Mecca — and that precedent generated the jurists' question about the offering's "place": some hold it means the place where it will be eaten, since most ritual sacrifices are consumed after slaughter; others require the animal to reach Mecca before the head is shaved. The Ḥanafī school's practical ruling extends the clause to every road-casualty — the lost, the stung, the bitten, the sick — who sends the offering or its value ahead and is by this released. The range of positions on what counts as hindrance, where the offering goes, and whether a missed attempt must be repeated is the verse's living jurisprudence.

**The Ransom of Fasting, Charity, or Rite**

The fourth clause provides for the pilgrim whose body will not keep the rule: whoever is ill or suffers a complaint of the head requiring the shave compensates with fasting, charity, or a rite. The word *nusuk* here means sacrifice specifically, though its literal sense is any act of worship. The compensation amounts were fixed by the jurists al-Qurṭubī records: the fasting is ten days; the charity is the feeding of ten poor people; the sacrifice is a sheep at minimum. The clause's architecture is the sūrah's familiar pattern — a duty, then its concession, then the concession's price — the same three-step legislation the fast received (2:184–185): the rule stands for the able, the unable are not simply excused but transferred to an equivalent, and the equivalence keeps the rite's gravity intact. The scalp-ailment case is not hypothetical decoration; it is the practical instance the road always produced — weeks of iḥrām in desert heat, with its prohibitions on grooming, made the head's affliction a common trial, and the verse legislates relief without relaxing the consecration: the head may be shaved, but the fast, the feeding, or the sacrifice answers for it.

**The Enjoyment: Three Ways to Combine the Rites**

The fifth clause — when you are secure, whoever enjoys the ʿumrah ahead of the ḥajj owes an offering within his means — legislates one of the three classical combinations of the two rites. The exegetes define all three. In *ifrād*, the pilgrim enters iḥrām and performs the ḥajj alone, exits, and may then perform an ʿumrah separately. In the mode this verse addresses — *tamattuʿ*, "enjoyment" — he enters iḥrām, performs the ʿumrah first, exits the sacred state, and enjoys the interval of ordinary lawful life before re-entering iḥrām for the ḥajj; for that enjoyed interval he owes the offering. In *qirān*, "joining," he performs both within a single unbroken iḥrām. The schools differ over which mode is most meritorious, and the verse's own historical setting explains the offering: the Arabs had frowned severely on performing the ʿumrah during the hajj-season and were reluctant to do so until the Prophet himself performed an ʿumrah in Dhū'l-Ḥijjah, the month of the ḥajj. The tamattuʿ concession — doing the lesser rite first, resting from iḥrām, then taking up the greater — is thus a mercy legislated against an old scruple, and the offering or its substitute fast is its acknowledged price: even the permission to perform the ʿumrah in the hajj-months is itself a gift.
verses.197:
> ˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason

**The Months Well Known**

The verse fixes the hajj's calendar: the pilgrimage belongs to appointed months — months well known, as the Arabic puts it, a phrase that presupposes a community already acquainted with them. The exegetes identify them as Shawwāl, Dhū'l-Qaʿdah, and Dhū'l-Ḥijjah, with some limiting the third month's share to its first ten days, since the sacrificial rules change after the Day of Sacrifice. The months are not arbitrary but the Arabian sacred season the previous verse's legislation had already engaged — the time in which the ʿumrah-in-hajj combination was performed, in which the pilgrim caravans moved, and whose sanctity the war-code protected (2:194). Juridically, the designation carries a ruling: according to many authorities it is disliked to enter the iḥrām for the hajj outside these months — a pilgrim should not consecrate himself early and carry the state across the intervening weeks until Dhū'l-Ḥijjah. The phrase *well known* is itself informative: the calendar of the pilgrimage was public knowledge, fixed by practice before the verse confirmed it, and the revelation legislates inside a living custom rather than inventing a season — the same method the fasting-legislation used with Ramadan's moon.

**No Iniquity, No Quarreling**

The second and third prohibitions — *fusūq* and *jidāl* — cover sin and strife. The iniquity named is wrongdoing in the general sense, the violations of God's law that iḥrām's holiness makes doubly grave; the quarreling is defined by the exegetes with precision: not intellectual disagreement, which the pilgrimage never forbade, but the interchange that ends in anger and insult — the argument as combat. Al-Qurṭubī supplies the historical instance: the Quraysh used to quarrel over the Station of Abraham (2:125), each party observing a spot different from the other Arabs', and he prefers to read the prohibition as covering disputes over the hajj's places and times — though it may equally target the boasting that accompanied the pre-Islamic pilgrimage, the claims that one's hajj was finer than another's, one's forefathers nobler. The three prohibitions together fence the pilgrim completely: the body (rafath), the deed (fusūq), the tongue (jidāl) — and the fencing is against the pilgrimage's own social conditions, the weeks of crowded travel, shared hardship, and tribal proximity in which these three exactly are the standing temptations. The tradition preserves a saying that gathers all three: an oath is reported that no work done under the sky excels striving in God's cause together with a pilgrimage kept faithfully — one free of lewdness, iniquity, and argument.

**O People of the Kernels**

The verse ends with an address that gathers its whole argument: be mindful of Me, O people of reason — ūlū al-albāb, the possessors of the lubb, the kernel within the shell. The title is the Qur'an's honorific for the wisdom-capable, used where its deepest thinking is demanded: over the qiṣāṣ's paradox of life-in-retaliation (2:179), over wisdom's gift, over the signs of creation. Its use here is pointed. The hajj is the rite most exposed to the shell-level reading — a journey of bodies, crowds, animals, shaved heads, and stones thrown at pillars — and the verse summons exactly the readers who can crack it: those who see in the provision-command a lesson about dependence, in the quarrel-prohibition a discipline of the soul's heat, in the months a calendar of consecrated time, and in the whole rite the rehearsal of the gathering to God. The shift from the third person to the first is the verse's final intimacy: after legislating the rite in the language of law — months, prohibitions, provisions — God commands in His own name, *be mindful of Me*, so that the pilgrimage's every external act is re-anchored in the internal relation. The people of the kernels are told where the hajj's kernel lies: not in the journey completed but in the Me remembered through it.
verses.198:
> There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray

**No Blame in the Market**

The verse's first clause lifts a scruple: there is no blame on you in seeking bounty from your Lord — that is, in trading during the pilgrimage. Al-Qurṭubī records the ruling the clause establishes: commerce during the hajj is permissible and does not nullify the rite, though refraining from it and devoting oneself wholly to the spiritual dimension remains the better course. The permission answers a real tension in the Arabian hajj: the pilgrimage season was also the peninsula's great fair — the markets of ʿUkāẓ and Dhū'l-Majāz ran alongside the rites, and the pre-Islamic pilgrim was merchant and worshiper at once. Early Muslim scrupulosity appears to have doubted whether the two could coexist inside the consecrated journey, and the verse resolves the doubt in the direction of permission — with a wording that keeps the priority straight: what the trader seeks is *bounty from your Lord*, the market's gain reframed as divine provision rather than secular interruption. The clause belongs to the same legislation as the provision-command before it (2:197): the hajj is a journey of bodies through a real economy, and the revelation sanctifies the economy's honest use instead of demanding its pretense of absence.

**The Pouring Forth from ʿArafāt**

The second clause places the pilgrim in the hajj's central geography: when you pour forth from ʿArafāt. The word for the departure — *ifaḍah*, a pouring out — describes the mass movement at sunset, when the whole assembly flows westward toward Muzdalifah in a single current of people. The verse legislates what happens at that flow's arrival: remember God at the sacred monument — al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām. The exegetes located the monument in two readings: some identify the hill named Quzaḥ at Muzdalifah, where the prayer-leader stands to lead the combined maghrib and ʿishāʾ prayers after the pilgrims come from ʿArafāt; others, al-Rāzī among them, take it as Muzdalifah itself — the place of prayer and remembrance where the pilgrims go after the standing, which the Qur'an's own phrase elsewhere calls the sacred monument.

**Remember God at the Sacred Monument**

The remembrance commanded at Muzdalifah has a defined content in the tradition's practice: the pilgrims remember God there through the standing formulas — al-ḥamduli'Llāh, praise be to God; Allāhu akbar, God is greatest; subḥāna'Llāh, glory be to God — recited through the night of gathering and at the prayers. The command's timing is instructive. The pilgrim has just come from the hajj's overwhelming moment — the standing on the plain, the sight of the whole ummah gathered — and the verse stations remembrance at the journey's next stage, so that the peak is not followed by emptiness but by named praise. The night at Muzdalifah is thus legislated as the plain's echo-chamber: what ʿArafāt held in presence, the sacred monument holds in words. The same structure of remembrance-after-rite governs the whole passage — the numbered days at Minā will be days of remembering God (2:203), and the rites' completion will end in the remembrance that outdoes the fathers' (2:200). The hajj, in this legislation, is a sequence of stations each capped by dhikr, so that the body's journey is continuously converted into the tongue's and the heart's.

**The Station in the Pilgrimage's Arc**

Within the passage's sequence the verse holds the middle station. The legislation began with the rites' completion and their concessions (2:196), moved to the months and the consecrated conduct (2:197), and now reaches the pilgrimage's heart — ʿArafāt and the night that follows it. What comes next in the sequence is the movement onward with the people (2:199), the remembrance after the rites' completion (2:200–202), and the numbered days of Minā (2:203). This verse is therefore the arc's summit and its pivot: the plain where the hajj's essence stands, and the monument where its meaning is spoken. The tradition's own geography confirms the pivot's weight — the pilgrim's whole journey moves toward the standing, and everything after it is descent into completion, the rites winding down through Minā's days toward the farewell circuit of the Kaʿbah. At the summit, the verse gives the pilgrim the two things to carry down: the permission that keeps his worldly life unbroken, and the remembrance that keeps his guidance unforgettable — bounty sought from the Lord on the road out, and praise rendered to the Lord at the sacred place, for having guided one who was astray.
verses.199:
> Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Surge Onward With the People**

The verse legislates the pilgrimage's great collective movement: then surge onward from where the people surge onward. The reference, the exegetes agree, is the pilgrims' flow from ʿArafāt to Muzdalifah — the ifāḍah the previous verse described at its arrival, now commanded at its joining. The word for the movement carries the image of water: a pouring, a streaming, a crowd moving as one body down the plain's western edge in the sunset. And the command's emphasis falls not on the movement but on its company — *from where the people* surge. The pilgrim is to go with the going multitude, from the place of its going, in its manner and its measure. Al-Qurṭubī notes a grammatical point that sharpens the emphasis: the *then* of the verse does not denote temporal succession — the going-forth is not simply the next item after Muzdalifah's remembrance — but functions as a logical connector, "so" or "and so," tying the command to the whole preceding legislation. The surge is thus the summed conclusion of the rites so far: the months kept, the iḥrām guarded, the bounty sought without blame, the plain stood upon, the monument remembered at — and now, with all of it done in the individual's own person, the person dissolved back into the people.

**The Ḥums and the Aristocracy of the Sanctuary**

The command was revealed against a specific practice of pre-Islamic exclusivism. The Ḥums — a confederation of Quraysh and the tribes linked to them by professed devotion to the Kaʿbah and its ḥaram — held themselves too sacred for the plain. Since ʿArafāt lies outside the ḥaram's boundary while Muzdalifah lies within it, the Ḥums would not stand with the other people at ʿArafāt and would not surge onward from there with them; they remained at Muzdalifah, reasoning that the entire hajj should take place inside the sacred precinct, and treating the other Arabs' station on the plain as beneath their rank. The verse abolishes the distinction by commanding the Ḥums — through the whole community — to surge from where the people surge: the aristocracy of the sanctuary is overruled, and the Quraysh's claimed holiness is required to stand, walk, and flow exactly where the herdsman of Najd stands, walks, and flows. The same group is identified by the commentators as the one addressed by the sūrah's earlier ruling on entering houses by their doors rather than their backs (2:189) — a pattern of sanctimonious custom corrected by plain obedience.

**Forgiving, Merciful**

The two names that close the verse are the istighfār's answer, and their pairing is the Qur'an's standard formula of comprehensive pardon. The pilgrim who is commanded to ask forgiveness is told in the same breath who is being asked: the Forgiving — the ghafūr whose forgiveness covers the faults just enumerated, the rite's small corruptions, the road's quarrels, the heart's mixed intentions; the Merciful — the raḥīm whose mercy exceeds the asking, so that the petition arrives before One already disposed to grant it. The names do structural work across the whole passage: the hajj-legislation has moved from severity (know that God is severe in retribution, 2:196) through knowledge (whatever good you do, God knows it, 2:197) to this pardon — the arc of a legislation that arms itself with awe and then opens into mercy, exactly as the pilgrimage itself moves from iḥrām's restrictions to the ʿīd's release. And the names answer the Ḥums' error at its root: the confederation that trusted its own sanctity is commanded to trust God's forgiveness instead — the aristocracy of lineage replaced by the democracy of pardon, in which the Qurayshī and the Bedouin ask in the same words and are answered by the same names.

**Between the Plain and the Days**

Within the passage's architecture the verse is the hinge between the hajj's peak and its coda. Before it: the months, the prohibitions, the provisions, ʿArafāt, Muzdalifah (2:196–198). After it: the rites' completion and the remembrance that outdoes the fathers (2:200), the two supplications and their portions (2:201–202), the numbered days at Minā with their easy departures (2:203). This verse stands at the turn — the surge onward, the forgiveness sought — and its two commands set the tone for everything that follows: the collectivity that the numbered days will keep (the takbīr recited by pilgrims and non-pilgrims alike) and the pardon that the completion will presume (the rites remembered before a Forgiving God). The pilgrim who has surged with the people and asked forgiveness has, in the verse's own logic, already received the hajj's inner substance; what remains is the working-out — the stones, the sacrifice, the days, the farewell circuit. The verse therefore closes the mountain-pass of the legislation and opens its descent: onward with the people, asking pardon, under the two names — and the plain behind, the valley ahead, and the gathered community streaming between them toward home.
verses.200:
> When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,” but they will have no share in the Hereafter

**When the Rites Are Done**

The verse addresses the pilgrim at the pilgrimage's completion: when you have carried out your rites — your manāsik — remember God. The word *manāsik* was explained by the exegetes at two scopes: the sacrifices of the ʿīd al-aḍḥā, the Feast of Sacrifice that marks the hajj's end, or the rituals of the hajj collectively — the circuit, the standing, the surge, the stoning, the shave — whose essential purpose, al-Qurṭubī notes, is the remembrance of God itself. The timing of the command is its first lesson. The danger-moment of a completed rite is the vacuum after it: the weeks of consecrated routine end, the iḥrām is exited, the crowd disperses into ordinary life, and the heart that was full stands suddenly empty. The verse stations remembrance exactly there — not as one more rite added to the list but as the rite that survives the rites, the dhikr that continues when the stations are behind. The whole hajj, in this legislation, is a machine for producing remembrance that outlasts the machine: months consecrated, conduct fenced, stations capped by praise — all so that when the manāsik are finished, the remembering is just beginning.

**The Prayer for This World Alone**

The verse's second half turns from remembrance to petition, and begins the duʿāʾ-diptych that the next two verses complete: among people are those who say, *Our Lord, give to us in this world* — and who have, in the Hereafter, no share. The prayer is quoted in its poverty: one clause, one horizon, one world. The askers are not described as praying falsely or for forbidden things; their petition is simply truncated — the whole of their wanting ends at the world's edge, and the verse reports the truncation as the diagnosis. What a person asks for reveals what a person is: the duʿāʾ as the register of the heart's actual eschatology. And the verdict follows the diagnosis with arithmetic precision: whoever asks only this world receives its terms — no share in the Hereafter, since no share was ever requested there. The sūrah of Consultation states the same economy from the side of desire: whoever desires the harvest of this world is given some of it, but has no share in the Hereafter (42:20). The verse thus completes the hajj's re-education of the tongue: the boast of the fathers transferred to God, and now the petition of the heart audited — the pilgrim who has just spent weeks performing rites for the Hereafter is caught, at the rites' end, praying like a man with no Hereafter.

**Remembrance and Petition at the Rites' End**

Read as a whole, the verse legislates the pilgrim's speech at the completion: first the remembrance measured against the fathers' boast, then the petition measured against the single-world prayer. Both measurements are comparisons to Arabian habit — the genealogical vaunt and the this-worldly want — and both are corrected in the same direction: toward God and toward both worlds. The custom after the rites had been ancestry and appetite; the legislation makes it dhikr and duʿāʾ, and audits the duʿāʾ's horizon. The names the diptych will end on — swift in reckoning (2:202) — already loom over this verse's verdict: the share in the Hereafter is not a metaphor but an accounting, and the prayer that omits the Hereafter is filed accordingly. The pilgrim leaves Minā with two sentences installed in his tongue: the remembrance more ardent than the fathers', and the petition wider than the world — and the verses that follow will give him the second sentence's exact wording, its prophetic provenance, and the portion earned by those who pray it.
verses.201:
> Yet there are others who say, “Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”

**Ḥasanah: The Beautiful Good**

The word the prayer uses for its two gifts — *ḥasanah* — carries more than the translation's "good." The root ḥ-s-n bears the sense of beauty: the ḥasanah is the beautiful thing, the good that is also fitting, radiant, whole. The righteous predecessors elaborated its content, and the tradition's glosses gather the concrete and the comprehensive: good in this world has been read as a righteous spouse — the prayer's most intimate petition — as sufficient and lawful provision, as security, health, and the ability to worship; good in the Hereafter as the Garden itself, with everything the name contains. The word's generosity is its point: the prayer does not itemize because the ḥasanah includes every beautiful thing the two worlds hold, and the asker commits the itemization to the Giver. The Qur'an's own usage confirms the breadth — Moses prays ordain for us good in this life and the next (7:156); the virtuous are told that for those who do good in this world there is goodness, and the Home of the Hereafter is better (16:30); Abraham is granted good in this world and stands among the righteous in the next (16:122). Each instance carries the same double grant in the same beautiful word, and the pilgrim's petition inherits them all.

**The Prophet's Most Frequent Supplication**

The verse's duʿāʾ is not only a Quranic sentence but the Prophet's own habitual prayer, and the report is among the best-attested in the tradition. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim preserves it (2690): Qatādah asked Anas ibn Mālik which supplication the Messenger of God made most frequently, and Anas answered that his most constant prayer was this — O Allah, grant us the good in this world and the good in the Hereafter, and save us from the torment of the Fire. Anas added his own practice to the report: whenever he made any supplication he included this one within it, so that every prayer he ever prayed carried the Quranic petition folded inside it. The identification is explicit in the sources — this is the verse's prayer, the duʿāʾ of 2:201, spoken by the Prophet more than any other words of asking. The report settles the verse's status in Muslim practice: not a text to be admired but a sentence to be repeated, the petition its Revealer chose to make the most-repeated petition of His Messenger. The pilgrim at Minā who prays it is praying the prayer the Prophet prayed most, at the stations the Prophet taught him, with Anas's inclusion as the model of how to carry it into every other asking.

**Against the Truncated Asking**

Set beside the previous verse's single-world prayer, this petition defines the Islam of the tongue. The first group asked for this world and received its limits — no share in the Hereafter; this group asks for both and, the next verse will state, receives a portion from what it earned. The contrast is not between material and spiritual temperaments: the second prayer is *more* material in one sense, since it asks for this world's good explicitly, naming what the ascetic might disdain to request. And the third clause does further work against a third error: the prayer that asks for both goods without the Fire's guard would be a prayer of presumption, as though the goods were owed; the guarding-clause keeps the asker in the posture the whole passage has trained — the pilgrim who asked forgiveness at his rite's summit (2:199), who remembers God more ardently than his fathers' boasts (2:200), and who now requests everything while taking refuge from the one loss that annuls everything.

**The Supplication as the Rites' Fruit**

The verse's position at the hajj-legislation's turning point makes the duʿāʾ the pilgrimage's stated product. The manāsik are completed (2:200); the remembrance replaces the boast; and the petition replaces the appetite. What the weeks of iḥrām, the plain, the surge, and the nights of Minā were for is now visible in a single sentence: a heart re-sorted in its wanting, praying with both horizons open and the Fire in view. The verses that follow will confirm the sorting — the portion earned by such askers, the reckoning swift upon it (2:202) — but the sort itself happens here, in the words. The tradition's reading of the prayer's clauses as a curriculum completes the picture: the righteous predecessors who read good in this world as a righteous spouse and lawful provision, and good in the Hereafter as the Garden, treated the duʿāʾ as the syllabus of a whole life — marriage, work, worship, death, judgment, all named or implied in three clauses. The pilgrim who learns the sentence at Minā carries home not a souvenir but a structure: every future asking already shaped by the double horizon, the beautiful good, and the guard against the Fire.
verses.202:
> It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning

**Swift in Reckoning**

The second clause names the speed of the settlement: God is swift in reckoning — *sarīʿ al-ḥisāb*. The attribute answers an objection latent in the portion-principle: the wage is promised, but the payer's audit of the whole creation would seem to require an age — how can the account of every asker be settled at all? The swiftness is the answer, and it is an attribute the Qur'an repeats at exactly such junctures: the People of the Scripture did not dispute until knowledge came to them, and whoever denies God's signs should know that God is swift in reckoning (3:19). The reckoning's speed follows from the reckoner's nature: an audit is slow in proportion to the auditor's distance from his accounts, and God's distance is zero — He knows the portion before it is asked, the earning before it is made, the prayer before the tongue forms it.

**The Reckoning and the Supplicant**

The swiftness has a personal edge for the praying pilgrim, and the passage's own structure supplies it. The verse before the duʿāʾ-diptych commanded the pilgrim at his rite's summit to ask forgiveness (2:199); the verse before the diptych stationed remembrance at the rites' end (2:200); the nearness-verse of the fasting legislation promised I respond to the call of the caller (2:186). The whole context is a theology of answered prayer, and swift in reckoning is its final guarantee: the portion of the earned prayer is not filed for a distant processing but settled by a reckoning that outruns the asking. The believer who prays 2:201's sentence at Minā, between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, in the night or the crowd, prays into an accounting already moving — the kasb registered, the nasīb assigned, the reckoning swift. The clause thus converts the portion-principle from a warning into a comfort: what you have earned is held for you by One whose audit needs no time, and the speed that makes the sinner's case fearful makes the asker's case sure. The two movements are one attribute — the reckoning is swift whether it convicts or pays, and the prayer decides which.

**The Verse as the Diptych's Hinge**

Structurally, this shortest of the three verses carries the whole weight of the settlement. Verse 200 quoted the truncated prayer and its verdict — no share in the Hereafter; verse 201 quoted the whole prayer without verdict; verse 202 supplies the verdict for the whole — and, on the comprehensive reading, for the truncated one too. The diptych's moral anatomy is by this completed in a single sentence: the asking reveals the earning, the earning fixes the portion, and the reckoning delivers it swiftly. The verse's brevity is proportioned to its function — it adds no imagery, no narrative, no elaboration, only the accounting — because the accounting is all the two prayers lacked. The single-world asker was told what he would not have; the both-worlds asker is told what he will: a portion, earned, paid by a swift reckoning. And the portion-language quietly answers the hajj's own economics: the pilgrim has spent wealth on the journey (2:195's spending, 2:197's provisions), earned hardship on the road, and invested weeks in rites whose yield is invisible; the verse credits all of it to the account — the kasb includes the journey — and settles it with the speed that makes the invisible yield as certain as the visible cost.

**Under the Swiftness, the Whole Passage**

The attribute's shadow falls across the legislation that follows as well. The numbered days at Minā are about to be legislated with their easy options — depart after two days or stay to the third, no sin on either for the mindful (2:203) — and beneath the ease stands the same swiftness: every choice in the rite, like every clause of every prayer, is registered instantly and settled exactly. The passage that began with the sacred month's ledger (2:194) and the spending in God's cause (2:195) has been building one continuous accounting — the retaliation measured, the offerings priced, the prayers portioned — and swift in reckoning is the seal on all of it: the ledger is kept in real time, by a knowledge that never pauses to compile. For the pilgrim the seal is mercy; for the Ḥums-type heart that prays with one horizon it is warning; and for the reader of the sūrah it is the standing condition of every verse's legislation — that the laws are not ideals posted against time but accounts entered the moment they are kept or broken. The portion from what they earned is, in the end, the hajj's final rite: the prayer completed, the earning closed, and the reckoning already swift upon it.
verses.203:
> And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered

**The Days Numbered**

The verse legislates the hajj's final station: remember God in the days numbered — the eleventh through the thirteenth of Dhū'l-Ḥijjah, which the pilgrims spend at Minā, the valley east of Mecca, and which the tradition calls the days of tashrīq, a word whose derivation is uncertain and whose sense the rites preserve: the three days after the Day of Sacrifice, not counting it. The station's central act is the stoning — the casting of pebbles at the columns (jimār) that represent Satan's three ambushes of Abraham on the road of the sacrifice — and the verse stations remembrance over the whole of it. The numbered days complete the pilgrimage's arithmetic: months appointed (2:197), a night at the sacred monument (2:198), a surge with the people (2:199), rites completed (2:200), and now days counted — three, named, and bounded, like the fast's numbered days before them. The numbering is the legislation's characteristic mercy: the rite has a defined end, the pilgrim knows his remaining obligation to the hour, and the remembrance that fills the days has a frame that keeps it from dissolving into the journey's fatigue.

**Remember God in Them**

The remembrance commanded in these days has a precise form in the tradition's practice: the takbīr — Allāhu akbar, God is greatest — recited while casting the pebbles at the columns and recited at the times of the prayers throughout the days. The litanies are the same ones the fasting-legislation produced — the verse of Ramadan's completion commanded magnifying God for having guided (2:185), and the formula the tradition recites there is the formula recited here: Allāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar, lā ilāha illa'Llāh, wa'Llāhu akbar wa li'Llāhi'l-ḥamd — God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest, and to God belongs the praise — with other litanies added in some practice.

**For the One Who Fears**

The flexibility carries a condition, and the condition is the verse's hinge: the no-sin ruling is *for the reverent* — for the one who keeps his taqwā. The exegetes read the qualifier in complementary directions. It attaches to both options: the hastener is sinless only if his hastening is not a flight from the rite's discipline but a traveler's necessity kept inside piety, and the delayer is sinless only if his staying is not self-righteous display. It also attaches, in the stricter reading, to the departing specifically: the one who hastens must have kept the fear of God in his whole pilgrimage — the rafath, fusūq, and jidāl avoided (2:197), the rites completed for God (2:196) — for the exemption to cover his early exit. The condition by this prevents the flexibility from becoming laxity: the option is not a discount on piety but a discount *for* the pious, the margin granted to the heart the rite has already formed. And the verse reinforces the point by repeating its command — be mindful of God — immediately after the options, so that both departures, the two-day and the three-day, are dispatched under the same taqwā, the only luggage whose inspection matters at the valley's exit.

**To Him You Will Be Gathered**

The verse ends by projecting the gathering at Minā into the gathering to God: know that to Him you will be gathered. The clause is the days' eschatological frame, and its fit to the setting is exact. The pilgrim at Minā stands inside the largest rehearsal the faith performs of the Day of Gathering — the nations assembled in one valley, ranked in tents like the ranks of the resurrection, performing the stoning of the devil who will be judged, awaiting the departure that resembles the final departure. The knowledge commanded is the rehearsal's lesson: this gathering disperses, that gathering does not; these days are numbered, that Day is not; this valley's exit is by the farewell circuit, that assembly's exit is by the portion earned. The clause also seals the passage's accounting-thread — the sacred month's ledger (2:194), the portion from what was earned and the swift reckoning (2:202) — with the destination of all accounts: the gathering to Him. The pilgrim who hastens after two days and the pilgrim who tarries to the third walk out of the valley under the same knowledge, and the verse leaves them both with it: the option was about days; the gathering is about the One who numbered them.
verses.204:
> There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries

**The Turn From the Pilgrim to the Impostor**

The sūrah makes one of its characteristic pivots here: the hajj-legislation closes with the pilgrims gathered at Minā, remembering God in numbered days (2:203), and the next movement opens on a man whose speech impresses and whose heart is war. The contrast is the point of the placement — the community that has just been legislated through remembrance, flexibility, and mindfulness is immediately shown its internal opposite, the person who performs the language of faith while carrying enmity inside it. The verses that follow (204–207) form a diptych: this portrait of the eloquent adversary, and its counter-portrait of the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure (2:207). Between the two figures the sūrah lays out the heart's two economies — the speech that markets the self, and the life that spends the self — and asks the reader, freshly returned from the valley of gathering, which trade he is in.

**The Speech About the Life of This World**

The portrait opens with the man's instrument: his manner of speaking about worldly affairs delights you. The verb carries the senses the exegetes list — to please, to evoke wonder, to delight — and its object is specified: not talk of God or the Hereafter but of *this world's life*, its affairs, its interests, its management. The hypocrite's eloquence is worldly fluency: he speaks the community's practical concerns — provision, politics, the arrangements of the road and the market — with a mastery that wins the listener's admiration. The specification matters. The sūrah's opening portrait of the hypocrites described their claim, we are only peace-makers (2:11); this portrait describes their competence. The dangerous deceiver is not the one who talks badly about sacred things but the one who talks brilliantly about worldly things and carries the brilliance into the sacred. The listener's admiration — the verse addresses the Prophet himself, *impresses you* — is the mechanism of the harm: the community is disarmed not by argument but by aesthetic surrender, the pleasure of a well-managed sentence doing the work a false doctrine could never do alone.

**Occasions and the Universal Portrait**

The exegetes record specific occasions for these verses and then, characteristically, prefer the general reading. Beside Akhnas, al-Thaʿlabī reports another incident behind the revelation: Meccan men feigned eagerness for Islamic instruction and requested that a party of teachers be dispatched to them; the men sent were waylaid en route and killed. But Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī agree in treating the passage as universal teaching on the nature of hypocrisy rather than as a locked historical caption — the portrait is drawn to be recognized in every generation. The preference is methodologically significant: a verse tied to one impostor would arm the community against a man; a verse describing the type arms it against the form. And the form is durable — the eloquent manager of worldly affairs, the invoker of God as heart-witness, the adversary inside the admiration — recurring in every community that judges its speakers by their speech. The universal reading also explains the diptych's second panel: the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure (2:207) is no less a type, and the two figures stand as the permanent alternatives of the religious life — the self marketed in God's name, and the self spent in God's cause. This portrait belongs to the sūrah's long anatomy of interior corruption, which began in its opening pages — the hypocrites who say we believe in God and the Last Day while believing not, who seek to deceive God and the believers while deceiving only themselves without awareness (2:8–9) — and now, two hundred verses deep, returns with its mature instruments: not the crude claim of belief but the accomplished performance of it.
verses.205:
> And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief

**When He Turns Away**

The verse follows the impostor out of the room. The portrait of 2:204 was drawn inside the encounter — the impressive speech, the oath to the heart, the listener's admiration — and this verse tracks what happens when the encounter ends: when he turns away, he strives in the land. The turning was read by the exegetes at two levels: the physical departure, his leaving the presence of those he has been deceiving, and the interior turn, the anger that shows the mask's underside. Both readings carry the same disclosure: the eloquence was a costume worn for an audience, and the audience's absence reveals the wearer. The verse thus completes the diagnostic pattern begun in the previous verse — the disjunction between the speech in your presence and the conduct out of it is the hypocrite's identifying mark. The community is taught where to look: not at the performance, which is flawless while watched, but at the interval, the going-away, the hours in which no admirer is present to be impressed. What a man does when he turns away is the report on what he was while facing you.

**Tillage and Offspring Destroyed**

The verse names the corruption's two targets: he destroys the tillage and the offspring. The tillage — the harth — is agriculture, the crops, the planted fields; the offspring — the nasl — is livestock on the primary reading, and on some commentators' extension any progeny including the human. The two named things are the Arabian world's entire wealth: what the land grows and what the herds bear, the standing crop and the multiplying stock, the food of this year and the food of all years to come. To destroy them is not to injure a competitor but to attack the conditions of life itself — the scorched field does not belong to the enemy alone but to the future, and the hamstrung animal ends a lineage of provision. The modern readings the verse has generated follow the same logic outward: Muslims have interpreted such corruption-verses as condemning injustice in society and the destruction of the natural environment, citing the Qur'an's own summary — corruption has spread on land and sea through what people's hands have done (30:41).

**God Loves Not Corruption**

The verse's final clause states the divine disposition: God does not love the fasād. The formula — the negation of divine love — is the Qur'an's characteristic verdict-language, marking not merely prohibition but divine aversion: God does not love the transgressor (2:190), the waster, the arrogant boaster, the treacherous. Its placement here is strategic, because the hypocrite's whole performance is built on claiming God's favor — the oath that God knows his heart, the religious language of his impressive speech. The clause answers the claim from the side of God: whatever the man asserts about the divine knowledge of his interior, the divine love does not attend his work, and the work is what the verse has just described — striving corruption, destroyed tillage, ruined offspring. The negation also disciplines the community's discernment: you cannot audit his heart, but you can audit his harvest — the fields he leaves burned, the herds he leaves hamstrung, the trust he leaves rotted — and the divine non-love is pronounced over exactly that audit. The verse by this hands the deceived a criterion that does not depend on eloquence: look at what his striving leaves growing, and what it leaves dead.

**The Anti-Economy of the Diptych**

Within the passage's architecture, this verse is the diptych's dark economy in full operation. The sūrah has just legislated an economy of cultivation and expenditure: spend in God's cause, the hands that withhold cast themselves into destruction (2:195); the pilgrim takes provision and seeks bounty without blame (2:197–198); the portion is from what is earned (2:202). Against that economy stands the hypocrite's: he spends nothing, earns nothing, and his one industry is the destruction of what others spend, earn, and grow. The tillage he burns is somebody's provision-command obeyed; the offspring he maims is somebody's bounty sought lawfully; the land he corrupts is the same land the verse of 30:41 describes as tasting the consequences of such hands. The diptych's second panel — the one who sells his soul seeking God's pleasure (2:207) — will complete the contrast from the other side: the believer's economy culminates in spending the self, the hypocrite's in destroying the harvest. Between the two, the verse's criterion of love divides them: the seller of the soul sells to a God who is kind to His servants; the spreader of corruption strives under a God who does not love corruption — and both dispositions are already, in this life, visible in the fields.
verses.206:
> When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,” pride carries them off to sin. Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest

**The One Sentence Every Counsel Needs**

The verse tests the portrait with the shortest possible intervention: when it is said to him, fear God. The counsel is the tradition's whole prophetic vocabulary in two words — the taqwā-command that every messenger brought his people, that the sūrah has legislated as the end of retaliation, bequest, fasting, and pilgrimage alike (2:179, 180, 183, 196–197). It is what a friend says to the eloquent impostor, what an elder says to the corrupter of the land, what the community says to its own admired speaker when the interval's report comes in. The verse's staging is precise: the admonition arrives, and what follows is the man's reaction to being told to fear God. Not to a refutation of his arguments, not to an exposure of his oath, but to the two-word counsel that names the only thing his whole performance lacks. The hypocrite's portrait is by this completed by its response to correction — the surface was drawn in 204, the industry in 205, and here the interior's reflex, the movement of the heart when the heart is addressed directly.

**What an Evil Resting Place**

The verse's last clause inverts the imagery of rest: what an evil cradle, an evil place to recline. The word mihād carries the bed-sense — the cradle, the made-up couch, the place where a person settles as into their own element — and the Qur'an uses it elsewhere for Hell's furnishing, the bed of the arrogant. The inversion bites against the whole portrait: the man who impressed you with his talk of this world's life was arranging his rest in the world — the estates the Anṣār were tempted back to (2:195), the position his eloquence maintained, the comfort his corruption protected — and the verse names the resting place his choices actually furnished. The man who could not bear the two words fear God is given the sufficient and evil substitute, the couch of his own ʿizzah.

**The Circuit Completed: Speech, Act, Reaction**

The three verses now read as one closed circuit of hypocrisy. 2:204 gave the surface: the eloquent speech about worldly affairs, the oath calling God to witness the heart, the enmity beneath the impression. 2:205 gave the work: the turning away, the striving corruption, the tillage and offspring destroyed. 2:206 gives the reflex: the counsel to fear God, the pride's seizure, the sufficient Fire. Nothing is missing from the anatomy — what he says, what he does, and what he becomes when corrected — and the circuit's third stage explains why the first two are fatal rather than merely bad. A man who spoke well and corrupted badly might still be reached; the counsel to fear God is the reaching, and the verse reports it fails, not for want of clarity but by pride's reflex. The failure of correction is hypocrisy's defining difference from ordinary sin: the sinner who can still hear fear God retains the road back — the repentance-legislation the sūrah has spread through its length stands open — but the man seized by ʿizzah into sin has closed the road from inside, and the sufficiency of Hell is the verdict on a self that made itself unaddressable.

**The Portrait Against the Pilgrims**

The diptych's dark panel is now complete, and its frame is the hajj it follows. The pilgrims of 2:196–203 spent weeks in the state where the interior is legislated — the intention audited by God alone, the tongue fenced from rafath and jidāl, the boast of the fathers transferred to the remembrance of God, the petition taught to span both worlds. The man of 2:204–206 is the inversion at every point: his tongue perfected for the world's affairs, his oath profaning the divine witness, his boast reasserted in the pride that refuses counsel, his petition truncated to the world whose harvest he destroys. The passage has thus built its two citizens — the one who leaves the valley remembering God in numbered days and knowing he will be gathered to Him, and the one who leaves the encounter striving corruption in the land and being carried by glory into a sufficient Fire.
