The verse that follows will draw the second citizen of the diptych's bright panel — the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure — and between the sold soul and the sufficient Hell the sūrah will have completed its most compact moral map: the heart that spends itself and the heart that markets itself, the ʿizzah that seizes and the raʾfah that receives.
verses.207:
> And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure. And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants

**The Soul Sold for Pleasure**

The diptych's second panel opens with the counter-figure: among people is the one who sells himself — his nafs, his soul, his self, his life — seeking the good pleasure of God. The verb is commercial and the verse means it: the same market-language the sūrah has used throughout — the traders who purchased error at guidance's price (2:16, 2:175), the concealers who sold revelation for a fleeting gain (2:174) — here receives its one holy instance. The seller is real, the merchandise is the highest thing a person owns, and the price is riḍwān Allāh, God's pleasure: not paradise as real estate, not safety as insurance, but the Divine good-will itself as the whole of the wanted. The transaction inverts the sūrah's bad trades completely. Those sold the eternal for the fleeting and received fire in their bellies; this one sells the fleeting — a life that ends regardless — for the eternal, and the verse's closing name will describe what the Buyer is: kind to His servants. The nafs sold is specified by the exegetes in its double sense, soul and life, because the sale runs at both levels: the self's desires given away, and where necessary the life itself laid down, in one undivided act of purchase-by-surrender.

**ʿUmar's Reading: The Man Who Enjoins and Is Slain**

The tradition's most cited application of the verse comes from the second caliph. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is reported to have read the seller as a man who sets out to enjoin the right and forbid the wrong — and is killed for it. The reading connects the verse to the Qur'an's great civic precept, al-amr bi'l-maʿrūf wa'l-nahy ʿan al-munkar, the commanding of good and forbidding of evil, a theme legislated across the scripture: let there be a community among you calling to the good, enjoining the right, forbidding the wrong — those are the successful (3:104); the believers, men and women, are protectors of one another who enjoin the right (9:71); and a dozen places more. On ʿUmar's reading the sale of the soul is not mystical withdrawal but public speech with a lethal price: the one who stands before a tyrant, a corrupt assembly, a community bent toward the corruption of 2:205, and says fear God — the very counsel the proud man of the previous verse rejected — knowing the saying may end him. The nafs as life makes the reading exact: the enjoiner sells his life in the sentence he speaks, and the verse records the transaction as the highest commerce available to a believer.

**ʿAlī in the Prophet's Bed**

The sīrah supplies the sale's most famous instance, reported by al-Thaʿlabī and the historians in connection with this verse. On the night of the Hijrah, with the Meccan assassins posted around the house waiting to strike at dawn, the Prophet commanded ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib to sleep in his bed and cover himself with his green mantle, so that the watchers, peering through the door's hole, would see a sleeper and believe him still present. ʿAlī — a young man lying down in a targeted bed, under a mantle that identified him as the target — asked whether the Prophet would be safe, was assured, and lay down; when the assassins rushed in at the hour they had chosen, they found ʿAlī and not Muhammad. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī gather the reports and keep, over all of them, the universal reading the passage prefers: whoever gives away his selfish desires or his life for God's sake has entered the virtuous bargain.

**The Virtuous Bargain**

The commentators' summary phrase for the verse — a virtuous bargain in the ultimate sense — states the economics the sūrah has been building since its opening pages. Every human being spends his nafs; the only question is the buyer. The traders of 2:16 spent their guidance on error and called the loss a trade; the concealers of 2:174 spent God's words on a fleeting gain and ate fire; the hypocrite of 204–206 spends his eloquence on this world's impression and is carried by pride into a sufficient Hell. The seller of this verse spends the same currency — the self, with its desires, its safety, its years — on the one counterparty whose payment does not fail: the good pleasure of God. The bargain's virtue is not that the seller receives more than he gives (he gives everything and receives a pleasure that is God's own) but that the transaction ends the selling: the self spent on the world must be re-spent forever, appetite renewing appetite, while the self sold to God is bought outright, and the buyer's name for the purchase follows in the same verse. The whole market-imagery of the sūrah — purchase, sale, trade, profit, loss — arrives here at its one transaction both parties will never regret.
verses.208:
> O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy

**The Command to Enter Completely**

The diptych of the two men gives way to a direct address, and the address gathers the whole community: O you who believe, enter into the silm — completely. The command's first word raised the exegetes' longest question: silm literally means peace, and many read it here as submission — islām itself — acknowledging, as al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī do, that this is not the word's plain lexical sense but its contextual one. Others take it as obedience in the general sense: enter into the state of obeying God wholly. The readings converge on the act commanded: a total entry, the believer's full-person immersion in the religion rather than a partial occupancy of it.

**The Footsteps of Satan**

The second clause names what partial entry actually is: do not follow the footsteps of Satan. The phrase is the Qur'an's fixed formula — the same command the food-legislation carried (2:168), the cattle-rulings of the sūrah of the Cattle repeat it (6:142), and the sūrah of Light legislates it for the believers directly: whoever follows Satan's footsteps, he commands immorality and wickedness (24:21). The word khuṭuwāt — footsteps, tracks, the prints of a walked path — carries the formula's whole psychology: Satan's method is not the leap but the step. He does not invite the believer from the mosque to the Fire in one motion; he lays a track — the small concession, the reasonable exception, the reservation kept from the old life, the room left unentered — and each step is short enough to take. The verse's two clauses are therefore one argument: the incomplete entry *is* the first footprint. The convert keeping his Sabbath, the believer skipping a rite, the community splitting into factions — each has placed a foot on a track that leads, step by undramatic step, away from the house he thinks he still lives in. The manifest-enemy clause at the verse's end confirms the reading: an enemy declared, an enemy known, is countered by watching the path rather than the horizon — the footsteps, not the face.

**The Enemy Manifest**

The closing declaration — he is your manifest enemy — states the enmity's two properties at once. Manifest: the hostility is not hidden, not debatable, not subject to reassessment — Satan declared his program at the beginning, in the Qur'an's own narration of his expulsion: to sit for them on the straight path, to come from before and behind, to prove them ungrateful. The enemy who has published his methods is the enemy whose footsteps can be recognized, and the verse's command to watch the tracks presupposes the declaration's clarity. And *your* enemy: the enmity is personal and collective — aimed at each believer and at the community's entry as a whole, which is why the two clauses address the individual's completeness and the community's togetherness together. The sūrah's earlier food-legislation ended its own footsteps-command with the same declaration (2:168), and the repetition is the verse's pedagogy: the believer is reminded, at each legislative station, that the track exists and the enemy is known. Between the impressed speech of the hypocrite (2:204) and the total entry commanded here, the sūrah has drawn the whole geography of the heart's danger — the eloquence from outside, the footsteps from below — and stationed one command against both: enter, completely, together, and watch the ground you walk on.

**The Verse at the Passage's Hinge**

The placement of this command completes the movement's architecture. The hajj-legislation formed the community through rite (2:196–203); the diptych displayed the heart's two economies (2:204–207); and this verse issues the summons that both prepared: enter completely. The summons is addressed to believers — to people already inside the door — which is its sharpest feature: the rite-formed, portrait-warned community is told that its membership is still an entry, a movement not yet completed, a house with rooms it has not walked into. The verse that follows will state the stakes of faltering in that entry — if you slip after the clear proofs have come (2:209) — and the one after it the scene the slipper is waiting for. But the hinge-verse itself holds the whole demand in two clauses: the totality of the entry against the partiality of reservation, and the watchfulness of the path against the subtlety of the enemy. The community that left Minā knowing it would be gathered to God is now gathered to one command, and the command is the religion's own name turned into a verb: become what you are called — enter the silm, all of you, into all of it, with the enemy's footsteps visible on the ground at the door.
verses.209:
> If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise

**The Slip After the Proofs**

The verse states the community's danger-case in one conditional: if you slip — after the clear proofs have come to you. The verb zalla is precise: not the rebellion of the defiant but the slip of the foot on smooth ground, the stumble of one who was standing, the error of one who was upright. The sūrah's vocabulary keeps the distinction sharp — the disbeliever rejects, the hypocrite conceals, the transgressor exceeds; the one who zalla was on the path and left it by a loss of footing rather than a decision of enmity. And the timing is the clause's aggravator: after the clear proofs — the bayyināt — have come. Al-Ṭabarī lists what the proofs comprehensively denote: the Prophet himself, the Qur'an, Islam as the embodied way, or all of them together.

**The Verse Against Despair**

Read beside the spending-verse of the same passage, this conditional performs a specific pastoral work. The sūrah had already named one self-destruction as the sinner's counsel of doom — the reading of 2:195 recorded by the exegetes, in which a person who believes his sin unforgivable goes on sinning, surrendering to moral despair instead of repenting. The slip-clause here could feed exactly that despair: I was given the proofs and I stumbled, so my case is closed. The verse's answer is the knowledge-command: the slipper is directed not into self-assessment but into theology — know God's might and wisdom rather than measure your own ruin. The direction matters because the two names hold the door open from both sides: the Mighty is the One whose strength the sūrah has repeatedly made the refuge of the weak, and the Wise is the One whose wisdom includes the repentance-legislation the sūrah has spread everywhere — the Forgiving turned toward every returner (2:160), the Forgiving and Merciful named over the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199). The verse thus refuses the slipper both escapes: it does not soften the slip into insignificance (the proofs were clear; the fall was real; the Might is over you) and it does not harden it into finality (the Wisdom that legislated the proofs legislated the return). Know, it says — and the knowing is the standing-up.

**The Footing of the Community**

The address is plural, and the slip it warns of is communal as well as personal. The clear proofs came to a community — the Prophet among them, the Qur'an descending on them, the legislation arriving verse by verse into their actual cases — and the community can slip where individuals slip: the rite kept in form while its wisdom drains (the boast returning after the remembrance, the prayer of this world alone replacing the double-horizon petition), the complete entry of 2:208 decaying into the provincial practice, the diptych's eloquent impostor admired again after his pattern was published. The verse's placement after the entry-command is deliberate: total entry is the footing, and the slip is what happens to the feet that stop walking into the house. The knowledge-command then reads as the community's maintenance — the regular re-knowing of the Might and the Wisdom that keeps the proofs from becoming furniture, the familiarity that precedes every communal zalla. The sūrah's own method models the maintenance: it re-states its proofs at every station, returns its names at every verdict, repeats its portraits — because a community that has received the bayyināt needs them re-delivered, not once but at every footing-risk, and the verse is the shortest form of that re-delivery: know.

**The Knowledge That Stands**

The verse's total demand reduces to its verb: know. Not perform more, not fear harder, not recover the lost ground by effort — know God's might and wisdom. The command identifies knowledge as the footing itself: the clear proofs came as knowledge, the slip happened despite knowledge, and the recovery is a knowledge deeper than the proofs' reception — the knowledge of who sent them and what His attributes guarantee. This is the same knowledge the hajj-legislation ended on: know that to Him you will be gathered (2:203); and the same knowledge the war-code ran on: know that God is with the mindful (2:194), severe in retribution (2:196). The sūrah's legislative stations all close in the commanded knowing, and this verse stations the knowing at the danger-point — the slip after clarity — because the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise is precisely what a slipping person has stopped having. The proofs inform the mind; this knowledge re-forms the posture: the heart that knows the Might cannot treat the slip as escape, and the heart that knows the Wisdom cannot treat the law as mistake. Between those two impossibilities the standing is rebuilt — and the verse, having rebuilt it, turns toward the horizon where all standing and slipping arrive.
verses.210:
> Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺

**Do They Wait for Anything Less?**

The verse answers the suspended question of the verse before with its full scene: do they wait for anything less than that God should come to them in the shadows of the clouds, and the angels, and the matter be decided? The verse thus names the posture it condemns: the life lived in the assumption that the decisive moment is indefinitely postponed, that the proofs can be received and slipped against (2:209) because the reckoning waits politely at the horizon. The clouds of the scene are the scripture's fixed apparatus of theophany — the same clouds the Day's own description uses: the day the heavens are split open with the clouds and the angels are sent down in ranks (25:25) — and the verse imports that whole imagery into the present tense of the waiting: what they wait for has a described form, a published manner of arrival, and a settled consequence, and the waiting is therefore not vagueness but appointment-keeping with their own end.

**The Matter Decided**

The scene's third element is the decision: and the matter has been decreed. Al-Rāzī explains the finality the clause carries: it refers to the Hereafter's decisive character — at that arrival the deeds have already been done, and there is no adding to them and no subtracting from them. The probation is over; the record is closed; the portion earned (2:202) is fixed. The Qur'an states the same closure in the sūrah of the Cattle's answer to the demand for visible angels: had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would be given no respite (6:8) — the angelic arrival and the decision's finality bound together there exactly as here. The clause is the verse's answer to the waiting posture at its root: what the deferrer is waiting for is the end of waiting — the hour whose whole function is to settle, after which no slip can be recovered (2:209), no entry completed (2:208), no soul sold (2:207), no portion altered. The matter decided is the swift reckoning arriving in scene-form: the audit the previous verses described as instantaneous disclosed at last as event — the clouds, the angels, and the book that no longer changes.

**To God All Matters Return**

The verse's final clause widens the decision into the cosmos's constant: to God all matters are returned. The formula is among the scripture's most repeated closures — to Him belong the matters' return in Āl ʿImrān, in the Spoils, in Hūd, in the Pilgrimage, in the Angels, in Iron (3:109; 8:44; 11:123; 22:76; 35:4; 57:5) — and its sense here is the waiting's refutation: the matters do not drift, defer, or belong to the interval; every affair is already in return-motion toward its Owner. The return is understood primarily as the Hereafter's gathering — the matters of every soul delivered back for the settlement — but its grammar holds the present tense too: the matter is returned at every moment of its existence, since nothing is ever out of His hands long enough to be lost. For the waiter the clause collapses the postponement's illusion: the arrival he defers toward is not a future interruption of the present order but the disclosure of the order the present already keeps — matters returning, accounts moving, the reckoning swift. The verse thus ends where the hajj-coda ended (to Him you will be gathered, 2:203) and where the whole sūrah's legislation has been pointing: every law a matter in return, every slip a matter in return, every prayer a matter already answered in the returning.

**The Verse Between Slip and Sign**

Within the passage's movement the verse holds the middle position between two addresses. Behind it: the command to enter completely, the warning of the slip after the proofs, the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise (2:208–209). Before it: the turn to the Children of Israel and their clear signs (2:211), the world made fair to the mockers (2:212), humanity's one community and the Book sent to judge its differences (2:213). The cloud-scene is the hinge between the community's internal danger and its historical lesson: the believers who might slip are shown the terminus their slipping defers toward, and then shown the people whose story proves the terminus real — the Israelites who received sign after sign and altered the favor after it came. The waiting-question binds both panels: the slipper waits as though the decision were far; the sign-recipients lived as though the favor were theirs to change; and the clouds arrive for both at the hour that ends both illusions. The verse leaves its reader with the posture the whole passage commands — the entry complete before the shadows fill the sky, the slip recovered before the matter is decided, the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise held until the return that holds every knower.
verses.211:
> Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺ should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

**The Question Put to History**

The verse turns from the cloud-scene to a standing witness: ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. The command to question is the verse's method — history summoned as testimony in the case the previous verses opened. The community that might slip after its proofs (2:209) is directed to the people who lived the slip at the largest scale the world has seen: a nation fed with signs, delivered by miracles, covenanted with God, and still the scripture's standing example of favor altered. The interrogative kam — how many — expects no number because the number is beyond counting; the question asks the witness to display its record, and the record itself is the argument. Al-Ṭabarī fixes the signs' identity: the miracles of Moses — the staff cast down and become a serpent, the hand drawn out white, the sea parted, the enemy drowned — the sign-cycle the sūrah of the Heights narrates at length (7:105–136). Each sign was a bayyinah, a clear proof in the exact sense 2:209 used for the proofs given this community: evidence so plain that rejection after it is not ignorance but choice. The verse thus establishes the comparison the passage needs — the proofs of this ummah against the signs of that — and asks the question whose answer is the warning.

**The Severe Retribution**

The verdict clause repeats the formula the hajj-legislation closed on: God is severe in retribution — shadīd al-ʿiqāb. The same phrase ended the pilgrimage's concessions-verse (2:196), where it guarded the rite's interior against exploitation; here it guards the favor against alteration, and the repetition across the passage is deliberate — the two domains where the law has no human auditor, the pilgrim's intention and the covenant-keeper's fidelity, are the two domains the severe-retribution formula oversees. The severity answers the crime's shape: an alteration performed after full receipt is not weakness but transaction — the favor traded, the verse says in the translation's gloss, for disbelief — and a transaction is answered by a price. The sūrah has been building this economics since its opening: the traders who purchased error at guidance's price (2:16), the concealers who sold revelation for a fleeting gain and ate fire (2:174–175), the covenant-sellers of Āl ʿImrān whose trade earns them no share in the Hereafter and no divine speech on the Day (3:77). The Israelite alteration is the pattern's first national instance, and the severe retribution is the pattern's fixed consequence: the favor exchanged is not only lost but avenged, because the exchange itself is the insult — the Giver's gift re-valued by the receiver as less than disbelief.

**The Signs and the Scripture's Own Case**

The verse's signs have a specific edge for a community whose central sign is a book. The miracles of Moses were public and physical — the staff, the hand, the sea — signs seen by multitudes and survived by no disputer; and the Children of Israel altered the favor built on them. The new community's clear proofs include a sign of a different order — the Qur'an itself, a bayyinah of speech rather than spectacle — and the verse's warning transfers without loss: the alteration Israel performed on signs it saw, a later generation can perform on a sign it reads, adjusting the Book's words toward desire, re-interpreting the covenant's terms, substituting for the favor a version of the favor that costs nothing. The sūrah has already legislated against exactly this on its own pages: the editors who write the book with their hands and say this is from God (2:79), the concealers who hide what was revealed (2:174), the far-schismatics who differ about the Book in truth (2:176).

**Between the Clouds and the One Community**

Within the movement's architecture the verse is the bridge between the horizon and the history. The cloud-scene (2:210) showed the waiting its terminus; this verse shows the slipping its precedent; and the verses that follow will show the whole human story its shape — the world made fair to the mockers (2:212), humanity one community then divided, the Book sent down to judge the division (2:213). The Israelite question is the middle term: the case-history that proves the terminus is not theoretical. A people asked, given signs, altered the favor, met the severe retribution — the sequence in completed form, available for the asking. The community reading these verses between the hajj's end and the coming trials-verse stands at the sequence's second step: proofs received, favor held. The verse tells it what the third step can be and what the fourth is — and the command to ask is the instruction for staying at the second: keep inquiring of the archive, keep the case-history present, keep the alteration visible in the witness's own record. The signs given Israel are counted; the favor they altered is named; the retribution's severity is published — and the whole testimony is left standing at the door of every community the proofs afterward reach.
verses.212:
> The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit

**They Mock the Believers**

The adornment's social expression is the mockery: they ridicule those who believe. Al-Thaʿlabī records the occasions — the verse was revealed about the Meccan idolaters, or the Medinan hypocrites, or the Jewish leaders of Medina who belittled the Muslim community for its composition: the poor, the weak, the slaves and laborers who filled its first ranks while the notables stayed away. The mockery has a fixed structure the verse assumes: the disbelievers measure the believers by the beautified world's metrics — wealth, status, comfort — and find them losing, then announce the verdict publicly, as though the ledger of adornment were the only ledger. The Qur'an answers this scene repeatedly and consistently: the sūrah of the Mockers devotes its opening to the woe of every scorner who counts his wealth (104:1–2); the Garden's people will call down to the Fire's people asking what their counting availed them (74:40–47 in substance); and the reversal the mockers cannot see is the verse's next clause. The mockery is also, in the passage's own logic, the diptych's continuation: the eloquent hypocrite whose worldly speech impressed (2:204) is the mocker in his community-role, and the mocked believers are the sellers of their souls (2:207) — the verse names both groups' worldly standing and then overturns it in the Day's.

**Above Them on the Day**

The reversal is stated in a single future tense: those who are mindful — the muttaqūn — will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. The elevation is the mockery's exact answer: the ranking the world performed in reverse, the Day performs in truth. Al-Qurṭubī notes the tradition's elaborations — reports describing how the belittled and mocked believers will receive great fame and standing on the Day while their abusers are humiliated and punished — and the verse's own wording carries the whole: above them, a spatial verdict in a scene the scripture consistently describes in the spatial terms of rank, the Garden's people calling down to the Fire's, the elevated couches and the lowered abode. The taqwā named as the elevation's criterion completes the passage's thread: the reverent are the ones the hajj-legislation formed (2:196–203), the ones the flexible options were granted for (2:203), the ones God is with (2:194) — and the verse now publishes the community's true standing against its mockers. The mockery measured by adornment; the Day measures by mindfulness; and the measured are placed above not by retaliation but by the simple disclosure of what the two currencies were always worth.

**Provision Without Reckoning**

The verse closes with the clause that re-reads everything before it: God provides for whomever He wills without reckoning. The exegetes unfold the phrase's several senses, and each cuts against the mockers' ledger. God does not give a reckoning to anyone for what He does — the Provider answers to no auditor, and the adorned life's distribution is His alone. The giving spans both worlds — provision in this life and provision in the next (al-Rāzī), so the adorned man's wealth is not the whole of what is being distributed. And the clause alludes to the incommensurability of God's giving altogether — the tenfold and beyond of the good deed (6:160), the grain that sprouts seven ears of a hundred grains (2:261), the provision found beside Mary in the sanctuary, from God, who provides for whom He wills without limit (3:37).

**The Verse Between the Diptych and the One Community**

The verse's placement binds the movement's three panels into one argument. The diptych (2:204–207) showed the heart's two economies in individual form — the marketed self and the sold self. The slip-and-cloud verses (2:208–211) showed the community's footing and its horizon — the proofs, the waiting, the altered favor of the witness-people. This verse shows the two economies at social scale: the beautified world with its mockers, the taqwā with its mocked, and the Day with its reversal — and the following verse will widen the scene once more to the species, humanity one community then divided, the Book sent to judge (2:213). The through-line is the currency-question the whole passage keeps asking: what is the world's adornment worth against the portion earned (2:202), the sold soul's price (2:207), the favor not altered (2:211)? The verse's answer is the provision-clause — the giving without reckoning, in which the mockers' wealth is a measured thing inside the Unmeasured's hand, and the mocked believer's standing is a weight already placed. The reader carried from Minā's gathering through the hypocrite's portrait to this verse arrives at the community's charter against contempt: the adornment is real but reckoned by another arithmetic, the mockery is loud but brief, and the above-them of the Day is provision without limit made visible.
verses.213:
> Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path

**Humanity Was One Community**

The verse opens the whole human story in a single clause: mankind was one community — ummah wāḥidah. The exegetes' readings map the possibilities, and al-Ṭabarī notes that the exact chronology is not what matters. Some locate the unity in the period between Adam and Noah; some understand it as a unity in disbelief and degradation, later corrected through Noah and then Abraham; others describe a unity in submission — all humanity following one religion, one community of believers before the loss. Another reading takes the oneness as Adam himself: humanity began as a single person and became many, and the Qur'an does use ummah of one man — Abraham was an ummah, rendered in the common translation as a model of excellence, devout and upright (16:120). A further reading connects the one community to the pretemporal covenant of 7:172, when all Adam's descendants testified Am I not your Lord? and answered yes — the unity of that original acknowledgment. The readings agree on the verse's structural point: the story begins in oneness, and everything that follows — prophets, books, differences — is the history of that oneness lost and its truth recovered. The sūrah of Yūnus states the same opening with the divergence explicit: mankind was nothing but one community, then they differed (10:19).

**Bearers of Glad Tidings and Warners**

The prophets are sent with a double office the Qur'an names as a fixed pair: bashīr — bearer of glad tidings — and nadhīr — warner. The two functions are the revelation's two hands: the good news that draws, the warning that drives, the Garden announced and the Fire announced, and no prophet sent with one hand only. With them — and the phrase binds book to messenger in one descent — God sent down the Book in truth, to judge between people in what they differed about. The Book here is read at two scopes: the general name for all the revealed books (al-Shaʿbī's reading), or the Torah specifically if the verse is tied to the Jews and Christians alone (al-Ṭabarī's alternative); the comprehensive reading carries the verse's universal frame better — one Book in successive descents, each installment in truth, each sent for the same adjudicating purpose. The phrase in truth is the same formula that grounded the far-schismatics' sentence (2:176): the Book descends bi'l-ḥaqq, its content corresponding to what is, its purpose the settlement of disputes by a standard no party controls. The verse by this states revelation's job-description: not to decorate the difference but to judge it — the Book as court, the prophets as its bearers, the glad tidings and warnings as its two verdicts.

**Only Those Given It Differed**

The verse's most searching clause reports the trial's outcome: none differed about the Book except those who were given it — after the clear proofs came to them — out of mutual injustice and envy. The paradox is the scripture's standing grief: the difference did not arise from the Book's absence but from its presence; the disputants were not the uninformed outsiders but the informed recipients; the proofs were clear and the division came after. The sūrah states the same sequence of the People of the Scripture: they did not dispute among themselves out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them (3:19); and the sūrah of the Clear Proof repeats it: the People of the Book became divided only after the clear proof came to them (98:4). The motive named — baghy, the envious overreaching — identifies the difference's engine: not honest interpretive struggle but rivalry, the competition of parties who want the Book's authority for themselves. The commentators draw the general lesson: there is something near-inevitable, given human nature, about difference arising after revelation arrives — the truth given to a community becomes, in envious hands, the truth disputed by that community. The verse thus completes the warning of 2:211: Israel altered the favor after receiving it; here the whole pattern is generalized — the recipients are the differers, the proofs precede the division, and the envy is the difference's parent.

**Guided to the Truth by His Leave**

The verse's penultimate clause turns from the divided to the guided: then God guided those who believe to the truth of what they differed about, by His leave. The sūrah of the Table states the framework the guidance operates in: to each community God ordained a law and a way, and had He willed He would have made you one community — but He tests you with what He has given you, so compete in good works; to God you all return and He will inform you of what you differed about (5:48). The verse of al-Baqarah is that framework's present tense: the differences are real, the competition is commanded, the final information is deferred to the Return — and in the meantime, by His leave, the believers hold the truth of the disputed matter, not as possession but as granted guidance.
verses.214:
> Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near

**The Question the Community Must Answer**

The verse opens with a question that dismantles an assumption: do you suppose you will enter the Garden without the likes of what befell those who passed before you? The interrogative form is not inquiry but correction — the community is addressed as people who have been entertaining, perhaps unconsciously, the idea that paradise is an inheritance of confession rather than an outcome of trial. The sūrah states the same principle twice more in identical terms: do you think you will enter Paradise while God has not yet proven who among you struggled and endured (3:142), and the sūrah of the Spider's opening — do people think they will be left to say "we believe" without being tested? We tested those before them (29:2–3). The three verses form a single doctrine of the tested faith: belief declares itself in words, and the trial verifies it in fact; between the declaration and the verification stands the whole life of the community. The verse's reference to those who passed before installs that verification in history — the test ahead is not novel but inherited, the same furnace every believing generation has entered, and its heat is not evidence of abandonment but of membership.

**The Trench, the Exile, and the Taunts**

The reports of occasion place the verse inside the community's hardest hours. Some connect it to the Battle of the Trench in the fifth year, when the confederated tribes besieged Medina and the Qur'an's own sūrah of the Parties remembers the days — when forces came against you and God sent a wind and hosts you did not see (33:9); others connect it to Uḥud in the third year, the defeat on the mountain. Al-Rāzī and al-Thaʿlabī preserve the social texture behind the shaking: the Emigrants were bearing the cost of exile — property left in Mecca, livelihoods interrupted, families divided — while the locals and the hypocrites taunted them, asking how long they would sacrifice themselves and their wealth for a cause that looked, by every worldly reckoning, like a losing one. The verse answers the taunt by relocating it in history: the question "when will this cost end?" is not a new question invented by Medina's cynics but the old question of every community under trial — asked, the verse will say, even by the Messenger and the believers with him.

**"When Will God's Help Come?"**

The cry is quoted: *When will God's help come?* The exegetes handled the question with care, because it issues from the Messenger and the believers together. Some read the Messenger here as Muhammad specifically; others took it generally — every prophet and his people at their trial's depth, since all the prophets encounter severe trials. Al-Qurṭubī records the reading that protects prophetic certainty: the Messenger knew the help was coming and the question sought its hastening — not doubt about whether but impatience for when. The Qur'an's parallel portraits confirm that prophethood does not exempt its bearers from the weight of trial: the messengers despaired and their people thought them denied, until Our help came (12:110); the breast straitened by what they say (15:97 in substance); the torment of the self over a people who will not believe (26:3 in substance); Job's affliction and his cry (21:83). The station of prophethood, in the Qur'an's presentation, includes human vulnerability to fear, sadness, and discouragement — and the verse quotes the cry rather than censoring it because the cry itself, at the trial's limit, is not disbelief but the last form of address to God: the question asked *to* Him, not about Him.

**The Verse as the Passage's Foundation**

The placement of this verse after the one-community history (2:213) and before the legislation of fighting (2:216) gives it an architectural office. The previous verse ended with the guidance granted by God's leave to those who believe; this verse states what the guided community must expect on the road — the trial of those before, carried to the shaking-point — and the verse after will legislate the obligation the community finds hateful. The sequence is pedagogy: guidance, then testing, then the hard command — the community is not given the command to fight before it is told what commands cost and what trials precede paradise. The verse also answers the mockery it will meet two verses on: the disbelievers for whom the world is beautified and who ridicule the believers (2:212) are exactly the taunters the reports describe, and the trial-verse tells the mocked that their shaking has a company, a purpose, and a near help. Between the one community of the past and the divided communities of the present, this verse installs the constant: every community that receives the truth is tried by it — and the trial's last word, spoken over the cry of the Messenger and the believers themselves, is the nearness of the help.
verses.215:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”

**The Standing Roster**

The five named recipients are not an ad hoc list but the Qur'an's standing roster of the people a righteous economy is measured by. The same names recur wherever the scripture legislates giving: the definition of righteousness counted kinsfolk, orphans, the poor, the traveler, beggars, and captives (2:177); the kindness-command of the sūrah of the Women lists parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbors near and far, the companion, the wayfarer, and those your right hands have (4:36); the war-booty legislation assigns its fifth to God and the Messenger, the near relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveler (8:41); and the sūrah of the Exile repeats the same five with its economic principle — so that wealth may not merely circulate among your rich (59:7). The recurrence is the point: the community is not given a different charity-list for each occasion but one list, installed across legislation, worship, and war alike, so that the same faces are seen in every distribution — the faces of the people the economy exists for.

**Whatever Good You Do, God Knows**

The closing clause returns the whole legislation to its unseen auditor: whatever good you do, God knows it. The same assurance stood inside the hajj-legislation — whatever good you do, God fully knows of it (2:197) — and in both places it does the same double work. It is a guarantee: the giving nobody sees, the relative supported quietly, the traveler relieved without witness — all of it is known, recorded, and answerable in reward; no act of charity is lost to the ledger for want of an audience. And it is a discipline: the knowledge of God audits the giving that *has* an audience, separating the charity performed for the eyes of people from the charity performed for the Face of God — the sūrah's recurring distinction, whose failure-mode it painted in the hypocrite who spends to be seen. The clause's placement after the list ties the two halves together: the recipients are named so the giving is directed rightly; the knower is named so the giving is motivated rightly. Direction and motive — the two coordinates of every act of charity — are fixed in one sentence.

**The Question-Verses as Classroom**

This verse is one of a dense cluster in which the community's actual questions are answered by revelation — the new moons and the doors of houses (2:189), the nearness of God to the caller (2:186), the sacred month's fighting (2:217), wine and gambling and the amount to spend (2:219), the orphans' affairs (2:220), menstruation (2:222). The cluster forms the sūrah's method of legislation: not a code delivered in the abstract but answers delivered to questions, the law growing at the points where the community's life actually presses against it. The question about spending — what should we give? — is the community asking to be directed in its daily economics, and the answer's form trains a habit: ask, and the revelation names the people. The method also honors the asking: the question is not rebuked as ignorance but answered as curriculum, and every generation inherits both the answers and the permission to bring its own cases to the text. The sūrah's legislation is thus dialogical — a community being formed through inquiry, with the roster of the needy installed at the center of the exchange.

**The Giver Between the List and the Knower**

Read whole, the verse places the giver between two presences: the visible claimants and the invisible Knower. The list makes the giving concrete — not "the poor" as abstraction but the father aging in the next room, the cousin fallen on hard years, the child whose guardian died, the beggar at the gate, the stranger whose caravan left without him. The knowledge-clause makes the giving pure — performed under an audit that sees the hand and the heart together. Between the two, charity becomes what the sūrah's whole economy intends: a transfer of wealth that is simultaneously an act of worship, directed to faces and offered to a Face. The verse that answers a simple question about spending thus carries the full moral architecture of Islamic giving — the priority of persons over amounts, the order of claims from kin outward, the surveillance that keeps the motive clean — and leaves the asker with a list to memorize and a Knower to remember.
verses.216:
> Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**The Third Kutiba**

The verse uses the sūrah's legislative formula for the third time: it has been prescribed for you — the same verb that wrote the retaliation for murder (2:178) and wrote the fast (2:183). The formula's repetition builds the community's constitution in three obligations, and the third is the hardest: fighting. The sequence is itself instructive — the law of blood, the law of the body's appetite, the law of the body's risk — each *kutiba*, each written rather than suggested. But this prescription arrives with a clause its two predecessors did not carry: *though it is hateful to you*.

**The Dislike Named, Not Rebuked**

The hateful-to-you clause has a precision worth marking. The Qur'an nowhere commands the emotional conversion of the reluctant fighter — there is no "fight and love it," no rebuke of the distaste as faithlessness. The dislike is treated as a fact of the human constitution, as real as the hunger the fast legislates over and the fear the battle produces. What the verse does is refuse the dislike a veto: the obligation is prescribed *while* the aversion is acknowledged, so the community learns to act from obedience rather than from appetite. The contrast with the hypocrites is immediate and structural: the diptych two movements earlier described the man whose speech delights while his heart is enmity (2:204) — the outward performance without the inner assent; this verse legislates the inverse, the inward reluctance carried by outward obedience. Between the eloquent impostor and the reluctant believer the sūrah has drawn its true line: God weighs what the hands do under the command, not what the feelings say about it — and the feeling of dislike, honestly held and honestly overridden, is closer to faith than the enthusiasm that performs.

**God Knows, and You Do Not Know**

The verse ends with the knowledge-clause that authorizes the whole transfer: God knows, and you know not. The formula is not a rebuke of ignorance in general but a specification of the gap that matters here: God knows the outcomes the fighting will produce — the persecution it will end, the community it will secure, the fitnah whose continuation the war-code named as worse than killing (2:191) — and the community knows only its own dislike. The clause is the epistemological ground of the two perhapses: the dislike-and-good and love-and-evil reversals are possible precisely because the divine knowledge spans the consequences and the human knowledge spans the moment. Read with the war-legislation behind it, the clause completes that legislation's frame: 2:190–193 bounded the fighting with reciprocity, proportionality, the sanctuary's immunity, and the cessation's pardon; this verse supplies the obligation's warrant — the bounded fighting is *written*, and its writing rests on a knowledge the commanded do not have. The believer's posture is therefore fixed between two knowledges: he does not know why this war and not another feels right; he knows that the One who does know has prescribed it within limits He Himself drew.

**The Verse Between Trial and Legislation**

The verse's placement completes the movement the trial-verse opened. The community was told it would be tested as those before were tested, shaken to the cry of *when comes God's help* (2:214); it was taught the roster of charity in the meantime (2:215); and now it receives the obligation the trial will chiefly run through — fighting, prescribed, disliked, defended by the knowledge-clause. The sequence trains a specific disposition: obedience under aversion, endurance under shaking, action under uncertainty of outcome. The verse that follows will take up the fighting's hardest case — the sacred month, the expedition that erred, the enemy's graver crimes — and the whole passage will legislate war inside a community whose feelings about war have been honestly legislated for. The reluctant believer of this verse is the same person the trial-verse shook and the roster-verse taught to give: one community, formed by trial, directed in charity, and commanded in what it dislikes — held together by the sentence that carries all three: God knows, and you know not.
verses.217:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**The Expedition at the Oasis**

The verse answers a crisis, and the reports preserve its details. Roughly eighteen months after the Hijrah — before Badr — a scouting party under the Companion ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh went out against Meccan movements. At a watering-stop between Ṭāʾif and Mecca they encountered a caravan: a man was killed — ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī — two captives taken, and the caravan's goods brought home. The killing, it emerged, had fallen on Rajab's opening day — sacred time — though the party had supposed Jumādā's final day still running — a confusion the crescent-based calendar made possible, since the month's beginning depended on the sighting the sūrah's moon-verse had legislated (2:189). The Prophet's response was immediate and severe: he declined the share of caravan-goods brought to him, and told the party that fighting in holy time was no order of his. The Quraysh seized the incident, condemning the breach and accusing the Prophet of transgressing the Arabian norm of the sacred months — spilling blood in the forbidden time. The affair was eventually resolved when the captives were ransomed back and ʿAmr's blood-price paid; and the verse descended, addressing all parties with a hierarchy of sins that neither side had calculated.

**Fitnah Is Graver Than Killing**

The weighing's summary clause repeats the war-code's foundational ranking: persecution — fitnah — is graver than killing. The same sentence stood inside the field-legislation (2:191), and its repetition here, in a case about an actual killing, is the verse's sharpest edge: the death of one man at the oasis is set against the campaign to destroy faith itself, and the campaign is named the greater evil. Fitnah in this usage carries the meaning the exegetes fixed — the trial and torture inflicted to make believers renounce their religion, the persecution whose end is apostasy, and in the commentators' gloss the idolatry the persecution aimed to restore. The clause by this answers the Quraysh's propaganda at its root: the party loudest about one bloodshed in a sacred month was the party operating a standing system of bloodshed against faith — and the verse measures the month's violator and the faith's persecutor in the same sight of God.

**They Will Not Cease**

The verse then states the enemy's objective as a permanent fact: the campaign against the community runs on, without pause, until apostasy succeeds — if it ever can. The clause is the war-legislation's intelligence report — the persecution named as not an episode but a program, bounded only by the enemy's ability, aimed not at territory or tribute but at the believers' faith itself. The conditional *if they are able* is not a softening but a realism: the objective stands whether or not the power currently matches it, and the community is instructed to plan against the objective rather than the momentary capacity. This is the verse's contribution to the whole war-code: 2:190–193 had legislated the fighting's limits and its end — fight until fitnah ceases; this verse confirms from the enemy's side that fitnah will not cease on its own, that the other program runs in the opposite direction with the same persistence. The two programs — the persecution aimed at apostasy, the fighting aimed at ending persecution — cannot both stop voluntarily, and the verse tells the community which one it is facing.

**The Apostate's Ledger**

The verse's final movement legislates the consequence of the enemy's success: whoever renounces his religion and dies in disbelief — the ledger of his deeds annuls itself across both lives, and the Fire becomes his lasting residence. The voiding is comprehensive: the whole ledger of a believing life — its prayers, its charity, its hijrah, its patience under trial — is annulled by apostasy carried to death. The exegetes note what the verse equally implies: the renouncer *can* return, and return restores him to the community, though some jurists held that certain obligations — notably the hajj — must be performed anew. And the tradition weighed carefully what the verse does and does not legislate about the community's treatment of the renouncer. The word irtadda is often translated as apostasy, but the commentators stress that mere change of religion is not, for many classical and contemporary scholars, a cause for communal punishment — in light of the Qur'an's own freedom-statements: the truth is from your Lord, so let whoever wills believe and whoever wills disbelieve (18:29); there is no compulsion in religion (2:256); to you your religion, and to me mine (109:6). On this reading the punishment the verse states is the Hereafter's, and the historical wars of Abū Bakr against the seceding tribes were directed at sedition — at apostasy amounting to a political act of destabilization, the changing of sides in a community where religion and polity were one — rather than at belief alone. The early authorities' practice points the same way: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAlī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and al-Thawrī barred executing a woman for renunciation alone, a distinction that makes sense if the capital matter is the treason and the sword, not the private turn of belief the verse leaves to the Fire's ledger.
verses.218:
> Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Three Deeds**

The triad the verse names — belief, emigration, struggle — is the early community's complete biography in three verbs. Believed: the inner assent, the creed's foundation. Emigrated: the hijrah, faith made geographical — property left in Mecca, homes abandoned, the material cost of allegiance paid in full, the act that gave the community its calendar and its name (the Emigrants, al-muhājirūn). Struggled: the jāhadū, the striving in God's way with wealth and person — the expenditure the previous verses had legislated (2:195) and the fighting the verse before had prescribed (2:16). The three are joined by a single article — *those who* — making one class of people defined by all three together: the believing emigrant striver, the person whose faith cost him his home and whose home-loss issued in striving. The Qur'an returns to this triad repeatedly, and wherever it appears it carries the community's highest social-spiritual rank: the sūrah of the Spoils will give the emigrants who strove a promise of provision without measure, and the sūrah of Repentance will rank the strivers and emigrants at the summit of the believers' degrees. The verse here installs the triad as the identity the promise addresses.

**The Theology of Hope**

The promise itself is couched in a word the exegetes weighed carefully: they *hope* for God's mercy — yarjūn. Al-Rāzī unfolds both readings the word supports. The first is doctrinal: hope reflects the principle that no reward is certain, that everything remains in God's hands, that a person might still die a disbeliever — so the greatest deeds are completed not in certainty of payment but in hope of mercy. The verse thus refuses the community the merchant's confidence: even the believing emigrant striver does not hold God's reward as a debt but approaches it as a hope. And the sūrah connects the hope to its earlier portrait of the humble — those who reckon that they will meet their Lord and to Him they return (2:46): the hoping and the reckoning describe both what believers do and what they are called to do, the expectation of the meeting shaping the life that precedes it.

**Emigration as the Verse's Social Text**

The triad's middle term deserves its social weight, because the verse speaks to a community of displaced people. The Emigrants were the trial-verse's addressees in person: the property left behind, the taunts of the locals and hypocrites about sacrificing for a losing cause (2:214), the years of exile in a city not their own. To such people the verse names emigration as a constitutive act of faith — not a misfortune endured but a deed counted, ranked beside belief and striving in the single clause that defines the promised class. The hijrah's cost becomes its credential: the homes and wealth left in Mecca are not losses written off but expenditures credited to the same account as the striving. And the verse's hope-clause answers the exile's particular temptation — the sense of having paid everything and received nothing yet: the payment is seen, the biography is the promise's addressee, and the mercy hoped for is the exile's eventual homecoming in a form larger than Mecca. The community that would return to the Kaʿbah within years first received this verse, and its hope-structure — deeds counted, reward hoped, mercy named — carried the Emigrants through the remaining seasons of the taunt.

**The Verse Between the Scales and the Questions**

Within the movement's architecture the verse is the hinge between war and domestic law. Behind it: the trial (2:214), the charity roster (2:215), the fighting prescribed despite dislike (2:216), the sacred month's scales (2:217). Ahead: the question-verses of wine and gambling, orphans, marriage, menstruation, oaths, divorce, and nursing — the great household legislation that fills the sūrah's remaining pages. The hinge-verse carries the whole transition: the community that has been legislated for war is assured of its hope before being legislated for home. The triad itself spans both legislations — belief undergirds the household's rules, the emigration built the households that the rules will govern, and the striving includes the patience the domestic law will require. And the verse's final word-order leaves the community inside the names: Forgiving, Merciful — the same names that closed the bequest-legislation (2:182), the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199), and the cessation of hostilities (2:192). The hope for God's mercy is the atmosphere the whole sūrah breathes: every law given inside it, every error absolved under it, every biography — believing, emigrating, striving — received at last by it.
verses.219:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect

**Two Questions, One Method**

The verse continues the sūrah's question-legislation with two inquiries answered in one descent: what about wine and gambling? and what should we spend? The first answer is a weighing rather than a prohibition — in them is great sin, and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit — and the method of the weighing is the verse's first lesson. The revelation does not begin by declaring the two evils pure and simple; it concedes that benefit exists, places it on the scale, and then out-weighs it. The concession is rhetorically and morally load-bearing: a community that knows wine loosens the miser's purse and gambling feeds the poor (the benefits the exegetes will enumerate) is not asked to pretend otherwise — it is asked to hold both columns of the ledger and accept the verdict of the total. *The spared* — the ʿafw, what can be given without strain.

**ʿUmar's Prayer and the Staircase of Prohibition**

The verse is the first of three steps in one of the Qur'an's clearest cases of gradual legislation, and the reports preserve the sequence with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb at its center. Before the prohibition was declared, ʿUmar used to pray: O Allah, give us a clear, satisfying ruling about wine. This verse was revealed — in them is great sin and benefits — and was recited to him; and he prayed again: O Allah, give us a clear ruling about wine. Then came the sūrah of the Women's clause — do not approach the prayer while intoxicated (4:43) — and was recited to him; and he prayed a third time. Then came the sūrah of the Table's decisive verses — Satan only seeks to cast enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you from the remembrance of God and from the prayer; so will you not desist? (5:90–91) — and when they were recited, ʿUmar said: we have desisted. The sequence, preserved in the Sunan collections, is the legislation's own pedagogy: a community weaned off a deeply rooted habit not by a single command but by staged revelation — first the weighing that educated judgment, then the prayer-time restriction that built the habit of abstention, then the final question that asked for the community's own consent. The verse of the weighing is the staircase's first step, and its method — benefit conceded, sin out-weighing — prepared minds the flat prohibition would have met with resistance.

**The Objectives of the Law**

The weighing's rationale entered Islamic legal theory as one of its foundational cases. The harms named for intoxication — beginning with the loss of the rational faculties — made the ruling on wine a central proof for the maqāṣid al-sharīʿah, the objectives-of-the-law doctrine, in which the protection of the intellect stands as one of the essential ends the Law exists to secure, beside the protection of religion, life, lineage, and property. Gambling's harms were analyzed in the same framework: al-Rāzī notes that it creates enmity and despair, produces ill-gotten gains, and diverts from the healthy pursuit of profit — and the risk-structure of the wager entered Islamic financial theory directly, where certain transactions are invalidated for entailing excessive risk, a doctrine connected by financial theorists to the prohibition of ribā, itself discussed by some as carrying a severe form of risk — the usury-legislation this very sūrah will deliver (2:275–280). The verse thus seeded two entire disciplines: a theory of law's purposes built on the intellect's protection, and a theory of finance built on the wager's distinction — gain by chance versus gain by work — with the maysir of the arrows as its founding case.

**The Spared, and the Sentence Left Open**

The second answer names the measure of giving: *the ʿafw* — what can be spared, what comes easily, given without difficulty; the same word elsewhere carries the sense of pardon, and al-Rāzī notes both. The exegetes debated whether the directive concerns voluntary giving or a required duty — some holding it abrogated by the later institution of the zakāh, others seeing no contradiction between a fixed alms-tax and a standing command of charity beyond it. The practical ruling they draw is a middle-path economics: be neither miserly nor improvident; never impoverish yourself through giving — the same balance the sūrah of the Night-Walk states as an image: let not your hand be chained to your neck, nor let it be fully open (17:29). The answer expands the earlier spending-verse — which named the recipients (2:215) — by addressing the amount, completing the curriculum of giving with its two coordinates: to whom, and how much. And the verse's closing opens into the next: thus God makes the signs clear to you, that haply you may reflect — the sentence continuing across the verse-division into the two worlds the reflection is to span. The clarity and the reflection are the whole passage's method in one clause: the signs made clear, the ledger set out, the totals stated — and the mind left to do what clear signs exist for: to think, across this world and the next, about what out-weighs what.
verses.220:
> upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**The Sentence That Crosses the Division**

The verse begins mid-sentence — *upon this world and the Hereafter* — completing the reflection-clause the previous verse left open: thus God makes the signs clear, that you may reflect upon the two worlds. The verse-division falls inside a single grammatical unit, and the effect is deliberate: the reflection commanded over wine and gambling is given its object here, the two horizons across which the weighing must run. The exegetes connect the objects explicitly — the theme of the Hereafter's superiority is joined here to the intoxicants and the wager: the mind is to weigh the passing satisfactions and enduring damages these things breed, judging both against the two horizons (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī).

**The Question About Orphans**

The verse then takes up the third of the cluster's questions: they ask you about the orphans. The occasion the reports preserve explains the question's urgency. The early community had received the scripture's fiercest property-legislation — the devourers of orphans' wealth eating fire into their bellies (4:10), the command not to come near the orphan's property except to improve it (6:152) — and the believers had responded with scrupulosity: guardians kept the orphans' property utterly separate, eating and drinking from completely distinct sources so that nothing of the orphan's might be touched. Al-Ṭabarī records the cost of the scruple: the separation became so burdensome that custodians sometimes withdrew from their wards altogether — and in the aloofness the property itself suffered, spoiling or falling into ruin. Another reading of the occasion looks behind Islam to a pre-Islamic custom: the Arabs had held it inauspicious, an ill omen, to eat with orphans or ride their mounts — a superstition of separation the verse also answers. Either way the question was real: how does a guardian obey the inviolability without destroying the estate — or the relationship — it exists to protect?

**The Economics of the Orchard and the Herd**

The answer's wisdom is embedded in a material fact the commentators supply: an orphan's inheritance in that economy was typically orchards and livestock — fruit trees and animals whose *value is maintained only through use*. An orchard unpruned and unpicked declines; herds unridden, unmilked, and unmanaged lose condition and fail to breed. The inviolability of the orphan's property, enforced as total hands-off separation, would have consumed the very wealth it guarded — the pedantic scruple producing exactly the ruin the legislation existed to prevent. The verse's ruling — set matters aright for them — legislates the estate's flourishing as the guardian's objective: the property is not a museum-piece but a working trust, and its improvement is the standard against which the guardian's every decision is measured. This is why the answer begins not with permissions or prohibitions but with a direction: iṣlāḥ, the setting-right, the making-whole — the same root-family as peacemaking (ṣulḥ) and righteousness (ṣāliḥ), the vocabulary of repair against its opposite, the corruption (fasād) the hypocrite-portrait had just described (2:205). The guardian stands between the two: his office is iṣlāḥ of the estate and of the child's place in the household.

**The Orphan-Legislation in the Sūrah's Whole**

This verse belongs to the scripture's longest sustained legislation for a single vulnerable class. The sūrah opened its social rulings with the orphan's property and its devourers (4:10's fire, echoed at 2:174); the definition of righteousness placed orphans second in charity's roster (2:177), and the spending-answer repeated the rank (2:215); the sūrah of the Women will legislate the estate's management across a whole passage (4:2–10); the Cattle's decalogue commands not approaching the orphan's wealth except to improve it, until maturity (6:152). This verse supplies the system's operating principle — improvement over isolation, brotherhood over segregation, intention audited by God — and its placement inside the question-cluster ties the orphan's welfare to the community's whole moral formation: the same people being taught to weigh wine against its benefits and to spare from their wealth for the roster are taught here that the roster's most vulnerable member is a brother in the house. The verse ends where the household-legislation that follows will begin: with the Almighty and Wise presiding over the intimate details of shared bread — the names that make the daily judgment of the guardian a matter of theology, and the orphan's flourishing a matter of divine interest.
verses.221:
> Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful

**The Legal Development: The People of the Book**

The verse's ruling generated one of the passage's most discussed legal questions, because the sūrah of the Table permits what appears broader: the chaste women of those given the Scripture before you are lawful to you in marriage (5:5). The exegetes record the positions. Some held that 5:5 partially abrogated this verse's ruling, opening marriage with Jewish and Christian women while the prohibition against idolaters stands — a reading that arises only if the People of the Book were classed among the polytheists the verse names. Many maintained the simpler harmonization: the prohibition was never directed at the People of the Book at all, whose scripture and monotheism place them outside the verse's category. A minority held the reverse abrogation — that this verse cancels 5:5, forbidding marriage with any non-Muslim. The operative ruling in Islamic law follows the permissive readings: Muslim men may marry Jewish and Christian women, with some jurists extending the category to Zoroastrians and, in the Indian context, to Hindus. And the asymmetry the verse's second clause established became the law's settled position: the command not to give Muslim women to polytheistic men is understood consistently as barring marriage between a Muslim woman and any non-Muslim man. The verse thus stands as the household-gate's foundation, with 5:5 as its specified opening — faith the rule, the People of the Book the exception the scripture itself legislated.

**They Call to the Fire**

The calling is not imagined as preaching — the polytheist spouse rarely sets out to damn the household — but as the direction of a shared life: the values a marriage runs on, the gods a home honors, the ends a family's daily choices accumulate toward. The clause's parallel structure states the two calls in their full scope: the Fire, against the Garden *and forgiveness* — God's call carries both the destination and the pardon for the road. The phrase *by His leave* keeps the calling gracious: the invitation to the Garden is not a transaction but a permission-granted gift, the same gratuity the previous verse's guidance and the trial-verse's help carried.

**The Signs Made Clear, That They May Remember**

The verse closes with the formula that has punctuated the whole passage: God makes His signs clear to people, that haply they may be mindful. The clarity-legislation and the taqwā-end are the sūrah's fixed pair — the same closing served the fast (2:185–187) and will serve the divorce-limitations ahead (2:230) — and its presence here marks the marriage-ruling as sign rather than mere rule: the gate of belief is legible as part of a coherent design, visible to the mind that reflects upon the two worlds the previous verse named. The mindfulness the verse aims at is precisely the faculty the domestic legislation will repeatedly demand: the guardian's intention audited by God (2:220), the husband's retention-or-release conducted honorably (2:229), the parent's weaning decided by mutual counsel (2:233). All of it requires people who have learned to see the revealed order as an order — clear signs read for their meaning, not mere commands obeyed without comprehension. The marriage-gate is the first sign of the household series, and its clarity is its mercy: the believer chooses his household's foundation with the design visible, choosing faith at the gate because the signs have shown him where each road's calling leads.

**The Verse in the Community's Formation**

Read within the movement, the verse completes the community's social architecture begun at the trial-verse. The believers were told their faith would be tested as the faiths before were tested (2:214); taught the roster of their charity (2:215); commanded in what they dislike (2:216); weighed in the scales of the sacred month (2:217); comforted with the hope of mercy (2:218); trained in the weighing of wine and gambling (2:219); instructed in the orphan's brotherhood (2:220). Now the household's gate: the intimate contract that will produce the next generation of the tested, the charitable, the obedient, the weighed, the hoping, the reflecting, the guardian-brothers. The verse's two comparisons — slave above free, belief above beauty — train the choosing heart in the community's inverted scale, the scale on which 2:212 had already ranked the tattered unknown above a world of the finely dressed. The marriage-gate is that ranking applied where it costs most: the desire of the eye overruled by the knowledge of the destination, the market's prices overruled by the Fire's and the Garden's callings — and the signs made clear so that the overruling is not mere submission but mindfulness, the household founded in the same reflective taqwā the whole passage exists to form.
verses.222:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”

**Against the Background of Exile**

The ruling's context makes its moderation visible. The commentators record that before Islam, menstruating women in Arabia were not slept with in the same bed and did not eat from the same plate — a separation customs possibly shaped by the neighboring religious law: the prescriptions of Leviticus (15:19–33) and the Zoroastrian Vendidad (16), both of which mandated substantial isolation for menstruating women and ritual purification of objects they touched. Against that background of household exile — and the Arabian custom sitting somewhere inside it — the verse's ruling is a deliberate middle: it prohibits one act and returns everything else. The woman is not exiled from the bed in the sense of isolation, not separated from the table, not treated as a contaminating presence; she is approached in every manner except the one the hurt forbids. The tradition's reports fill in the practice: in many hadiths the Prophet is described as not staying aloof from his wives during their periods but showing them affection — kissing and fondling — short of intercourse. And the ruling on touch is explicit in the commentators' summary: apart from cleaning any item that menstrual blood contacts, Islamic teaching does not deem the touch of a menstruating woman unclean, and does not treat her as rendering anything unclean.

**Your Menses Are Not in Your Hand**

The tradition preserves a scene that fixes the verse's atmosphere with unforgettable economy. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records it (298), from ʿĀʾishah: the Messenger of God said to her — bring me the small mat from the mosque. She answered: I am menstruating. And he said: *your menses are not in your hand*. The exchange is a ruling in miniature: the flow is located in the body, not in the hand that reaches; the woman in her period is not a contamination that spreads by contact but a person whose one bounded restriction leaves her hands — and her service, her presence, her household life — untouched. The report has been read in the legal tradition as addressing the mosque's boundary too: remaining inside the mosque and the retreat of iʿtikāf are restricted for the menstruating woman — restrictions the commentators connect more to protecting the mosque from blood-staining than to any defilement of the woman — while passing through and reaching into it stand. The verse's wider jurisprudence follows the same logic of bounded restriction rather than exile: the canonical prayer and the fast are suspended during the period (the fast made up later), the circumambulation of the Kaʿbah deferred, loud recitation and touching of the Qur'an withheld — suspensions of specific acts, never of the person's standing, her household, her affection, or her nearness to God.

**The Verse in the Household Series**

The verse's position in the domestic sequence completes its meaning.
