The marriage-gate legislated faith as the household's foundation (2:221); this verse legislates the body's cycle within the household; the verse that follows will legislate the marriage's intimacy itself and end in the meeting with God (2:223); and the oaths, the abstention-oath, the divorce, the waiting-periods, and the nursing will follow. Across the whole series the same method runs: a question from real life, an answer that acknowledges the fact (the hurt, the desire, the anger, the womb), a boundary that protects without exiling, a resumption that restores, and names of God — Forgiving, Merciful, Hearing, Knowing, loving the repentant and the pure — presiding over the details. The menstruation-verse is the series' clearest case of the method's genius: a subject the surrounding cultures handled with exile and pollution-mythology, the question-verses of other traditions left largely unaddressed, receives here a ruling of surgical narrowness wrapped in love — one act withheld while the flow lasts, everything else returned, and at the ruling's end the declaration that both the sinners' turning and the washers' purity are, in God's reckoning, objects of love.
verses.223:
> Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers

**The Tilth**

The verse's central image is agricultural and its meaning generative: your wives are a tilth — harth, cultivated land, sown field — for you; come to your tilth as you will. The commentators read the symbolism straightforwardly: the tilth is the place of sowing, and the sowing's harvest is the child; the image locates the marriage's intimacy inside the same order as the field's — seed, soil, season, fruit — and by that locating, bounds it. A tilth is approached for what a tilth is for; the field's meaning governs the coming to it. Some exegetes took the verse as giving permission for any manner of vaginal intercourse, the symbolism referring to procreation as the act's natural end (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī). The image also carries the whole ethic of cultivation the sūrah has been building: the hypocrite strives to destroy tillage and offspring (2:205) — the same two words, harth and nasl — while the believer comes to his tilth as a cultivator, and the verse that destroys and the verse that cultivates stand twelve verses apart, the field appearing in both as the measure of the heart.

**The Occasion: Two Customs, One Ruling**

The reports behind the verse preserve a clash of marital customs in the young community. The Emigrants from Mecca — Quraysh and their fellows — practiced intercourse in various positions; the Helpers of Medina held to a single manner and considered the others reprehensible. When Emigrant men married Helper women, the customs collided: one account names a Muhājir who married an Anṣārī woman and attempted his customary manner, and she refused him — the tradition preserves her objection in substance: we are approached in one way; do that, or keep away from me. The matter came to the Prophet, and this verse was revealed: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records it from Jābir (1435) — the ruling permitting the positions, from the front or from behind, so long as it is in the one orifice; and in some narrations the Prophet summarized the verse in a phrase: a single orifice (al-Ṭabarī).

**Send Forth for Your Souls**

The verse's second command turns the intimacy outward in time: send forth for yourselves — qaddimū, put forward, as one sends goods ahead to a destination. The exegetes read the sending as the performance of good deeds that will benefit the doer in the Hereafter, the same forwarding the Qur'an describes elsewhere: the day a soul finds what it did of good present (3:30 in substance), the provision sent ahead in the sūrah of the Cleaving and the Resurrection passages the commentators cross-reference. Within the marriage-context the command carries its immediate senses too: the child is the sending-forth par excellence, the soul's deposit into the future; and every act of the household — the affection kept lawful, the rights rendered, the kindness stored — is provision forwarded to the meeting the next clause names. The imperative transforms the verse's subject: the intimacy legislated is not a closed circuit of pleasure but a field whose harvest is forwarded — seed sown in the tilth of this world reaped in the soil of the next. The marriage, like the charity-verse's spending and the hajj's provisions, becomes an instrument of the two-worlds reflection the passage commanded (2:220): the household runs in this world and ships its yield to the other.

**The Verse Between Its Neighbors**

The verse's placement completes a pair with the menstruation-ruling and opens the series that follows. Before it: the question about menstruation answered with bounded restriction and beloved purification (2:222). After it: the oaths not made into hindrances (2:224), the oath against the wife legislated to four months (2:226–227), and the whole divorce-architecture (2:228–233). The pair 222–223 thus legislates the marriage's body in its two states — the cycle's suspension and the intimacy's permission — and both end where the series will keep ending: in the names and the meeting. The tilth-image holds the whole domestic legislation together: a field is a thing of seasons (the cycle), of bounded cultivation (the orifice), of forwarded harvest (the sending), and of the owner's audit (the meeting) — and the marriage that follows, through its oaths and estrangements and divorces and nursings, will be legislated as the care of that field in every weather. The verse's last word — the believers given glad tidings — leaves the household under the promise: the field cultivated in mindfulness, the harvest sent ahead, and the cultivators met, at the season's end, by the Giver of the news.
verses.224:
> Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good, not guarding against evil, or not making peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**The Oaths Condemned**

The exegetes specify the cases the verse targets: swearing never to speak to relatives, never to give charity, never to make peace between two people, never to perform some good deed — oaths against righteous behavior in every direction (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The list's first item has a social history: the sworn boycott of kin was an Arabian instrument of pressure, a man binding himself by God to silence against his own blood until some grievance was satisfied. The second and third items turn the same instrument against the community's charitable and reconciling life.

**The Oath-Culture Corrected**

The verse legislates inside a culture dense with oaths, and the commentators note the culture's own ambivalence: even in pre-Islamic Arabia, immoderate oath-taking was counted a vice — the man forever swearing was suspected precisely because his sacred words were cheap. The Qur'an's own portraits carry the judgment: the sūrah of the Pen's list of the despicable characters to be obeyed-not includes the vain oath-monger — the habitual swearer, the one whose oaths are so frequent they mean nothing (68:10). And the sūrah of the Table legislates the oath's serious tier alongside its casual one: God does not take you to task for what is frivolous in your oaths, but He takes you to task for the oaths you have pledged in earnest — with the expiation defined: feeding ten poor people from the family's ordinary food, or clothing them, or freeing a bondsperson, or, for the one who cannot, fasting three days (5:89). The two verses together draw the oath's whole map: the casual invocation exempted, the deliberate pledge binding, the pledge against good dissolved with expiation — and over the whole territory, the name of God treated as the weight it is, neither banalized by frequency nor weaponized against the good it should serve.

**Hearing, Knowing**

The verse closes with the two names that preside over all speech-legislation: God is Hearing, Knowing. The pairing audits the oath from both ends. Hearing: the sworn sentence is a sound in the world, and the One whose name it invokes heard it — the words, the tone, the audience, the moment. Knowing: the intention behind the words is known — whether the oath was heat or calculation, whether the good it blocks was ever intended, whether the piety it claims is real. The names together defeat the abuse at its root: the man who swears against charity and then pleads the oath's sanctity is pleading before the Hearer of his swearing and the Knower of his purpose, and the verse leaves the plea in Their hands rather than in the community's. The same names closed the war-legislation's hearing of the cease (2:227's coming pair) and will preside over the divorce-resolutions ahead — the domestic legislation runs, clause by clause, under this surveillance: every word of the household spoken before the Hearing, every motive of the household held before the Knowing.

**The Oath-Block's Opening**

This verse opens a short block in which the sūrah legislates the whole life of the sworn word. Here: the oath misused against good. Next: the oath uttered carelessly, exempted from reckoning, with accountability reserved for what hearts have earned (2:225). Then: the oath sworn against a wife — the īlāʾ — bounded by four months and forced to resolve into return or divorce (2:226–227). The block's architecture is complete jurisprudence in four verses: the abusive oath, the empty oath, the harmful oath, and each one's ruling. Its placement matters: the oath-block stands between the household's intimacy-legislation (2:222–223) and the household's dissolution-legislation (2:228 onward), because the oath is the hinge between them — the speech-act by which a marriage's daily life can be poisoned or a divorce's drama staged. A community being taught to govern its bedrooms and its divorces is first taught to govern its swearing: the tongue that invokes God is the tongue that will pronounce the ṭalāq, and the verse that forbids making God a barrier to good is training the same organ that will soon hold a wife's fate.
verses.225:
> Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing

**The Honest Mistake, and the Angry Word**

Two further cases were gathered under the exemption by the commentators. The first: a person swears to something he believes true — I did not do it, he was there, the goods are mine — and later discovers the belief was wrong. The oath was sincere, the assertion false, and the verse exempts it: no expiation falls on the man whose heart meant truth and whose information failed. The second case al-Qurṭubī records: oaths taken in anger are excluded from the tasking — the word sworn in the heat that the cooled heart never willed. The jurisprudence this generated distinguishes the laghw from the muʿaqadah — the oath knotted in earnest, which the sūrah of the Table's legislation binds with its expiation of feeding, clothing, freeing, or fasting (5:89) — and the line between the two runs exactly where this verse draws it: through the heart.

**What Your Hearts Have Earned**

The verse's second half states the positive rule: He takes you to task for what your hearts have earned. The earning-language — kasb — is the sūrah's accounting term: the portion from what they earned settled the two prayers (2:202), the hypocrite's corruption was his striving's earn, the believer's good is sent ahead as earnings. Here the heart itself is the earning organ, and the oaths it knots are its kasb: the deliberate pledge, the intended commitment, the sworn word that the will stands behind. The verse by this relocates the oath's jurisdiction from the tongue to the heart — a move consistent with the whole domestic legislation's surveillance-theology, from the guardian's intention known to God (2:220) to the concealment of the womb forbidden before the Last Day's reckoning (2:228). The heart's earnings are the real ledger: the reflex-swear adds nothing to it, the knotted oath adds its full weight, and the expiation-rulings that follow exist to let the heart unwind what the heart bound. The sūrah's final verse will legislate the same interiority as its closing principle — God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity, and the accounting runs on what the soul earned and sent ahead (2:286) — with this verse as its early statement in the grammar of swearing.

**The Speech-Legislation's Inner Court**

Read with its neighbors, the verse forms the oath-block's inner court. The verse before governed the oath aimed at good — God's name made a barrier against righteousness, taqwā, and peacemaking, with the Hearing and Knowing presiding (2:224). This verse governs the oath aimed at nothing — the habit, the mistake, the heat — with the Forgiving and Clement presiding. The verse after governs the oath aimed at a marriage — the forswearing of the wife, bounded and forced to resolve (2:226–227). Across the three rulings the sūrah legislates the full spectrum of the sworn word by its object: against good, against meaning, against a person — and calibrates both the ruling and the divine names to each. The spectrum's lesson is the heart's jurisdiction throughout: the barrier-oath is condemned because the heart wields the name against the good; the laghw-oath is excused because the heart is absent from the words; the īlāʾ-oath is bounded because the heart's harm cannot be allowed to run without term. The tongue is legislated exactly in proportion to the heart's presence in its speech — and the Forgiving and Clement names assure the community that the proportion is kept by a mercy that has already, in this very verse, pardoned the vast majority of what human tongues do with the name of God.

**The Verse's Standing Comfort**

The exemption has carried pastoral weight across the tradition's life precisely because the habit it excuses is universal. The believer who counts his casual oaths and fears their tally is answered by this verse before he asks: the wa'Llāh of conversation is not on the ledger. The person tortured by a remembered oath sworn to a false belief is answered: the honest heart is not tasked. The man haunted by words sworn in rage is answered: the anger's output is excluded. The verse's comfort is not leniency for its own sake but the accuracy of divine audit — God takes the heart's earnings and leaves the tongue's noise — and the accuracy is itself the mercy: an audit that counted reflexes would drive the scrupulous to despair, and the sūrah's whole project (the hope of 2:218, the ease of 2:185, the latitude of 2:220) refuses despair as a legislative outcome. The Clement's forbearance with human speech is the atmosphere in which the serious oath can be serious: because the careless is forgiven, the knotted can bind; because the tongue's dust is pardoned, the heart's pledges carry weight — and the community learns to swear rarely, mean always, and expiate when meaning must be unwound.
verses.226:
> Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Suspended Wife**

The verse addresses a specific pre-Islamic institution of harm, and the commentators describe it plainly: a man would stay away from his wife without divorcing her — swearing against marital relations and leaving her in a limbo that could last for years (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī). The suspended woman had neither of marriage's two goods: not its intimacy, since the oath withheld it, and not its exit, since no divorce freed her to marry another. She was a wife in law and a prisoner in fact — bound to a man who had sworn against the marriage's central act while refusing the word that would release her.

**If They Return**

The first exit is reconciliation: if they return — the resumption of marital relations — God is Forgiving, Merciful. The exegetes defined the return concretely: the resumption of intercourse itself; and they extended its validity — the return counts even where the husband intends it and is hindered by some obstacle, since the intent to harm has ceased; for some, bearing witness to the return suffices. The legal question the return generated concerns the oath itself: many understood the Forgiving-Merciful clause to mean that no expiation is necessary when the husband returns (al-Ṭabarī) — the reconciliation absorbs the oath without ransom; others held that some expiation, such as feeding the poor, remains due, since returning to the wife constitutes going back on the sworn word. The two readings compose a coherent policy: reconciliation is made as cheap as possible — the verse's names are forgiveness and mercy, not audit — while the oath's gravity is not entirely dissolved. The decisive point is the welcome: the swearer who comes back is met by the same names that closed the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199) and the comfort of the Emigrants (2:218), and the marriage that resumes after estrangement resumes inside pardon rather than under penalty.

**The Oath's Scope**

The jurists debated the boundaries of the īlāʾ — which oaths fall under the four-months law — and the debate maps the verse's concern. Some held the ruling applies only when the oath is made in anger with intent to harm: the man who swears against relations for another reason — protecting the well-being of a nursing child, for instance — stands outside the verse's ruling (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). Others extended it to any oath that keeps a man from relations with his wife, regardless of motive. Others extended further still: the forswearing need not concern relations at all but may cover any withdrawal intended to harm the wife — not speaking to her, not touching her. The three positions share the harm-criterion the four-month term installed and differ only on the harm's vehicles; the nursing-child exemption shows the criterion at work, since a withdrawal serving the child's welfare is not a withdrawal against the wife. The verse's legislative achievement is visible in the debate's shape: a pre-Islamic practice with no term, no definition, and no remedy became a bounded institution whose every boundary — which oaths, which motives, which harms — the law could now argue about, because the scripture had first made it a matter of law.

**The Verse in the Household's Legislation**

The īlāʾ-verse sits at the hinge of the domestic series. Behind it: the marriage's gate of faith (2:221), the body's cycle and its beloved purifications (2:222), the tilth and the meeting with God (2:223), the oaths' general legislation (2:224–225). Ahead: the second exit — the resolved divorce, heard and known (2:227) — and the whole dissolution-architecture of waiting periods, counts, ransoms, and nursing (2:228–233). The verse's office in the series is to legislate the marriage's estrangement: not its daily friction, which the oaths-verses handled, and not its ending, which the divorce-verses will handle, but the suspended state between — the estrangement that pretends to be marriage. The four months force that pretense to choose, and the two exits the pair of verses provides — return under Forgiving and Merciful, divorce under Hearing and Knowing — cover the whole field: the marriage resumes or it ends, and what may not resume or end is the wife's captivity. The harm-criterion the verse installs will govern everything that follows — the retention that harms (2:231), the concealment of the womb (2:228), the taking-back of gifts (2:229) — making this short ruling the domestic legislation's declaration of principle: in the household God governs, no person's suspense may be another person's weapon.
verses.227:
> But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**Hearing, Knowing**

The names presiding over the second exit differ from the names that presided over the first, and the difference is the verse's theology. Reconciliation was received by the Forgiving, the Merciful — names of welcome over the marriage resumed. Divorce is received by the Hearing, the Knowing — names of audit over the marriage ended. The Hearing attends to the divorce's word: the pronouncement is a speech-act, uttered and heard, with legal consequences that attach to its utterance; God hears the ṭalāq as the community's courts must, and the name guarantees that the word spoken in the household's privacy is spoken in the presence of the Hearer. The Knowing attends to the divorce's interior: the resolve behind the word — whether it is the settled decision the verb requires or the masked continuation of harm, whether the estrangement's history carried injustice into the dissolution, whether the wife's rights will survive the husband's decision. The two names together install the divorce inside the same surveillance the whole domestic series has run under: the guardian's intentions known (2:220), the oaths' hearts earned (2:225), the womb's secrets legible to belief in the Last Day (2:228 as it will legislate) — and now the marriage's ending heard and known. Nothing about the exit escapes the audit, which is why the exit can be left so brief: the One who hears and knows requires no elaboration here to protect the departing wife.

**The Pair as One Law**

The two verses are read in the tradition as a single legislation — the commentators treat 226–227 together, and their joint architecture repays the reading. One institution is abolished: the oath-suspension without term. One diagnostic is installed: four months as the harm-line. Two exits are opened: return with pardon, divorce with resolve. Two name-pairs preside: Forgiving-Merciful over the reconciliation, Hearing-Knowing over the dissolution. And one state is left without existence: the marriage that is neither lived nor ended. The pair's economy — a long verse and a short one, the machinery and the exit — enacts the law's proportion: the reconciliation, which the legislation prefers and helps, receives the fuller treatment and the warmer names; the divorce, which the legislation permits and polices, receives the brieest clause and the names of audit.

**The Divorce-Legislation's Threshold**

This verse is the threshold of the sūrah's divorce-code, and its position determines everything that follows. The waiting-period legislation (2:228) presupposes a divorce properly declared — resolved, heard, known — and its rules about the waiting, the return-right, and the womb's truthfulness all operate downstream of this threshold. The count-legislation (2:229) presupposes divorces that are decisions rather than harassments: twice, then retention in honor or release in grace. The harm-prohibition (2:231) exists because the threshold can be abused — the resolve reversed and re-declared as sport — and the Knowing at this verse is the abuse's standing witness. Read as the code's entrance, the verse performs the entrance's whole office: it establishes that divorce in this legislation is a grave, deliberate, divinely audited act — not a husband's casual instrument, not a drifting default, not a weapon of suspense. The tradition's famous description of divorce as the most hateful of permitted things to God finds its textual ground in exactly this architecture: permitted at the threshold, audited by the names, bounded by the counts, and preferred at every point by the reconciliation the previous verse welcomed — the permission real, and surrounded on every side by the machinery that makes its use deliberate.

**The Household Under the Names**

The verse leaves the estranged marriage — and the reader — inside the divine names, and the whole domestic series is now visibly a legislation of named presences. The marriage's gate stands under the clarity that produces mindfulness (2:221); the body's cycle under the love of the repentant and the purifying (2:222); the tilth under the meeting with God and the glad tidings (2:223); the oaths under the Hearing and Knowing of speech and the Forgiving and Clement of habit (2:224–225); the īlāʾ's return under Forgiving and Merciful (2:226); and its divorce under Hearing and Knowing (2:227). No chamber of the household — its founding, its bed, its quarrels, its estrangements, its dissolutions — is left outside a named relation to God; every act, from the sworn word to the resolved divorce, occurs in the presence of attributes that see its interior and answer its need. The brevity of this verse is thus not thinness but density: two names doing the work that lesser legislation would need paragraphs to do, because the Hearing requires no procedure to hear and the Knowing requires no evidence to know. The husband who resolves on divorce speaks his word into that hearing; the wife whose release the resolve begins stands under that knowing; and the code that follows will legislate their separation in the same light — heard, known, and bounded by the One who does both.
verses.228:
> Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**The Right of Return**

The third clause preserves the reconciliation the waiting exists to make possible: their husbands have the better right to restore them in that period, if they desire peace — the maʿrūf reconciliation, the restoration of the marriage. The right's logic follows the divorce's origin: the husband — initiator of the ṭalāq — holds the initiative of its undoing — the declaration was his, and within the waiting-period its withdrawal is his, conditioned on the desire for reconciliation rather than for harm. The condition matters and the verses that follow will enforce it: the return-right exists for peace, and its abuse — retaining to harm, the cycling of divorce and revocation as captivity — is legislated against at 2:231. The wife's position within this architecture is the jurists' noted asymmetry: her options for ending the marriage do not run through the ṭalāq but through the khulʿ, the divorce she initiates with a ransom, legislated in the next verse (and at 4:20). The waiting-period thus holds the marriage in a reversible state under the initiator's hand, with the reconciliation desired as the outcome the period prefers — the law's tilt toward preservation visible in the structure of the right itself.

**The Reciprocity Clause**

The verse's fourth movement is its most far-reaching: the women have obligations the like of what is owed to them, in what is honorable — and the men have a degree over them. The reciprocity-clause generated a range of readings the commentators preserve, and the range is the clause's wealth. Some read it as mutual duty: each side owes what the other owes — wives their part, husbands theirs, in honorable exchange. Some read it as the mutuality of intimate right: the wife's claim on her husband in this respect resembling his on her (al-Ṭabarī). Some read it as mutual protection from harm: the husband not harming the wife through endless cycles of divorce and reconciliation, the wife not harming the husband by concealing her womb — the two harms the verse itself has just legislated against, gathered into one principle of reciprocity. Others grounded it in the marriage's purpose: closeness, love, and peace shared between the spouses — with al-Rāzī's striking verdict that in this sharing, one might even say the woman's portion is more abundant. And Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have lived the clause in its most domestic sense: I adorn myself for my wife as she adorns herself for me. The clause installs, at the center of divorce-law, the marriage's own constitution — reciprocal rights and duties in maʿrūf — and makes the waiting-period's conduct a matter of that reciprocity rather than of the husband's prerogative alone.

**The Degree**

The degree-clause — a degree named for men over women — has been read by the commentators in directions that share a common structure: the degree is load-bearing rather than dignifying. Ibn ʿAbbās's reported reading is the most cited: the degree consists, he explained, in men's fostering of good relations and their largesse toward women in property and conduct — the upper hand is bound to incline against its own interest. On this reading the degree is noblesse oblige legislated: the advantage carries the obligation of self-disadvantaging generosity, the headship measured by what it gives up. Other readings the commentators record ground the degree in men's economic advantages and their corresponding obligations — the maintenance and clothing the marriage-law assigns — in their role in the community's defense, and in qualities such as physical strength. Al-Qurṭubī gathers the positions without collapsing them, and the verse's own closure — Almighty, Wise — places the degree's measure with God rather than with the degree-holder: the Mighty enforces the reciprocity the degree sits inside, and the Wise has ordered the household's asymmetry as an ordering whose wisdom is His to know. The degree, in the verse's architecture, never escapes the reciprocity-clause that precedes it: the obligations owed and owing are mutual and honorable, and the degree stands over that mutuality as responsibility, not exemption.
verses.229:
> Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers

**Retention in Honor, Release in Grace**

Between the counts the verse states the marriage's only two lawful postures: retain honorably — in maʿrūf — or release virtuously — in iḥsān. The formula is the divorce-code's ethical constitution. Retention in honor is the marriage maintained: the wife kept not as captive or servant but in the honorable exchange the previous verse legislated — the reciprocal rights and duties, the adornment Ibn ʿAbbās described as mutual, the closeness and peace al-Rāzī named. Release in grace is the marriage ended well: the divorce declared without spite, the rights rendered, the departure dignified, the ex-wife sent out with what the law assigns her rather than stripped of it. And the formula excludes the third posture — the retention in harm, the release in vengeance, the suspended state between marriage and divorce — which is exactly what the īlāʾ-verses abolished and 2:231 will legislate against by name. The two options together make every moment of a marriage's life and death a choice between two graces: how it is kept, or how it is released. The verse leaves no middle term because the middle is where the harm lives — the neither-kept-nor-released existence that the whole code exists to make impossible.

**The Bridewealth Not Taken Back**

The third clause legislates the divorce's economics in the wife's favor: it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them. The bridewealth — the mahr stipulated in the marriage contract — is the wife's property absolutely, and the husband-initiated divorce leaves it untouched: in the ṭalāq, the wife everything the wife owns stays hers. The clause's exception is narrow and specific: a marriage not consummated allows the return of half the stipulated amount (as 2:237 will legislate). And the clause carries an anti-abuse rule the commentators make explicit: the husband may not abuse his wife into purchasing her own release — refunding, through the manufactured "request," the mahr he had given — the pressure-divorce, in which cruelty manufactures the wife's "request" and converts it into a refund, is forbidden at its root. The economics complete the count's work: the man contemplating serial divorce now spends not only his revocable chances but nothing of his wife's wealth in the process — the declarations cost him opportunity, never her. The protection is total in its domain: what he gave at the marriage's founding remains hers at its ending, and the verse surrounds that remainder with the anti-coercion rule that keeps it real.

**The First Khulʿ**

The tradition preserves the door's first opening with documentary precision. The case is described as the first khulʿ in Islam: a woman brought her case to the Prophet, complaining of her husband — the reports carried by Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī describe her aversion to his physical appearance, while Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī preserves her words in another register (5273, and Ibn ʿAbbās's account at 5275–5276): the wife of Thābit ibn Qays said — O Messenger of God, I do not blame Thābit for any defect in his character or his religion, but I, being a Muslim, dislike to behave in an un-Islamic manner if I remain with him; in one account, I cannot endure to live with him; in another, I fear I may become ungrateful for God's blessings. Her complaint was not of abuse but of aversion — the fear that a marriage without love would drive her to contempt, and contempt to sin. The Prophet's ruling established the mechanism: will you return the garden he gave you as your mahr? She said yes — in one account, yes, and more. His answer fixed the ransom's measure: no, the garden alone — and to Thābit: accept your garden, and divorce her once. The case legislated the door's whole character: the wife's aversion received as sufficient ground, her property as the ransom, the excess refused, the release commanded — the marriage dissolved without blame on either, in the precise economy the verse had laid down.

**The Limits and Their Transgression**

The verse closes with the ḥudūd-formula that governs the whole code: these are the limits of God — do not approach transgression; whoever transgresses the limits of God, those are the wrongdoers. The limits are the rules the verse has just legislated — the count of two, the retention and release, the bridewealth's inviolability, the khulʿ's conditions and ransom — and the formula's force is the same as the fasting-legislation's (2:187): the limits are established, named, and fenced with the divine ownership. The commentary tradition filled in the limits' rationale with social wisdom: a bad marriage, al-Rāzī notes, can lead to further evils — adultery, social instability — and a couple starved of companionship slide toward bitterness, then toward sin; the discord the khulʿ answers (the nushūz of the marital-strife passages) is read from the verse's dual form as coming from both sides, or as originating in the wife's expressed hatred and aversion — the two readings complementary, since her aversion, even without ill-treatment by the husband, produces his resentment in turn.

The jurists debated the fear's distribution: some require both spouses' fear; others hold the wife's fear sufficient while the husband's alone is not — if she wishes to remain and he does not, no khulʿ is permissible and he can take nothing of her property; others read the you-fear as the community's assessment of the pair, with some opinions granting the arbiters of 4:35 power to divorce or recommend divorce where reconciliation is impossible.
verses.230:
> So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge

**The Deterrence Built Into the Bar**

The commentators read the rule as the deliberate completion of the code's anti-harm architecture: an extension of the logic limiting declarative divorce (2:229) and the forswearing of marital relations (2:226). Their reasoning is precise. Were the husband free to remarry his thrice-divorced wife, he would be free to declare three more divorces and repeat the process continuously — cycling her through serial waiting-periods, married on paper, never free in fact, barred from every other suitor. The prohibition against remarriage until she has married and been divorced by another caps the damage available to him at a finite sequence, and it deters the declaration itself: the prospect of recovering a wife who has meanwhile been another's is, in most cases, unlikely — and the unlikelihood is legislated on purpose.

**The Intervening Marriage's Conditions**

The jurists drew the rule's necessary conditions from its wording and purpose. Most hold that the intervening marriage must have been real — entered and lived — before the first pairing may lawfully resume (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) — the marriage must be real, not a paper transaction, since a nominal contract divorced without consummation would circumvent the bar as easily as the serial cycling it prevents. The consummation-requirement keeps the intervening marriage's dignity intact in the law's own terms: the wife's second marriage is a true marriage with its full rights and its own possible future, not a legal device — and its ending in divorce must be that marriage's own real event. The verse's scope-clarification completes the conditions: this bar applies to the thrice-divorced pair; remarriage after a single declaration belongs to the different legislation the code will supply — the completed-waiting-period remarriage of 2:232, where the couple's honorable consent suffices and no intervening marriage is required. The three-declaration case and the single-declaration case are thus governed by opposite logics: the first barred absolutely until another life has intervened; the second open as soon as the waiting ends — the law's severity exactly proportioned to the abuse each case represents.

**Clear to a People Who Know**

The verse ends with the ḥudūd-formula's rarest qualification: The bounds are made plain, the verse closes, for those endowed with knowledge. The clarity-clause has run through the sūrah's legislation — the signs made clear that people may be mindful (2:187, 2:221), the verses made clear that they may reflect (2:219–220) — and each instance names its audience by the faculty the legislation requires. Here the faculty is knowledge: the divorce-code is addressed to knowers, and the address is the code's final instruction about itself. The machinery this verse completes — counts, bars, intervening marriages, ransom economics, prospective deeming — is intricate, and its intricacy is not accidental but pedagogical: a law this precisely articulated against the abuses it foresees demands readers who can hold its structure, trace its deterrents, and apply its conditions case by case. The people who know are the code's intended administrators — the judges who impose divorce at the īlāʾ's deadline, the arbiters who assess the khulʿ's fear, the jurists who debate consummation and ceilings and the dual of the limits — and the verse names them as the clarity's recipients because the limits' keeping depends on their knowledge as much as on the spouses' obedience. Between the clarity and the knowledge stands the code's whole claim: the household's hardest cases are not left to power or custom but legislated in detail, made plain, and entrusted to understanding.

**The Code's Keystones**

Read with its neighbors, this verse is the divorce-code's keystone — the piece that locks the arch. The count (2:229) gave the structure its numbers; the bar and its sequel (2:230) give the numbers their consequence; the harm-prohibitions that follow (2:231–232) give the consequence its manners — the retention without injury, the remarriage without obstruction; and the nursing-legislation (2:233) extends the code's care past the divorce to the children it produces. The keystone's own logic gathers everything: the marriage is a covenant whose dissolution must be deliberate (the counts), whose final dissolution must be costly (the bar), whose restoration must be reformed (the deeming), and whose whole law must be understood (the knowers). The wife the pre-Islamic practice suspended for years now has a calendar; the husband who cycled declarations now has a terminus; the couple who return now have a condition; and the community now has a code whose severity — the third word's irreversibility — is entirely in the service of its mercy: that no marriage be a prison, no divorce a weapon, and no return a repetition of the harm the limits were made clear to prevent.
verses.231:
> When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

The verse legislates against the divorce-code's most specific cruelty, and al-Ṭabarī's description of the practice is exact: a man declares divorce, then takes his wife back just before the waiting period ends — revoking the declaration at the last permissible hour — then divorces her again when a new waiting period begins, and repeats the action to harm her. The count-legislation of 2:229 barred the cycle's infinity — twice, then finality — and this verse bars its spirit: even within the lawful count, the revocation-right may not be exercised *as harm*.

**Wronging Oneself**

The verdict on the abuser is the sūrah's standing arithmetic: whoever does that has wronged himself. The clause is not a softening of the harm — the cycling husband has wronged his wife in fact, and the code's other provisions answer her — but a statement about the wrong's full account. The harm he engineers is harm he houses: the soul that learns to play with sacred signs, to use a person as a lever, to convert law into cruelty, is a soul being deformed by its own devices, and the deformation is registered on the self that the deeds return to. The sūrah has run this accounting throughout — the concealers' fire eaten into their own bellies (2:174), the traders' purchase of error at guidance's price (2:175), the transgressor after settlement carrying his painful punishment (2:178) — and here the formula enters the domestic law: the husband who harms through the waiting-period is not only liable but self-damaged, the wrong returning to its author as the author's own diminished soul. The clause's function is deterrent and diagnostic at once: it tells the would-be cycler that his cleverness has a cost booked to his own account, and it tells the reader that every abuse of the household's law is, in the scripture's vision, first a mutilation of the abuser.

**Remember the Favor, the Book, and the Wisdom**

The verse's third movement turns from prohibition to remembrance: remember God's favor upon you, and what He sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, exhorting you by this. The favor is comprehensive — the guidance itself, the community's rescue from the pre-Islamic household's injustices, the legislation that gives the wife a calendar and the marriage a law — and the remembering is the antidote to the mockery: the heart that holds its inheritance in memory does not play with its instruments. The Book-and-Wisdom pairing is the verse's notable formula, recurring where the revelation's wholeness is named — the Prophet's prayer for the community to be given the Book and the Wisdom (2:129), the gifts bestowed on the prophets and the believers across the sūrah of the Women and the Table and the Assembly (3:48, 4:113, 5:110, 45:16, 62:2) — and its presence here elevates the divorce-legislation from case-law to bestowed wisdom: the counts, the waitings, the honors of retention and release are not juristic inventions but the sent-down Wisdom itself, exegeting the community through its households. The exhorting clause names the sending's mode — the Book and Wisdom arrive as admonition, as counsel addressed to hearts — and the verse by this answers its own abuse-case: the man who plays with the signs has forgotten that the signs were sent to exhort him, and the remedy prescribed is memory.

**The Code's Conscience**

Within the divorce-legislation this verse holds the office of conscience. The count (2:229) gave the code its arithmetic; the bar (2:230) gave the arithmetic its finality; this verse gives both their manner — the honor that must govern every exercise of every right the code confers. Its three movements form the conscience's full address: to the hands (do not retain to harm, do not cycle, release at the term), to the tongue (do not play with the signs, do not joke with the divorce-word), and to the heart (remember the favor and the Wisdom, be mindful before the Knower). The wife the legislation protects receives her protection through all three: her waiting-period secured against the trap, her freedom secured against the jest, her case secured before the audit that reads the pattern no court can see. And the husband is addressed not as a defendant but as a beneficiary — the favor upon him includes the law that bounds him, the Wisdom sent down includes the code he administers, and the honor commanded at both edges of the waiting period is his dignity as much as hers: the man who releases honorably is the man the legislation exists to form, and the verse leaves him the choice the whole code has left at every count — retention in maʿrūf, release in iḥsān, and never, under the all-knowing gaze, the harm that wrongs the doer first.

The sūrah of the Table will legislate the same gravity against those who mock the call to prayer (5:57–58 in substance), and the verse here establishes it where the mockery is most costly — in the chamber where a woman's freedom waits on a man's seriousness.
verses.232:
> When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**The Obstruction Forbidden**

The verse legislates the waiting-period's other end: when the divorced women have fulfilled their term — the ʿiddah complete, the marriage fully dissolved — do not hinder them from marrying their husbands, when the two have consented honorably. The prohibition is addressed to the people with power to hinder: the guardians, the families, the brothers and fathers whose consent the custom required and whose refusal could block the marriage. The case the verse answers is not the couple's — the couple's consent is assumed and named as honorable — but the third parties': the divorce is complete, the woman is free, the former spouses wish to remarry each other lawfully, and the verse forbids anyone from standing between them.

**The Sister's Case**

The occasion the tradition reports gives the ruling its human shape: the verse was revealed, al-Ṭabarī records, when a man balked at the idea of his sister — divorced and single — remarrying the man who had divorced her. The brother's balk is the verse's whole subject in miniature. His motives are the family's familiar ones: the divorce was an injury to the household's honor, and the remarriage reopens it; the sister deserves better, or the former husband proved himself unworthy, or the family has begun arranging another match; the children of the first marriage complicate a second. The verse answers every such motive with a single prohibition: the brother's judgment about his sister's former husband is not a legal fact — the honorable consent of the two adults is the only fact the law recognizes at the waiting-period's end. The case also shows the prohibition's addressee in his social reality: the guardian is not a villain by definition but a family member exercising what custom gave him, and the verse legislates against the custom itself — transferring the marriage's decision from the household's honor-politics to the couple's consent, and making the transfer binding on the believers precisely as believers.

**God Knows, and You Know Not**

The verse ends with the knowledge-formula that closed the fighting-prescription (2:216): God knows, and you know not. The formula's return at the household-legislation's turn is structural — the two clauses bracket the whole passage from the war's obligation to the marriage's remarriage, and the bracket is the passage's epistemology: at both of the community's hardest legislations, the human judgment is submitted to the divine knowledge. Here the submission is specific: the brother who balks believes he knows what protects his sister — the character of the former husband, the scandal of the remarriage, the family's standing; the verse tells him that the knowledge operative in the case is not his. God knows the couple's consent and its honor, knows the harm the obstruction will produce, knows the purity of the lawful path and the corruption of the blocked one — and the guardian's knowledge is the family's interest, dressed as judgment. The formula is not a rebuke of the brother's love but a relocation of the decision: the love may remain, the counsel may be given, the concern may be voiced — but the hindrance is forbidden because the case belongs to a knowledge the family does not have. The same relocation ran through the fighting's prescription: the community's dislike overruled by the divine knowing of the good (2:216); here the family's objection overruled by the divine knowing of the pure. Both legislations end in the same posture — obedience inside admitted ignorance — and the posture is the passage's formed heart.

**The Consent-Centered Household**

Within the divorce-code this verse completes the legislation's transfer of the marriage's center from the households to the spouses. The count and the bar (2:229–230) bounded the husband's power; the harm-prohibition (2:231) policed its exercise; and this verse establishes the couple's consent as the fact the whole system serves — honored at the marriage's founding (the gate of 2:221), protected at its dissolution (the release in grace of 2:229), and sovereign at its renewal (the honorable agreement of this verse). The remarriage-clause is the code's most complete statement of that sovereignty: two people who have been married, divorced, and freed may marry again on their own honorable consent, and every third party — guardian, brother, family, custom — is legislated out of the decision. The verse's closing counsel binds the arrangement to faith rather than to force: it is the believer in God and the Last Day who is enjoined, and the community's families are reformed not by the court's compulsion but by the counsel addressed to their belief. Between the war-legislation's God knows and this verse's God knows, the sūrah has legislated the community's two most contested domains — its violence and its households — under one epistemic rule: human judgments submitted, divine knowledge sovereign, and the purest path the one the Lawgiver named.
verses.233:
> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**The Nursing Legislated**

The verse extends the divorce-code past the marriage's end to its longest-lasting consequence: the child. The mothers shall nurse their children the breast — two full years — to whoever wishes the nursing completed. The addressees are the divorced mothers the preceding verses legislated for: the marriage is dissolved, the waiting complete, the couple separated — and the nursing obligation survives the dissolution, because the child's need outlives the marriage's life. The two years are the completion's measure, not an absolute command on every mother: the verse's own qualifier — for those who wish to complete — and its later consultation-clause allow shorter periods by agreement, and the jurists draw the full ruling from the wording: the two years cap the father's support-duty toward the nursing mother; she may stop earlier, and no power of his can force her to continue — while the support runs, when the nursing does, to the full term (al-Qurṭubī). The period's coherence with the rest of scripture is exact: the sūrah of Luqmān states the weaning at two years (31:14), and the sūrah of the Dunes gives the arithmetic — bearing and weaning together, thirty months (46:15) — from which the tradition derives the six-month minimum gestation and the twenty-four-month nursing as the two terms that sum to the whole. The child's first two years are by this legislated across three sūrahs as one continuous provision: carried, born, nursed, and supported under a calendar God set.

**The Father's Provision**

The verse's second clause assigns the nursing's economics: upon the father is their provision and their clothing, in what is honorable — bi'l-maʿrūf. The provision covers the nursing mother's maintenance through the nursing period, and the honorable-qualifier carries the standard the domestic legislation has used throughout: what is fitting, recognized as right, proportionate to the case. The verse immediately bounds the standard by capacity: no soul is charged beyond its scope — the same principle the sūrah will close with as its final verse's comfort (2:286), and which the scripture repeats as a rule of all obligation (6:152, 7:42, 23:62, 65:7). The two clauses together produce the provision's actual measure: the father gives according to his means, honorably — the wealthy father's maʿrūf and the poor father's maʿrūf are different amounts under one standard, and the verse acknowledges the difference explicitly: fathers differ in capacity, and the obligation is defined by the honorable within the possible. The child's support is thus secured without crushing its source: the law takes the child's need seriously enough to bind the father for two full years, and takes the father's capacity seriously enough to bind him only within it.

**No Parent Harmed by the Child**

The verse's third clause legislates the child against weaponization: neither parent may be wounded through the child — not the mother through hers, nor the father through his. The commentators read the mutual prohibition in both directions with concrete cases: the mother may not wound the father by withholding her nursing or by using the child as a wall between them; nor may the father wound the mother by holding the child back from a breast that wishes to give (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The clause's scope covers nursing and custody together — the two domains where the divorced parents' conflict has its instruments — and its principle is total: the child is not a lever. The divorced couple, whose marriage the preceding verses dissolved with counts and honors and prohibitions of harm, are here forbidden the last remaining harm available to them: the use of the child they share as an instrument against each other.

**The Seeing, and the Custody's Afterlife**

The verse closes with the domestic legislation's final name-pair movement: hold God in awe, since His seeing misses no act. The seeing is the clause's enforcement and its comfort in one: the nursing's details — the milk given or withheld, the provision rendered or shorted, the counsel sought or bypassed, the wage paid fairly or meanly — are the invisible transactions of a household under strain, audited by no court in most of their moments, and the verse stations the all-Seeing over every one. The jurists drew the verse's remaining question — custody beyond the nursing — from its logic rather than its letter: most agree that the mother has the stronger custody-claim while she remains unmarried — the reasoning being that a new husband would not willingly raise another man's child; positions differ, and some grant the child a choice upon reaching years of discretion (al-Qurṭubī). The custody-debate inherits the verse's two constants — the child's interest as the fixed point, and the harm-prohibition as the governing rule — and extends them past the two years the verse legislates. The whole domestic series now stands complete: from the marriage's gate of faith (2:221) through the body's cycles, the tilth's harvest, the oaths, the estrangement's four months, the divorces' counts and honors, the remarriage's consent — to this verse, where the legislation ends at a nursing child and the All-Seeing watches the milk. The household's law began with belief as its gate and ends with a fed child as its final subject: the code's last word is not about the spouses at all, but about the small person their union produced and their separation must not harm.
verses.234:
> As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**The Widow's Term Fixed**

The family code turns from the divorced woman to the widow, and its first act is arithmetic: four months and ten days. The term, like the divorced woman's qurūʾ-count, serves the womb's evidentiary function — the community must know whether a new life was begun before death — but it runs longer, and the commentators note the reason pregnancy is handled separately: a widow who is pregnant waits until delivery, the two reckonings compared and the longer one observed, a rule the sūrah of Divorce states plainly — *As for those who are pregnant, their waiting period ends with delivery* (65:4). The ten extra days beyond the four lunar months have been read as completing the count with certainty, since lunar months vary between twenty-nine and thirty days and the added ten absorb the shortfall of four short months. The precision matters: a fixed term replaces guesswork, and a fixed term also ends — which, for a woman whom custom had buried alongside her husband socially, is the verse's real gift.

**Mourning and Waiting: Two Rules, One Term**

The prophetic tradition ties the two obligations together with a boundary that clarifies both. Zaynab bint Abī Salamah narrates that when news of Abū Sufyān's death reached Medina, Umm Ḥabībah asked for perfume on the third day and scented her cheeks and forearms, saying she had no need of it except that she heard the Prophet say: it is not lawful for a woman who believes in God and the Last Day to mourn any deceased person more than three days — except a husband, for four months and ten days (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī). The same wording is reported from Zaynab bint Jaḥsh at her brother's death, and from Umm ʿAṭiyyah, who added that mourners were barred from kohl, perfume, and dyed clothing during the term. The three-day ceiling for every other death throws the widow's four-months-and-ten into relief: it is not grief regulation — grief is permitted its three days for anyone — but a legal status attached to the marriage bond itself, combining the womb's clarification with the husband's honor.

**Seclusion or Celibacy: The Jurists' Split**

What the widow must actually do during the term divided the early jurists. One reading, supported by narrations restricting the widow's use of perfume, ornaments, and dyed clothes and keeping her in her home, treats *let them wait by themselves* as prescribing cloistering: she stays in the marital home, unadorned, for the duration. The exegetes record this as the position grounded in those aḥādīth. The other reading, associated with prominent early authorities including Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, takes the waiting to mean simply refraining from marriage: the term binds her eligibility, not her movements, and she goes about her life without adorning herself for suitors. The practical difference is considerable — confinement versus celibacy — and the majority of the legal schools settled between the poles, requiring the widow's nights in her late husband's home while permitting her daytime business. The disagreement itself testifies to what the verse's wording leaves open: it fixes the term with precision and the conduct with a single phrase.
verses.235:
> There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing

**The Inner Permission**

The verse's second allowance is quieter: *or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts*. Thinking about marrying a woman in her waiting period is itself unblamed — and the permission is psychologically precise, since a rule that criminalized the thought would be unenforceable and corrosive. The clause then grounds itself in divine knowledge: *Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺*. The formulation does something subtler than prohibition or permission: it acknowledges that the consideration is happening, names God as its witness, and declines to legislate the heart — legislating instead the two thresholds where the heart goes public, the word spoken and the contract signed. The structure mirrors the orphan verse's surveillance clause (2:220): discretion is granted where human audit cannot reach, and God's knowledge is stationed over the grant, converting the private space from a loophole into a trust.

**Beware of Him**

The verse's closing movement returns to the heart it opened with. *Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him* — the same khubr-expertise named at the end of the widow's verse (2:234), now turned explicitly inward. The sequence is deliberate: knowledge, then wariness. A person who is certain that his unspoken calculation is known relates to his own heart differently; the intimation he permits himself, the direction he angles his allowable sentences, the private agreement he does not voice — all of it stands in a lit room. The commentators connect this interior surveillance to the verse's whole legislation: the rules about words are enforceable by courts only crudely, since the difference between honorable intimation and secret commitment lives in tone and intention, and so the verse installs its own enforcement in the heart's awareness of being known. The external law is thin; the internal audit is total.

**Forgiving, Forbearing**

The final name-pair is the one the code has used at moments of interior legislation before — the oaths verse closed with the Forgiving, the Forbearing (2:225), and the pairing does its distinctive work here. Ghafūr addresses the heart's trespasses that no court will ever see: the consideration that shaded toward scheming, the intimation that leaned too hard, the intention hidden a little less innocently than the verse assumes. Ḥalīm — the Forbearing, the One who does not strike at once — addresses the interval the whole verse legislates: the waiting period is itself a divine ḥilm, a suspension of resolution in which nothing is concluded and everything is given time. The suitor is told that God's knowledge of his heart is paired not with immediate reckoning but with patience and pardon — and that this pairing, rather than licensing the hidden commitment, obliges him. A law this gentle about what it cannot see is a law that trusts the heart it has made visible to God.
verses.236:
> There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers

**The Unconsummated Marriage**

The code now takes up a case at the margin of its own subject: a marriage contracted but never consummated, and possibly never priced — the bridewealth undesignated — dissolved by divorce. The opening clause lifts blame: there is no fault in this divorce. No waiting period attaches — the sūrah of the Confederates legislates the same case with the same conclusion: a believing woman divorced before she has been touched has *no waiting period for you to count* (33:49) — because the waiting's function, the womb's clarification, has no object where consummation never occurred.

**What Remains: The Provision**

Blame is lifted, but the woman does not leave empty-handed. *But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation* — the mutʿah, a consolatory grant distinct from the bridewealth, and the verse's legislation is entirely about its scaling: *the rich according to his means and the poor according to his*. The formula appears twice in the sentence, and the doubling is the point — the obligation is universal and its amount is personal, measured against the giver's capacity rather than against any fixed schedule. The same bi-māʾūn logic governed the nursing provision two verses earlier (2:233) and the code's whole treatment of maintenance: the law binds the conscience at full strength and binds the purse proportionally. The jurists add a fallback for disputes: where the couple cannot agree on the amount, the measure becomes half of what a woman of similar standing would have received as bridewealth — the compensation anchored to the social arithmetic of the marriage that never was.

**An Obligation on the Good-Doers**

The verse's closing formula names the addressee's character rather than his legal status: *A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers* — ḥaqqan ʿalā'l-muḥsinīn. The word choice has been read two ways that reinforce each other. Legally, it confirms the obligation: the mutʿah in this case is not a courtesy but a ḥaqq, a claim — and the sūrah's later general ruling, *Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺* (2:241), restates the same duty on the register of taqwā. Spiritually, it describes the payer: the man who pays honorably is enacting iḥsān, the excellence the Qur'an consistently places beyond the minimum — and the verse assigns the minimum itself to the excellent. The effect is characteristic of this code's drafting: the floor of obligation is installed at a height that only the good-doer's conscience will recognize, so that the law's least demanding clause still calls its addressee upward.

**The Seam in the Code**

Positioned where it sits, the verse functions as the code's seam-piece. Behind it stand the divorce verses proper — the twice-counted ṭalāq, the retention in honor or release in grace, the waiting periods and the reciprocal rights (2:228–232). Ahead lies the general provision-ruling (2:241) and then the pivot to prayer (2:238) that carries the sūrah out of domestic law. The unconsummated-marriage case tests the code at its edge and demonstrates its method: the same instruments — blame, waiting, compensation, capacity — recalibrated for a case where the marriage's substance never materialized. The exegetes' cross-reference to the general bridal-payment legislation (4:24) completes the picture: the Qur'an's marriage law knows the price of every configuration, including the configuration that ended before it began. No woman leaves this code without a settled claim, and no man leaves it obligated beyond his means — the two guarantees, in the smallest of the code's cases, stated together.
verses.237:
> And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**The Two Waivers**

*Unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full.* The half-dowry is a default, not a cage, and the two exceptions are assigned one to each party: she may release her claim to the half, or he may surrender his right to keep it. The symmetry is deliberate and rare — the code that elsewhere allocates initiative asymmetrically (the reversal-right of 2:228, the khulʿ-ransom of 2:229) here gives each spouse one act of pure generosity, identical in structure and opposite in direction. The exegetes note what the doubling accomplishes: the settlement's floor is the half, its ceiling is the whole, and the space between is governed by nothing but the parties' grace. A divorce that could end in ledger-balancing is made capable of ending in a gift — from either side — and the verse's next clause ranks the gift above the ledger.

**The Hand That Holds the Knot**

The identity of the second waiver's agent produced one of the code's most discussed phrases. The Arabic phrase — the one whose hand holds the marriage-knot — was read by the dominant interpretation as the husband himself: he who holds the knot's power, the ṭalāq-prerogative legislated at 2:228, is the one positioned to forgo the half he could legitimately reclaim. The alternative reading identified the holder as the wife's marriage guardian, the wakīl whose consent a woman's marriage requires — in which case the guardian could release, with her approval, the half she had been entitled to keep. The exegetes record the difficulty with this position directly: the guardian is necessary to the contract but has no legal standing over the bridewealth, which is the wife's personal property; a man cannot donate what is not his. The majority reading therefore prevailed — and it prevailed by the code's own logic, since the hand that holds the knot is the hand the code gave the knot to.

**Seclusion and the Full Dowry**

The jurists pressed one further question out of the verse's architecture: is consummation the only trigger for the full dowry? An opinion recorded by Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī holds that it is not — where the husband was secluded with his wife in circumstances making consummation possible, the full bridewealth becomes due even without it. The reasoning treats privacy itself as the marriage's activation: the seclusion is what the contract purchased, and its occurrence obliges the price. The opinion matters beyond its case, because it shows the halving-rule functioning as the jurists read the whole code to function — not as letter to be gamed but as a map of the marriage's realities. A man cannot dissolve a marriage at its threshold, after the threshold-crossing has occurred in every sense but the last, and claim the discount of a contract never begun. The half belongs to the marriage that truly never started; the seclusion opinion polices the word truly.

**The All-Seeing**

The verse closes with the name the nursing-verse closed with (2:233): *Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do*. The placement is exact to the legislation. The acts this verse governs — the waiver, the full payment, the remembered bounteousness, the forgotten — are mostly invisible transactions: no court witnesses the moment a husband decides to keep the half or release it, and no register records the spirit in which a settlement was paid. The All-Seeing name stations the code's final auditor over its quietest clauses, and it does double duty: for the generous, the unseen grace is seen; for the exacting, the unseen hardening is seen. Between the two the verse leaves its addressee with the choice it has been building toward — the arithmetic half, or the gracious whole — and with the knowledge that whichever is chosen, chosen is exactly the word: the seeing covers the deed and the deliberation alike. The code's domestic legislation ends where it began, under surveillance that is also an invitation.
verses.238:
> Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah

**The Pivot from House to Mosque**

The domestic code, which has run from marriage-gates through divorce arithmetic, ends abruptly on a dowry settlement — and the next verse is prayer. The pivot is the sūrah's method rather than an interruption: the legislation has just finished assigning rights, waiving them, and stationing God's sight over the waiving, and it now assigns the practice that makes such legislation livable. *Observe the prayers* — ḥāfiẓū, from the same root as the code's guarding-language, the keepers of the trusts (2:283). The commentators define the guarding doubly: observance at the appointed times, and presence within the observance — the prayer performed on time and performed attended. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr both press the second half; a prayer guarded in schedule but abandoned in attention is not what ḥifẓ means. The verse thus installs, over against the household's transactions, the day's fixed stations — five anchors around which the code's honesty, generosity, and patience are meant to be reassembled five times daily.

**The Middle Prayer**

*Especially the middle prayer* — al-ṣalāt al-wusṭā — is the verse's famous crux. The five canonical prayers are meant, but which is the middle one has no settled consensus: the exegetes record identifications with each of the five in turn, with the Friday congregational prayer, with the ʿĪd prayer, with the five taken together, and with the deliberate position that its identity is unknown. The strongest identification is ʿAṣr, the afternoon prayer, and it rests on the most documented reading of the Prophet's own words. On the day of the Trench, ʿAlī narrates in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4533), the Prophet said of the besieging pagans: they have kept us from the middle prayer until the sun set — may God fill their houses and graves with fire. The same day's report from Sulaymān ibn Surd (Bukhārī 4109) glosses the middle prayer explicitly as ʿAṣr. The Fajr identification rests on other narrations, and the wusṭā-question has stayed open in the tradition precisely because the evidence supports plurality — and because, as the unknown-identity position argues, an unspecified middle keeps every prayer suspect of being it.

**Why Ambiguity May Be the Point**

The reading that the middle prayer's identity was withheld — or lost — on purpose has exegetical weight. If one prayer is singled out for special guarding and the community cannot agree which, the practical result is maximal: every prayer is guarded as though it were the middle. The strategy mirrors the withheld knowledge of the Night of Power and the Greatest Name — a specified excellence with an unspecified location, converting a single observance into a vigilant many. The Trench incident supplies the historical pressure behind the singling-out: ʿAṣr is the prayer whose window falls in the working day's thick, the hour when engagement — with an enemy, with a market, with a household dispute of the kind the preceding verses legislate — most easily swallows it.

**Qunūt: Standing in Devotion**

The verse's final clause governs the prayer's interior: *and stand in true devotion to Allah* — qānitūn, from qunūt, a word the exegetes gloss as combining obedience, humility, and silence. The three components are not a list but a single posture described from three sides: the obedience that stands when standing is commanded, the humility that stands before rather than merely in, and the silence that lets the standing be listening. The qunūt-vocabulary threads the Qur'an wide — the devout men and devout women of the sūrah of the Confederates' catalogue, the standing of Maryam who was commanded to bow with those who bow — and its appearance here, inside a verse about guarding times, sets the two obligations side by side: the prayer's schedule and the prayer's quality. A guarded prayer performed without qunūt meets the count and misses the clause; the verse demands the devotion inside the observance, the stillness inside the station.
verses.239:
> If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know

**The Prayer Under Fear**

The guarding-command of the previous verse is immediately qualified by its hardest case: what happens to the prayer when keeping it may cost a life? The verse answers with the condition first — *if you are in danger*, khawf, which the commentators extend across battle and persecution alike — and then with the concession: pray on foot or riding. The two modes name a prayer released from its normal architecture: no fixed stance, no stationary row, no required orientation. The exegetes detail what the release covers. The praying person faces the qiblah if he can and any direction if he cannot; the bow and prostration become the head's inclinations, nodded at the corresponding degrees; and according to some readings the prayer itself may be shortened to a single cycle where the normal count is two, three, or four.

**The Concession as Command**

The verse's grammar deserves notice: the fear-prayer is not only permitted but prescribed — *pray on foot or while riding* is an imperative, not a license. The jurists read the implication plainly: in conditions of real danger, insisting on the full form is not piety but disobedience, since the verse has redefined the prayer's obligation to fit the danger's shape. This is the same logic the sūrah applies to fasting on a journey and in illness (2:184–185) and to the pilgrimage interrupted (2:196) — the worship is not suspended by hardship but re-specified by it, and the re-specification comes from God rather than from the worshipper's discretion. The fear-prayer thus protects two things at once: the life that would be spent praying standing, and the prayer that would be lost if it could only be performed standing. Between the two protections stands the verse's quiet claim — that the religion's forms exist for its purposes, and that God Himself redraws the forms when the purposes require it.

**The Detailed Legislation Elsewhere**

This verse gives the fear-prayer its principle; the sūrah of Women gives it its choreography.
