The commentators cross-reference the detailed legislation directly: *When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer—˹especially˺ if you fear an attack by the disbelievers* (4:101), and then the congregation's procedure — one group praying with the imām while armed, the second group standing guard behind them, then the rotation, the weapons carried through the prostrations, the rain-and-illness exemptions (4:102). The two passages divide the legislation the way the code often divides it: the Baqarah verse names the concession's spirit — pray however the danger allows — and the Women verses build its order, a communal prayer conducted in shifts with a guard posted mid-worship. Together they describe a community that prays under attack without ceasing to be either an army or a congregation, the verse here supplying the permission that makes that double existence lawful.

**When You Are Safe**

The concession's boundary is its second half: *But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah*. The dhikr commanded at safety's return has been read in two registers that the verse's wording holds together. The first is the prayer restored — the full standing, the complete cycles, the direction recovered — resumed the moment the danger lifts, since the concession was coextensive with the fear and not a moment longer. The second is remembrance in its own right: the gratitude of the survivor, the recollection that the safety itself is a gift and that the shortened prayer was prayed under the shadow of a death that did not arrive. The exegetes' gloss *take time to* — the Qur'anic verb carrying the sense of full, unhurried performance — marks the contrast the verse is built on: the fear-prayer is contracted, and the safety-prayer is expanded; what the danger compressed, the peace is to stretch back out, in the prayer's length and in the rememberer's attention.
verses.240:
> Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**The Year Bequeathed**

The widow's verse returns — this time from the side of the estate rather than the calendar. The four-months-and-ten term (2:234) fixed how long the widow waits; this verse legislates where she waits and on whose purse: the dying husband is to make provision for his wife — maintenance for a year, and residence in his house *without forcing them out*. The bequest-form is explicit: the maintenance is something he is to arrange, a charge laid on his estate ahead of its division, and the expulsion-ban is its physical half — the year's maintenance is meaningless if the house it is spent in can be closed to her. The commentators read the two halves as one protection: sustenance and shelter, ordered together, owed by the dead man's wealth to the woman his death leaves standing in it. The verse extends the code's pattern — provision scaled and owed at every dissolution — to the dissolution no one contracts: death itself.

**The Abrogation Question**

The year and the four-months-and-ten stand in obvious tension, and the exegetes record the classical solutions. One position holds this verse abrogated by 2:234 — the waiting-term of four months and ten days replacing the year's provision, a reading supported by the verse-order oddity that the abrogating verse appears before the abrogated one, which the tradition explains by the revelation's sequence differing from the compiled arrangement. A second position finds the abrogation in the inheritance legislation of the sūrah of Women — the widow's fixed share, *your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless* (4:12), supersedes the year's bequest. A third position, recorded by al-Qurṭubī and argued on the no-contradiction principle, dissolves the tension without abrogation: 2:234 governs the waiting period — the term of remarriage-eligibility — while this verse governs maintenance and residence, two different questions with two different durations.

**The Harmonizing Reading**

The third position deserves its full statement, because it makes the two verses a single coherent institution. On this reading the widow's waiting period is four months and ten days, fixed and unextendable; her right to remain in her late husband's house with maintenance from his estate runs up to a year; and the two rules interlock rather than conflict. If she remarries before the year ends, the maintenance stops — her new husband assumes her support — and there is no blame on the heirs for ceasing it. The jurists who preferred abrogation answered that a year's charge on the estate conflicts with the heirs' fixed shares; the harmonizers answered that the bequest precedes the shares — *after the fulfilment of bequests and debts* (4:12) — and the year's provision is exactly such a bequest.

**Bequest, Share, and the Estate's Order**

The verse sits inside the Qur'an's wider legislation of the estate, and its mechanics repay that context. A bequest (waṣiyyah) in Qur'anic law is discharged before the fixed shares are computed — the estate's first charges are debts and bequests, and only the remainder divides among the heirs (4:12). The widow's year, on the harmonizing reading, rides in that first rank: not a share competing with the quarter or the eighth the same verse assigns her, but a charge ahead of them. The jurists debated whether the year's provision survives the later inheritance-legislation's arrival precisely because the two operate at different stages of the estate's arithmetic — and the debate produced the position al-Qurṭubī records, that the widow takes her fixed share and, on some readings, was additionally housed for the waiting-term's duration from the estate. The verse's practical legacy in the schools is thus layered: everywhere it informs the widow's housing-right during her waiting, and in one school's history it legislated a full maintained year.
verses.241:
> Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺

**One Sentence, Every Divorce**

The code's divorce legislation, which has run twenty-odd verses through counts, waiting periods, ransoms, halves, and waivers, is gathered into a single sentence — and the sentence is universal. *Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women*: not the unconsummated wife of 2:236, not the priced-and-released wife of 2:237, not the twice-divorced or the thrice-divorced — every divorced woman. Ibn Kathīr records the verse's import in exactly these terms: where the earlier ruling concerned the marriage not yet consummated, this one carries the general obligation, binding every man who divorces to make provision for the woman he releases. The verse is the code's safety-net clause — the rule that closes every gap the preceding rules' case-by-case structure might leave — and its position after the widow-verses extends the net's reach: by the time the sentence arrives, no dissolution of marriage, by divorce or by death, has left the woman's material claim unlegislated.

**Maʿrūf: The Custom Standard**

The provision is bi'l-maʿrūf — the code's recurring formula, rendered here *reasonable* and elsewhere *honorable* or *fair*. Maʿrūf is the standard of the recognized-good: what the community's decent practice acknowledges without being told. The word does the legislative work that fixed sums cannot do — it scales automatically with wealth, locality, and era, and it imports the community's own best behavior as the law's floor. The same word governed the nursing mother's provision (2:233), the retained-or-released wife's treatment (2:229), the widow's own decisions (2:234), and the wet-nurse's payment. Its recurrence across the code amounts to a drafting philosophy: where amounts cannot be fixed universally, the Qur'an fixes the standard and delegates the number to the honorable — and then, as here, attaches the standard to the conscience rather than to the court. A maʿrūf-provision argued down to its minimum has met the letter and missed the word.

**A Duty on the Mindful**

The verse's second half names its enforcement: *a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺* — ḥaqqan ʿalā'l-muttaqīn. The formula appeared two verses earlier with a different noun: the compensation for the unconsummated marriage was *an obligation on the good-doers* (2:236), assigned to the muḥsinūn. Here the same grammatical structure — a ḥaqq laid ʿalā a named company — assigns the general provision to the muttaqīn, the God-fearers. The exegetes read the pairing as cumulative: the code's financial duties are owed by everyone and claimed by the excellent and the reverent as their specific honor. The phrasing also does precise legal-ethical work: calling the provision a ḥaqq — a right, a claim — makes it enforceable in principle, while attaching it to taqwā locates its real operation in the conscience, since no court can audit the spirit of a settlement.

**The Provision's Range**

What the provision consists of, the jurists debated within the maʿrūf-standard, and the debate maps the verse onto the code's other rulings. For the unconsummated marriage it was the mutʿah-compensation scaled by capacity (2:236). For the consumed marriage with a named dowry, the retained wife's maintenance during her waiting and the released wife's settlement (2:229, 65:1–7's later legislation). For the nursing mother, provision and clothing (2:233). The general verse gathers these into a single expectation: whatever the configuration, the departing woman leaves with something — a gift, a half, a maintenance, a wage — and the something is measured by his means and the community's honor. The exegetes' note that the obligation falls on all who divorce, not merely on those who divorced well, closes the range's far edge: there is no divorce in this code so clean, so faultless, or so early that it releases the husband from giving.

The particular cases (2:236–237) established the code's method on the easiest instances: the marriage never begun, the price never set, the arithmetic clean.
verses.242:
> This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand

**The Seal on the Code**

One sentence closes the longest continuous legislation in the Qur'an. The family code — marriage-gates, ʿiddahs, ransoms, nursing, custody, widows, provisions — ends not with a new ruling but with a statement about the rulings: *This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you*. The demonstrative *this* — kadhālika, thus, in this manner — has a specific referent the exegetes mark: the clarity just witnessed, the clarity of everything from 2:221 onward, is itself the thing being pointed at. The verse is the code's seal and its self-description in one: God has made the signs clear, the clearing has taken exactly this form — case by case, clause by clause, right against right — and the form is named so that the reader knows what kind of book he is holding. A legislation that ends by describing its own method is a legislation that intends its method to be recognized, retained, and extended by the minds it has just trained.

**The Refrain Across the Book**

This sentence is one instance of the Qur'an's most characteristic closing-refrain, and the pattern's repetitions define its function. The same formula closes the garden-parable later in this very sūrah — *This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect* (2:266) — and appears in the sūrah of the Table's legislation (5:89), the sūrah of Light's household rules (24:61), and the sūrah of ʿImrān's counsel (3:103). Each instance stands at the end of a unit of instruction, and each does the same double work: it names what has just happened — divine clarification, not human drafting — and it states the clarification's purpose in a single verb of the mind. The recurrence converts the individual verses into a signature: wherever the refrain appears, a legislative or parabolic unit has completed and the Book is marking the completion. The reader who has learned to hear the formula can find the seams of the Qur'an's architecture by ear.

**Understanding and Reflecting**

The refrain's final verb varies, and the variation is precise. Here the purpose-clause is *so perhaps you will understand* — taʿqilūn, from ʿaql, the intellect's binding-and-comprehending. At 2:266 it is *so perhaps you will reflect* — tatafakkarūn; at the wine-and-gambling verse the same reflection-verb closed a pair of legislations (2:219). The exegetes note the fit of each verb to its unit: reflection suits the parable and the weighing of two worlds; understanding — ʿaql, the root that carries both reason and restraint — suits a code of binding rules whose clauses interlock, qualify, and limit one another. The family legislation just completed is precisely a structure to be ʿaqled: held together in the mind, its exceptions grasped as exceptions, its general sentence (2:241) recognized as the summary of its cases. The verse's verb is thus a claim about the code's intelligibility — it can be understood, it was drafted to be understood, and its understanding is the stated purpose of its clarity.

**The Hinge Between the Two Halves**

The verse's position is structural as well as rhetorical. Behind it, the sūrah's great legislative block — qiblah, fasting, pilgrimage, war, family — has run nearly unbroken from verse 183. Ahead, the sūrah's narrative mode resumes: the stories of the fleeing thousands, of the requested king, of the tested army, which carry the sūrah toward its second half. The one-sentence verse is the hinge between them, and hinges of this kind do interpretive work: the legislation just sealed is the community's law, and the narratives about to begin are the community's memory — law and memory, the two materials of a formed people, joined by a sentence that describes the first as made clear and the purpose of the clarity as understanding.
verses.243:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful

**The First of the Stories**

The hinge-verse turns, and the sūrah's narrative sequence opens with a scene of pure paradox: thousands flee their homes *for fear of death*, and death is exactly what meets them — by direct divine command. *Allah said to them, "Die!" then He gave them life.* The two imperatives frame the whole event: the command to die arrives at the fleeing thousands in their thousands, and the giving of life follows — a resurrection inside history, witnessed, reported, and made a sign. The opening formula, *Have you not seen*, is the Qur'an's summons to the mind's eye: what follows is not presented as speculation but as a scene the hearer is to see, and its seeing is the lesson's vehicle. The commentators note the verse's function at this exact position: the legislation has just closed with a call to understanding (2:242), and the first narrative unit delivers the understanding's first object — a demonstration, in thousands of simultaneous deaths, of the proposition every preceding ruling assumed: that life and death are God's property, and that no human arrangement reaches them.

**Who They Were**

The tradition's account, recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, places the scene among the Children of Israel: a community — a town's population or an army's multitude — that fled either a plague or a war, in circumstances the narrations describe as disobedience, seeking a place of safety. They left in thousands, the numbers themselves part of the sign: flight at that scale is a society's decision, not a panic's. Death overtook them anyway, all of them, and God then raised them — the narrations describe a prophet sent to or passing the scene, at whose intercession or by whose witness the thousands stood up alive again. The exegetes also record the position that treats the particulars as beside the point: who they were, when they lived, and where they fell matter less than the verse's demonstrative core — God kills and God gives life, the fleeing is futile, and the revival is grace. Both readings coexist in the commentaries without tension, since the narrative's historicity and its typology carry the same claim.

**The Plague and Its Protocol**

The plague-identification connects the verse to a body of prophetic legislation the commentators cite at this point. When plague breaks out in a land, the Prophet commanded, do not enter it; and when it breaks out in a land where you are, do not flee it (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī). The two rulings look like quarantine law and are also theology: the first refuses to carry the disease toward the healthy, the second refuses the flight this verse depicts — the departure *for fear of death* that the fleeing thousands undertook and that did not, in the event, save them. Al-Ṭabarī's commentary sets the command beside the verse precisely because the verse is the tradition's proof-text for the futility the plague-protocol assumes: death is not a geography one can leave, and the believer's posture in an epidemic is neither flight nor fatalism but stay-and-trust, since *Allah said to them, "Die!"* reaches the runner and the rester alike. The revival then supplies the protocol's second half: life, too, is not a geography — it is a word, and the same voice that commanded the dying commanded the rising.

**Ezekiel's Valley**

Some commentators see in this verse an allusion to the vision in Ezekiel 37 — the prophet set down in a valley full of dry bones, commanded to prophesy over them, and watching the bones come together, take flesh, and stand as an exceeding great army. The parallel is real and the differences are instructive, and the exegetes mark both. Beyond the revival itself, al-Ṭabarī notes, the two accounts share almost nothing — no valley, no bones, no prophesying-over in the Qur'anic scene.
verses.244:
> Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**The Command Between Two Scenes**

Nine words in English and two clauses in Arabic: the imperative, and the knowledge attached to it. Its position is the first interpretive question, and the exegetes answer it two ways. Some read the command as addressed to the revived thousands of the preceding scene — the community God killed and then restored, now conscripted by the One who has just demonstrated that its life is His to give twice. Others, al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī among them, press the grammar: the verb-form is a direct address, not a historical narration, and the command belongs to the believers hearing the sūrah — a standing injunction delivered through the story rather than into it.

**In the Cause of Allah**

The qualifier *in the cause of Allah* — fī sabīl Allāh — is the command's entire legislation compressed into three words. The fighting the verse orders is defined not by its enemy, its territory, or its grievance but by its direction: the way, the road, the cause that is God's. The sūrah's earlier fighting-legislation (2:190–193) supplied the content of the phrase — fight those who fight you, do not transgress, until persecution is ended and the religion is God's — and this verse restates that whole architecture as an intention-test. Al-Rāzī draws the implication the tradition kept repeating: the same act of arms, performed in the same battle, is fī sabīl Allāh or it is not, depending on the cause it serves and the heart it proceeds from — and the difference between the two is invisible to every witness except the One the second clause names. The phrase converts the verse from a military order into a criterion, and it is why the tradition could read the struggle, as al-Qurṭubī records, as spiritual as well as physical: the sabīl is wide enough for the soul's campaign against itself, provided the campaign is really God's.

**The Imperative's Weight**

Read against the sūrah's own history, the command marks a threshold. The permission to fight had come recently — *Permission ˹to fight back˺ is ˹hereby˺ granted to those being fought* (22:39) and the Baqarah's own fighting-verses — after years of Meccan patience under persecution; this verse is among the passages the exegetes cite as evidence of its post-permission revelation, since an imperative to fight presupposes the fighting's legitimacy already established. The sequence matters for the command's tone: it is not the eagerness of a new power but the obligation of a community that has learned, through the fleeing thousands and through its own thirteen years of Meccan endurance, that survival is God's gift and that gifts carry assignments. The imperative also stands bare — no enemy named, no campaign specified — which is why the general reading could carry it forward: whatever the community's battles, their legitimacy is measured by the sabīl-qualifier and their conduct by the knowledge-clause that follows.

**The Same Pair the Code Just Used**

The name-pair is not new to the sūrah, and its reappearance here does deliberate work. The Īlāʾ-verse closed with the Hearing, the Knowing (2:227) standing over the marriage's most private deliberations; the same pair now stands over the campaign's. The pairing's distribution across the code is instructive: God hears and knows wherever human acts have an unseen interior — the oath in the heart, the resolve about a wife, the intention in a war. Al-Rāzī's spiritual reading rests on exactly this continuity: the struggle legislated here, physical or inward, is subject to the same surveillance the domestic legislation invoked, and the fighter's sincerity is audited by the same names that audited the swearer's. The verse thus binds the sūrah's two great subjects — the house and the battlefield — under one divine attention, and its message to both is identical: the outward act is legislated; the inward cause is known.
verses.245:
> Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**The Question That Is an Invitation**

The verse opens with a question that has no addressee's answer in it — *Who will lend to Allah a good loan?* — and the question-form is the invitation's genius. God, who owns the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, asks to borrow; the borrower names Himself and the loan's quality together: qarḍ ḥasan, a goodly loan, given willingly, from the lawful, without reminder or reproach attached. The commentators note the inversion the verse performs on every ordinary loan: in human lending the poor borrow from the rich, and the rich stipulate their terms; here the Rich asks the poor to lend, and the stipulation runs the other way — the loan must be *good*, and the repayment is promised at a multiplication no human creditor could offer. The transaction-language is not accidental; the Qur'an consistently frames the human relation to God as commerce — a bargain, a sale, a loan — and consistently assigns the guaranteed side of the ledger to God.

**Abū al-Daḥdāḥ's Garden**

The tradition's own answer to the question is a story. When this verse was revealed, the narrations collected by Ibn Kathīr relate, Abū al-Daḥdāḥ al-Anṣārī came to the Prophet and asked: does God truly seek a loan from us? The Prophet said yes, and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ asked for his hand, took it, and said: I have lent my garden to my Lord. The garden held six hundred date-palms, and his wife and children were living in it. He went to them and called his wife: Umm al-Daḥdāḥ. She answered: here I am. Leave the garden, he said, for I have lent it to my Lord. Her reply became proverbial: a profitable transaction — or words to that effect — and she moved herself and the children out. The Prophet's response, in the narrations, praised what Abū al-Daḥdāḥ now had: how many a date-cluster, heavy with pearls in Paradise, hangs for Abū al-Daḥdāḥ. The story is the verse performed: the question asked aloud, the loan contracted by handshake, the whole estate lent rather than a portion given, and the multiplication acknowledged before it arrived.

**The Loan Verses as a Network**

This is not the Qur'an's only loan-invitation, and the repetitions define the institution. The covenant with the Children of Israel made the good loan one of its conditions — *lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow* (5:12); the sūrah of Iron asks the same question with the same multiplication and adds the honorable reward (57:11); the sūrah of Mutual Disillusion attaches the forgiveness and names God Most Appreciative (64:17); and the wrapped-in-garments sūrah repeats the call (73:20). The exegetes draw the network's conclusion: serving God and doing good is always, in the Qur'an's economics, a profitable transaction — and its inverse is legislated too, in the condemnation of those who sell God's signs for a paltry price (2:41). The two sides of the ledger give the loan-language its seriousness: every person is transacting with God constantly; the only question is the terms, and the verse's terms — a loan repaid many times over — are the generous side of a trade both sides must make.

**The Multiplication's Arithmetic**

*Which Allah will multiply many times over* — adʿāf kathīrah, multiples upon multiples — and the Qur'an elsewhere supplies the arithmetic's floor and ceiling. The floor is the sūrah of the Cattle's rule: *Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold* (6:160), while the evil deed draws one. The ceiling is this sūrah's own grain-parable — the spent-in-God's-way wealth likened to a grain growing seven ears, each with a hundred grains, and God multiplying further for whomever He wills (2:261). Between ten and seven hundred and beyond, the multiplication is undefined — which is precisely the invitation's form: a creditor who fixes the interest invites calculation; a creditor who says *many times over* invites trust. The commentators note that the verse's own second clause removes even the calculation's motive: since increase and decrease belong to God alone, the wealth kept back was never secure and the wealth lent out was never lost — the multiplication is not an addition to the lender's estate but a revelation of where the estate always stood.
verses.246:
> Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**The Second Summons to See**

*Have you not seen* — the formula that opened the fleeing-thousands scene (2:243) opens this one, and the repetition binds the two stories into a single exhibit. What the eye is summoned to now is not a multitude dying but a council deliberating: the chiefs — the malaʾ, the leading men — of the Children of Israel in the generation after Moses, bringing a political request to a prophet. The tradition identifies the prophet as Samuel, the last of the judges, and the period as the era before the monarchy: the tribes under Philistine pressure, their shrines violated, their leadership failing. The verse compresses the whole situation into its opening exchange, and the compression follows the pattern the previous scene established — the narrative will move from a human proposal to a divine demonstration, and the demonstration will concern not the enemy but the proposers.

**The Request and Its Biblical Twin**

*Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the cause of Allah.* The request has a documented parallel the commentators cite: the elders' demand to Samuel in the first book of Samuel — a king to *go out before us and fight our battles*, so that Israel may be like the nations (1 Samuel 8:19–20). The two accounts share the structure — monarchy requested as a military solution — and differ in emphasis instructively. The biblical elders want to be like the nations, a king visible at their head; the Qur'anic chiefs frame the request entirely in the divine cause: the king's function is to make their fighting possible, and their fighting's definition is fī sabīl Allāh. The Qur'an's version thus sharpens the coming collapse: these are not men asking for pomp but men pledging a holy war conditional on a commander — and the condition, once granted, will reveal what the pledge was worth.

**God Knows the Wrongdoers**

The verse closes with the knowledge-clause: *And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers*. The wrongdoers named are precise — not the enemy, not the fleeing crowd in general, but those whose flight constituted ẓulm: the pledge-breakers, who had invoked their expulsed homes and separated children as the guarantee of their fighting and then withheld the fighting the guarantee promised. The commentators connect the clause to the story's function for its first hearers: the community receiving this sūrah had its own chiefs, its own pledges, and its own approaching orders, and the knowledge-clause stands over all of them — the audit that caught the fleeing thousands (2:243) and will audit the fighters of the following verses begins here, at the council. The clause also does narrative work: God's knowledge of the wrongdoers is the story's quiet statement that the flight was seen, recorded, and named — and that the few who stood were seen too. Between the two sightings the verse leaves its reader with the question the prophet asked: what will you do when the order comes?
verses.247:
> Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”

**The Appointment and the Protest**

The request is granted, and the grant detonates the story's second crisis: the king named is Saul — Ṭālūt, his Qur'anic name carrying the length that the verse's answer will explain — and the chiefs' first response is not allegiance but objection. *How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?* The protest has two grounds, and the exegetes note that both are claims about entitlement: we are more deserving — a claim of comparative right residing in the claimants — and he lacks wealth — a claim that the office requires an endowment he does not have.

**Saul in the Biblical Record**

The objection's historical basis is documented, and the commentators cite the parallel record. When Samuel first speaks to him, Saul himself argues his own improbability: *Am I not a Benjaminite, of the least tribe and the humblest family?* (1 Samuel 9:21). And after his anointing, the scripture records the same objection the Qur'an preserves: certain base men asked, *How can this man save us?* — they despised him and brought him no gift (1 Samuel 10:27). The Qur'anic account adds the genealogical detail the exegetes draw from al-Rāzī: Saul came from neither the kingly line — Judah — nor the priestly line — Levi — but from Benjamin, outside both pedigrees of power. The objection was thus, by the lights of its makers, entirely reasonable: the tribes had a constitutional expectation of where kings come from, and the appointment violated it. The narrative's whole design is to show that the expectation was the error.

**The Mirror of the Prophet's Own Rejection**

The commentators do not let the story stand alone, and the connection they draw is the verse's sharpest edge for its first hearers: the ground of the objection to Saul was the ground of the objection to Muhammad. The Quraysh's notables asked why the revelation had not descended on a great man of the two cities — wealth and station were their stated criteria; the Jewish tribes objected on lineage, the prophet from outside the prophetic houses. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī both note the parallel with the sūrah of ʿImrān's sovereignty-verse (3:26), where kingship is likewise God's disposal. The Israelite chiefs, in this reading, are not an ancient curiosity but a mirror held up to Mecca and Medina: every generation re-enacts the protest that divine election ignores human resumes, and every generation's protest is answered with the same two words the prophet answers with here — God has chosen. The story's placement in a sūrah addressed to a prophet whose own credentials were disputed on exactly these grounds is the placement's purpose.

**Kingship Is Given**

*Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills.* The sentence is the objection's formal refutation: the chiefs had spoken of deserving as though kingship were a wage earned by pedigree, and the verse names it a gift conferred by will. The Qur'an's parallel statements gather around this one — the sovereignty-verse of ʿImrān, which gives dominion to whom God wills and takes it from whom He wills (3:26); the sūrah of Women's question — *do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty* (4:54); and Joseph's prayer at the end of his own rise, *My Lord! You have surely granted me authority* (12:101) — the same vocabulary of grant, the same recognition that the office was received. The theological stake is the objection's root: if kingship is earned, the chiefs' resumes are valid grievances and God's choice is appealable; if kingship is given, the objection is not against Saul but against the Giver — which is why the verse's final clause names the Giver's two relevant attributes rather than answering the chiefs further.
verses.248:
> Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”

**The Sign Announced**

The prophet's answer to the objection moves from argument to evidence: the appointment will be confirmed by a sign, and the sign is the Ark — the tabūt, the sacred chest of Israel's sanctuary-history, missing from the community's life, now promised back. The verse's structure is precise about what the sign does: it authenticates the kingship (*the sign of Saul's kingship*), and it authenticates the prophet who announced it — al-Ṭabarī reads the prophet's gesture as self-validating: the Ark returns while I am your judge, so believe my prophecy about your king.

**Sakīnah: The Reassurance Inside**

The Ark's first content is *reassurance from your Lord* — sakīnah, the tranquility-word the Qur'an reserves for divine calm sent into human hearts. The commentators divide on its mode here: an object inside the Ark whose presence arouses tranquility, or the sakīnah itself — the quality, contained. Al-Rāzī notes the grammar permits a third reading: the Ark comes *on account of which* there will be tranquility — the chest as the sign's vehicle rather than the calm's container. Whichever mode is meant, the word's Qur'anic network is fixed and martial: the sakīnah sent down upon the Messenger and the believers after the battle's shaking (9:26), sent down again in the cave and at the treaty-year's crisis; the serenity sent into the believers' hearts *so that they may increase even more in their faith* (48:4). In every instance the word names God's answer to a community's fear — and its placement here, ahead of a campaign, tells the objecting chiefs what their king's real equipment is: not wealth, but the divinely-sent steadiness the Ark carries.

**The Relics of the Two Houses**

The second content is *relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron* — baqiyyah, a remnant, a remainder. The exegetes enumerate the candidates the tradition preserves: the staff of Moses — the rod that struck the sea and the rock (2:60); the fragments of the stone tablets brought down from Sinai, the broken pieces preserved after the first tablets' shattering (7:150); the manna of the wilderness years (2:57); and the vestments of the two brothers, including the sandals Moses was told to remove in the sacred valley (20:12). The list's significance is cumulative rather than archaeological: everything inside the Ark is a residue of revelation — objects that touched the founding events of Israel's faith, kept by God's people and lost by them, now returned. The two families named are the two offices of that founding — prophecy in Moses, priesthood in Aaron — and the remnant of both houses, riding in one chest, tells the objecting chiefs that the kingdom being authenticated stands in the line of both.

**The Biblical Background and Its Divergence**

The exegetes are candid that much of the surrounding material is biblical, and the divergences are as instructive as the parallels. In the books of Samuel the Ark was captured by the Philistines, afflicted its captors with plagues until they returned it, and then sat for decades in a private house at Kiriath-jearim — a period the biblical record itself marks as religious decline, Israel indifferent to its own sanctuary; David would later say, *we did not turn to it in the days of Saul* (1 Chronicles 13:3). The Bible's chronology thus places the Ark's return long before Saul's reign and records its neglect during it; the Qur'an gives no chronology at all, and al-Ṭabarī records the reading that resolves the tension: the Ark's restoration to Israel's life — functionally, as a sign — occurs around this appointment, whether or not the chest had sat physically nearby. One Muslim narration adds that from its Philistine return until Saul's time the people were prevented from approaching the Ark, a single family guarding it: present but inaccessible, its blessing withheld. On every reading the Qur'an's interest is identical — not where the chest was, but what its coming means: a neglected sacred history returning as the credential of God's chosen king.
verses.249:
> When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”

**Gideon's Water, Saul's Water**

The commentators set this scene beside its scriptural twin: Gideon's army at the water in the book of Judges (7:4–7), reduced by a drinking-test to three hundred men. The parallels are typological rather than historical — Gideon lived generations before Saul — and the differences are as structured as the similarities. Gideon's test was known only to Gideon: the soldiers were not told they were being sorted, and the criterion (lapping from the hand versus kneeling to drink) was applied after the fact, its meaning explained by God alone. Saul's test is proclaimed to the whole army, its criterion stated as a command, its consequence named as belonging or exclusion. Both tests reduce an army to a few so that the victory's attribution will be unambiguous — Judges states the purpose explicitly, that Israel might not boast against me, saying, my own hand has saved me — and both echo the Qur'an's wider water-motif, the parted sea of the exodus and the Jordan crossed before Jericho: the waters as the threshold where God's people are separated and reconstituted. The reenactment-reading follows naturally: sacred history repeating its forms, the river-test as a recurring station on the road God's armies travel.

**The Company of the Certain**

The verse's designation of the second group — *those who were certain they would meet Allah* — is the story's theological center, and it explains the maxim's power. Certainty (yaqīn) about the meeting reorders the soldier's arithmetic completely: if death is an appointment kept with God, then the numerical disparity between two armies concerns only the manner of the meeting, not its fact or its outcome. The few who drank nothing at the river had already demonstrated the same ordering — thirst governed, appetite deferred, belonging chosen over comfort — and the maxim is that governance extended from the mouth to the mind. Al-Qurṭubī connects the certainty-clause to the fleeing thousands of the sūrah's earlier scene (2:243): those fled death and met it; these expect death and by this meet God, and the difference between the two multitudes is the verse's whole instruction. The remnant that survives both sifts — the river's and the arithmetic's — is defined not by strength but by a settled relation to its own end, which is why so few have it and why the campaign needs so few.

**Allah Is with the Steadfast**

The maxim closes with the companionship-claim: *And Allah is always with the steadfast* — maʿiyyah, divine withness, attached to ṣabr. The formula is the sūrah's own standing promise, announced in its patience-verses — seek help through patience and prayer, for God is with the patient (2:153) — and its repetition here, in the mouth of the certain few, shows the promise functioning as doctrine under fire: not a comfort quoted after the battle but a premise used inside the arithmetic. The companionship is what makes the small-over-large record explicable — the mighty army fights alone in the sense that matters, and the small force does not fight at all alone — and it converts the maxim from battlefield folklore into theology. The verse's final word-order leaves the army on the far bank with the claim spoken: the river has sifted the indulgent, the maxim has answered the counters, and the companionship of God has been declared over what remains. What remains is very small, very certain, and — as the next moment will show — at prayer.
verses.250:
> When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**Pour Down Patience Upon Us**

The first petition's verb is a pouring: *afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabrā* — empty out, pour in abundance, patience upon us. The metaphor is rain and vessel at once: the ṣabr asked for is not the patience the men already have, deployed and rationed, but patience as a divine downpour filling them beyond their capacity — the word choice the commentators contrast with ordinary requests for patience, which ask for endurance within existing strength. The petition acknowledges what the river-test proved: the human stock of steadfastness is finite, drinkable in a handful or gulped past its limit, and the army facing a host of giants knows its own stock has already been spent down to a remnant. What remains must be supplied from above, and the supplying verb is generous — not give us patience but pour it, the abundance-form that matches the disparity. The Sufi commentators read the petition as the station of the certain: the men who know they will meet God ask, before the meeting's battle, for the quality that makes the meeting survivable in either direction.

**The Third Petition and Its Parallel**

*And give us victory over the disbelieving people* — the exterior request arrives last, and its placement after the two interior petitions is the verse's ethics of prayer: victory is asked for a people already asking to be made worthy of it. The petition has a documented twin, and the Qur'an itself preserves the parallel: at the battle of Uḥud's crisis, the sūrah of ʿImrān records the believers' prayer — *Our Lord! Forgive our sins and excesses, make our steps firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people* (3:147). The two duʿāʾs share their second and third petitions almost word for word, and the shared middle — make firm our steps — is the link the tradition treasures: the community of Muhammad praying the same prayer, in the same order, as the remnant of Saul. The parallel does interpretive work in both directions: it identifies the Ṭālut-army's prayer as the believers' standing battle-duʿāʾ, and it reads Uḥud's shaken ranks into the story's remnant — a small force facing a large one, asking not for numbers but for feet.

**The Duʿāʾ Preserved**

That this prayer is written down, in the revealed Book, is its own final lesson, and the commentators draw it: the Qur'an archives the words of God's servants at their moments of extremity, and the archive is an instruction. The duʿāʾ of the remnant joins the book's standing collection — the prayer of the patient (2:153's company), the prayer of those shaken at Uḥud (3:147), the prayers of Abraham, of Jonah, of Zachariah — each preserved as a form the community may inhabit. The preservation teaches that prayer under disparity is not a private resource but an inherited one: the believer facing his own Goliath does not need to compose a theology of the few from scratch, because the few have prayed before him and their words were kept. The verse's placement — between the maxim and the outcome the narrative now carries — makes the prayer the story's hinge: everything the sifting produced converges into these three petitions, and what the petitions ask for is exactly what a remnant needs to remain one. The army advanced, it prayed; the Qur'an, characteristically, wrote the prayer down and let the advancing speak for itself.
verses.251:
> So they defeated them by Allah’s Will, and David killed Goliath. And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all

**The Boy and the Two Inheritances**

The verse's second movement turns from the battle to the victor: *And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom*. The dual gift is read by al-Ṭabarī as a double inheritance: wisdom means the prophethood — David inherits the prophetic office of Samuel, the story's announcing prophet; kingship means the throne — he inherits the royal office of Saul, whose line the narrative will not continue. The shepherd thus gathers into one person the two authorities the tribes had held apart, and the gathering is the verse's quiet answer to the chiefs' old objection about pedigree: the man who ends up holding both offices came from neither house, chosen the way Saul was chosen, for what God knew. The Qur'an's David-portrait continues elsewhere — the sūrah Ṣād's account of him as authority in the land, commanded to judge with truth and warned against desire's misdirection (38:26) — and the kingship-plus-wisdom pairing here is that portrait's origin-story: the office and the character to carry it, granted together, at the moment of the sling.

**Taught Him What He Willed**

The third clause widens the gift: *and taught him what He willed*. The teaching's content is unnamed, and the naming is withheld deliberately — the tradition associates David with the Zabūr, the Psalter, with the mountains and birds joining his praise, with the craft of mail taught by divine instruction (21:80); the verse subsumes all of it under a single principle: what God teaches, He teaches by will, and the recipient's qualification is election rather than curriculum. The commentators connect the clause to the story's leadership-theology: Saul was increased in knowledge and stature (2:247), David is taught what He willed — both men carry endowments whose measure and timing belong to the Giver. The clause also frames the coming verses' subject, the messengers and their preferments: before the sūrah generalizes the principle — some messengers raised above others — it exhibits it in one career, a boy given a kingdom, a prophethood, and an education no school administered. The will that chose the unlikely king chooses the unlikely champion, and teaches him out of the same freedom.

**The Repelling Principle**

The verse's fourth movement steps back from the story to a law of history: *Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth*. The principle — God repels some people by means of others — is the Qur'an's answer to the question every holy war narrative raises: why does the divine administration run through human conflict at all? The verse's answer is counterfactual and total: without the repelling, the earth's corruption would not merely occur but prevail — the fa-sada that consumes societies would go unchecked, and the checking is done, in God's arrangement, by human forces set against one another. The parallel statement in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage specifies the repelling's stakes in the register of worship: *Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, destruction would have surely claimed monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah's Name is often mentioned* (22:40). The two verses together state the principle's scope: the repelling protects the earth's order and the earth's sanctuaries, and it protects them through exactly the kind of event the story just narrated — a remnant set against a host.

**Gracious to All**

The verse closes by naming the repelling's source: *but Allah is Gracious to all* — dhū faḍlin ʿalā'l-ʿālamīn, the Possessor of bounty toward the worlds. The name answers the counterfactual's darkness: the sentence begins with the corruption that would have dominated and ends with the generosity that does not let it, and the bounty's range — the worlds, not the believers, not the remnant — includes the repelled and the repellers, the defeated host and the boy with the sling. The echo with the fleeing-thousands scene is deliberate: that story closed on God's bounty toward mankind and mankind's ingratitude (2:243); this one closes on the same bounty, extended through a war, over all worlds. The story-unit that began with a multitude dying for fear of death ends with the principle that keeps the earth alive through the few who did not fear it — and the principle's engine, the verse's final word insists, is not necessity but faḍl.
verses.252:
> These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers

**The Address Turns**

The story ends, and the verse turns from the story's world to the Prophet's: *These are Allah's revelations which We recite to you*. The shift of addressee is the verse's whole function — everything narrated since the fleeing thousands (2:243) has been third-person history, and the seal now makes it second-person property. The demonstrative tilka, those, gathers the whole sequence: the thousands killed and revived, the council and its pledge, the appointment and the protest, the Ark and its angels, the river and the remnant, the prayer and the rout — and names all of it āyāt, signs, the same word the code's closing refrain used for the legislation just completed (2:242). The recitation is placed in God's own voice with the Qur'an's characteristic grammar of revelation: We recite — the divine first-person performing, in the verse itself, the very reciting it describes. The Prophet is told, in the act of being told, that what he has been reciting to his community is not his narrative but a delivery — and the delivery's source is named so that its authority is not his to defend.

**In Truth**

The recitation's qualifier — bi'l-ḥaqq, in truth — does double work, and the commentators divide it between the two. The first work is ontological: what has been recited is true, the stories are accounts of what was, not edifying inventions; the Qur'an's parallel declaration in the sūrah of ʿImrān states the claim at its strongest — *Certainly, this is the true narrative, and there is no god worthy of worship except Allah* (3:62), the story's truth and the creed's truth in one sentence. The second work is purposive: the reciting is *in truth* in the sense of *for truth* — the stories are delivered not as antiquarian interest but as vehicles of the revelation's claim, each carrying the doctrines the sūrah has been legislating: God's command of life and death, the hollowness of pledges untested, election over pedigree, the few and the many, victory by leave. The two readings converge in the verse's context: the Prophet's recitation of these stories to a community containing their skeptics is itself an act of truth-telling, and the qualifier arms him for it — the stories he tells are true, told truly, and told for the truth they carry.

**The Consolation Reading**

Al-Ṭabarī records the verse's pastoral dimension: the stories of 2:243–251 were sent, on this reading, to hearten the Prophet against the enemies pressing him — the past's messengers and prophets, he is reminded, endured trials of the same shape. The reading fits the sequence's content precisely. The fleeing thousands faced death and were commanded onward; Samuel's council pledged and collapsed; Saul was appointed to a nation that disputed his right to exist as king; the remnant faced a disparity their own ranks could not bear. Every scene is a mirror of the Prophet's circumstance — a messenger with a pledged community that keeps failing its pledges, facing enemies who dispute his appointment on grounds of wealth and pedigree — and the verse's seal tells him that the mirrors were sent on purpose. The consolation is not that the past prophets won easily but that they were where he is: outnumbered, objected-to, dependent on leave. The sūrah's earlier consolation-verse had promised the believers help until the last messenger despaired (2:214); this verse delivers the help in narrative form, addressed to the messenger himself.
verses.253:
> We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills

**Preferment and the No-Distinction Creed**

The verse opens on a claim that sounds, to the creed-trained ear, like a contradiction: *We have chosen some of those messengers above others*. The sūrah's own closing confession will have the believers say *We make no distinction between any of His messengers* (2:285), and the same no-distinction formula governs belief elsewhere in the Book (2:136, 3:84). The tradition's resolution, which the exegetes state as settled doctrine, distinguishes two objects: belief makes no distinction among the messengers in their truthfulness, their prophethood, and their protection from sin — every one of them maʿṣūm, every one of them to be believed in without exception — while God's preferment ranks their missions, not their persons. The sūrah of ʿImrān supplies the ranking's formula: *They each have varying degrees in the sight of Allah* (3:163). To believe all and to acknowledge the degrees is not double-bookkeeping but one creed with two clauses: the messengers are equal in what they are, and differentiated in what they were sent with and given.

**The One Spoken To**

*Allah spoke directly to some* — the kalām-privilege, and the tradition identifies its bearer without hesitation: Moses, the kalīm Allāh, the one to whom God spoke. The identification rests on the Sinai accounts — *When Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him* (7:143) — where the speaking is unmediated, without the angelic embassy that carries revelation to every other prophet. The exegetes mark what the privilege does and does not imply: it does not make Moses the highest-ranked (the tradition's ranking places the highest elsewhere), and it does not imply a divine mode of speech like human voices — the theology of the attribute is contested ground the verse does not enter.

**The Proofs and the Spirit**

The verse's one named messenger after Moses is Jesus: *To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit*. The proofs — the bayyināt — are the visible signs catalogued elsewhere in the sūrah and in the Table: the healings of the blind and the leper, the quickening of the dead by God's leave, the bird of clay breathed into life, the table sent down (5:110). The support is the same pairing the sūrah stated in its address to Israel — *We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit* (2:87) — and the Spirit's identity is the exegetes' question. Al-Rāzī records the three identifications the tradition carries: the angel Gabriel, the Spirit who brought the revelation and strengthened the prophets; the spirit God breathed into human being (15:29), the life-principle in its divine origin; and the Gospel itself, the revelation given to Jesus. The three, he notes, share one quality — each is life-giving, whether the quickening of bodies or the nourishment of hearts and intellects — and the sharing is the identification's real content: whatever the Spirit is, its function in Jesus' mission is the same, the divine reinforcement carried alongside the proofs. The word's root, qudus, carries purity as well as holiness: the support named here is the clean, uncreated side of every miracle the verse's Jesus performs.

**Had God So Willed**

The verse's second half turns from the messengers to their aftermath, and its refrain begins: *If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought among themselves after receiving the clear proofs*. The subject is precise — not the pagans but the generations after the messengers, the communities of revelation, fighting each other *after* the bayyināt arrived: the very proofs the verse just named as gifts became the occasion of war, because clarity divides as surely as it guides. The refrain has its network, and the network is the doctrine: *If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but His Will is to test you with what He has given each of you* (5:48); *Had your Lord so willed, He would have certainly made humanity one single community, but they will always choose to differ* (11:118); and the sūrah's own earlier statement that humanity was one community before it differed, the messengers sent with the Book to judge between them (2:213). The verse adds nothing to the mechanism and removes nothing from its hardness: difference after revelation is willed — not approved, not authored in the sense of commanded, but permitted inside a will whose alternative (one undiffering community) is named and declined.

**But Allah Does What He Wills**

The verse's final sentence is the refrain's resolution and the whole preferment-doctrine's ground: *But Allah does what He wills*. The clause answers the objection the verse's first half invites — if some messengers are raised and some are not, if the speech is given to one and the Spirit to another, if the proofs arrive and the communities fight anyway — who adjudicates the arrangement? The answer declines adjudication: the will is the last term, and the verse places it last. The commentators are careful about what the clause does not say: it is not arbitrariness dressed as sovereignty, since the same verse names what the will has actually willed — gifts, proofs, support, clarity — and the Qur'an elsewhere attaches the willing to wisdom (2:269, 3:74 in the tradition's citation). It is, instead, the closing of every appeal: the ranks are not negotiable by the ranked, the difference is not litigable by the differers, and the fighting after the proofs is not excusable by its participants, since the proofs they fought over were given. The verse ends where the story-sequence began — with a divine administration whose dispositions are seen, named, and not explained away — and leaves its hearer with the only response the administration has ever asked for: belief on one side of the difference, and the deeds that follow.
verses.254:
> O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers

**The Three Currencies Refused**

The Day is defined by three refusals, and each names a currency the world runs on. No bargaining — the world's transactions: ransom, price, negotiation, the deal struck at the margin. No friendship — the world's networks: the ally who intervenes, the connection who vouches, the kinship that opens doors. No intercession — the world's hierarchies of access: the patron who stands between the accused and the judge. The Qur'an states the same economics elsewhere: the sūrah of Abraham orders the believers to donate *before the arrival of a Day in which there will be no ransom or friendly connections* (14:31); the sūrah of the Believer pictures the Day *when the hearts will jump into the throats* and the wrongdoers have *neither a close friend nor intercessor to be heard* (40:18).

**The Intercession Question**

The third refused currency deserves the precision the commentators give it, because the Qur'an's intercession-teaching is not a flat denial. The sūrah's own early verse stated the Day's rule absolutely — *No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given* (2:48) — while other verses condition intercession rather than abolish it: who can intercede with God except by His leave. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record the reconciliation here: the ability to intercede is unavailable, on this Day, to the disbelievers — the refusal is scoped to those who refused God. The tradition's picture of the Day includes intercession exercised by permission — above all the Prophet's intercession for his community and for the world, attached to the praiseworthy station promised him (17:79) — and the theological literature extends the permission to others by rank, al-Ghazzālī among the saints and the faithful, the Shīʿī tradition through the Imams. The verse's clause, read in that light, does not erase the institution but empties it of everything the world meant by it: no intercession that is bought, owed, or leveraged — only what the Judge permits, to whom He permits, for whom He permits.

**Friends Become Enemies**

The friendship-refusal has its own Qur'anic elaboration, and the elaboration sharpens the warning. The sūrah of Ornaments states it as a reversal: *Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous* (43:67). The exception is the verse's hidden door: the friendships that survive the Day are the ones that were already righteous — bonds whose content was the good rather than the useful. The sūrah of Smoke adds that on the Day *no friend will avail a friend in any way*, and the sūrah of the Stairways pictures the loyal friend not asked about by his loyal friend (70:10) — each soul too occupied to plead another's case. Read together, the network-verses tell the believer something actionable in the interval: the worldly friendship that will be worthless on the Day is the friendship of mutual advantage, and the only social capital that crosses is the righteousness shared — which is why the verse's command is a command to spend: the donation is precisely the act that converts wealth, the most worldly of currencies, into the only form that the refusals do not touch.

**The Verse as Threshold**

Positioned where it sits, the verse opens the sūrah's second great theme-block — spending — and opens it with the eschatology that will govern every spending-verse to come. The parables of the grain and the garden, the prohibitions on reminders and injury, the ranking of secret over public, the recipients who do not beg: all of it operates inside the deadline this verse states. The three refusals also gather the sūrah's earlier material — the Day described in its opening eschatological verses, the intercession-question raised at 2:48, the spending-from-provision commanded from 2:3 — and compress it into a single imperative. The reader is left with the verse's arithmetic, which is deliberately simple: everything a person owns is provided, everything provided can be donated, everything donated before the Day crosses it, and on the Day the three currencies of the world are refused to everyone. The command is therefore not a tax on the believer's wealth but the only available exchange rate — and the wrongdoers named at the end are the ones who waited for a better one.
verses.255:
> Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest

**The Greatest Verse**

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (810), the Prophet asks Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: O Abū'l-Mundhir, do you know which verse of God's Book is the greatest? Ubayy answers by reciting this verse — *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa'l-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm* — and the Prophet strikes his chest and says: may knowledge gladden you, O Abū'l-Mundhir. Other narrations call the verse a quarter of the Qur'an, direct the Companions to recite it before sleep, and promise — in a report of the Sunan collections — that whoever recites it after every obligatory prayer is kept from Paradise only by death. The tradition of its protective recitation has a famous story behind it: Abū Hurayrah, set over the Ramadan alms-store, caught a night-thief three times running, and the third time released him in exchange for words of benefit — recite Āyat al-Kursī when you go to bed, and a guardian from God will stay with you and Satan will not approach you until morning. The Prophet's verdict, in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (2311): he told you the truth, though he is a liar — the thief was Satan himself.

**The Living, the Self-Subsisting**

The verse opens with the shahādah's Qur'anic form — God, there is no god but He — the phrasing that dominates the text's own declarations of unity (2:163, 3:2, and many more), and then names the two divine titles the tradition counts among the mothers of the Names, ummahāt al-asmāʾ. Al-Ḥayy, the Living, occupies in Islamic theology a place the commentators equate with Being itself: a living thing, al-Rāzī formulates it, is one able to fully actualize all its perfections — and the theological cascade runs from there, God's Power directed by His Will, His Will determined by His Knowledge, all of them depending on His Life. Al-Qayyūm, the All-Sustaining, is an intensive form from the root of standing and establishing: God subsists through Himself, and — the second half of the intensity — all things subsist through Him. The two names together state the verse's whole architecture: a Life that cannot lapse and a Subsistence that cannot be borrowed, which is why the next clause denies the lapse's slightest forms.

**Ownership and Permission**

*To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth* — the ownership-clause grounds the intercession-clause that follows, and the intercession-clause is the verse's great reconciliation. The sūrah's earlier Day-verse had denied intercession flatly (2:48); here it is affirmed conditionally: *Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission?* The rhetorical question concedes nothing to the intercessor — the permission is God's, wholly — and everything to the institution: intercession exists, and it exists as a function of the leave. The tradition's supreme instance is the Prophet's intercession on the Day of Judgment, for his community and for the world, attached to the praiseworthy station (17:79); theologians like al-Ghazzālī extend permission-granted intercession to the saints and ordinary believers according to rank, and Shīʿī doctrine places the Imams at its center. The commentators' deepest observation is structural: every prayer one person makes for another already assumes intercession — the angels' forgiveness-prayers for the believers (40:7), Jacob's promised prayer for his sons (12:98), the command to the Prophet to seek forgiveness for the faithful — since to pray for another is to believe God answers. Intercession, on this reading, is a special kind of supplication, and the verse's permission-clause is its charter: no one stands before God for anyone except by His leave — and His leave is why anyone stands.

**The Knowledge That Cannot Be Grasped**

*He knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them* — the phrase's referents are read three ways by al-Rāzī and the tradition: the Hereafter ahead and the world behind; what comes after death and what preceded creation; the deeds yet to be done and the deeds already done. The pronoun covers both the would-be intercessors and those interceded for — every party to any plea, past and coming. Then the verse closes the knowledge in the other direction: *no one can grasp any of His knowledge — except what He wills to reveal*. Knowledge here, the commentators note, is used in the sense of the known — the content rather than the faculty — and the exception-clause is the Qur'an's standing epistemology: the unseen is disclosed only where God approves its disclosure, *except messengers of His choice* (72:27); the angels' own confession is the verse's echo from the sūrah's opening — we have no knowledge except what You have taught us (2:32). The intercession-clause and the knowledge-clause are thus two statements of one rule: no access to God's court and no access to God's knowledge except by His leave and His will — and both accesses, the verse affirms, are real.
verses.256:
> Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**The Sentence and Its Grammar**

Lā ikrāha fī'l-dīn — *no compulsion in religion* — is among the most cited sentences in the Qur'an, and its first interpretive question is grammatical: is it descriptive or prescriptive? Read as description, it states a fact about faith itself — religion cannot be compelled, because belief coerced is not belief; the heart under threat produces compliance, not īmān. Read as prescription — *let there be no compulsion* — it legislates the fact, forbidding what would in any case be futile. The traditional commentaries carry both readings without conflict, and the second clause supplies the reason either way: *the truth stands out clearly from falsehood* — rushd has become distinct from ghayy, and what is distinct does not need to be imposed. The Qur'an's parallel statements gather behind this verse: *Had your Lord so willed, all people on earth would have certainly believed. Would you then force people to become believers?* (10:99); and the command to say: *Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve* (18:29). The compulsion-verses share one assumption — that faith is a seeing, not a yielding — and this verse states the assumption as a principle of law.

**The Occasions of Revelation**

The narrations behind the verse are specific and domestic, and they matter for its scope. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record three occasions, all involving children and belonging. In the first, Muslim parents had children among the Banū Naḍīr — the Jewish tribe exiled from Medina after its plotted betrayal — and asked whether they might force the children into the Muslim community; the background is a pre-Islamic custom of Yathrib, where women whose infants kept dying vowed that any child who survived would be raised Jewish, and it was such vowed children who now stood between two communities. In the second, a Muslim man's two sons were converted by merchants and left for Syria as Christians. In the third, Muslims who had been wet-nursed by Jewish families wanted to depart with the exiled clans, and their families were forcing them to remain. In every account the verse arrives to stop a compelled belonging — and in every account the compelling party is the one with the better religion, which is precisely why the case is hard and the ruling general.

**Scope, Jizyah, and the Abrogation Debate**

The jurists asked how far the principle reaches, and the commentary records the debate honestly. Some sources restrict the verse to the People of the Book, or to anyone from whom the jizyah-protection tax may be taken (9:29's legislation) — noting that the idolatrous Arabs were not offered the option of remaining idolaters, and reading the no-compulsion rule as governing the recognized protected religions. Others claimed the verse was abrogated by the fighting-commandments, the sword-verse of sūrah 9 among them. The commentators answer the abrogation-claim on chronology: all three occasions of revelation follow from conflicts with the Jewish tribes — conditions resulting from banishments already carried out — so the verse is late, not early, and cannot have been repealed by verses whose campaigns preceded it. The deeper answer is doctrinal: compulsion in religion negates taklīf, the accountability before God that gives both this life and the Hereafter their meaning — and an ethical pronouncement of that kind is not subject to abrogation at all.

**Ṭāghūt and the Handhold**

The verse's second half describes the act of faith in two movements: renouncing ṭāghūt and believing in God. Ṭāghūt — rendered *false gods* — is built on the root of rebellion and trespass: al-Rāzī glosses it variously as Satan, as soothsayers and magicians, as idols, as any being who rebels against God and is followed in the rebellion; the longer treatment waits in the sūrah of Women (4:51). The renunciation comes first in the syntax, and the order is the theology: the handhold is grasped by a letting-go. The image — *the firmest, unfailing hand-hold* — has its parallel in the sūrah of Luqmān: whoever submits to God and does good *has grasped the firmest hand-hold* (31:22). The commentators identify the handhold as faith itself or as the shahādah-word, and they note the precision of *unfailing*: the Arabic break it denies is the fracture that does not show — the handhold that fails imperceptibly, the faith that parts silently under strain. What is grasped, the verse promises, does not give way even slightly, and the grasping is available to whoever performs the two movements — renounce, believe — with no one compelled into either.
verses.257:
> Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**The Walī**

The verse opens with a single relational noun carrying the weight of everything that follows: God is the walī of those who believe — guardian, protector, ally, friend, patron; the word holds all of them at once, and the tradition's glosses move across the range. A walī is the one who stands nearest with power to help: the guardian of an orphan, the protector of a client, the ally of a confederation, the friend whose friendship has consequences.

**Out of the Darknesses, Into the Light**

The movement ascribed to God's guardianship is an extraction: *He brings them out of darkness and into light*. The Arabic's asymmetry is the image's first teaching, and the commentators mark it: the darknesses are plural — ẓulumāt — while the light is singular, nūr. Error, in the Qur'an's idiom, is many; truth is one. The plural darknesses are the unbelief's varieties — the idols, the doubts, the appetites, the inherited errors — and each extraction is particular: this believer out of these darknesses. The singular light is the destination's unity: one faith, one direction, one God. The symbolism runs through the whole Qur'an, and this verse is its most explicit statement of movement — elsewhere the sūrah of the Table names the Book *a light by which Allah guides* (5:16), the sūrah of Light builds the symbol into its greatest verse — *Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth* (24:35) — and the extraction-formula recurs: out of the darknesses into the light at 14:1, 33:43, 57:9, 65:11. Al-Ṭabarī records the majority gloss plainly: light is faith and guidance, darkness is denial and error — and the bringing-out is the work of the walī, not the achievement of the brought.

**The Reverse Migration**

The verse's second sentence is its most disturbing symmetry: the disbelievers' guardians *lead them out of light and into darkness*. The migration is real and it runs backward — and its starting point is the verse's quiet claim about unbelief: it begins in light. The ṭāghūt-guardianship does not operate on people who never saw; it takes people who did — the clarity established in the preceding verse, the rushd distinguished from ghayy, the handhold within reach — and leads them out of it. The commentators read the reversal as the work of false patronage: whatever is followed in rebellion against God performs, for its followers, the inverse of God's walāyah — it has the shape of guardianship (devotion given, direction taken, trust extended) and the function of undoing. The plural returns in the destination as in the cause: out of the one light, into the darknesses — the single truth abandoned, the many errors entered, each idol and appetite its own chamber. The symmetry denies any neutral ground: every person is migrating, under one guardianship or the other, and the verse's two sentences are the two itineraries.

**Guardianship as Pedagogy**

The bringing-out and the leading-out share a structure the exegetes draw out: both are gradual, both are relational, and both are performed on the person rather than by him. Light and darkness in this idiom are not information but states — a person is in them, and getting out requires a hand. The believer's extraction is the history of revelation itself: the Book sent *that you may bring people out of the darknesses into the light, by their Lord's permission* (14:1) — the messenger's mission defined as the same bringing-out the verse ascribes to God, since the walī's work runs through the means the walī appoints. The disbelievers' leading-out has its ministers too: the callers to the ṭāghūt, the merchants of Syria in the occasion-narrations of the preceding verse, the inherited customs of Yathrib's vowed children. The verse's pastoral instruction is to audit one's guardianships — to ask of every attachment that shapes the heart's direction whether it is extracting toward the one light or conducting toward the many darknesses — because the migration is underway either way, and nobody travels unaccompanied.
verses.258:
