The first is increase through deferment — ribā al-nasīʾah: a charge added to a debt at its maturity in exchange for time. The second is increase through surplus — ribā al-faḍl: an excess taken in the exchange of like commodities, gold for gold, or one grade of a staple for a better grade in unequal measure.

**The Slogan Refuted**

The verse names the devourers' argument and answers it in one movement: *That is because they say, "Trade is no different than interest." But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest.* The slogan's form is an equivalence-claim — bayʿ, ordinary sale, is mithl ribā, the same thing as the increase — and the traditional glosses preserve its historical voice: the Meccan creditor-class's defense of the practice, sale is only money-for-goods and ribā is money-for-money, both are trade. The refutation declines the terrain entirely. It does not argue the equivalence false on economic grounds; it states the legislative fact: God has allowed the one and forbidden the other, and the permission-and-prohibition are themselves the difference. The Qur'an's wider treatment supplies the economics the slogan hides — the sūrah of the Byzantines states it flatly: *Whatever loans you give, seeking interest at the expense of people's wealth will not increase with Allah. But whatever charity you give, seeking the pleasure of Allah—it is they whose reward will be multiplied* (30:39). The increase taken from people's wealth does not increase where increases are actually recorded; the two transactions are not the same because they run in opposite directions — one toward the debtor's loss, one toward the needy's gain.

**Whoever Refrains After the Warning**

The verse's amnesty-clause legislates the prohibition's arrival: *Whoever refrains — after having received warning from their Lord — may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah.* The commentators' rulings give the clause its exact reach: what is cancelled is the outstanding — the increases accrued and not yet collected at the warning's arrival; what has already been consumed is not reclaimed. The Prophetic statement attached to the clause fixes the formula: all the ribā of the Age of Ignorance is remitted; you have your principal; you neither wrong nor are wronged (the declaration made at the Farewell Pilgrimage's sermon, weeks before the Prophet's death). *Their case is left to Allah* covers the amnesty's interior: the desisting's sincerity, the past's weight, the heart's history with the practice — the file closed to human jurisdiction and left open with God. The clause is the verse's mercy-statement, and its timing is the tradition's observation: this passage is said to be among the very last revelations — some count it the last of all, with 4:176 and 5:3 the rival candidates — which the exegetes cite to explain why the ḥadīth record on ribā's fine mechanics is comparatively thin: the law arrived late, and its elaboration fell to the jurists of the following generations.

**Those Who Persist**

The final sentence closes the alternative: *As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.* The going-back — the return to the practice after the warning — is what the residency answers, and the verse's structure makes the persistence, not the past, the operative fact: the pre-warning gains were remitted, and only the post-warning return carries the Fire. The residency-language is the sūrah's permanence-formula, and its assignment here places ribā's operators in the company of the verse-sequence's other final residents — the apostates of 2:217, the darkness-led of 2:257 — while its occasion, an economic practice, is the sequence's sharpest statement that the ledger's deepest entries are commercial. The devourer's portrait is now complete in three strokes: the convulsed rising, the slogan refuted by permission-and-prohibition, and the residency earned by persistence after amnesty. Between the amnesty and the residency stands the verse's only open question — *their case is left to Allah* — and the case it leaves is every reader's own: what he will do with the increase in his ledger, now that trading has been permitted and this forbidden.
verses.276:
> Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful. And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer

**The Blight's Operation**

The commentators read the blighting across both registers the sūrah has established. In the visible register, the ribā-estate carries the devourer's curse inside its own structure: the compounding that swallowed the debtor's possessions (3:130's doubling and redoubling) builds a wealth whose preservation requires the debtor's ruin, and the tradition's Prophetic saying quoted at the next verse states the visible end — ribā, even when it swells, ends in loss. In the unseen register — the one the section's parables have trained the reader to read — the blight is the dust-on-rock effect at the scale of an estate: amounts that looked like soil over substance, stripped bare by the downpour of the reckoning (2:264). The two registers converge in the parable-language the sūrah already supplied: the grain sown in charity multiplies to seven hundred (2:261), the garden on the height doubles under rain (2:265), and the orchard of a lifetime burns in an hour (2:266) — the ribā-wealth is the orchard whose fire was lit at its planting, and the verse's maḥq names the burning as already underway, invisible to the ledger and total in the fact.

**The Growth's Operation**

The causing-to-grow answers the blight point for point, and the section's own imagery supplies the mechanics. The date-given-in-charity is taken into God's hand and nurtured like a foal until it stands like a mountain — the ḥadīth the garden-verse's commentary carried; the single grain returns seven hundredfold and God multiplies beyond for whom He wills (2:261). The growth is not metaphorical in the tradition's insistence: the charity's increase is a real accretion in the only ledger that survives, deposited with the Lord (2:262, 2:274) where the maḥq cannot reach it. The verse thus restates the two preceding verses' eschatology as economics: the devourers' rising in convulsion (2:275) is the blight made visible at the standing, and the givers' no-fear-no-grief (2:274) is the growth made visible at the same hour. The sūrah of the Byzantines states the same opposition with the same verbs' logic — the interest seeking increase in people's wealth does not increase with God, while the charity seeking God's pleasure is multiplied (30:39) — and the two verses together are the Qur'an's complete rebuttal of the devourers' slogan: they claimed sale and ribā were one thing, and the answer is that ribā and charity are the two things, the false increase and the true.

**Why the Thesis Stands Alone**

The verse's placement between the devourers' portrait (2:275) and the believers' portrait (2:277) gives it the function of a fulcrum, and its brevity is the fulcrum's requirement. What precedes is the case of the ribā: its image, its slogan, its amnesty, its residency. What follows is the case of the community: belief, righteous deeds, the prayer kept, the alms paid, the reward deposited, the fear and grief removed. Between the two cases the sūrah needs one sentence stating the principle both are instances of — that God presides over two opposite arithmetic operations, effacement and increase, and assigns each to one of the two economies — and the sentence is this verse. The commentators' observation that the section's legislation (the commands to the believers in the next three verses) presupposes the thesis is exact: leave what remains of ribā (2:278) is a command that only makes sense to someone who believes the blight is real, and the respite-and-charity upgrade (2:280) is an invitation only attractive to someone who believes the growth is real. The one-line verse is therefore the block's axiom, and the axioms of divine economics, the Qur'an's structure suggests, fit in one line: two verbs, one root, two names of what a person can be.
verses.277:
> Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**The Four Named**

The verse states the community's positive economy in four terms, and the terms' order is the verse's architecture: *those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax*. The first pair is the sūrah's standard opening dyad — believed and worked the righteous — the interior assent and the deeds that verify it. The second pair names the two institutions: the ṣalāt established (āqāmū, the same causing-to-stand the prayer-verse commanded, 2:238) and the zakāt given. The commentators note the dyads' division of labor: belief and righteous work are personal and unlimited, while prayer and alms are the instituted forms the personal takes — the fixed stations of the day and the fixed levy on the year, the two pillars whose performance is measurable and whose neglect is public. The verse's listing is the same four that structure the sūrah's opening portrait of the successful (2:3–5: belief in the unseen, the prayer established, spending from the provision, belief in the revelation) — and the ring it closes is deliberate: the Book that began by defining the guided in these four terms ends its economy-legislation by restating the same four and attaching their reward.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The reward-formula is now so established in the section that its recurrence is itself meaningful: *they will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve*. The custody-clause — the reward with, at, from the Lord — has sealed the un-reminding givers (2:262) and the four-quadrant givers (2:274), and its assignment here to the pillar-community extends the custody from the charitable act to the instituted life: the zakāt-payer's reward sits in the same divine keeping as the secret night-gift's. The no-fear-no-grief formula, which the tradition reads as the sūrah's language of final security, has by this point appeared across the revelations' faithful (2:62), the sūrah of the Table's parallel (5:69), the section's complete givers, and now the community's four-term portrait — and each recurrence narrows the distance between the formula's bearers until this verse, where it rests on the instituted believers themselves. The commentators' note that the verse's content parallels 2:62 and 5:69 sharpens the point: the security once stated for the faithful of every revelation is here stated for the community that keeps its two pillars — the same reward, the same custody, the same two negations, now as a description of institutional life rather than of creed alone.

**The Establishment-Verb**

The prayer-clause's verb deserves the attention the tradition gives it: āqāmū — they established, they caused to stand. The sūrah's prayer-guarding verse (2:238) commanded the keeping — ḥāfiẓū — of the prayers and their middle; this verse describes the community's characteristic act as the establishing, and the commentators gloss the difference as the difference between performance and institution: the prayer established is the prayer given standing — in the person's day (its times kept, its devotion honored) and in the community's space (its congregation maintained, its mosques built, its children taught). The same verb has run through the sūrah from its opening — those who establish the prayer (2:3) — and its reappearance in the economy-block is the verse's quiet structural claim: the market's ethics are anchored in the mosque's discipline. The zakāt-clause inherits the anchoring: the alms-tax is not occasional generosity but established giving — assessed, owed, distributed — the charity-section's free quadrants (2:274) crystallized into an institution that survives the moods of the giver.
verses.278:
> O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers

**If You Are Believers**

The verse's final clause is its sharpest instrument: *if you are true believers* — in tuʾminūn, the condition attached to the abandonment. The commentators read the conditional in the register the Qur'an reserves for such attachments: not a doubt cast on the addressees' faith but a definition of it. The faith named is being tested against its own content — the community that has just been described as believing, doing good, establishing prayer, and paying alms (2:277) is told that the outstanding ribā in its ledgers is incompatible with the description, and the conditional makes the incompatibility active: belief, if it is belief, gives up the remainder. The structure echoes the sūrah's own faith-verses — the handhold grasped by the renouncing and believing (2:256), the fear-of-God that the annulment-prohibitions assumed — and it does the same work here on the economy: faith is not a state that coexists with the increase-claims but a state that releases them. The tradition's ascetic commentators draw the clause's full edge: the verse makes the abandoned ribā the criterion, so that a believer's ledger is itself a testimony, and what remains in it after the command is the measure of what the in tuʾminūn found inside.

**The Taqwā-Frame**

The fear-of-God that heads the command connects the economy-block to the sūrah's whole legislation, and the commentators mark the connection deliberately: this is the same taqwā the code invoked at its thresholds — nearer to reverence in the waiver-ranking (2:237), the duty on those mindful in the provision-ruling (2:241), beware of Him in the heart-knowledge verse (2:235). The placement means that the ribā-relinquishment is legislated as an act of taqwā rather than as a commercial adjustment: what makes the abandonment possible is not economic argument but the feared-and-hoped relationship the sūrah has been installing since its opening portrait of the God-fearers (2:2–5). Al-Rāzī's cascade in the two-voices verse (2:268) is the psychology behind the frame: the soul that obeys the poverty-threat keeps and compounds, and the soul that fears God releases — the taqwā-clause is the command's statement of which fear it expects to find operative. The verse thus does not argue with the creditors' self-interest; it addresses the fear that outranks self-interest, and makes the argument's conclusion — leave the remainder — that fear's immediate act.

**The Community Addressed as Creditors**

One feature of the verse's address has drawn the commentators' notice: it speaks to believers as people who hold ribā-claims — the community's own ledgers, not the enemy's. The address assumes what Medina's economy actually contained: Muslim creditors holding pre-Islamic deferment-claims against Muslim and non-Muslim debtors alike, the mechanism of the Age of Ignorance still running inside the believing community's own books. The verse's legislation is therefore internal reform at its most concrete — a community ordered to rewrite its own contracts, cancel its own accrued income, and absorb the loss as the cost of the faith it claimed. The commentators connect this internality to the sequence's structure: the portrait-verse (2:277) described the community's four terms, and this verse tests the fourth — the alms-payters against the interest-takers are supposed to be the same people, and where they are not, the command makes them so by force of the conditional. No external enemy is named in the ribā-block; the war-declaration that follows is addressed to whoever among the believers does not comply — which is why the taqwā-frame comes first: the battlefield of this legislation is the believer's own ledger, and the fear of God is the only authority that can order a man to burn his own outstanding income.
verses.279:
> If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger! But if you repent, you may retain your principal—neither inflicting nor suffering harm

**Neither Wronging Nor Wronged**

The settlement's formula is the verse's most quoted clause: *neither inflicting nor suffering harm* — lā taẓlimūna wa-lā tuẓlamūn, you shall not wrong and shall not be wronged. The commentators note the formula's double fairness with care. The creditor is not wronged: his capital returns to him intact, and the repentance-clause exists precisely so that the prohibition does not become a confiscation — the religion does not make the abandonment of ribā a punishment of the lender's estate. The debtor is not wronged: the increase that was absorbing his possessions — the doubling and redoubling of 3:130 — stops at the principal, and the wrong of compounding is lifted from him forever. The two negations thus state the settlement as a symmetry, and the symmetry is the ribā-block's moral core: the forbidden transaction is the one that requires a wronging — the increase taken from the debtor's need is a wrong inflicted, and its cancellation without capital-loss ensures no wrong rebounds onto the creditor. The tradition reads the same formula as the economy's standing principle, the Prophetic declaration at the Farewell Pilgrimage using it as the ribā-amnesty's own closing words: you have your principal — neither wronging nor wronged — and the jurists extended the principle to the whole of muʿāmalāt: no transaction in the Islamic order may be built on either party's ẓulm.

**The Principal and the Loan's Nature**

The retention-of-principal ruling carries an implication the commentators draw out in the block's wider context: the legitimate loan, in this legislation, is a loan that returns exactly what was given. The Islamic tradition's ideal of the qarḍ — the loan — is therefore charitable in structure: money lent for a term, repaid in the same amount, the time-value surrendered by the lender as an act of the giving the section has been legislating (the invitation to turn the difficult debtor's respite into outright charity follows at the next verse). The profit-seeking uses of capital are not forbidden by this structure but channeled — into the trade God permitted (2:275's permission-clause), the credit-sale with its negotiated price, the lease, the partnership where profit and loss are shared — instruments in which the return compensates real risk or real exchange rather than time alone. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī both frame the principal-rule this way: the creditor's capital is protected because capital is legitimate property; the increase is cancelled because the increase was the wrong. The verse thus legislates not the abolition of lending but its purification — the loan restored to the form in which it can be, as the tradition insists, an act of charity with a contractual body.

**The Sequence's Position**

This verse and its neighbors form the block's enforcement-triad, and the triad's order is deliberate: the portrait of the pillar-community (2:277), the command to the believers to fear God and abandon the remainder (2:278), the war-and-repentance alternative (this verse), the respite-and-charity treatment of the struggling debtor (2:280), and the Day-return that seals the whole (2:281). The commentators read the movement as descending from the community's identity to its ledgers to its debtors to its final audit — each verse narrowing the frame: believers, creditors, debtors, souls. Within the triad this verse is the alternative-statement, the point where the command's two exits are named in full: persistence is war, repentance is settlement, and the settlement's terms are fixed at the principal. Nothing between the two exits is legislated — no partial compliance, no negotiated retention of some increase — and the binary is the verse's rhetorical force: the ribā-holder stands, in the moment of the command, at the fork the verse describes, and the fork's two roads have been named with their destinations, war on one side and neither-wronging on the other, with the principal waiting intact on the road of return.
verses.280:
> If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew

**The Struggling Debtor**

The ribā-block turns from the creditor's sin to the debtor's distress, and its legislation begins with recognition: *if it is difficult for someone to repay a debt* — the ʿusrah, the straitness, the hard circumstance that makes the due date arrive against an empty hand. The verse does not treat the struggling debtor as a defaulter to be pressed but as a condition to be waited out: *postpone it until a time of ease*. The commentators mark the command's addressee and its force: the creditor who holds a matured debt against a debtor in genuine straits is ordered to grant the respite — the inaẓār, the looking-along, the patience of the term extended. The jurisprudence that grew from the clause distinguished the straitened debtor from the evasive one (the mūsil, the procrastinator with means, whose delay is ẓulm in the tradition's famous saying), and assigned this verse to the former: where the difficulty is real, the postponement is not the creditor's option but his obligation until the ease arrives. The verse thus completes the block's debtor-protection: the increase was cancelled at the principal (2:279), and now the principal itself is granted patience — the debt survives, and the debtor survives it.

**The Respite as Charity**

The verse's second movement converts the obligation into an invitation and ranks the conversion: *if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you*. The waiving — the ṣadaqah-word the giving-section built its fifteen verses on — is applied here to the debt itself: the creditor may release not the increase (already cancelled) but the principal, turning the loan's remainder into a gift. The tradition's arithmetic of the respite makes the invitation's gradient explicit: a ḥadīth the exegetes cite states that whoever grants delay to one in difficulty is credited an act of charity for each day of the delay — the patience itself generating the giving's reward day by day — while the outright waiving is the section's own better, the excellence beyond the duty. Al-Qurṭubī's ruling fixes the two ranks' legal relation: the respite is commanded because the debtor's difficulty is real, but the principal remains the creditor's claim — the verse encourages the waiving without requiring it, since the lender's capital is legitimate property the law protects (the neither-wronged half of 2:279). The structure is the sūrah's characteristic ethics one final time: the floor legislated (postpone), the height pointed at (waive), and the better named without being imposed.

**If Only You Knew**

The closing conditional — *if only you knew* — is the verse's rhetorical hinge, and the commentators note its unfinished grammar: the apodosis is absent, the knowing left hanging over what it would change. The tradition reads the ellipsis as deliberate: had you known what the respite earns day by day, what the waiving weighs at the reckoning, what the debtor's distress is in God's sight — the sentence breaks off because the knowledge, if it arrived, would make the choice immediately and argument would be unnecessary. The formula matches the giving-section's whole pedagogy, which has consistently relocated the arithmetic from the visible ledger to the unseen one: the reward deposited with the Lord (2:262, 2:274, 2:277), the date nurtured into a mountain, the blight and growth operating where the amounts do not show (2:276). The creditor considering his struggling debtor is asked to perform the same relocation: the principal in his ledger is a visible amount, and the better the waiving carries is an invisible one — but the invisibility is an artifact of the vantage, not of the value, and the if-only-you-knew is the verse's promise that the vantage exists and is coming. The ribā-block ends its legislation on the word knew, and hands the whole matter, like the amnesty-clause before it, to the knowledge of God.
verses.281:
> Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged

**The Seal on the Economy**

The ribā-block closes as the sūrah's great legislative blocks have consistently closed — not with a new ruling but with the Day held up behind the rulings: *Be mindful of the Day when you will all be returned to Allah*. The ittiqāʾ — the mindfulness, the same God-wariness that headed the command (2:278) — is now directed at a Day rather than an act, and the direction is the verse's legislation: the economy just governed is not a province life walls off from the fear of God but one of the fear's densest terrains, where every ledger-entry, every postponed term, every waived remainder is a transaction conducted in the Day's full jurisdiction.

**Returned to Allah**

The return-clause's grammar carries the verse's first precision: *you will be returned* — the passive, the returning done to the returner. The commentators note the formula's kinship with the sūrah's own opening movement — how can you disbelieve, when you were dead and He gave you life, then causes you to die, then gives you life, then to Him you are returned (2:28) — and the kinship is the verse's argument: the return is not a journey the soul undertakes but an appointment it is brought to, the same divine passive that governed the first giving of life. The Day named is yawm — unspecified, undated, definite only in its certainty — and its content here is a single event: the return to God. Not the return to the earth, the tribe, the market, or the grave's silence but the return to the party every transaction in the block was secretly with: the Provider whose provision was spent or hoarded, the Warner whose warning arrived at the ribā-ledgers, the Lord whose principal-rule protected both creditor and debtor. The verse asks its reader to perform the block's whole economics as preparation for a meeting, and names the meeting's location as the meeting's meaning: to Him.

**Every Soul Paid in Full**

The Day's operation is stated in the verse's middle clause: *then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done*. The tawfiyah — the full paying-out, the completion of the wage — is the verse's economic verb, and its use at the Day's description is deliberate: the block that legislated debts, principals, respites, and waivers closes by describing the ultimate settlement in the same vocabulary. Every soul — kullu nafs, the individual in her singularity, the collective nouns of creditor and debtor dissolved into the unit that actually acted — receives the payment in full: nothing held back from the wage and nothing added to the bill. The commentators connect the clause to the resurrection of the devourers (2:275) as its double: the ribā-eater's convulsed rising and the soul's complete payment are the same Day seen from the two ledgers — the one whose increase was blighted arrives to find the blight total, and the one whose charity was grown arrives to find the growth counted to the last grain.

**None Will Be Wronged**

The verse's final clause is the block's own formula lifted to the Day: *and none will be wronged* — wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn. The commentators mark the echo deliberately: the same no-wronging that described the creditor's right at the settlement — you shall have your principal, neither wronging nor being wronged (2:279) — now describes every soul's position at the final audit. The parallel is the verse's quiet theorem: the settlement that the ribā-legislation imposed on the community's ledgers was a rehearsal of the Day's arithmetic, and the Day's arithmetic is the settlement's guarantee. Where the community's courts could only approximate the neither-wronging — the straitened debtor misjudged, the respite refused, the waiver uncredited — the Day performs it exactly: no soul overpaid, no soul underpaid, no increase surviving the blight, no charity lost from the growth. The commentators note the clause's double edge for the block's two parties: for the devourer who persisted, the no-wronging means the war-declaration's consequence arriving with full precision; for the repenter, the waiving creditor, the patient lender, it means the if-only-you-knew finally known — the better that was withheld from sight paid in full, to the last day of respite credited as the ḥadīth promised, to the last hidden gift found in the deposit with the Lord.
verses.282:
> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**The Longest Verse**

This is the longest single verse in the Qur'an — a fact the tradition states with the gravity of a marker: the Book that runs from the Fātiḥah's seven short āyāt to its own final page reserves its maximum extension for the documentation of a debt. The commentators give the verse its occasion and its range together: it is said to have been revealed in connection with the agricultural forward sales practiced in Medina — payment now for harvests deliverable one, two, or three years out — but it applies generally to every deferred agreement, loans included: wherever payment and delivery do not meet in the same moment, the verse's machinery engages. The Prophetic rule the tradition attaches to the forward sale states the verse's minimum content: whoever contracts a forward sale should fix a known amount, a known measure, and a known term. The forward sale itself is the verse's exhibited exception to the wider prohibition on selling what one does not yet have — permitted, al-Qurṭubī explains, because the farmer genuinely needs the funds for seed and care while his wealth stands in the ground in a yearly cycle, and because the social benefit outweighs the transaction's risk. The longest verse legislates, in other words, the longest transactions: the ones that stretch across years and therefore across the failures of memory, good faith, and life itself.

**The Witnesses**

The witnessing-legislation is the verse's most discussed clause, and the discussion repays care. Two men are called as witnesses; *if two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice* — the doubling attached to its rationale in the verse's own words: *so if one of the women forgets, the other may remind her*. The commentators establish first what the exegetes agree on: the provision is peculiar to the commercial testimony this verse governs and differs from the Qur'an's treatment of testimony elsewhere — the sūrah of Light explicitly equates husband and wife as testifiers in the gravest of accusations (24:6–9), and the classical tradition, while generally excluding women from the corporal-punishment and qiṣāṣ cases, treated even there as preference rather than incapacity, admitting women's testimony when no male witness existed. The erring named is forgetting — a lapse of memory in the contract's particulars, not a character deficiency — and the classical readings of the reminder's effect ran in two directions: the reminded woman becomes legally equal to the man, or the two women together stand equal to him, the latter the more widely held. The modern and classical commentators converge in refusing the intrinsic-inferiority reading, and their structural argument is the verse's own: nothing here excludes a transaction between two women with two men witnessing; women in Islamic law transact sales and loans independently, without witnesses at all, across the whole range of ordinary commerce. The provision addresses, rather, the specific transaction's expertise-demand — the from-among-those-whom-you-approve phrasing signals competence in a domain, and complex multi-year forward contracts were, in the verse's society, a domain women rarely worked in. Al-Qurṭubī adds the social reading: participation of this kind was itself a major change for the women of the time, and the doubled presence functions as protection against bullying or manipulation in a long-term financial proceeding — while Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī's recorded puzzlement (why could not one man remind one woman if she erred? he could not answer it) testifies that the tradition itself never settled the clause into a verdict on women's minds. The witnesses' duty-clause closes the paragraph symmetrically with the scribe's: *the witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned*.
verses.283:
> If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found, then a security can be taken. If you trust one another, then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺—and let them fear Allah, their Lord. And do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do

**The Pledge in Hand**

The security named is the rahin maqbūḍah — the pledge in hand, the collateral physically seized and held by the creditor: property given by the debtor, or by the forward-sale's seller, as guarantee in the absence of the written, witnessed contract. The fiqh of the pledge that grew from this clause is one of the tradition's settled chapters — the pledge held, not merely promised; its value answering the debt at default; its care incumbent on the holder — and the Prophetic practice the tradition preserves gives the institution its most cited instance: the report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī that the Prophet died with his shield pledged to a Jewish merchant of Medina against thirty ṣāʿ of barley for his household's food.

**Do Not Conceal the Testimony**

The verse's third movement turns from the debt's instruments to its witnesses, and its prohibition is the testimony's concealment: *do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful*. The commentators connect the clause backward to the documentation-verse's summons — the witnesses who must not refuse when called (2:282) — and forward to its rationale: the whole machinery of writing and witnessing exists to make the truth available at the dispute, and the concealing witness defeats the machinery at its terminal point, holding in his memory the very fact the document was built to preserve. The sin-clause's organ is the verse's precision: the concealer's *heart* is named sinful — al-Ṭabarī and the tradition read the attribution as the sin's location and its totality, the heart being the seat whose corruption the concealment constitutes. The Qur'an's testimony-ethics elsewhere carry the same weight — the sūrah's own earlier verse legislated the witnesses' non-refusal and God's knowledge of what they do, and the sūrah of the Starving's picture of the record that leaves nothing out, small or great, unlisted (18:49) is the concealment-clause's eschatological guarantee: the withheld testimony is withheld from men only, and the heart that withheld it is registered.

**The Knower of What You Do**

The verse closes with the knowledge-clause the whole documentation-sequence has been building toward: *And Allah fully knows what you do*. The commentators read it as the sequence's enforcement-summary: the scribe's justice, the dictator's honesty, the witnesses' availability, the pledge-holder's care, the trusted debtor's fidelity, the testifier's disclosure — every actor in the contract-machinery has an interior the documents cannot capture, and the closing name captures it. The clause also answers the verse's ladder-structure with its final consolation: at the top rung, where trust operates without instrument, the creditor who relied and lost is not simply defrauded in an unenforceable deal — the transaction stands recorded where enforcement is perfect; and at every lower rung, where the document or the pledge may still fail (the forged term, the disputed collateral, the pressured witness), the same record stands behind the human machinery as its audit and its guarantee. The knowledge-verse thus completes the sūrah's documentary legislation the way the Day-return verse completed its ribā-legislation (2:281): the human instruments are commanded, calibrated, protected — and then handed over to the Knower, in whose knowledge the contract's final copy has been kept since the moment the scribe's pen, or the trusting hand, first moved.

**The Sequence's Completion**

Read with its two neighbors, this verse completes the sūrah's movement from the economy's morals to the economy's paperwork and back to the paperwork's morals. The ribā-block legislated the debt's ethics — the increase forbidden, the principal protected, the straitened debtor respited, the whole sealed at the Day (2:275–281). The documentation-verse built the debt's instruments — the writing, the scribe, the dictation, the witnessing, the harm-protections (2:282). This verse handles the instruments' limits and their interior: the road without a scribe, the pledge that substitutes, the trust that transcends, the testimony whose concealment is a sin of the heart. The three movements together are the Qur'an's complete treatment of the deferred obligation — its ethics, its documentation, and its conscience — and the verse's own structure enacts the completion: it descends from the ideal machinery to the emergency substitute, ascends from both to naked trust, and closes with the knowledge that holds all three levels equally. The believer who has traveled the sūrah's economy from the devourers' rising to the pledged shield and the trusted word now carries, the verse's closing clause assures him, a ledger kept at every altitude: documented where possible, secured where necessary, trusted where grace allows, and known — in every case, completely — to God.
verses.284:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything

**The Sovereignty Premise**

The sūrah's closing movement opens by restating its property-law at the widest possible scale: *To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth*. The ownership-clause is the same formula āyat al-kursī carried (2:255), and its placement here does the same preparatory work: the accounting that follows is legitimate because the Accountant owns everything the account concerns — the wealth whose documentation the preceding verses legislated, the hearts whose concealments the testimony-clause policed, and the souls the Day-return verse (2:281) gathered from every economic identity into their singular kasb. The commentators read the clause as the ground of the verse's second sentence rather than its decoration: universal ownership makes universal accounting coherent, since nothing in any soul's contents falls outside the Owner's jurisdiction. The sūrah that began by describing the Book as the guidance in which there is no doubt ends its legislative career by naming the jurisdiction in which there is no outside.

**Accounting Is Not Punishment**

The tradition's clarification of the verse is precise and comes from al-Ṭabarī's own commentary: bring you to account need not mean punish. The muḥāsabah — the reckoning, the calling-to-account — is the Day's procedure, and in Islamic belief every person will first be brought to account for all his deeds before entering Paradise or Hell, except the elect who pass to Paradise directly (the sūrah's own verse on whom God wills among the reckoned-without-punishment, 2:212's discussion). The verse's forgiveness-and-punishment clause then names the accounting's two possible outcomes as divine dispositions: *He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills* — the will operating at the audit's end, not the audit's fact. The sūrah of the Cave's picture supplies the accounting's texture, quoted by the exegetes here: the record laid open, the wicked crying out — woe to us, what a book this is, leaving nothing out, small or great, but numbering it all (18:49). The verse's claim is thus total in knowledge and open in outcome: every heart-content is registered, and the registered stands before a will whose two movements are forgiveness and punishment — the dread the Companions wept at being the dread of the registration's completeness, which the verse affirms, and of the outcome's severity, which the verse leaves with the will that also forgives.

**No Abrogation, Two Descriptions**

Some held that the capacity-principle of the sūrah's final verse (2:286) abrogates this verse's audit-clause, and the commentators answer the claim on two grounds. The first is textual: there is no contradiction between the two — God's knowledge-and-reckoning of the heart's contents and God's not-tasking any soul beyond its capacity describe different relations (the audit's range and the obligation's measure), and both stand. The second is categorical: these are descriptions of God's acts, not legal rulings, and descriptions of the divine action are not subject to abrogation at all — naskh operates on commands and prohibitions, not on statements of what God knows, wills, and does. The clarification matters for reading the whole closing sequence: the verse is not a law later repealed but a doctrine permanently stated — the heart's contents are within the divine jurisdiction, full stop — and what the following verses adjust is not the jurisdiction but the community's burden under it.

**Power Over All Things**

The verse's closing name gathers its three movements: *Allah is Most Capable of everything* — the qadr that owns the heavens and earth, registers the heart's concealed and revealed, and holds the forgiveness and the punishment in one will. The commentators connect the power-clause to the audit's feasibility: an accounting of every heart-content across every soul is an operation of infinite capacity, and the name states the capacity the clause assumes. The power is also the verse's answer to the sūrah's economic sequence, which ends here: the documentation legislated because human memory fails, the pledge because the road lacks scribes, the trust because instruments run out — and the divine power because nothing in the final audit depends on instruments at all. The God who teaches the scribe (2:282), who knows what the trusted debtor does (2:283), and who owns both worlds (this verse) is the God before whom the sūrah's last movement now begins — the believers' creed and their prayer, revealed, the tradition holds, into the very distress this verse's audit-clause created. The sovereignty-statement is the closing sequence's foundation: the heart is audited by its Owner, the outcome rests with its Forgiver-and-Punisher, and the community's response — stated in the two verses that follow — is the response the audit was sent to elicit: belief, hearing, obedience, and the prayer of the capacity-bounded to the All-Capable.
verses.285:
> The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. ˹They proclaim,˺ “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.” And they say, “We hear and obey. ˹We seek˺ Your forgiveness, our Lord! And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.”

**The Articles Enumerated**

The four named objects are the tradition's standard enumeration, and the commentators locate the verse inside the Qur'an's creed-network: the same articles appear in the sūrah's own righteousness-verse — belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets (2:177) — and in the sūrah of Women's faith-command, where denying Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day is named as the far straying (4:136). The three passages together give the articles their canonical form, and this verse's list is the one that runs in the order of descent: Allah, then the angels who carry, then the Books carried, then the messengers who receive — the revelation's chain of custody stated as the belief's structure. The commentators note what the verse's position adds: the creed arrives immediately after the audit-verse's account of God's total knowledge and sovereign will (2:284), and the tradition preserves the connection — the Companions' distress at that verse was answered by the revelation of these closing verses, whose first sentence describes the response the audit sought: not evasion but belief, held by the Messenger and shared by the believers. The articles are thus not abstract theology but the distressed community's answer, revealed as the shape faith takes when the heart's contents are known and the will forgives or punishes as it wills.

**We Make No Distinction**

The creed's next clause is spoken in the believers' own voice: *We make no distinction between any of His messengers*. The formula is the sūrah's recurring confession — commanded at 2:136 (we believe in what was revealed to us and to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes; we make no distinction between any of them), at 3:84 in nearly identical words, and listed among the markers of true faith at 4:152 — and the commentators explain its double work. The first work is internal to the faith: the no-distinction clause stands in deliberate tension with the preferment-verse (2:253 — some messengers raised above others), and the tradition's resolution governs both: the ranking concerns the missions and endowments, not the persons' truthfulness or their claim on belief, so the believer ranks what God ranked and distinguishes no one God sent. The second work is polemical, and the commentators state it plainly: the confession distinguishes the believers from the communities that accepted some messengers and rejected others — the Jews who rejected Jesus and Muhammad, the Christians who rejected Muhammad. The no-distinction clause is therefore the sūrah's final word in its long argument with the selective faith of the People of the Book: the community this verse describes receives the whole chain, and its creed is the chain's unbroken acknowledgment.

**We Hear and Obey**

The believers' speech continues into its operative clause: *We hear and obey* — samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā, the formula whose meaning the sūrah has been building since its early covenant-scenes. The commentators' cross-reference is exact and deliberate: when the mountain was raised over the covenant-community and they were told to hold firmly and obey, they answered *we hear and disobey* (2:93) — and the calf's love was rooted in their hearts. The closing verse's samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā is that answer reversed: the same hearing, the same covenant-context of a book received, and the obedience where the disobedience stood. The tradition reads the reversal as the sūrah's ring-closure at the level of response: the Book that documented one community's hearing-without-obedience documents this community's hearing-with-obedience as its final confession, and the difference between the two is the difference the whole sūrah has been legislating toward — the law heard and the law kept, the ribā abandoned at the command, the debt written at the command, the heart's contents surrendered at the audit-clause.

**To You Is the Final Return**

The verse's last words return the prayer to the sūrah's first theology: *And to You alone is the final return* — the masīr, the journey's end, the same return the sūrah's opening argument named (to Him you are returned, 2:28) and the Day-return verse legislated mindfulness of (2:281). The commentators mark the ring: the Book began with the return as a proof against disbelief and ends with the return as a prayer's horizon — the same destination, held at the beginning as doctrine and at the end as address. The return-clause also gathers the verse's own movement: the belief (in the Revealer), the no-distinction (among the sent), the hearing-and-obeying (toward the commanded), the forgiveness-ask (for the performance) — all four terminate at the One to whom the journey ends, and the termination is the verse's final definition of faith: belief lived as a journey with a known destination, whose travelers confess their creed, keep their obedience, beg their covering, and walk. The sūrah's last legislative word (the documentation, the audit) and its last creedal word meet here in the return: everything written is kept, everything concealed is known, everything obeyed is forgiven — and everything, the verse's closing phrase insists, comes back. The believers' first sentence said they believe in what was revealed from their Lord; their last says where they are going. Between the two stands the whole sūrah, and after the two stands only its final verse — the prayer of the capacity-bounded, which the tradition recites with this one, as the two verses the night is sufficient with.
verses.286:
> Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian. So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**The Capacity Principle**

The Book's final verse opens with the sentence the tradition quotes more often than almost any other: *Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford*. The principle has the Qur'an's standing formulation — la yukallifu Llāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā — and the commentators list its recurrences as a network: the nursing-provision legislation bound the father only within his capacity (2:233), the sūrah of the Cattle legislates full measure with the same clause (6:152), the sūrah of the Heights places it inside the Paradise-promise (7:42), and the sūrah of the Believers states it beside the record that speaks truth (23:62). Its position as the sūrah's closing legislation is the tradition's answer to the audit-verse's distress: the Companions wept at the heart's total registration (2:284), and the response revealed — these final verses — begins by bounding the obligation while leaving the knowledge total. God knows the heart's every content; God requires of the soul only its width. The distinction is the verse's whole mercy: the audit's range is infinite, the assignment's is capacity-shaped, and the community lives between the two — fully known, partially tasked.

**Earned and Perpetrated**

The verse's second sentence pairs two near-synonyms and sets them in opposite directions: *All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss*. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī mark the roots' kinship — kasabat, earned, and iktasabat, perpetrated, are from one stem, their difference contextual and deliberate — and gloss the pair as the ledger's two columns: what the soul earned is added to its merit, and what it perpetrated is what it is held to. The commentators connect the clause to the spending-section's own economics — whatever you spend is for your own good (2:272), whoever does good does it for his own soul (41:46) — and to the Day-return verse's payment-in-full (2:281): the soul's earnings travel with the soul, benefit and loss both deposited in the only account the return will open. The clause is also the capacity-principle's corollary: since the assignment never exceeds the width, everything assigned falls within the soul's power to earn — and everything earned, good or evil, returns as the soul's own. No transferred guilt, no borrowed merit, no burden carried from another's ledger: the verse states, in two clauses, the personal arithmetic the whole sūrah's legislation has assumed.

**The Three Do-Not-Petitions**

The verse's second half is the believers' prayer, and its first three petitions each open with the same call — Our Lord, Our Lord, Our Lord — a triple invocation the commentators read as the prayer's deliberate rhythm. Ibn Kathīr glosses its range as sins of omission — the canonical prayer forgotten until its window closes — and of commission, the wrong done in error's grip. Al-Ṭabarī reads the burden as the covenant-conditions laid on earlier communities, and Ibn Kathīr states the tradition's consensus: Islam is, in much of its legislation, an alleviation and reduction of the ritual and legal obligations borne by the peoples before — the same sūrah's widow-legislation halving the mourning-year (2:234), its fear-prayer bending the ritual to the danger (2:239), its fasting legislating the night's full permission (2:187). The third: *Do not burden us with what we cannot bear* — al-Rāzī reads it as the plea against commands and afflictions beyond the strength to uphold them, and the commentators note the petition's harmony with the verse's own opening clause: the soul tasked only within its width prays that the width be honored — the principle stated as doctrine and then begged as mercy, because the doctrine's keeper and the petitioner's needer are the same God.

**The Two Verses from Beneath the Throne**

The tradition's verdict on this verse and its predecessor is the sūrah's own epilogue, and the ḥadīth-record states it in three reports the exegetes gather. The Prophet said of the two closing verses: whoever recites them in a night, they suffice him (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, 5009; also in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim) — the sufficiency read as protection, as the night's worship, as the household's covering. He said of their origin: I was given the two verses that close the sūrah of the Cow from a treasury beneath the Throne — the kanz taḥt al-ʿarsh report that places the sūrah's ending at the highest point of the revelation's geography, the same Throne āyat al-kursī (2:255) describes as encompassing all. And the Miʿrāj-tradition reports that at the Night Journey — the night the sūrah of the Night Journey opens (17:1) — the Prophet was given three things: the five daily prayers, the two closing verses of the Cow, and the forgiveness of his community's sins save the associating of partners. The three reports converge on the verse's function in Muslim practice: the sūrah that legislated the community's law ends in a gift carried down from the Throne and up from the Night Journey, recited every night by millions who may not have read the legislation it seals — the creed-verse and the prayer-verse, belief and capacity, the articles and the asking, sufficient for the night, sufficient, the tradition has always understood, for more: the whole Book folded into its last two sentences, the Cow's long road from guidance-without-doubt to victory-over-disbelief ending where every road the sūrah described ends — at the Guardian, in the prayer, before the return.

The commentators note the sūrah's ring-closure in the request: the Book opened with the disbelievers' sealed hearts and hearing (2:6–7), legislated two hundred verses of a community's formation, narrated its battles and its Bani Israil mirror, and ends with the formed community asking its Guardian for the victory the opening described as withheld from the sealed.
